# about Witchcraft.

It is plain enough in the records of ancient times that there were nations that actually worshipped the **Devil**. Some even read that passage in the Psalms as, *The Gods of the Heathen are Devils* <note>Psalm 96:5</note>; and we know **Satan** is called the *God of this World* <note>2 Corinthians 4:4</note>. Indeed, our author himself admits that the nation of the **Jews** was strictly prohibited from practicing **witchcraft** and all dealings with evil **spirits** because of their tendency to worship them. 

But what more evidence is needed? Even today, there are those who offer sacrifices and all sacred homage to the Evil One in a visible form. It is well known to our own countrymen who trade and reside in those regions that the **Caribbeans** <note>Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean islands</note> worship the **Devil** under the name of **Maboya** <note>A spirit or deity in Caribbean mythology often equated with the Devil by European writers</note>, who frequently reveals himself and interacts with them. Travelers relate similar stories concerning various other parts of the "uncivilized" **Indies**. Furthermore, it is confidently reported by sensible, intelligent men who have visited those places that most of the **Laplanders** <note>The Sámi people of northern Scandinavia, who were frequently associated with magic in early modern literature</note> and some other northern peoples are **witches**. 

Thus, it is plain that there are **national alliances with devils**. Even if there were none, I do not see how it could be inferred that there are no individual alliances. That would be no more logical than saying there were never any **demoniacs** <term>people possessed by demons</term> because we know of no nation where everyone is possessed, or that there are no **lunatics** <term>people with mental illnesses, historically believed to be affected by the phases of the moon</term> in the world because there is no country made entirely of madmen. But our author offers another argument:

->(2) To this effect: That profligate <note>original: "profligate" — meaning reckless, immoral, or dissolute</note> persons, who are vulnerable to such blatant temptations, are already secured [to the Devil's side]; therefore, such a covenant would be unnecessary and of no use to the Tempter's plans.<-

I have already answered this objection in my remarks on the ninth prejudice. I remind you again here that if the goals of those evil **spirits** were only to secure wicked men for the **dark kingdom** in general, one might better argue that we cannot give a reason for their **temptations** and efforts of this kind. However, as I have speculated, it is likely that each of those infernal **tempters** has a specific "property" or claim over those he has seduced and secured by such **compacts** <term>formal agreements or contracts, specifically with the Devil</term>. Their individual pride and tyrannical desire for **slaves** may reasonably be thought to motivate them to pursue such attempts, as their own personal interest is involved.

But I will add a more direct point: namely, that such desperate sinners are made more secure for the infernal kingdom at large by such hellish **covenants** and **combinations**. Through these, they confirm and harden their hearts against God and place themselves at a greater distance from His grace and His **Spirit**.

<summary>The author argues that devil-worship is a historical and global reality, citing indigenous Caribbean and Northern European cultures as evidence. He also contends that formal "compacts" with the Devil are real because they satisfy the personal pride of individual demons and further alienate sinners from God's grace.</summary>

These are certainly sure ways of being destroyed, and we see that the Devil has a great interest in a project whose success results in such outcomes. (3) That to attempt such an express <term>Covenant</term> <note>A formal, binding legal agreement, here referring to a "deal with the Devil."</note> is contrary to the *interests of Hell*, which are actually promoted mightily in this way. And whereas he suggests that something so horrific is likely to *startle the conscience* and awaken the soul to *consideration* and *repentance*, I reply: indeed, considering *man* in general as a rational creature—driven by hopes and fears and aware of the *joys* and *miseries* of another *world*—one would expect *it to be so*. 

But then, if we look at man as he really is—*sunk into flesh and physical senses*, darkened in his *mind*, and governed by his *imagination*; blinded by his *passions* and made foolish by *sin* and *folly*; hardened by evil habits and hurried away by the torrent of his inclinations and desires—I say, looking at man in this miserable state of evil, it is not incredible that he should be persuaded by the Tempter and his own lusts to act with a wonderful degree of madness, and continue unconcerned and senseless <note>original: "stupid"</note> in it. He remains intent upon his present satisfactions, without any sense or consideration of the dreadfulness and danger of his condition. By this, I am also prepared to meet a *fourth objection* from our *author*, namely:

(4) That it is not probable on the part of <term>Witches</term> that they would be so desperate as to renounce *God* and eternal *happiness*, and so everlastingly ruin their bodies and souls for a *short and trivial interest*. This way of arguing only suggests that mankind sometimes acts with a prodigious degree of *brutishness* <note>Behaving like a beast or animal, lacking human reason or morality.</note>, and we actually see this in examples every day.

There is no lust so base and so contemptible that there are not those continually before our eyes who feed it with the *sacrifice* of their *eternity* and their *souls*. Daring sinners rush into the darkest villainies with so little remorse or awareness, as if it were their goal to prove they have nothing left in them that makes them human. So, nothing can be inferred from this argument except that human nature is incredibly degenerate. The vileness and stupidity of men are truly so great that such things are customary and common,

Thus, I <unclear>suppose</unclear>, I have also answered the *argument* of this great *man* <note>Likely referring to a specific skeptical author discussed on the previous page</note> against the *covenants* <note>Contracts or pacts with the Devil</note> of *witches*. I am almost inclined to imagine that there is little more to be said to the purpose which may not, by the further development of my *CONSIDERATIONS* <note>Referring to the author's book, *Considerations touching Witchcraft*</note>, be easily answered. I am even further strengthened in my opinion because, since the former *edition* of this book, I have sent word to several acute and ingenious persons of my acquaintance to beg for their *objections* (or those they have heard from others) against my *discourse* or *accounts*, so that I might consider them in *this* edition. But I can obtain none except for those *few* I have now discussed; most of my friends tell me that they have not met with any objections that *need* or *deserve* my *notice*.

## Section 19.

**From** all this, it is clear that there were witches in ancient times under the Law <note>original: "Dispensation of the Law," referring to the era of the Old Testament.</note>. It will not be much more difficult to prove that there were also such people in the times of the Gospel <note>The era of the New Testament.</note>. I recently had the opportunity to write about this in a letter to a person of the highest honor, and I will now borrow some points from that for my current purpose.

**I** say, then, (2) that there were also pacts with evil spirits in those times. I think this is strongly suggested by the Jews' claim about our Savior—that *he cast out demons through Beelzebub*. In his response to this, he does not deny the general possibility of such a thing, but instead clears himself by appealing to the actions of their own children, whom they would not judge so harshly. I cannot understand why those times should be exempt from witchcraft and diabolical pacts any more than they were from demonic possessions, which we know were more frequent then (as far as we can tell) than ever before or since. Besides this, there are clear enough hints in the Apostles' writings about the existence of sorcery and witchcraft. St. Paul lists **witchcraft** right after **idolatry** in his list of the "works of the flesh" (Galatians 5:20). Sorcerers are again grouped with idolaters in that solemn warning in Revelation 21:8. A little later, in Revelation 22:15, they are listed again among idolaters, murderers, and others who are "outside." It seems to me that the story of **Simon Magus** <note>A practitioner of magic in Acts 8 who opposed the Apostles.</note> and his diabolical opposition to the Gospel in its early days should provide clear proof. To all this, I add this more general consideration:

(3.) Even if the **New Testament** had mentioned nothing of this matter, its silence in such cases does not prove anything <note>original: "is not argumentative."</note>. Our **Savior** spoke as the occasion arose, and, as one of his biographers suggests <note>Referring to the Gospel of John 21:25, which states the world could not contain all the books that could be written about Jesus.</note>, not even a thousandth part of what he did and said was recorded. He said nothing about the large, unknown lands of **America**, nor did he even hint at the existence of those many people, much less leave instructions for their conversion. He provides no detailed account of the state of the afterlife, other than the general point that some will be happy and others miserable. He revealed nothing of

(5.) The consequence of this imagined *decorum* <note>the idea that things must happen in a certain "proper" way</note>, if it is pursued, would be this: that *Satan* would now be deprived of all the *ways and tricks of deception* <note>original: "cozenage"</note> by which he deceives us, and mankind, since the coming of *Christ*, should have been secure from all his *temptations*. For there is a greater consistency in believing that, when he was forced from his *haunts in temples and public places*, he should also be removed from *those closer ones, around us and within us, in his daily temptations of all mankind*, than believing that, upon relinquishing *those public places*, he should be made to leave all *professed communication and correspondence* with those *profligate persons whose vileness had made them fit for such company.*

So it seems *these reasoners* are very close to denying all internal diabolical *temptations*. And because I dare not trust them, I will ask your permission here to add some thoughts concerning *those*.

To do this, and to win the favor of those cautious people who are so hesitant to give their agreement, I admit that men frequently—out of a desire to excuse themselves—lay their *own* guilt upon the *Devil* and charge him with things for which he is not actually responsible. For I do not doubt that every *wicked man* has enough of the *Devil in his own nature* to prompt him to evil and does not need another tempter to incite him. Yet, the idea that *Satan* endeavors to further our *wickedness* and our *ruin* through his *enticements*, and "goes to and fro seeking whom he may devour," is too evident in the *Holy Scriptures* <note>original: "holy Oracles"</note> to require my particular effort to prove it. However, those skeptical men perhaps cannot understand the *manner of this operation*, and are therefore tempted to believe that no such thing really exists. Therefore, I judge it necessary to explain *this*, and it is not irrelevant to my general subject.

In order to explain it, I consider that *sense is primarily caused by motion in the organs*, which is continuously conveyed to the *brain*, where *sensation is immediately experienced*. It is nothing more than a signal triggered in the *soul* by the *impulse* of an external object. This is how *simple outward sense* works. But *imagination*, though also caused immediately by material motion, differs from the external senses in this: it does not come from an *impression* directly from the *outside*, but rather the primary and original motion comes from within *ourselves*. Thus, the *soul itself* sometimes strikes upon those...

At other times, the loose spirits <note>In 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were thought to be subtle fluids or vapors that traveled through the nerves to cause movement and thought.</note> wandering up and down in the brain by chance strike those filaments and fibers whose motion triggers a thought, which we call a fancy or imagination. Besides the natural causes of the motions that stir the imagination, there is little doubt that spirits, both good and bad, can move the instruments of sense in the brain to awaken whatever imaginations they intend to provoke. Since the imagination has a powerful influence upon the emotions <note>original: "affections"</note>, and the emotions upon the will and outward actions, it is very easy to understand how good *angels* may stir us up toward *religion* and *virtue*, while *evil* ones tempt us toward *lewdness* and *vice*—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, through the representations they create on the stage of the imagination. These representations invite our emotions and allure our wills, though they cannot compel them.

I believe this is an understandable explanation for temptations and for *angelic* encouragement. Perhaps this is the only way that spirits from the other world have a direct influence on us. Through this explanation, it is easy to account for *dreams*—both those that are *monitory* <note>warning of the future</note> and those caused by our physical temperament—as well as *enthusiasms*, *fanatic ecstasies*, and similar phenomena, as I have suggested.

So, Sir, that addresses the first point. But the other claim must also be examined.

## S E C T. XX.

(2.) *Miracles have ceased; therefore, the alleged actions of witchcraft are merely stories and illusions.*

To respond properly to *this*, we must consider a great and difficult *problem*: *What is a real miracle?* To answer this weighty *question*, I think:

(1.) **T**HAT we should not conclude a *miracle* has occurred simply because a thing is *strange* or *unaccountable*. If we did, we would have to classify all the *great wonders* <note>original Latin: "Magnalia"</note> of nature and all the *mysteries* of those honorable *arts* <note>referring to sciences or specialized trades</note> that we do not understand as miracles.

# Considerations

Furthermore, (2) this is not the criterion of a miracle: that it is an action or event beyond all natural *powers*. This is because we are ignorant of the *extent* and *boundaries* of *nature's sphere* and its possibilities. If this were the *character* and *essential mark* of a miracle, we could not know what was one, unless we could determine the *extent* of natural causes <note>original: "causalties," referring to the range of cause and effect in the physical world</note> and fix their *boundaries*. We would have to be able to say to nature: "*This far you can go, and no farther.*" Anyone who uses this as his *measure* to judge a miracle is himself the greatest miracle of *knowledge*—or of arrogance <note>original: "Immodesty"</note>. Besides, although an effect may truly transcend all the powers of mere nature, there is still a *world of spirits* that must be taken into our account; and concerning them, I also say:

(3) Not everything done by *supernatural agents* is a *miracle*. There is no doubt that evil spirits can create wonderful combinations of natural *causes*. They may perhaps immediately perform many things that are prodigious and beyond the *furthest* reach <note>original: "longest Line"</note> of nature. Yet, these are not to be called miracles for that reason; for miracles are *sacred wonders* and imply that the *power is divine*. But how shall the *power* be known to be divine, when we understand so little of the *capacities* and reach of the *abilities of lower agents* <note>original: "lower Agents," referring to spirits or demons who are beneath God but above humans in power</note>? The answer to this *question* will reveal the criterion of miracles. They must be assumed to have all the previous characteristics—*they are unaccountable, beyond the powers of mere nature, and performed by supernatural agents*—and to these must be added:

(4) They have unique circumstances that indicate they are of a divine origin. Their human instruments <note>original: "mediate Authors"</note> declare them to be so, and these people are always individuals of simplicity, truth, and holiness, free from ambition and all worldly <note>original: "secular"</note> designs. They seldom use ceremonies or physical methods <note>original: "natural Applications"</note>, yet they surpass all the activities of *known nature*. They perform those wonders not to gain admiration or out of the vanity of being talked about, but to seal and confirm some divine *doctrine* or *commission* in which the good and happiness of the world is concerned. I say that by circumstances such as these, wonderful *actions* are known to be from a divine cause; it is this that defines and distinguishes a miracle.

And thus I am prepared for an *answer* to the *objection*, to which I make this brief return: although WITCHES, through their *confederate spirit* <note>original: "Confederate Spirit," referring to a demon or familiar with whom a witch has allegedly made a pact</note>, do the odd and astonishing things we believe of them, they are still no *miracles*. There is *evidence* enough from the *badness* of their *lives* and the

...ridiculous ceremonies of their performances, and from their malice and mischievous designs, that the power that works and the end for which those things are done is not *divine* but *diabolical*. And by singular providence, they are not usually permitted even to pretend to any *new sacred discoveries* in matters of religion, or to do anything to confirm false doctrines <note>original: "Doctrinal Impostures"</note>. Therefore, whether miracles have ceased or not, these acts of witchcraft are certainly not miracles. However, we have a recent great piece of evidence in the famous Greatrakes <note>Valentine Greatrakes (1628–1682), known as the "Irish Stroker," was a famous faith healer who claimed to cure diseases by stroking his patients with his hands.</note> that such "miracles"—which are merely strange and unaccountable performances above the common *methods* of *art* or *nature*—have not ceased. Regarding him, it will not be out of place to add the following account, which I received in a letter from the Reverend Dr. Rust, Dean of Connor <note>Dr. George Rust (died 1670), a theologian and member of the Cambridge Platonists.</note>, a person of great truthfulness and a philosopher. This learned gentleman was pleased to write the following:

> "The major topic of conversation now at the coffee houses and everywhere else is about Mr. Greatrakes, the famous *Irish Stroker*, concerning whom you likely expect an account from me.
> 
> He undergoes various criticisms here: some take him to be a *conjurer* <note>original: "conjurer"; here meaning a magician or someone who summons spirits.</note>, and some an *impostor*, but others adore him as an *apostle*. I confess, I think the man is free from any ulterior motives, very pleasant in conversation, not addicted to any vice or to any specific sect or party, but is, I believe, a sincere *Protestant*. I spent three weeks with him at *Lord Conway's* <note>Ragley Hall, the home of Edward Conway and his wife, the philosopher Lady Anne Conway, where many thinkers gathered to investigate Greatrakes' abilities.</note> and saw him (I believe) lay his hands upon a thousand people. Really, there is something in it more than ordinary, but I am convinced it is not miraculous. I have seen pains strangely fly before his hand until he has chased them out of the body; *dimness* of sight cleared, and *deafness* cured by his *touch*. Twenty people at various times, in fits of the *falling sickness* <term>falling sickness: an archaic term for epilepsy.</term>, were brought to their senses in two or three minutes, so as to tell where their pain was, and then he pursued it until he drove it out at some extremity. Running sores of the *King's Evil* <term>King's Evil: scrofula, a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes, which was traditionally believed could only be cured by the touch of a reigning monarch.</term> were dried up, and swellings <note>original: "kernels"</note> brought to a head <note>original: "suppuration"</note> by his hand; grievous sores of many months' duration were healed in a few days; obstructions and blockages were removed, and cancerous knots in the breast were dissolved, etc.
> 
> Yet I have many reasons to believe that none of this is miraculous: he does not claim to provide evidence for any religious doctrine; the way he operates suggests it is natural; the cure seldom succeeds without repeated touches; his patients often relapse; and he fails frequently..."

### S E C T. I.
#### *The Opinions of the <term>NULLIBISTS</term> <note>original: "Nullibists"; philosophers who believed spirits exist but have no spatial location (from the Latin "nullibi," meaning "nowhere")</note> and <term>HOLENMERIANS</term> <note>original: "Holenmerians"; those who believed a spirit is "whole in the whole and whole in every part" of the space it occupies (from the Greek "holos," meaning "whole," and "meros," meaning "part")</note> proposed.*

**T**HAT we may explain the *essence* or *concept* of *incorporeal beings* <note>original: "incorporeal beings"; entities that do not have a physical or material body</note> or *spirits* with the greater satisfaction and success, we must first remove two vast mounds of darkness with which the ignorance of some has burdened and obscured their nature.

And the first consists of those who, though they readily acknowledge there are such things as *incorporeal beings* or *spirits*, yet very stubbornly contend that they are *nowhere* in the whole world. This opinion, although at first glance it appears very ridiculous, is nonetheless firmly held by the maintain—

# The true Notion of a Spirit.

...followers of it, and that not without some <term>fastuosity</term> <note>original: "Fastuosity"; meaning haughtiness or arrogance</note> and superciliousness, or at least some more sly and silent contempt of such philosophers as hold the contrary, viewing them as less intellectual and as men who indulge far too much in their imagination. Those others, because they so boldly affirm that a spirit is *Nullibi*—that is to say, *nowhere*—have deservedly earned for themselves the name or title of **Nullibists**.

The other obstacle of darkness placed upon the nature of a spirit is by those who willingly acknowledge that spirits are *somewhere*, but add further that they are not only entirely or totally in their whole <term>Ubi</term> <note>Latin: "Where"; referring to the spatial location or presence of a being.</note> or place (in the most general sense of the word), but are totally in every part or point of it. They describe the peculiar nature of a spirit to be such that it must be *Totus in toto & totus in qualibet sui parte* <note>Latin: "The whole in the whole and the whole in any part of itself."</note>. Therefore, the Greeks would aptly and briefly call this an *ousian holomere* <note>Greek: οὐσίαν ὁλομερῆ; an essence that is entirely present in each of its parts.</note>, and this property of theirs—*tes asomaton ousion ten holomereian* <note>Greek: τῆς ἀσωμάτων οὐσιῶν τὴν ὁλομέρειαν; the "wholeness-in-parts" of incorporeal beings.</note>—is the **Holenmerism** of incorporeal beings. From this, these other philosophers, who are diametrically opposite to the former, may most significantly and concisely be called **Holenmerians**.

## S E C T. II.

### That Descartes is the Prince of the Nullibists, and wherein chiefly consists the force of their Opinion.

**T**he opinions of both kinds of philosophers having been sufficiently explained, we will now propose and refute the reasons of each of them. First, we will address the **Nullibists**, of whom the chief author and leader seems to have been that witty and pleasant *René Descartes*. Through his playful *Metaphysical Meditations*, he has so dislocated and distorted the rational faculties of some otherwise sober and quick-witted persons (who, in this point, were not sufficiently cautious because of their over-great admiration of Descartes) that they have been deceived. Partly by his counterfeit and deceptive subtlety, and partly by his authority, they have persuaded themselves that such things were most true and clear to them which—had they not been blinded with these prejudices—they could never have thought to have been even possible. And so, they having been so industriously taught, and diligently in-

...instructed by him so that they might not be deceived—not even by the most powerful and malicious, deceptive deity—have nonetheless, by not sufficiently standing on their guard, been deceived and deluded by a mere man of pleasant but abundantly cunning and obscure genius. This shall clearly appear after we have searched and examined the reasons for this opinion of the Nullibists <term>Nullibists: A term coined by Henry More for philosophers (specifically followers of René Descartes) who argued that spirits exist but have no location in space (from the Latin *nullibi*, meaning "nowhere").</term> to the very bottom.

The whole force of their argument is comprised of these three axioms: the first, *that whatever thinks is immaterial, and vice versa.* The second, *that whatever is extended <term>extended: The property of taking up physical space or having dimensions (length, width, and height).</term> is material.* The third, *that whatever is unextended is nowhere.* To which third axiom I shall add this fourth, as a necessary and manifest corollary <note>original: "consectary"</note> thereof: *that whatever is somewhere is extended.*

The Nullibists will easily grant me that this fourth point is most true; otherwise, they could not seriously argue for their opinion, by which they affirm spirits to be *nowhere*. If they did not grant this, they would be found to hold their position only as a way of indirectly and secretly mocking the existence of spirits—saying indeed that they *exist*, but then hiddenly and cunningly denying it by affirming they are *nowhere*. Therefore, if they are in earnest, they undoubtedly affirm spirits to be *nowhere* for this reason only: they fear that if they granted spirits to be *somewhere*, it would be immediately forced from them (even according to their own principles) that spirits are *extended*—since whatever is extended is material, according to their second axiom. It is therefore manifest that we both agree on this: that whatever real being exists *somewhere* is also *extended*.

### *The fallacious weakness of the Nullibists' reasoning: concluding that because we can conceive of thinking without conceiving of matter, whatever thinks must be immaterial.*

**W**ith this truth, notwithstanding, we are furnished and supported; I do not doubt that we shall easily overthrow and utterly root out this opinion of the Nullibists. But so that their lack of seriousness and their gullibility may more clearly...

# The True Notion of a Spirit.

To make this manifestly appear, let us examine the principles of this opinion part by part, and consider how well they support each member.

The first is, *Whatever thinks is immaterial*, and vice versa. I will not examine the reversal of this axiom because it contributes little to the present purpose; I will only note in passing that I suspect it may be false, although I easily grant the axiom itself to be true. However, it is this new method of demonstrating it that I call into question. This method concludes that *Whatever thinks is Immaterial* from the fact that we can conceive of <term>Cogitation</term> <note>original: "Cogitation"; the process of thinking or mental action</note> while at the same time not conceiving of <term>Matter</term>. 

Now, they say it is manifest that we can conceive of thinking without conceiving of matter from this: even if one should suppose there were no body in the universe, and should not flinch from that position, he would nonetheless remain certain that there was a <term>Res cogitans</term> <note>Latin: a thinking being</note> in the world, finding himself to be such. But I add further: even if he should suppose there was no immaterial being in nature (nor indeed any material one) and should not flinch from that position, he would still not cease to be certain that there was a *thinking being* (no, not even if he should suppose himself not to be a thinking being), because he can suppose nothing without the act of <term>Cogitation</term>. I thought it worthwhile to note this in passing so that the great flippancy of the <term>Nullibists</term> <note>From the Latin "nullibi" (nowhere); a term for those, like the Cartesians, who argued that spirits exist but occupy no physical space or "where."</note> might appear more clearly.

But I add further: such is the nature of the human mind that it is like the eye, better suited to contemplate other things than itself. Therefore, it is no wonder that while thinking nothing of its own essence, the mind fixedly and intently considers and contemplates all other things—even those very things with which it has the nearest affinity—and yet does so without reflecting that it is of a similar nature itself. 

From this, it may easily happen that when the mind is so wholly taken up in contemplating other things without reflecting upon itself, it may either carelessly consider itself in general as a *mere thinking being* without any other attribute, or else do so by later deliberate resolve and by forcing its own faculties. But there is no one who does not discern that this reasoning is wonderfully weak and trifling as it pertains to proving that the mind of man is nothing else—that is to say, that it has no other attributes but mere thinking.

# SECTION IV.

## The true method that ought to be taken for proving that matter cannot think.

**L**astly, if René Descartes <note>original: *Cartesius*</note> and his "Nullibists" <note>Nullibists: A term used by the author to describe philosophers, like Descartes, who argued that spirits or souls exist but have no spatial extension or location.</note> had acted in good faith <note>original: *bona fide*</note>, they should have avoided all those windy and circuitous paths of fake abstraction. They ought to have directly addressed the subject itself, analyzing *matter* and searching the nature of *thought* <note>original: *cogitation*</note>. From there, they might have clearly demonstrated that there was some inseparable attribute in *matter* that is incompatible with the <term>thinking faculty</term> <note>original: *cogitative faculty*</note>, or something in *thought* that is incompatible with *matter*. But to conclude that attributes are separable or *really* distinct—or even contrary and incompatible—merely because we have different ideas or notions of them, is a foul violation of the essential laws of *logic*. It confuses *different things* <note>original: *diversa*</note> with *opposite things* <note>original: *opposita*</note>. To anyone who understands *logic*, such a mistake must appear very crude and absurd.

However, so that the weakness and instability of this method may appear even more clearly, let us suppose what certain philosophers of significant reputation seriously maintain: namely, that thinking substance is either *material* or *immaterial*. Does it not clearly follow from this that a thinking substance can be conceived precisely without the concept of *matter*, just as *matter* can be conceived without the concept of *thought*—even though, in one part of this classification, they are joined closely together?

How, then, can this new-fashioned method of Descartes convince us that this supposition is false and that the division is invalid? Can it do so simply because *matter* can be conceived without *thought*, and *thought* without *matter*? Everyone grants the first point, and the second is assumed by the classification itself; yet the classification remains firm and certain. Therefore, it is very evident that we must return to the known and ratified laws of *logic*. These laws were established and approved by the common agreement of humanity many ages before this upstart method of Descartes appeared. They teach us that in every legitimate

<summary>The author critiques René Descartes' logical method, arguing that simply being able to conceive of "mind" and "body" separately does not prove they are fundamentally incompatible substances. He asserts that Descartes confuses "different" concepts with "opposite" ones, violating established logical principles.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Nullibists, Cogitation, Matter, Logic, Dualism, Philosophy of Mind, Thinking Faculty</keywords>

...legitimate distribution, the parts ought *to agree with the whole and disagree among themselves* <note>original: *consentire cum toto, & dissentire inter se*</note>. Now, in this distribution, it is very manifest that they do sufficiently disagree. It remains only to be proved that one of the parts—namely, the one that supposes a *thinking substance* <term>original: *Cogitative Substance*</term> may be *material*—is contrary to the nature of the whole. This is the clear, solid, and manifest way or method according to the known laws of logic; but that "new way" is a kind of sophistry and a pleasant mode of trifling and evading the point.

# SECTION V.

## *That all things are extended in some way, demonstrated from the corollary of the third principle of the Nullibists.*

**A**s for the second axiom or principle—*namely, that whatever is extended is material*—no new arguments are needed to prove its falsity, if one simply refers to the sixth, seventh, and eighth chapters of the *Manual of Metaphysics* <note>original: *Enchiridium Metaphysicum*, a work by Henry More published in 1671</note>. There, by unanswerable reasoning, it is demonstrated that there is a certain immaterial and immovable *extension* <term>original: *Extensum*; the property of taking up space</term> distinct from movable matter. However, from the corollary <note>original: Consectary</note> of their third principle, we shall prove once and for all that all spirits are extended (meaning they are "somewhere"), against the wild and ridiculous opinion of the *Nullibists* <note>Nullibists: from the Latin *nullibi* (nowhere); philosophers, such as followers of Descartes, who argued that spirits do not exist in space or have spatial dimensions.</note>.

Their third principle, from which they immediately and precisely conclude that spirits are nowhere, is: *Whatever is unextended is nowhere*. I grant this very willingly, but only on the condition that they, in turn, concede (as I have no doubt they will) that *whatever is somewhere is also extended*. From this logical consequence, I will prove with mathematical certainty that God, our soul, and all other immaterial beings are, in some sense, extended. For the Nullibists themselves acknowledge and assert that the operations by which the soul acts on the body are *in* the body, and that the power or divine virtue <note>virtue: here used to mean an inherent power or spiritual influence</note> by which God acts on matter and moves it is present in every part of that matter. From this, it is easily gathered,

<summary>The author argues against the "Nullibists" by asserting that if spirits (like the soul or God) act upon the physical world, they must exist "somewhere" and therefore possess a form of immaterial extension.</summary>
<keywords>Nullibists, extension, immaterial substance, soul, God, Enchiridium Metaphysicum, logic, metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>The text continues the argument that a spirit must be located where its effects are felt, following the previous page's discussion on the presence of the Soul and God.</meta>

That the operation of the *Soul* and the moving *Power* of *God* is somewhere—namely, in the *Body* and in *Matter*. However, the *Operation* of the *Soul* by which it acts on the *Body* and the *Soul itself*, and the *Divine Power* by which *God* moves *Matter* and *God himself*, are joined together. They cannot even be imagined as separate from one another—namely, the *Operation* from the *Soul*, and the *Power* from *God*. Therefore, if the *Operation* of the *Soul* is somewhere, the *Soul* is somewhere—namely, there where the *Operation* is. And if the *Power* of *God* is somewhere, *God* is somewhere—namely, there where the *Divine Power* is: *He* is in every part of *Matter*, and the *Soul* is in the *human Body*. Anyone who can deny this might as well, by the same logic, deny that common *notion* in *mathematics*: quantities that are individually equal to a third thing are equal to one another.

## S E C T. VI.

### *The open confession of the* Nullibists <note>original: "Nullibists"—a term used for those (often Cartesians) who believed that because spirits are not extended in space, they are "nowhere."</note> *that the* ESSENCE *of a* Spirit *is where its* OPERATION *is; and how they contradict themselves and are forced to acknowledge that a* Spirit *is extended.*

**A**ND truly, the very point we are arguing for seems to be openly asserted by the *Nullibists* themselves, even in their own express words. This is evident in *Lambertus Velthusius* <note>Lambert van Velthuysen (1622–1685), a Dutch physician and philosopher who sought to reconcile Cartesianism with theology.</note> in his *On the Principles of First Philosophy* <note>original: "De Initiis Primæ Philosophiæ"</note> in the chapter *On Location* <note>original: "De Ubi"</note>. Although he clearly affirms that *God* and the *Mind of Man* are in every part or some specific part of *Matter* through their *operations*, and that in that sense—namely, in respect of their *operations*—the *Soul* may be truly said to be *somewhere* and *God everywhere* (as if that were the only way they are present); yet he expressly grants that the *Essence* <note>original: "Essence"—the fundamental nature or being of a thing.</note> is never separate from *that* by which *God* or a *created Spirit* is said to be present (the one *everywhere*, the other *somewhere*). He does this so that no *man* should imagine the *Essence* of *God* to be in a place where his other *attributes* are not—for example, that the *Essence* of *God* is in *Heaven*, but that his *Virtue* <note>original: "Vertue"—meaning his power or efficacy.</note> spreads itself beyond *Heaven*. "No, by no means," he says. "Wherever *God’s Power* or *Operation* is, there is the *Nature* of *God*; because *God* is a *Substance* free from all composition <note>original: "composition"—being made of distinct parts; God was traditionally viewed as "simple" or non-composite.</note>." But now, whereas being is derived from the *essence*, and *operation* flows from the *power*, by joining the *essence* they impart being, and by bequeathing the *power* they communicate the *operations*; so that out of the union <note>original: "congress"</note> of soul and body, there is made one *living creature* <note>original: "animal"</note>."

## S E C T. VII.

### *The more superficial reasonings of the Nullibists by which they try to confirm their opinion. The first of these is that the soul thinks of things that are "nowhere."*

**B**ut we shall not ignore their more minor arguments in so great—or rather, so monstrous—a matter. The first of these is that the human mind thinks of things that are *nowhere* and have no relation to place, not even to a *logical* place or "where-ness" <note>original: *Ubi*</note>. Many truths, whether *moral*, *theological*, or *logical*, are of this sort. Because these truths are of such a nature that they are *nowhere*, the Nullibists argue that the human mind which conceives them must necessarily be *nowhere* as well. 

However, it is apparent to anyone—and should be especially so to the *Nullibists* themselves—how foolishly and illogically they conclude that the human soul is *nowhere* simply because it thinks of things that are *nowhere*. By that same logic, it would follow that the *mind* of man is *somewhere*, because sometimes (if not almost always) it thinks of things that are *somewhere*, as all *material* things are. Yet they dare not grant this, because it would clearly follow from their *doctrine* that the human mind or soul was *extended* <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "extension" meant occupying space or having physical dimensions.</note>, and would therefore become physical and devoid of all *thought* <note>original: *Cogitation*</note>. Furthermore, these things which they say

[Those who] say are nowhere—namely, certain moral, logical, and theological *truths*—are actually somewhere, specifically in the *soul* itself which conceives them; but the *soul* is in the *body*, as we proved above. From this, it is manifest that the *soul* and those *truths* which she conceives are just as much "somewhere" as the *body* itself. I grant that some *truths*, in how they act as *representations*, respect neither *time* nor *place* in any sense. But as they are *operations*, and therefore *modes* <note>original: "Modes"; in philosophy, a "mode" is a specific quality or state of a substance, like the shape of a piece of wax.</note> of some *subject* or *substance*, they cannot be conceived of in any other way than as being within some substance. And because there is no substance that does not have some <term>amplitude</term> <note>original: "amplitude"; here meaning spatial extension or the quality of taking up some amount of space.</note>, they exist in a substance which is, in some way, extended. Thus, by reason of their *subject* (the soul), they are necessarily conceived to be "somewhere," because a *mode* is inseparable from its *subject*.

Nor am I at all moved by that dizzying and reckless evasion which some resort to here. They say we are wrong to distinguish between *thought* (such as all conceived truths) and the *substance* of the *soul* that is thinking. They claim that thought itself is the very *substance* of the *soul*, just as *extension* <note>original: "Extension"; the property of taking up physical space.</note> is the substance of *matter*; and therefore, they argue the *soul* is just as much "nowhere" as any thought would be (which ignores time and place) if it were found in no *subject*. 

But here the <term>Nullibists</term> <note>From the Latin "nullibi," meaning "nowhere." This was a term used for philosophers (like followers of René Descartes) who argued that the mind or spirit has no physical location.</note>, who hope to escape this way, fail to notice that while they acknowledge the *substance* of the *soul* to be *thought*, they are simultaneously acknowledging that the *soul* has a *substance*—and therefore it must have some amplitude. Furthermore, *this assertion*—by which they claim *thought* is the very substance of the *soul*—is clearly false. For many *operations* of the soul are, as they say, <term>specifically</term> <note>meaning "different in kind" or belonging to a different "species" of thought.</note> different. If thoughts were the substance itself, then as they succeed one another, there would be many *substances* that are *specifically* different. In that case, the *soul* of *Socrates* would not always be the same *kind* of soul, and much less the same <term>numerical</term> <note>In philosophy, "numerical identity" means being one and the same individual thing over time.</note> soul. What could be imagined that is more <term>delirant</term> <note>original: "delirant"; delirious, insane, or completely irrational.</note> and further removed from common sense?

To this you may add that the soul of man is a *permanent being*, but her *thoughts* are in a state of flux or succession. How then can the very substance of the soul be its successive *operations*? When the *substance* of the soul so constantly ceases or perishes [to be replaced by the next thought], what, I ask you, will become of *memory*? From this, it is clearly evident that there is a certain *permanent* substance of the soul, which is as distinct and different from her succeeding *thoughts* as *matter* itself is from its changing shapes and motions.

## SECTION VIII.

### *The second reason of the Nullibists, namely: That* **THOUGHT** <note>original: "COGITATION"</note> *is easily conceived without* **EXTENSION** <note>In this context, "extension" refers to the property of occupying physical space.</note>.

**T**HE second reason overlaps somewhat with some of those we have already examined; but it is briefly proposed by them thus: There can be no conception, not even of a "logical place," or *ubi* <note>Latin for "where."</note>, without extension. But thought is easily conceived without conceiving of any extension. Therefore, the thinking mind, being free from all extension, is also free from all locality, whether physical or logical; and it is so detached from it that it has no relation or applicability to it; as if those things had no relation or applicability to certain other things simply because they might be conceived without them.

The weakness of this argument is easily detected <note>original: "deprehended"</note> from this: the intensity of heat or motion is considered without any respect to its extension, and yet it is referred to a physical subject, namely, a fired bullet or a red-hot iron. And although in focused <note>original: "defixed"</note> and intent thoughts upon some either difficult or pleasing object, we do not notice at all how time passes, nor take the slightest notice of it, nothing prevents those thoughts from being applied to time anyway. It can be rightly said that they began, for instance, at six o'clock in the morning and continued until eleven; and in the same way, the place where they were conceived may be defined—within the walls of someone's study, for example—even though perhaps during that entire time this focused thinker did not notice whether he was in his study or in the fields.

And to be blunt, to infer the real separation of things based only on the mental isolation <note>original: "precision"; the logical act of considering one quality while ignoring others</note> of our thoughts is a very foul <note>original: "putid"</note> and childish fallacy <note>original: "sophism"</note>. It is even more outrageous and wild to conclude from this that they have no relation or applicability to one another. For we may have a clear and distinct understanding <note>original: "apprehension"</note> of a thing that is connected to another by an essential tie, even if that tie is not noticed (and much more so when they are connected by a circumstantial one). However, this is not a full and adequate understanding, nor one that sees through and penetrates all the [aspects of the thing...]

From this, it appears how greatly René Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> has misled others, if not himself. By using a mental abstraction <note>original: "percision," meaning the act of mentally separating one thing from another</note> to strip "thought" <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> away from "occupying space" <note>original: "Extension"</note>, he defined a **Spirit** (such as the **human soul**) by thought alone, and **Matter** by physical extent alone. He then divided all **Substance** into two categories: "thinking" and "extended," as if these were their primary types. However, this division is as discordant and absurd <note>original: "absonous"</note> as if he had categorized all **Animals** as either "sensitive" or "rational"—since all **Substance** occupies space, just as all **Animals** possess senses. He focused his critical attention <note>original: "Animadversion"</note> on the specific nature of the human soul; however, he either intentionally or by mistake failed to notice its general nature as a substance, as has been noted in the *Handbook of Ethics* <note>original: *Enchiridion Ethicum*</note>, book 3, chapter 4, section 3.

## S E C T. IX.

*The third and last Reason of the Nullibists, namely: That the Mind is conscious to itself that it is nowhere, unless it is disturbed or jogged by the Body.*

**T**he third and last reason, which is the most clever of them all, is found in the work of *Lambertus Velthusius*. He argues it is a truth that God has instilled into the mind itself: that it is "nowhere." He claims we know from experience that we cannot tell from our spiritual operations where the mind is located. According to him, we only know the mind is in our body because we perceive the operations of **Sense** and **Imagination**, which the mind cannot perform without the body or the body's movement.

The meaning of this, if I guess correctly, is this: that the mind, through a certain internal sense, is conscious that it is **nowhere**, unless it is occasionally disturbed by the motions or "joggings" of the body. This is, as I said, a clever suggestion, but it is not true. It is one thing for the mind to perceive itself to be "nowhere," and quite another for it simply to not perceive itself to be "somewhere."

For she <note>The author refers to the mind or soul as "she," following the gender of the Latin *anima*.</note> may not perceive herself to be somewhere, even though she is somewhere, just as she may not take notice of her own individuality or *numerical* distinction <note>original: "numerical Distinction"; the unique identity of a single, countable thing.</note> from all other minds, although she is one *numerical* or *individual* mind distinct from the rest. For, as I hinted at above, such is the nature of the human mind that, like the eye, it is better suited for contemplating all other things than for contemplating itself. And indeed, that which is designed for clearly and purely seeing other things ought to have nothing of itself actually perceptible within it, which it might mingle with the perception of those other things.

Because of this, the human mind is not to have any stable and fixed sense of its own *essence*, such as it cannot easily set aside when necessary. Therefore, it is no wonder—given that the human mind can set aside the sense and consciousness of its own *essence* and *individuality*—that it can also set aside the sense of its being somewhere, or simply not perceive it. This happens when it does not perceive its own *essence* and *individuality* (of which <term>Hic & Nunc</term> <note>Latin: "Here and Now"</note> are the known characteristics), and because the chief objects of the mind are *universals* <note>General or abstract concepts, such as "truth" or "beauty," which are not tied to a specific location.</note>.

But as the mind, although it does not perceive its *individuality*, can still prove to itself through reason that she is one specific *numerical* or *individual* mind, so she can by the same means—although she does not perceive where she is through inward sense—nevertheless prove that she is somewhere. This is based on the general account of things, which by their own nature are extended, singular, and located somewhere. Besides, Velthuisius <note>Lambert van Velthuysen (1622–1685), a Dutch philosopher and physician who wrote on the nature of the soul and its relation to the body.</note> himself plainly grants that from the operations of sense and imagination, we know our mind to be in our body. How then can we be ignorant that she is somewhere, unless the body itself is nowhere?

## S E C T. X.

### *An Appeal to the internal sense of the Mind, whether she be not environed with a certain infinite Extension; together with an awakening of the Nullibist out of his Dream, by the sound of Trumpeters surrounding him.*

**The** reasons of the *Nullibists* <note>original: "Nullibiſts"; those who believe that spirits exist nowhere in space</note> by which they endeavor to maintain their opinion are sufficiently weakened and overturned. Nor do we have need of any arguments to establish the contrary *doctrine*. I will only ask, in passing, that anyone who thinks his *mind* is *nowhere* would test his faculty of *thinking*. When he has detached himself from all thought or sense of his *body*, and fixed his *mind* only on an idea of an indefinite or infinite *extension*, and also perceives himself to be some *particular thinking being*, let him test, I say, whether he can in any way avoid perceiving at the same time that he is *somewhere*—namely, *within this immense extension*, and that he is surrounded by it on all sides. Truly, I must honestly confess that I cannot conceive of it otherwise; I cannot help but conceive an idea of a certain *extension, infinite and immovable*, and of necessary and actual existence. I clearly perceive <note>original: "deprehend"</note> that this idea was not drawn in by the outward senses, but is innate and essentially inherent in the mind itself. Thus, it is the genuine *object* not of *imagination*, but of the *intellect*. It is perversely and without any judgment determined by the *Nullibists*, or *Cartesians* <note>followers of the philosopher René Descartes</note>, that whatever is extended is also *phantaston* <note>original: "φανταστὸν"; the object of imagination or something that can be pictured</note> or the *object of imagination*. Yet, despite this, there is nothing imaginable, or an object of imagination, which is not *sensible* (perceived by the senses), for all *phantasms* <note>mental images or sensations</note> are drawn from the *senses*. But this infinite *extension* has no more to do with things that are *sensible* and fall under *imagination* than that which is most *incorporeal*. But perhaps it will be more appropriate to speak of this elsewhere.

### *The Explanation of the Opinion of the Holenmerians,*

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>The true Notion of a Spirit.</header>

...as much as it respects the *Holenmerism* <note>original: "Holenmerism" — a philosophical concept from the Greek words "holos" (whole) and "meros" (part), meaning a substance is whole in the whole and whole in every part.</note> of Spirits. The first reason is that, while they grant that the whole soul pervades and occupies the whole body, they thought it would then follow that the soul is divisible. They tried to correct this by saying that the soul is in the whole body in such a way that it remains entirely, at the same time, in every part of it. By this logic, they felt certain that the soul could not be argued to be divisible or corporeal in any way, but would remain purely spiritual.

The other reason is that this concept makes it easy to understand how the soul, being in the whole body (points C, D, and E), immediately perceives whatever happens in point C or B at point A. Because the whole soul is perfectly and entirely in C or B as it is in A, it is necessary that in whatever way **C** or **B** is affected, **A** should be affected in the same way. This is because it is entirely and perfectly one and the same thing—namely, the whole soul—in **C** or **B** as in **A**. From this comes that common saying in the Scholastic schools: *If the eye were in the foot, the soul would see in the foot.*

## S E C T. XII.

### The Examination of the Opinion of the Holenmerians.

**BUT** now, according to our custom, let us weigh and examine all these things in a free and just balance. In their assertion that the whole soul is in the whole body, and that the body is entirely penetrated by the soul's essence, they seem willing to acknowledge a certain "essential amplitude" <note>The idea that a spirit has a non-physical "spread" or presence.</note> of the soul. In this, I say, they come near to our position: we contend there is a certain *metaphysical* and *essential extension* in all spirits, but one that is <term>without magnitude and without parts</term> <note>original Greek: ἀμεγέθης καὶ ἀμερὴς</note>, as *Aristotle* defines his "separate substances" <note>Immaterial beings, such as God or the celestial movers, that exist independently of matter.</note>. For there is no magnitude or bulk which cannot be physically divided, nor are there any "parts" in the proper sense where there is no such division. Therefore, the *metaphysical extension* of spirits is rightly understood to be incapable of either [bulk...]

### The True Notion of a Spirit.
<meta>The previous page likely introduced the "Holenmerian" view of the soul—the idea that the soul is "all in the whole and all in every part" of the body—which the author is now critiquing.</meta>

Since a spirit lacks bulk or parts, and in that sense has no parts, it cannot justly be said to be a "whole." In that respect, we plainly agree with the *Holenmerians* <note>original: "Holenmerians"; from the Greek "holos" (whole) and "meros" (part), referring to those who believed the soul exists entirely in the whole body and entirely in every part of it</note> that a soul or spirit may be said, by its essence, to penetrate and possess the whole body (C, D, E). But we differ from them in this: we dare not affirm that the *whole* spirit or *whole* soul penetrates and possesses the body, because something that has no parts cannot properly be called a "whole." Though I will not contend too stiffly against using that word to explain our meaning more easily, according to the old, common proverb: *Speak a little more unlearnedly, so that you may speak more intelligibly or plainly* <note>original Greek: "Ἀμαθέστερόν πως εἰπὲ καὶ σαφέστερον λέγε"</note>. But we must remember that when we do so, we are not speaking with technical accuracy, but rather adapting our speech to common understanding.

<margin>See Fig. 2. Section 11</margin>
But now, when the *Holenmerians* go further and add that the whole soul is in every part or physical point of the body (D, C, E)—specifically in points A and B and all the rest of the points the body consists of—that seems a harsh expression to me. It is something that may justly be considered close to an open inconsistency and contradiction. For when they say the whole soul is in the whole body (D, C, E), if they understand the essence of the soul to be commensurate <note>equal in extent or area</note> and, as it were, equal to the body, and yet at the same time claim the whole soul is contained within point A or B, it is manifest that they make one and the same thing many thousand times greater or smaller than itself at the same time; which is impossible. 

Even if they affirm that the *essential amplitude* <note>the inherent size or "spread" of an essence</note> of the soul is no bigger than what is contained within the physical point A or B, but that the *essential presence* of the soul is diffused through the whole body (D, C, E), the argument will fare no better. While they plainly profess that the whole soul is in Point A, it is manifest that nothing remains of the soul to be in Point B, which is distant from A. It is as if one should say that there is nothing of the soul which is not included within A, and yet in the same moment of time, not only something of the soul (which might be a milder contradiction), but the *whole* soul is in B. This would mean the whole soul is totally and entirely outside of itself, which is surely impossible for any singular or individual thing. As for "universals" <note>general concepts like "humanity" or "circularity," which can apply to many things at once</note>, they are not actual things, but notions we use when contemplating them.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the "Holenmerian" view of the soul—the belief that a spirit is "all in the whole and all in every part" of a body. The author argues that this theory logicially reduces the size of a spirit to a single infinitesimal point.</meta>

<page-num>19</page-num>

# The true Notion of a Spirit.

Again, if the **essential size** <note>original: "essential Amplitude"</note> of the soul is no greater than what may be contained within the limits of a **physical point**, it cannot extend or show its **essential presence** through the whole body—unless we imagine in it such an incredible speed that it could be carried within one moment into all parts of the body to be present to them. Since it is so hard to conceive this happening even in the small **structure** <note>original: "compages," meaning a framework or joined structure</note> of a human body, with the soul occupying every part of it in a single moment, how much more outrageous and utterly impossible is it to understand this regarding that Spirit which perpetually shows his **essential presence** to the whole world, and whatever exists beyond the world?

To this, lastly, you may add that this hypothesis of the **Holenmerians** <note>Those who believe that the soul or spirit is "all in the whole and all in every part" (from the Greek *holos*, "whole," and *meros*, "part").</note> necessarily makes all spirits the most **tiny** <note>original: "minute"</note> things that can be conceived. For if the whole spirit is in every physical point, it is plain that the **essential size** itself of the spirit (which the two former objections assumed) is no bigger than that physical point in which it exists. You may call this, if you will, a **physical monad** <note>A term for a simple, indivisible, and ultimate unit of existence.</note>; nothing is or can be smaller in the entire universe. If you apply this to any **created spirit**, it cannot help but seem very ridiculous; but if you apply it to the majesty and **vastness** of the **Divine Being** <note>original: "Divine Numen"</note>, it is intolerable—not to say plainly insulting and blasphemous.

## S E C T. XIII.

### A Refutation of the First Reason of the Holenmerians.

But now, regarding the reasons why the **Holenmerians** cling to such an absurd opinion: truly, they are such that they can in no way outweigh those huge difficulties and contradictions that the opinion itself struggles with. For the first reason, which so anxiously provides for the **indivisibility** of spirits, it seems to me to undertake a task that is either **unnecessary** or **useless**. It is **unnecessary** if extension <note>Taking up space or having dimensions.</note> can exist without divisibility—as it is clearly demonstrated that it can, within that infinite, immovable extension distinct from moveable matter, in the *Manual of Metaphysics* <note>original: "Enchirid. Metaphys. cap. 6, 7, 8"</note>, chapters 6, 7, and 8.

7, 8. However, this argument is *ineffectual* if all *extension* <note>original: Extension; the quality of taking up space or having physical dimensions.</note> is divisible. If the *essential presence* of a *spirit*—which spreads through and is extended across the entire body C D E—can be *divided* for that very reason, then the whole *essence* occupying that body would be split into *parts*. But you will certainly say, "No, by no means," because you believe the spirit is entirely present in every single part of the body.

Therefore, the spirit would be divided (if I may put it this way) into many *totalities*. But what *logical ear* can tolerate a statement so absurd and contrary to all reason: that a "whole" should be divided not into parts, but into other "wholes"? 

You might argue instead, "Grant us at least that an *essential presence* can be distributed or divided among many distinctly located *totalities* which occupy the entire body C D E at the same time." Yes, indeed—this shall be granted to you, but only after you have proved that a *spirit* no larger than a *physical monad* <note>original: Physical Monad; an indivisible, infinitesimal point of matter or existence.</note> can occupy all parts of the body C D E at the same instant. However, this is on the condition that you acknowledge that it is not various *totalities*, but only one *total essence*—even the smallest imaginable—that can occupy that whole space and, when necessary, occupy an infinite space in an instant. 

The *Holenmerians* <note>original: Holenmerians; from the Greek *holos* (whole) and *meros* (part), referring to thinkers who believed a soul or spirit is "whole in the whole and whole in every part."</note> must necessarily hold this view regarding the Divine Essence. This is because, according to the second interpretation of their opinion (which squeezes the entire essence of a spirit into the smallest possible point), the Divine Essence itself would be no larger than a single *physical monad*. From this, it is clear that the three objections we raised at the beginning return here and completely overwhelm the primary reasoning of the *Holenmerians*. Thus, their "remedy" for the problem is far more unbearable than the original "disease" of the argument.

# SECTION XIV.

### A Refutation of the Second Reason of the Holenmerians.

**A**nd truly, the other reason which from this "Holenmerism" <note>Holenmerism (from the Greek *holos*, "whole," and *meros*, "part") is the Scholastic theory that the soul is present in its entirety in the whole body and also entirely present in every single part of the body.</note> of spirits claims an easier way of conceiving how it happens that the soul—suppose at point A—can perceive what happens to it at points C or B, and altogether in the same circumstances as if it were perfectly and entirely at C or B, while it is actually at A; although at first glance this seems very plausible, yet if we look thoroughly into it, we shall find it far from performing what it so fairly promises. 

For besides the fact that nothing is more difficult, or rather impossible to conceive, than that an essence no larger than a physical point <note>original: "Physical point"</note> should occupy and possess the whole body of a man at the same instant, this hypothesis is moreover plainly contrary and opposed to the very laws of the soul’s perceptions. For physicians and anatomists unanimously declare that they have found by very solid experiments that the soul perceives only within the head, and that outside the head there is no perception. 

This could by no means be the case if the soul herself were wholly in point A, and the very same soul again wholly in points B and C, and nowhere possessed an *essential size* <note>original: "essential Amplitude"</note> larger than a *physical monad* <term>Physical Monad: A single, indivisible, and dimensionless point of existence.</term>. For from this it would follow that one and the same thing would both perceive and not perceive at once; that it would perceive this or that object, and yet perceive nothing at all; which is a total contradiction.

And from here, the falsehood of that common saying is detected: *That if the eye were in the foot, the soul would see in the foot*; whereas the soul does not even see in those eyes which it already has, but somewhere within the brain. Nor would the soul see through an eye in the foot, unless by fitting nerves—not unlike the optic ones—extending from the foot to...

...to the head and brain, where the soul, so far as it is *perceptive*, resides. In the other parts of the body, its functions are only *vital* <note>Functions necessary for life, such as growth and involuntary processes, rather than conscious thought or sensation.</note>.

Again, the nature of some perceptions of the soul is such that they are suited for moving the body. It is therefore obvious that the very same thing which perceives also has the power of moving and guiding the body. This seems impossible to be done by a soul which, according to the opinion of the <term>Holenmerians</term> <note>Followers of the "Holenmerian" theory, which argues that the soul is "whole in the whole and whole in every part" (from the Greek *holos*, "whole," and *meros*, "part"). The author is arguing against the idea that the soul is a tiny, indivisible point that somehow exists everywhere at once.</note>, does not exceed the size of a small <term>physical monad</term> <note>The smallest possible unit of matter; a physical atom or point.</note>. And lastly, if it is permissible for the human mind to offer conjectures regarding the immortal spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> (whether they inhabit <term>vehicles</term> <note>In Neo-Platonic philosophy, "vehicles" are the subtle, non-fleshly bodies (airy or ethereal) that souls or spirits inhabit.</note> or are without them), and regarding their *perceptions* and *essential presences*—whether invisible or those in which they are said sometimes to appear to mortal men—surely no one can admit that any of these things are compatible with such a spirit as the <term>Holenmerians</term> describe. For how can a <term>metaphysical monad</term> <note>An indivisible, non-physical point of spiritual substance that has no extension in space.</note>—that is to say, a spiritual substance no larger than a physical atom—fill out an *essential presence* <note>The actual space or volume occupied by a spirit's essence.</note> larger than an atom? Unless it does so by a very swift vibration of itself in all directions, just as boys, by rapidly moving a fire-stick, create a fiery circle in the air through that quick motion. But that spirits without "vehicles" should have no greater *essential presence* than that occupied by a naked and unmoved metaphysical monad seems such an <note>original: "absonous"</note> absurd and ridiculous spectacle to the human mind that, unless a person is deprived of all wisdom and spiritual feeling, he cannot help but abhor such a foolish opinion.

As for those *essential presences* through which they sometimes appear to men, reaching at least the height of a human, how can a single metaphysical monad form such a large amount of air or <term>ether</term> <note>A hypothetical substance once thought to occupy all space beyond the Earth's atmosphere.</note> into a human shape, or govern it once it is formed? Or how can it perceive any external object during this swift motion and quick vibration, by which the <term>Holenmerians</term> understand this metaphysical monad to be present in all parts of its "vehicle" at once? For there can be no perception of an external object unless the object to be perceived acts with some stability upon the thing that perceives it. Furthermore, if an object could be perceived by this metaphysical monad while it is moving so swiftly and vibrating in all directions at once, it would not be seen in one place, but in many places at once—and those places might be very distant from one another.

## S E C T. XV.

### The egregious falsity of the Opinions of the Holenmerians
### and Nullibists, as also their uselessness
### for any Philosophical ends.

**B**UT truly, I am ashamed to waste so much time in refuting such mere trifles and foolish ideas <note>original: "Dotages"</note>—which indeed are such (I mean those of the *Nullibists* <note>Those who believe spirits exist nowhere in space</note>, as well as this other of the *Holenmerians* <note>Those who believe a spirit is "all in the whole and all in every part" of a body</note>) that we may very well wonder how such distorted and strained conceits could ever enter into the minds of men, or by what trick they have so spread themselves in the world. But the prejudices and enchantments of superstition, and the mindless admiration of certain men's persons, are so strong that they may utterly blind the minds of men and charm them into foolishness.

But if anyone, setting aside all prejudice and bias <note>original: "Parts-taking"</note>, will attentively consider the thing as it is, he shall clearly perceive and acknowledge (unless all belief is to be denied to human faculties) that the opinions of the *Nullibists* and *Holenmerians* regarding *incorporeal beings* <note>Beings without physical bodies, such as souls or spirits</note> are miserably false. Not only that, but for any philosophical purpose, they are altogether useless.

Neither hypothesis makes it any easier to conceive how the **mind** of **man**, or any other *spirit*, performs the functions of *perceiving* and *moving bodies*. It is no easier to imagine this by supposing they are *nowhere* than by supposing they are *somewhere*; or by supposing them to be entirely in *every part* of a body than by supposing them to occupy the whole body by an *essential* or *metaphysical* extension <note>The author's theory that spirits have a non-material kind of "spread" or presence in space</note>. On the contrary, both of these hypotheses entangle and involve the **doctrine of incorporeal beings** with greater difficulties and contradictions <note>original: "Repugnancies"</note>.

Therefore, since there is neither truth nor usefulness in the opinions of the *Holenmerians* and *Nullibists*, I hope it will offend no one if we dismiss them entirely from our philosophical inquiries <note>original: "Philosophations"</note> regarding an *incorporeal being* or *spirit*, as we deliver the **true idea** or **concept** of it.

### SECTION XVII

*The definition of Body in general, with so clear an explanation that even those who complain of the obscurity of a Spirit cannot help but confess they perfectly understand the nature of Body.*

**B**ut now, for those who thus despair of any true knowledge of the nature of a *Spirit*, I would entreat them to test the abilities of their wit in recognizing and thoroughly considering the nature of *Body* in general. Let them honestly tell me whether they cannot help but acknowledge this to be a clear and evident definition of it: *namely, that Body is a material substance of itself, altogether lacking all perception, life, and motion.* Or this: *Body is a material substance, growing or clustering together into one by virtue of some other thing, from which that unified whole, through this clustering, has or may also have life, perception, and motion.*

I do not doubt they will readily answer that they understand all of this (regarding the terms) clearly and perfectly. Nor would they doubt its truth, except that we deprive Body of all *motion from itself*, as well as of *union, life*, and *perception*. But they cannot help but very willingly admit that it is *substance*—that is, a being existing by itself, not a <term>mode</term> <note>original: "mode"; a philosophical term for a quality or state of a thing, like "roundness" is a mode of a ball, rather than the ball itself.</note> of some being—and also that it is a *material substance* composed of <term>physical monads</term> <note>original: "physical Monads"; the most basic, indivisible particles of matter that make up larger objects.</note>, or at least of the most minute particles of matter into which it is divisible. Because of their **impenetrability**, it is impenetrable by any other body; thus, the essential and positive difference of a body is that it is impenetrable and physically divisible into parts. But that it is <term>extended</term> <note>original: "extended"; occupying space in three dimensions (length, width, and depth).</note> belongs to it immediately simply because it is a *being*. Nor is there any reason why they should doubt the other part of the *dif-* <note>The word concludes on the next page as "differentia," meaning the distinguishing characteristic.</note>

## S E C T. XVIII.

### The perfect *Definition* of a *Spirit*, with a full *Explication* of its *Nature* through all *Degrees*.

**A**ND if the *notion* or *essence* is so easily understood in *corporeal* nature or the *body*, I do not see why the same ease of understanding cannot be found in the species immediately opposite to the *body*, namely the *spirit*. Let us try, therefore, and define a *spirit* according to the law of opposites: *an immaterial substance intrinsically endowed with life and the faculty of motion.* 

This slender and brief definition, which flows so easily without any fuss, encompasses the whole nature of a *spirit* in general. Because its thinness <term>original: exility</term> and brevity might make it less perceptible to the understanding—just as a spirit is to the sight—I will add a more complete explanation. This will show everyone that this definition of a *spirit* is not at all inferior to the definition of a *body* regarding clarity and distinctness. By the method we are now using, a full and perfect knowledge and understanding of the nature of a *spirit* may be achieved.

Come then, let us observe the properties of the *thing being defined* <term>original: definitum</term> through all its stages. We will see what precise and immediate properties each of them contains, from which a most distinct and perfect knowledge of the whole subject will finally reveal itself. Let us begin from the very top. First, let us note that a spirit is a *Being* <term>original Latin: Ens</term>. From the very fact that it is a *Being*, it is also *One*, *True*, and *Good*. These are the three acknowledged properties of a "Being" in metaphysics: that it exists at some time and in some place, and is in some way extended <note>meaning it occupies some form of space, a key point of the author's philosophy</note>, as is shown in the *Manual of Metaphysics* <note>original: Enchirid. Metaphys.</note>, Chapter 2, Section 10. These last three terms are self-explanatory. As for the first three, "*One*" signifies that it is undistinguished or un-
