...divided within itself and from others. "One" signifies that a thing is not divided within itself, but is distinguished from all other things. "True" denotes the correspondence of the *thing* to its own proper *Idea* and implies the correct *Matter* and *Form* duly joined together. Lastly, "Good" refers to its fitness for its purpose in a broad sense, so that it includes the common saying of theologians: "God is His own purpose." These concepts are commonly known to logicians and philosophers. That these six <note>In his *Enchiridion Metaphysicum*, More identifies the six "affections" or properties of "Being as Being" as: One, True, Good, Thing, Something, and Measure.</note> are the immediate properties of "Being as Being" is made clear in the previously cited *Manual of Metaphysics* <note>original title: *Enchiridion Metaphysicum*</note>; it is not necessary to repeat those arguments here. Every *Being* is either a *Substance* or a *Mode* <note>A "mode" is a specific way in which a substance exists, such as its shape or state.</note> of a substance, which some call an *Accident*. But almost everyone declares that a *Spirit* is not an accident or mode of a substance. It can be proven through many arguments that there are spirits which are no such *accidents* or *modes*, as is demonstrated in the said *Manual* and other treatises by Doctor Henry More.

Therefore, the second essential stage of a spirit is that it is a *Substance*. From this, it is understood to exist by itself and does not require any other thing to serve as a *Subject*—in which it might exist, or of which it might be the *mode* or *accident*—in order for it to exist.

The third and last essential stage is that it is *Immaterial*. According to this definition, it is a *Being* that is not only "one," but "one by itself" or by its own inner nature rather than by another. This means that although it is a being that is in some sense extended <note>meaning it occupies space</note>, it is utterly *Indivisible* and <term>Indiscerpible</term> <note>Indiscerpible: A term favored by Henry More meaning "incapable of being torn asunder" or separated into physical parts.</note> into real physical parts. Moreover, it can *penetrate* matter and (which matter cannot do) penetrate things of its own kind—that is, pass through spiritual substances. In these two essential attributes (as should be the case in every perfect and logical classification of a category), spirit is fully and accurately the opposite of its counterpart, namely, *Body*. Spirit also possesses those immediate properties by which it is understood to have *Life* inherently within itself and the faculty of *moving*. This is true in some sense for all spirits whatsoever, because life is either *Vegetative* (growth), *Sensitive* (feeling), or *Intellectual* (reason). Every spiritual substance has at least one of these, as well as the power of *moving*. Consequently, every spirit either moves itself by its own power, moves matter, or moves both—either directly or indirectly. For in this way, all things that move are moved by God, who is the fountain of all life and motion.

## SECTION XIX.

### *Since the definition of a Body is clear, the definition of a Spirit is also necessarily clear.*

**T**herefore, I dare appeal here to the judgment and conscience of anyone who is not completely uneducated or of a dull and slow mind, whether this concept or definition of a Spirit in general is not as understandable and clear <note>original: "perspicuous"</note>, and as clear and distinct in every way, as the idea or concept of a *Body*, or of anything else whatsoever that the mind of man can contemplate in the entire scope of Nature. And I ask whether he cannot as easily—or rather with the same effort—apprehend the nature of a *Spirit* as of a *Body*, since they both belong to the same immediate category <note>original: "Genus"</note>, namely *Substance*. Their distinguishing characteristics <note>original: "Differentiæ"</note> clarify one another through their mutual opposition; it is so connected that it is impossible for someone to understand what *Material Substance* is without immediately understanding what *Immaterial Substance* is. Likewise, one cannot understand what it is *not* to have *Life* and *Motion* inherently <note>original: "of it self"</note> without immediately perceiving what it is *to have both within itself*, or to be able to grant them to others.

...tually destroy one another. <note>The word "tually" is the completion of "mutually" from the preceding page.</note> For this *extension*—which is mixed with or included in the nature of a *spirit*—seems to take away its *penetrability* and *indivisibility*, as well as its ability to *think*. Likewise, its *penetrability* takes away its power to *move any bodies*.

I. First, *extension* removes *penetrability*. This is because if one extended thing penetrates another, of necessity either one of them must be destroyed, or two equal sizes <note>original: "Amplitudes"</note> that completely penetrate each other will be no larger than either one of them alone, since they are contained within the same boundaries.

II. Second, it removes *indivisibility*. Anything that is extended has <term>parts outside of parts</term> <note>original: *partes extra partes*; a philosophical concept describing how physical objects take up space by having distinct, separate parts in different locations</note>—one part distinct from another—and is therefore *divisible*. It could not even have parts unless it could be divided into them. Furthermore, since these parts are *substantial* and do not depend on one another, it is clearly evident that—at the very least by Divine Power—they could be separated and exist apart from each other.

III. Third, *extension* deprives a *spirit* of the ability to *think* by dragging it down to the same level as physical *bodies*. There is no reason why an extended *spirit* should be more capable of *perception* than extended *matter*.

IV. Lastly, *penetrability* makes a *spirit* unable to *move matter*. Because it slides so easily through *matter* due to this penetrability, it cannot effectively unite with *matter* to move it. Without some union or connection <note>original: "inherency"</note> (since a *spirit* lacks all *impenetrability*), it is impossible for it to push <note>original: "protrude"</note> *matter* in any direction.

The sum of these four difficulties is this: we should understand that although this *idea* or *notion* of a *spirit* we have presented is clear and easy to understand, that very clarity makes it abundantly obvious that it is not the *idea* of a *possible* thing, let alone a *really existing* thing. Its defining characteristics are clearly contradictory <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to one another.

## SECTION XXI.

### *An Answer to the first of the Four Objections.*

I. **B**UT against both the *Nullibists* <note>original: "Nullibists"; a term for philosophers who believed that spirits exist but occupy no space or location (from the Latin *nullibi*, "nowhere")</note> and the *Hobbians* <note>original: "Hobbians"; followers of the materialist philosopher Thomas Hobbes, who argued that only physical matter exists</note>, who both argue that *Extension* and *Matter* are one and the same thing, we will prove that the Notion or Idea of a *Spirit* which we have presented is a possible concept. 

As for the *Nullibists*, who think we rely too much on physical imagination in our opinion regarding the *Extension* of *Spirits*, I hope to show the opposite. I shall show that it is only because the *Hobbians* and *Nullibists* have not sufficiently cleansed and purified their imaginations from the filth and unclean stains of *Materiality* <note>original: "Corpority"</note> that they have stripped spirits of all *Amplitude* <note>original: "Amplitude"; the quality of having size, extent, or breadth</note>. Rather, their minds are so addicted and enslaved to *Material* things, and so disordered, that they do not know how to free themselves from gross *Physical Phantasms* <note>original: "Corporeal Phantasms"; mental images or illusions based solely on physical bodies</note>.

All those difficulties by which they endeavor to overwhelm our *Notion of a Spirit* have sprung from this source, as we shall clearly demonstrate by going through each of them and carefully weighing <note>original: "perpending"</note> them. It is due to their coarse imagination that they conclude that if two equal "amplitudes" (or extents of being) penetrate one another completely, one of them must perish, or else—being joined together—they are no larger than either one of them taken alone. This happens because their minds are so ensnared <note>original: "illaqueated or lime-twigged"; a metaphor of a bird caught in sticky glue (birdlime) smeared on a twig</note> with the ideas and properties of *Physical* things. They cannot help but infect things that have nothing physical in them with this material stain and contagion. Thus, they altogether confuse this *Metaphysical Extension* with *Physical Extension*. 

I say, it is from this mental "disease" that their insight has become so dull and blunt. They are unable to distinguish that common attribute of existence—I mean *Metaphysical Extension*—from *Specific* and *Material Extension*. They cannot assign to *Spirits* their proper *Extension* while leaving to *Matter* hers. Nor can they, according to the well-known logical or metaphysical methods of intellectual abstraction, separate <note>original: "prescind"</note> the *General* nature of *Extension* from the specific kinds mentioned above. ## SECTION XXII.

### *That besides those THREE dimensions which belong to all extended things, a FOURTH must also be admitted, which belongs properly to SPIRITS.*

And so that I do not hide or conceal anything, although all *material* things, considered in themselves, have only *three* dimensions, there must still be admitted in nature a *fourth*, which I think may aptly be called *Essential Spissitude* <term>original: "Spiffitude" (an OCR error for "Spissitude"); a term coined by Henry More to describe the "density" or "thickness" of a spirit when it occupies the same space as other spirits or matter</term>. While this most properly belongs to those *spirits* which can contract their *extension* <note>the space an object occupies</note> into a smaller *ubi* <note>Latin: "where"; a philosophical term for a specific location or spatial presence</note>, it can also be applied, by a lesser analogy, to *spirits* penetrating both *matter* and *one another* mutually. Thus, wherever there is more than one *essence*, or more of the same *essence* in the same *location* than its size would normally allow, this *fourth dimension* must be acknowledged, which we call *Essential Spissitude*.

This certainly involves no greater contradiction than what might seem, at first glance to an inattentive observer, to exist in the other *three* dimensions. For instance, unless one believes that a piece of wax stretched out to the length of an *ell* <note>a historical unit of measurement, roughly 45 inches</note> and then rolled into the shape of a globe loses some of its former *extension* by being made into a ball, one must admit that a spirit, by contracting itself into a smaller space, has not lost any of its *extension* or *essence*. Just as in the wax mentioned above, the reduction of its *length* <note>original: "Longitude"</note> is compensated for by the increase of its *width* <note>original: "Latitude"</note> and *depth* <note>original: "Profundity"</note>, so in a spirit contracting itself, its *length*, *width*, and *depth* are lessened and compensated for by *Essential Spissitude*, which the spirit acquires through this contraction.

In both cases, we must remember that only the *position* <note>original: "Site"</note> is changed, while the *essence* and *extension* remain completely unimpaired.

Truly, I perceive these things so perfectly in every way, and they are so certain and tested, that I dare appeal to the mind of anyone who is free from the moral prejudices of the *imagination*—

But I confidently deny that all **perception of extension** is such "imagination." There is an idea of infinite **extension** that is not drawn or taken from any external **sense**, but is natural and essential to the very faculty of perceiving. The mind can by no means pluck this idea out of herself, nor cast it away. But if she will rouse herself and fix her attention upon it through earnest and attentive thinking, she will be constrained—whether she wants to or not—to acknowledge a truth: even if all the matter in the world were removed from the universe, there would still remain a certain subtle and immaterial extension. This immaterial extension has no agreement with material extension in any way, except for the fact that it is extended. It does not fall under the senses, it is not impenetrable, it cannot be moved, and it cannot be torn apart <note>original: "discerped"</note> into pieces. This idea is not only possible but necessary; we do not invent it for our own pleasure, but find it so innate and ingrained in our mind that we cannot remove it by any force or artifice. This is a most certain demonstration that all **perception of extension** is not "imagination" properly so called.

For we see they confess their own guilt: namely, that their mind is so corrupted by their imagination and so immersed in it that they can use no other faculty when contemplating any extended thing. Therefore, when they use their imagination instead of their **intellect** in contemplating extension, they necessarily look upon it as an object of imagination—that is, as a corporeal thing that can be divided into parts. As I noted above, the sight of their mind is made so heavy and dull by this *material disease* <note>original Greek: ὑλοειδὴς (hyloeidēs), meaning "matter-like" or "pertaining to matter"</note> that it cannot distinguish any **extension** from that of **matter**. They cannot allow extension to belong to another kind of being, nor can they separate the concept of extension from matter through **logical** or **metaphysical abstraction**.

## S E C T. XXIV.

### *That extension as such includes in it neither divisibility nor impenetrability, neither indivisibility nor penetrability, but is indifferent to either pair of those properties.*

Therefore, because a thing is extended, people immediately imagine that it has "parts outside of parts" <note>original Latin: *partes extra partes*</note> and is not a "being that is one in itself and not by virtue of another" <note>original Latin: *Ens unum per se & non per aliud*</note>. They think it is constructed from the side-by-side placement of parts, when in fact the idea of *extension*, strictly considered in itself, includes no such thing. It includes only a three-dimensional distance, or solid amplitude—that is to say, not just in terms of lines and surfaces (if we may use those terms which properly belong to mathematical magnitude), but reaching out in every direction and extending toward every part. 

This amplitude surely, and nothing else, is what this bare and simple *extension* includes. It includes neither penetrability nor impenetrability, nor divisibility, nor yet indivisibility. Instead, it is altogether indifferent toward either pair of <term>Affectiones</term> <note>original: properties or attributes</note> or essential differences—namely, to divisibility and impenetrability, or to penetrability and indivisibility. If considered in itself, extension can be determined to either of these two pairs.

Therefore, we acknowledge that there is a certain kind of *extension*—namely, *material* extension—which is endowed with such a stout and invincible <term>antitypia</term> <note>Greek: 'Αντιτυπία (resistance or the quality of striking back)</note> or impenetrability, that it necessarily excludes and pushes out all other matter that encounters it and attempts to penetrate it. It does not allow other matter to enter at all, thanks to an insuperable <term>Renitency</term> <note>original: renitency (the physical resistance of a solid body to pressure)</note>. 

However, this marvelous power is not contained within the simple idea of *extension* itself, but is plainly omitted as something not belonging to it immediately. Why then may we not as easily conceive that another kind of *extension*—namely, an *immaterial* one—is of such a nature that it cannot be <term>discerped</term> <note>original: discerped (torn apart or divided into separate pieces)</note> into parts by any other thing, whether material or immaterial? Even though *extension* in itself does not include such a trait, this immaterial substance could be so united and held together by an indissoluble, necessary, and essential tie. ### *That everything that is extended does not necessarily have parts that are physically separable, though they may be logically or intellectually divisible.*

...number of monads <note>original: Monads; fundamental, indivisible units of being</note>, which the intellect nevertheless divides into two equal parts. And truly, in a *metaphysical monad*—such as the *Holenmerians* <note>original: Holenmerians; from the Greek "holos" (whole) and "meros" (part), referring to those who believed the soul is "all in the whole and all in every part" of the body</note> imagine the mind of man to be, and meanwhile to possess and occupy the whole body—there may again be made a *logical distribution* <note>a conceptual division rather than a physical one</note>, for example, *e subjectis* <note>original: e subjectis; Latin for "from the subjects," referring here to dividing a thing based on the different objects or areas it occupies</note>, as they call it. This occurs insofar as this *metaphysical monad*, or *soul* of the *Holenmerians*, is conceived to occupy the head, trunk, or limbs of the body; and yet no man is so delirious as to think it follows from this that such a soul may be discerped <term>discerped: torn apart or divided into separate physical pieces</term> into so many parts, or that the parts so divided could exist by themselves.

## SECTION XXVI.

### An answer to the latter part of the second objection, which infers the separability of the parts of a substantial extension from the idea that said parts are substantial and independent of one another.

**F**rom this, a sufficiently fitting and accommodated answer may be drawn for the latter part of this difficulty—namely, to the argument that because the parts of a substance are **substantial** and **independent** of one another, and exist by themselves (as being **substances**), it must follow that they can be discerped (at least by divine power) and disjointed, and once so disjointed, exist by themselves. I confess this is the main point or "sting" of the entire difficulty, and yet it is one that I hope I shall easily file down or blunt. For first, I deny that in a thing that is *absolutely* one and simple, as a *spirit* is, there are any *physical parts*, or parts properly so called; rather, they are only falsely feigned and imagined to be in it by a clouded imagination. But when the mind itself is sufficiently cleansed and purged from the impure dregs of fancy <note>original: Fancy; here meaning the faculty of imagination which relies on physical images</note>, although for some external reason she may consider a *spirit* as having parts, yet at the very same time she observes and notes within herself, with close attention, that such an *extension* in itself has none; and therefore when—

<summary>The author argues that while we can conceptually divide a spirit or soul based on the body parts it occupies, it remains a single, indivisible "monad" that cannot be physically torn apart. He asserts that the "parts" of a spirit are merely imaginary constructs and do not exist as independent, separable substances.</summary>
<keywords>Holenmerians, monad, soul, spirit, divisibility, discerped, substantial extension, metaphysics, philosophy of mind</keywords>

--- Page 52 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of spirits and whether they can be divided into parts, following the previous section's exploration of spiritual substance.</meta>

Since it has no parts, it is plain it has no *substantial parts*, nor any that are *independent* of one another or subsisting on their own. Furthermore, regarding those parts which a dull and weak imagination fancies to be in a spirit, it does not follow—simply because they are *substantial*—that they may *subsist separately by themselves*. For a thing *to subsist by itself* only means that it does not need the support of some other *subject* in which it must exist (as <term>accidents</term><note>original: "Accidents"; in traditional philosophy, these are properties like color or shape that cannot exist without a substance to inhabit.</note> do). Thus, the parts of a *spirit* may be said to subsist by themselves even though they cannot be separated, and therefore they remain a *substance* still.

## SECTION XXVII.

### *That the mutual independence of the parts of an extended substance may be understood in two ways; with an answer to the first interpretation.*

**B**UT what they mean by that "mutual independence of parts," I do not fully understand. However, I can see that they must mean one of two things: either that the parts are not the *mutual* and effective *causes* of each other's *existence*, or that their existence is thought to be connected by *no necessary condition at all*.

Regarding the first meaning, I willingly admit that the parts people imagine in a spirit are not the mutual causes of each other's existence. However, I also firmly deny that it follows that they may be <term>discerped</term><note>original: "discerped"; meaning to be torn apart, separated, or divided into distinct pieces.</note>. Once torn apart, they could not be preserved separately, any more than the conceptual parts of a *physical monad* <note>original: "Physical Monad"; here referring to a theoretical indivisible unit of matter.</note> which is divided into two only by our reason or intellect. These parts are certainly not the mutual causes of each other’s existence. 

The same applies to the divisions of a *metaphysical monad* according to the doctrine of the <term>Holenmerians</term><note>original: "Holenmerians"; from the Greek "holos" (whole) and "meros" (part), this refers to thinkers who believed the soul is present in its entirety in every part of the body, rather than being spread out like a liquid.</note>—namely, that the soul is totally present in every part of the body. No one in their right mind could ever hope that these could be <term>discerped</term>, even though the parts of that division are not the mutual causes of each other's existence. For they are but one and the same soul, which is not the cause of itself, but was wholly and entirely caused by God.

<summary>The author argues that while we can conceptually imagine "parts" within a spirit or soul, these parts are not independent entities that can be physically separated or "discerped." He refutes the idea that lack of mutual causation between parts implies they can exist apart from the whole.</summary>
<keywords>Spirit, Substance, Accidents, Discerption, Physical Monad, Metaphysical Monad, Holenmerians, Indivisibility, Soul, Theology</keywords>

But you might argue that there is clearly an existing and obvious reason why these parts of the division cannot be torn apart <note>original: "discerped"</note> and kept as separate pieces after being torn away. This is because the same indivisible unit <term>monad</term> <note>original: "Monad," referring to an ultimate, indivisible unit of being</note> exists in every part of the division. Since it is a single thing, it is impossible for it to be torn apart from itself. To this, I respond that it is equally clear and obvious how frivolous—and therefore foolish—it is to draw arguments from *logical* or *intellectual divisions* to conclude that parts can be physically separated in reality. I further add that just as that imaginary *metaphysical unit* cannot be torn or plucked into pieces away from itself, neither can any real spirit. This is because a spirit is a *most simple* thing and *most absolutely one*. A *pure mind*, unclouded and free from the prejudices of the *imagination* <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "imagination" often referred to the faculty of forming mental images of physical objects, which the author believes misleads people into thinking spirits have physical-like parts.</note>, recognizes that no real parts exist within it at all. If it had parts, it would *by that very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> be a *compound thing*.

### S E C T. XXVIII.

#### *An answer regarding the independence of parts, understood in the second sense.*

**T**his provides an easy way to answer the difficulty when understood in the second sense—that of the *mutual independence* of a spirit's parts, where their existence together and their union are thought to be connected by *no necessary law* or *condition*. I state firmly and without hesitation that this is false. The coexistence of the parts (as they call them) of a spirit is connected by an *absolutely necessary* and clearly *essential* law or condition. This is because a spirit is a *most simple being*, or a being that is *one in itself and not through another* <note>original: "unum per se & non per aliud"</note>. This means it is one by its very own nature, and not because of some other *substance* or *quality*. None of those "parts," as the *Nullibists* <term>Nullibists</term> <note>From the Latin "nullibi" (nowhere); a term used by Henry More to describe philosophers like Descartes who believed spirits exist but have no location in space.</note> call them, can exist except under this condition: that they all exist together, joined and united. This condition or law is contained within the very idea or nature of every spirit. Therefore, a spirit cannot be created or produced in any way unless it meets this condition—that all its parts are inseparably and indivisibly <note>original: "indiscerpibly"</note> one. This is similar to how a *right-angled triangle* <note>original: "Rectangle Triangle"</note> cannot exist unless it meets certain conditions—

...that the powers of the vertical side and the base are equal to the power of the hypotenuse <note>This is a reference to the Pythagorean theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$), implying that mathematical truths are necessary and inseparable.</note>. From this, the *indiscerpibility* <note>original: "indiscerpibility"; the quality of being impossible to divide or tear apart</note> of a *spirit* cannot be removed from it—not even *by divine power* <note>original: "virtute Divina"</note>, as the *Scholastic philosophers* <note>The "School-men" were medieval theologians and philosophers who used Aristotelian logic.</note> say—any more than the aforementioned property could be separated from a *right-angled triangle*. ## SECTION XXIX.

*An Answer to the third objection concerning the inability of an extended substance to perceive: namely, that whatever exists is extended, and that the* **NULLIBISTS** <note>From the Latin "nullibi" (nowhere); philosophers who argued that spirits or minds have no location in space.</note> *and* **HOLENMERIANS** <note>Philosophers who believed that the soul is "whole in every part" (tota in qualibet parte) of the body simultaneously.</note> *themselves cannot explain the faculty of perception in spirits based on their own hypotheses.*

III. **N**or is it any hindrance (which is the third point) to the faculty of *perceiving* and *thinking* in *spirits*. For by attributing *extension* to a *spirit*, we do not demote it to the rank of *bodily beings*; for there is nothing in all of nature that is not, in some sense, *extended*. Whatever *essence* exists in anything, it either is or can be actually present to some part of matter. Therefore, it must either be *extended* or be *contracted* to the narrowness of a single point and be *mere nothing*. As for the *Nullibists* and *Holenmerians*, I have already utterly defeated their opinions and completely overturned them from their very roots, so that no one may seek excuses or hiding places there. Therefore, it is a necessity that something which is extended must possess *thought* and *perception* within it, or else there will be nothing left that does.

As for what this objection further urges—that there seems to be no reason why an extended *spirit* should be more capable of perception than extended matter—it is truly, in my judgment, a very unlearned and unskillful <term>argument</term> <note>original: "argutation"; a formal or pedantic way of reasoning.</note>. For we do not take all this trouble to demonstrate the *extension* of a *spirit*...

### S E C T. XXXI.

*That although the Holenmerians and Nullibists can give no reason why that which perceives should be TOTALLY in every part, or should be NOWHERE rather than being in any way extended or somewhere, yet there are reasons obvious enough why an extended spirit is more likely to perceive than extended matter.*

This is surely much more than either the *Holenmerians* <note>from the Greek "holos" (whole) and "meros" (part); those who believed a spirit exists "entirely in the whole and entirely in every part" of a space</note> or *Nullibists* <note>from the Latin "nullibi" (nowhere); those, like Descartes, who argued that spirits have no location in space</note> can boast of. But now, since *matter* or *body*—which is *divisible* <note>original: "discerpible"</note> and *impenetrable*—is in itself devoid of all life and motion, it is certainly consistent with reason that the *category* <note>original: "Species"</note> opposite to *body* (which is conceived to be *penetrable* and *indivisible* <note>original: "Indiscerpible"</note>) should be naturally endowed with life in general and motion. And whereas *matter* is nothing else than a certain dull and loose...

Because of the *Unity* and *Subtlety* of its nature, spirit is a better fit for these functions than *Matter*, which is so dense <note>original: "crass"</note> that it is impenetrable. Matter is so far from having a unified *Essence* that it consists only of parts placed side-by-side <note>original: "juxtaposited"</note>. I hope that by this explanation I have fully resolved this third difficulty.

# S E C T. XXXII.

## An Answer to the fourth Objection as much as respects the HOLENMERIANS and NULLIBISTS, and all those that acknowledge that the Matter is created of God.

IV. Let us proceed, therefore, to the fourth and last objection. This argument concludes that because a spirit has "penetrability" <note>The ability of one substance to pass through another without resistance.</note>, it is unfit to move matter. The reasoning is that a spirit cannot move matter except by pushing it; and it cannot push matter because it passes through it so easily, without any resistance. Here, once again, the imagination plays tricks on us. It measures the nature of a spirit by the laws of matter, imagining a spirit to be like a physical body passing through an oversized or wide hole, where it cannot gain any traction because the passage is too loose.

In the meantime, however, it should be noted that neither the *Holenmerians* <note>Philosophers who believed a spirit is "whole in the whole and whole in every part" of the body it occupies.</note> nor the *Nullibists* <note>Philosophers, such as Descartes, who argued that spirits exist but are "nowhere" because they do not occupy physical space.</note> can rightfully raise this objection against us. It is far more unbelievable that either a *metaphysical monad* <note>original: "Metaphysical Monad"; defined here as a single, indivisible spiritual point.</note>, or any essence that is *nowhere*, should be better suited for moving matter than a spirit that has some extent (amplitude) and is actually present within the matter that is to be moved.

Therefore, we now only have to deal with those philosophers who argue that the entire universe consists of physical bodies alone. For those who acknowledge that there is a God and that matter was created by Him, it is not hard to conceive that there may be a certain faculty in the soul. This faculty, though only a faint shadow, corresponds to God’s power to create matter. Specifically, just as God—though the purest of all spirits—creates matter, which is the most solid of all things, so too might created spirits emit a certain *material virtue* <note>original: "Material Vertue"; a spiritual power or influence that can act upon physical objects.</note>. This power, whether exercised spontaneously or naturally, allows them to intimately inhabit the subject matter and be sufficiently and closely united with it. In the *Appendix* to the *Antidote against Atheism*, this faculty of spirits is called <term>hylopathy</term> <note>original: ύλοπάθεια; from the Greek roots for "matter" and "to be affected."</note>, or the "hylopathy of spirits"—the power of affecting or being affected by matter. But I confess that this answer is less effective when we are dealing with those who deny the creation of matter, and even less so with those who deny the existence of God.

<summary>The author refutes the idea that spirits cannot move matter due to their lack of physical solidity, proposing instead a spiritual faculty called "hylopathy" that allows spirits to bond with and influence physical substance.</summary>

# SECTION XXXIII.

## *An Answer to those who think there is nothing in the Universe but Matter or Body.*

Therefore, since we have to deal with such stubborn <note>original: "insense," meaning unfeeling or obstinate</note> adversaries who are so distanced from any knowledge or acknowledgment of *incorporeal* <term>immaterial or non-physical</term> *things*, we truly ought to behave very cautiously and carefully. We must consider the title of the question more precisely: it is not whether we can accurately describe and explain the specific way a spirit moves matter, but whether its *penetrability* <term>the ability of a spirit to occupy the same space as matter</term> is incompatible <note>original: "repugnant"</note> with the faculty of *moving matter*. Now, it is clear that if a spirit could be united and, as it were, cohere <term>stick together</term> with matter, it could easily move that matter. After all, if such a thing as a spirit exists at all, it is recognized by common opinion to be the true principle and fountain of all life and motion. Therefore, the entire controversy hinges on this one point: whether it is impossible <note>original: "repugnant"</note> for any *spirit* to be *united* and, so to speak, *cohere* with matter, or be joined to it by any bond or fastening (whether permanent or temporary).

I hope to clearly demonstrate that this is not impossible, based on the principle that the *uniting* of spirit with *matter* is just as understandable as the *uniting* of one *part* of matter with *another*. In reason, it should be held as a firm and sure axiom <term>a self-evident truth</term> that *something is possible if it presents no greater (if not even less) difficulty than something we already know to exist.* We see parts of matter truly and actually united with one another, and in some bodies this union has an almost invincible firmness—as seen in certain stones and metals, which are considered the hardest of all bodies. To understand this business more fully, let us imagine a body that is absolutely and perfectly hard, made of no particles except for the *physical monads* <term>the most basic, indivisible units of matter</term> themselves, and without any pores or gaps.

I ask, therefore: by what power or in what way do the parts of such a perfect solid hold together? Undoubtedly, they can claim nothing here except immediate *contact* and *rest*. For if they resort to any other qualities <note>original: "affections"</note> which are related to...

Life and sense are more rightly and more easily understood to be in a *spirit* than in *matter*; and we will presently show that a *spirit* may adhere to *matter* by the same virtues.

But the idea that the parts of *matter* cohere <note>original: "cohere"; to stick together</note> by bare, though immediate contact, seems as difficult—if not more difficult—than the idea that a *spirit* penetrating *matter* should join together into one with it. For the contact of the parts of *matter* is only superficial everywhere, but one and the same <term>indiscerpible</term> <note>original: "indiscerpible"; a philosophical term meaning a substance that cannot be divided, separated, or torn into smaller parts</note> *spirit* penetrates and possesses the whole *matter* at once.

Nor need we fear at all that it will not stick because it can so easily slide in, and therefore (as it may seem) might slide through and pass away.

For in a body that is perfectly solid—suppose cube *A*—in which we will imagine some particular internal <term>superficies</term> <note>original: "superficies"; a surface or boundary layer within or on a body</note>, suppose E, A, C. This surface E, A, C, is assuredly so <note>original: "glib"; meaning perfectly smooth or slippery</note> smooth and slippery that nothing could be imagined more smooth and slippery. Therefore, why does the upper part of this solid cube (C, D, E) not slide upon the lower part of the cube (E, F, C) by even the slightest push?

Can a spirit, which our imagination suspects can so easily pass through any body, be united to a body with equal firmness? This is no more difficult than the other; indeed, it is much easier if one considers the matter as it is, setting aside all *prejudice*. But now, since the *penetrability* of a spirit is not incompatible with its *union* with matter, it is obvious that its faculty for moving a body is not at all incompatible with its *penetrability*. This is the point that was to be demonstrated.

But I almost regret that I have attacked such a small difficulty with so much preparation and pomp, and have struggled so long with mere elusions and deceptive tricks of the *imagination*—which casts such a mist of fictitious contradictions upon the true idea of a spirit—as if fighting so many phantoms and ghosts of a restless night. But in the meantime, I have made it abundantly clear that there are no other contradictions or inconsistencies in our notion of a spirit than what the minds of our adversaries—polluted with the impure dregs of *imagination* and unable to separate *metaphysical extension* <note>The concept that even non-physical things occupy a kind of space or have "spread."</note> from *bodily properties*—foully and slovenly <term>clart</term> <note>original: "clart"; to smear, soil, or dirty, as with mud.</note> upon it. This idea, looked upon by itself, clearly appears to be a notion of a thing that is at least *possible*; which is all we aim for in this place.

For it is impossible that the human mind—unless it were weighed down and polluted by the dregs and waste of physical <term>corporeal</term> imagination—would allow itself to sink into such a crude and foul opinion.

However, the <term>Nullibists</term> <note>original: "Nullibiſts"; from the Latin *nullibi*, meaning "nowhere." These were philosophers, like René Descartes, who argued that spirits do not exist in any physical location or occupy space.</note> themselves seem almost ready to acknowledge as true and certain that everything which exists is extended (occupies space). They do not hide the fact that if a *spirit* is *somewhere*, it necessarily follows that it is also *extended*. Moreover, they grant that through its *operation* (its actions), a spirit is present to or within matter, and that the *essence* of a *spirit* is not separate from its *operations*.

Yet, the idea that a thing could exist and yet not be anywhere in the entire universe is such a wild and mad claim <note>original: "Vote"</note>—so discordant <note>original: "abſonous"</note> and repellent to all reason—that no one in their right mind could say it, except perhaps as a joke or a clever prank, as I suggested earlier. Because of this, the situation of those who are captivated and blinded by their admiration for the main author of such an absurd opinion <note>Likely referring again to Descartes.</note> is even more pitiable; they solemnly and seriously embrace it, and work diligently to refine it.

Finally, as for the <term>Holenmerians</term> <note>original: "Holenmerians"; from the Greek *holos en merei*, meaning "the whole in every part." These thinkers argued that the soul is entirely present in the whole body and also entirely present in every single part of the body.</note>, those among them who are more cautious and thoughtful explain their opinion in a way that seems hardly different from our own. They claim that the soul is in every part of the body, yet they say they do not mean the *quantity* or *extension* of the soul (by which it fills the whole body), but rather the *perfection* of its *essence* and *virtue* (its power). While this may be true of the *soul*, it is most certainly true of the *Divine Presence* <note>original: "Divine Numen"</note>, whose life and essence is most perfect and completely present everywhere, since He contains infinite *goodness*, *wisdom*, and *power* in all places.

Thus we see that this idea or notion of a spirit presented here is not only possible in itself, but very plausible and beyond objection. All parties, if they are understood correctly, will be found—whether they intend to or not—to contribute to the discovery of its truth and soundness. Therefore, this concept serves as a useful and timely conclusion to this first part of *Saducismus Triumphatus* <note>The title of Joseph Glanvill's book, meaning "Sadducism Conquered." Sadducism refers to the denial of the existence of spirits or the afterlife.</note>, which discusses the *possibility* of *ghosts* <note>original: "Apparitions"</note> and *witchcraft*. It makes it easier to accept the strength of the arguments in the second part—namely, the many *accounts* <note>original: "Relations"</note> provided to prove the *actual existence of spirits and ghosts*.

# A farther Defence of the

...inadequate concepts <note>original: "Conceptus's"</note>, as you call them—and I intend to use your phrases throughout, which are like those that occur in the writings of Mr. Richard Baxter <note>original: "Mr. R. B."</note>, just as the ideas in your letter are very similar to the ideas in Judge Hale's writings and his own—from those two partial concepts, I say, one adequate concept does result. This concept must encompass all spirits and nothing but spirits, or else we miss our mark.

Now, for the first inadequate concept, which you call the *fundamental concept* <note>original: "Conceptus Fundamentalis"</note> and acknowledge to be *substance*, we are both agreed that *it is substance*. But the *formal concept* <note>original: "Conceptus Formalis"</note>, by which it is distinguished from all substance that is not *spirit*, is where we do not seem to agree. For unless everything that exists is *spirit*, we must define spirit as a substance that is specifically opposite to all other substance in the universe besides itself, or else we achieve nothing.

Now I ask whether there is not *matter* in the world as well as *spirit*, and whether the immediate, known, and universally acknowledged notion of *matter* is not the real *divisibility* <note>original: "Devisibility"</note> and *impenetrability* of its parts to one another. This is body or matter according to the common notion of philosophers: *that which is extended in three dimensions and resistant* <note>original: "τὸ τριχῇ διάστατον ἀντίτυπον"</note>. 

And if this is the immediate character of matter, it naturally and logically follows that the immediate character of its opposite species, *spirit*, must be *indivisibility* and *penetrability*. Therefore, those essential characters must be a part of the *formal concept* of a spirit, by which it is distinguished from body or *matter*. 

So, these two substances, *matter* and *spirit*, stand opposite to one another, specifically distinct by their immediate, essential, and inseparable attributes: the one being truly separable <term>discerpible: capable of being torn apart or divided into pieces</term> and impenetrable, and the other penetrable and inseparable <term>indiscerpible: incapable of being torn apart or divided; a single, unified whole</term>. They are sufficiently distinguished in this way before we even consider any principle of *activity* in either. 

And this much being conceded—that there are these two kinds of substances in the world so described—I appeal to any person's faculties: which of the two, *spirit*, is more likely to be the fountain of all life and motion, and *matter* a merely passive principle? That is to say, matter is inactive by itself, and is not moved unless the other principle moves it and modifies it. 

Therefore, the true notion of a *spirit* in general is what I have set down in *Section 18, namely: An immaterial (which is, a penetrable and inseparable) substance, intrinsically endowed with life and motion.* Whatever fits this description is spirit, and whatever substance is not this, is no *spirit*, but *matter*. It is more logical that life, motion, sympathy, and synergy <note>original: "Synenergy"</note> should intrinsically result from a substance that is so much *one* as to be inseparable, and so subtle as to be *penetrable* in the manner described, rather than from *matter*, which is the opposite...

# S E C T. VII.

## *That Matter and Substance differ as Genus and Species, and what Substance properly and adequately is. And that the bare and naked Substance of a thing is not knowable neither in this Life, nor perhaps in the Life to come—but only its Essential Attributes, Behaviors, and Operations.*

Moving on to the *fundamental concept* <note>original: *Conceptus Fundamentalis*</note>, you say this: *“But truly I am at a loss about the fundamental concept wherein the true difference lies between substance and matter.”* It seems to me the difference is quite obvious to any observant eye: namely, that substance <note>original: *Substantia*</note> and matter <note>original: *Materia*</note> differ as a general category <note>original: *Genus*</note> and a specific type <note>original: *Species*</note> differ, just as "animal" and "beast" <note>original: *Brutum*</note> differ. You may complete the classification this way: substance is either matter or spirit, just as an animal is either a beast or a human <note>original: *Homo*</note>. I am satisfied with such a simple analysis. But you proceed:

Do we mean by substance a real concept <note>original: *Conceptus Realis*</note> or only a relative one <note>original: *Relativus*</note>? To say it "stands under accidents" <note>original: *substare accidentibus*; in traditional philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties like color or shape that must exist within a substance</note> describes only a relationship and leaves the question unanswered: *What is it that stands under the accidents?* To say it is not an "accident" does not tell us what it is, but what it is not. To say it "exists by itself" <note>original: *subsistere per se*</note> either says nothing more than that it is a real being <note>original: *Ens reale*</note>, or else fails to tell us what it is that actually exists. 

(1) As for that relative meaning, we do not care much for it here. It looks more like the logical notion of a "subject" <note>original: *Subjectum*</note> which relates to an "added quality" <note>original: *Adjunctum*</note>. (2) And though saying it is not an accident tells us what it is *not* rather than what it *is*, it still clarifies its nature through contrast (as the logical maxim teaches us: *Opposites placed next to each other become clearer* <note>original: *Contraria juxta se posita magis elucescunt*</note>). 

The nature of an "accident" is such that it cannot exist except within something else. The nature of a substance is such that it needs no "inherence" <note>original: *inhæsion*; the state of existing inside or being attached to a subject</note> as an accident does in another subject, but exists by itself and stands, as it were, on its own legs.

This is the proper character of substance, insofar as <note>original: *quatenus*</note> it is substance. What could be clearer than this? And one should consider whether it is not a sign of a lack of education <note>original: *’Απαιδευσία* (apaideusia); specifically a lack of training in logic or philosophy</note> to ask further what it is, once such a complete definition has been given—to ask, "what is that

(1) If *discrete quantity* <note>original Latin: "Quantitas discreta," referring to things that can be counted as individual, distinct units</note> is granted to spirits, why may they not also be granted an *indivisible* <note>original: "indiscerpible"</note> continuation of *extension* <note>original: "amplitude"</note>? You will reply that they may not—and this is one of the most clever arguments I have encountered—because then a spirit could be measured by a ruler made of wood or brass, and be declared to be so many inches or feet long or wide. This, you argue, would prove it is not a *spirit*, but *matter* or a *body*. Why? Because it is measured by wood or brass? Would it follow that these spirits are physical bodies simply because the brass counters are physical? The logic is just as firm in one case as the other, as I have noted more fully elsewhere.

(2) And now, regarding the idea that *forms multiply themselves* <note>original Latin: "Formæ se multiplicant"</note>, I wish to know what is meant by "forms"—whether they are the qualities and modes of a substance, or substances themselves acting upon other substances. If the former is meant, it does not apply to our case, as our argument concerns spirits that are substances. I say that no substance can multiply itself; for if a substance, while remaining the same entire substance, should multiply into other substances, it would be an act of creation, which is impossible for a created being to perform. But if it sheds or parts with a portion of its own substance, that in my view is not *multiplication* but *division*.

(3) What follows is a sound and golden saying, if understood correctly: *That generation* <note>the process of coming into being or biological formation</note> *is the work of spirits and not of bodies*. For *body* or *matter* is passive by itself and can do nothing except as it is either indirectly or directly moved by a spirit. This includes fire, water, air, and all other bodies that are moved either by the *spirit that sustains matter* <note>original: "Holostatick Spirit of the Universe," likely referring to the "Hylostatic" spirit or World Soul that governs physical matter</note> throughout the universe, or by their own specific spirit, such as brute animals, angels, and men. In this way, all "inanimate" creatures (as they are commonly called) are generated by the *Spirit of Nature*. Likewise, all specific animals—both beasts and men—are generated, or rather *formed*, by their own souls. The Spirit of Nature prepares the matter as far as is appropriate, but in the meantime, all things depend upon that universal Creator of all things, *God*, who is blessed forever.

Otherwise, for what are commonly called *inanimate creatures*—such as *plants* and all other *inanimate bodies* that appear to be different *species* of things—they are held together in their specific forms by the *Spirit of the Universe* <note>A common 17th-century concept of a non-rational, pervasive force that organizes the physical world according to God's laws</note>. According to the course of nature, I know of no other ways for many substances to become one besides these.

# S E C T. XIV.

*A summary of the Psychopyrist's <note>original: "Psychopyrist"; literally "soul-fire-user," a term used by Henry More to describe Richard Baxter's view that the soul consists of a spiritual form of fire.</note> philosophical arguments concerning a Spirit. The first four particulars of it are presented, where, among other things, the author notes the insufficiency of the Psychopyrist's reasoning for setting aside the use of the words "immaterial" and "material" and his preference for holding only to the distinction between "active" and "passive" natures.*

I may perhaps have been too tedious already, but yet because you have been pleased to share your thoughts regarding this present subject with me even more specifically, though briefly, I shall offer some criticisms or brief comments upon each of them in the order they appear. *I am currently,* you say, *compelled to keep my thoughts within the following scope.*

First, *I know spirits best by their* **Triune Formal Vital Power** <note>original: Virtus Vitalis Formalis Una-Trina; a three-in-one life force.</note>. But here I ask: how do you know that this **Triune Formal Vital Power** belongs to *Spirit* and not to *Matter*, unless you have a prior notion of *Spirit* as distinct from *Matter*, and also know the nature of *Matter* so distinctly—as well as the operations of that **Vital Power**—that you can conclude they are incompatible with one another? Otherwise, even if you find that **Vital Power** in a subject, you do not know whether the principle from which it comes, or in which it resides, is *Material* or *Spiritual*.

Secondly, *I maintain,* you say, *that for created spirits,* **Substance** <note>original: Substantia</note>, *as it designates a* **Real Basis** <note>original: Basis Realis</note>, *must be the* **Fundamental Concept** <note>original: Conceptus Fundamentalis</note>. This is solid and beyond reproach, as far as I can discern. From this, it is evident that since the soul is a spirit, and a spirit is a substance, those who hold that the soul is <term>derived from the parents</term> <note>original: ex Traduce; the doctrine of Traducianism, which suggests that the soul is transmitted from parents to children during procreation rather than being created individually by God.</note> must also hold that a substance can be derived in this way. As I noted above, the comparison of one lamp being lit from another does not apply to this. I also previously mentioned the difficulties involved in the idea of a parent's soul shedding part of itself to produce a child's soul.

Thirdly, *The word "immaterial,"* you say, *signifies nothing but a negation, and since "matter"* <note>original: Materia</note> *was used by many ancient writers in the same sense that we use "substance," I usually set aside these words.* The

I do not think the first reason is very strong. For a negative prefix added to a word that denotes imperfection implies something positive and perfect, such as in *Infinite*, *Immortal*, and the like. These terms remove the imperfections found in *finiteness* and *mortality*, and imply something positive of a better nature. In the same way, the word *Immaterial* removes the imperfections of <term>discerpibility</term> <note>original: "Discerpibility"; the quality of being able to be torn or divided into parts</note> and <term>impenetrability</term> <note>original: "Impenetrability"; the property of matter that prevents two bodies from occupying the same space at the same time</note>, and it implies the opposite, positive qualities. 

As for the reason for the second avoidance: *Matter* <note>original: "Materia"</note> might indeed be used by the ancient philosophers in the same sense that the "Subject" <note>original: "Subjectum"</note> is used in logic, or as "substance insofar as it underlies its properties" <note>original: "Substantia quatenus substat Accidentibus"</note>. However, when it is precisely defined as "a being existing by itself" <note>original: "Ens per se subsistens"</note>, I believe it is not easy to find an example where *hyle* <note>original: "ὕλη"; the Greek word for matter</note> or *Matter* is used as a substitute for *Substance* in that full sense. 

But my main question is this: since the definitions of *Substance* and *Matter* are so well known in the learned world, why do you use *Substance*—which is only the general category—instead of *Matter* or the other species of substance, which is *Immaterial* or *Spiritual*? These terms are more certain and distinct. It seems you only avoid them out of a shyness to state clearly which properties or operations belong to which subject (material or immaterial), or perhaps you doubt whether there is any real and proper distinction between "body" and "spirit" in the created universe. But you know your own reasons best.

Fourthly, you say that you hold to the distinction between *natures* or *substances* that are *active* and *passive*. However, since every created substance is both *active* and *passive* in some sense or another, this is a distinction that confuses everything and distinguishes nothing. Instead, *spiritual* and *material substance* are the permanent characteristics of two orders of things that are fundamentally different. This clear way of philosophizing is more satisfactory to me than blending and confusing these categories of things. Your approach looks as if there were some paradoxical mystery beneath it, which is perhaps better left alone than investigated too closely.

## SECTION XV.

### *The Fifth Particular, concerning the Purity of Spiritual Substances, and how prone those who do not understand that the most subtle Material Substances consist of Particles are to think that what is really Material is Spiritual.*

**F**ifthly, you say that I distinguish *Spiritual Substances as such by the purity of their Substances in addition to their formal Differences*. I suppose you mean by "purity" the subtlety and thinness <term>tenuity: thinness or lack of density</term> of their substances, just as the interpreter of *Trismegistus's Pæmander* <note>original: *Trismegist's Pæmander*. Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric wisdom known as Hermeticism.</note>, chapter 12, translates the Greek *τὸ λεπτομερέστατον τῆς ὕλης* <note>original: *tò leptomeréstaton tês hýlēs*</note> as "The purest portion of matter." The Latin text is: *Purissimaque materiæ portio Aer, Aeris Anima, Animæ Mens, Mentes denique Deus* <note>Translation: "The purest portion of matter is Air; of Air, the Soul; of the Soul, the Mind; and finally of Mind, God."</note>. The Greek is, "The most subtle part of matter is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the mind; and of the mind, God." And yet *leptomereia* <note>original: *λεπτομέρεια*</note> properly signifies the subtlety, thinness, or smallness of the parts or particles of which a thing consists; even so, the translator calls this "purity." However, I am quite certain that your "purity" of spiritual substances is not of the kind that you believe consists of particles, because you do not accept that hypothesis <term>hypothesis: here, the scientific theory that matter is composed of discrete particles</term> any more than *Judge Hale* <note>original: *Judge Hales*. Likely referring to Sir Matthew Hale (1609–1676), a famous English jurist and natural philosopher.</note> does.

This is a strong temptation for someone to judge what is really *material* to be *spiritual* when it is not, merely because it is conceived to be one continuous, subtle substance. But a man would be loath to admit that a collection <term>congeries: a collection or mass of items</term> of *atoms*, no matter how small or subtle they are, is a spirit—any more than he would admit that the powder of some dense <term>crass: thick, coarse, or dense</term> body is a spirit, when it was so obviously a body before. For *more and less do not change the species* <note>original Latin: *magis and minus non variant speciem*. A Scholastic maxim meaning that a change in degree (more or less of a quality) does not change the essential nature or category of a thing.</note>, as that *Scholastic maxim* puts it.

<summary>The author argues that "purity" or extreme thinness in a substance does not automatically make it spiritual, warning against mistaking very subtle matter (like air or atoms) for a spirit.</summary>

## S E C T. XVI.

The Sixth Particular. *That all created Spirits are in some way Passive: That the density <note>original: "Spissitude"</note> which is attributed to Spirits by the Psychopyrist’s <note>literally "fire-soul," referring to an opponent who believes the soul is a form of fire or matter</note> Antagonist argues a Spirit to be Immaterial rather than Material: That "Body" sometimes has a less gross meaning than "Matter": And in what sense the Psychopyrist seems to allow created Spirits to be Incorporeal: And what might be the chief ground of this Mistake.*

**S**ixthly, you say that you do not doubt that *all created Spirits are somewhat passive, because they receive the influence of the First Cause <note>original: "quia Influxum causæ primæ recipiunt"; referring to God as the source of all existence</note>,* and you grant them *density* and *extension*, which signifies the same as what many people mean when they call them *Material*. That is to say, if I understand you correctly, all created Spirits—no matter how pure and refined—are not so far transformed from the condition of *Matter* that they cease to be *passive* in relation to the First Cause and His *influence* upon them. I will easily admit this even for the highest level of created spirits as I define them, which are most properly and truly spirits. 

Regarding all created Spirits: though I grant them *density and extension*, I grant the former in a sense that signifies only more substance within a smaller space <note>original: "compass"</note>. It does not imply any hardness or coarseness resulting from the folding <note>original: "Reduplication"</note> of that same substance into a narrower area. In this way, the spirit remains just as spiritual as before and does not resemble *Matter* in this regard. In fact, it proves itself to be the opposite of matter: *Matter* implies that its parts cannot occupy the same space <note>original: "Impenetrability of Parts"</note>, whereas spirit allows for such penetration <note>original: "Penetrability"</note>. 

As for *extension*, that in itself has nothing of the nature of matter in it. There is such a thing as *metaphysical extension* as well as *metaphysical numerality*, both of which belong to *beings as they are beings <note>original: "Entia quatenus Entia"</note>*. There is no *being <note>original: "Ens"</note>* that lacks all size or "amplitude," or that is not capable of being counted as a second, third, or fourth in a sequence. Therefore, if those men mean no more by these words *density* and *extension* in *Spirits* than I do, and yet still call Spirits *Material*, I must take the liberty to say that, in my judgment, they are misnaming them.

<summary>The author argues that spirits are fundamentally different from matter because they are "penetrable" and can exist with varying degrees of density without becoming physical. He asserts that "extension" (occupying space) is a property of all existence, not just material things.</summary>

# A further Defence of the

But you say that custom has caused *Materia* <note>Matter</note>, and especially *Corpus* <note>Body</note>, to signify only such coarse substance as the three *passive elements* <note>Earth, water, and air</note> possess. I agree, in that sense, to say that *spirits* are not *corporeal* or *material*. It is apparent that *Corpus* does not always signify something more solid than *Materia*, but can mean a mere three-dimensional metaphysical or mathematical space. This is clear from the expressions of some *Platonists* who describe the space in which the worldly bodies move—which *Democritus* and *Epicurus* called *the void* <note>original: τὸ κενόν (*to kenon*)</note>—as an *immaterial body* <note>original: Σῶμα ἄϋλον (*Soma aylon*)</note>. To have called it "immaterial matter," however, would have been a contradiction. From this, it is suggested that *matter* fundamentally and specifically implies a coarser nature than *body*. 

But we will not argue about words. What is most notable here is that you seem to concede or imply that no created *spirits* are to be considered *incorporeal* or *immaterial* in any sense other than that they are not as coarse in consistency as those *three passive elements*: *earth, water, and air*. It is as if *fire* and *ether* <note>original: Æther</note>, which are far thinner than *air*, were *immaterial* and *incorporeal beings*, and as if no other created *beings* could be called *immaterial* or *incorporeal* in any other way than they are—namely, for the *thinness* <note>original: tenuity</note> or *subtlety* of their *substance*.

I consider this opinion—though I have known pious and intelligent persons to hold it—to be a major mistake. It arises from another false assumption or suspicion: namely, that the bodies of the world do not consist of small, minute parts of *matter*, and that *water*, *air*, *ether*, and *fire* are each a continuous *substance* rather than a collection <note>original: congeries</note> of touching particles that make up such fluid *substances*. This, I say, seems to be the fundamental error of those who philosophize according to your method. If they had not swallowed this first error, they could not have so easily absorbed the second: namely, that there are no created *incorporeal substances* in any sense other than that *ether* or *fire* may be said to be *incorporeal*—that is, being freed from that coarseness or grossness that the *three passive elements* seem to have.

<summary>The author argues that spirits are truly immaterial, rejecting the opponent's view that they are simply "thin" physical substances like fire or ether. He attributes this misunderstanding to a denial of atomism, or the idea that matter is composed of minute particles.</summary>

## SECTION XVII.

### *Reasons why Atomic Philosophy is to be preferred over that of the Psychopyrist <note>original: "Psychopyrist"; one who believes the soul is composed of a "soul-fire" or fiery matter</note>. And where he may find enough instruction to be certain of such an important truth.*

**B**UT here we two disagree very much; for I believe that all bodies consist of atoms, or little particles of matter. Hard and solid bodies, such as stones, iron, and the like, consist of particles that are somehow more firmly joined to one another. But in fluid bodies, such as water, air, ether <note>original: "Æther"; the substance once believed to fill the upper regions of space and the gaps between particles</note>, and fire, they consist of particles that are merely touching and moving past one another. I think I have good reason to embrace this way of philosophy over any other. 

First, because in this industrious and searching age, it is most universally accepted by independent and thoughtful philosophers. This is that "philosophical age" <note>original: "saculum Philosophicum"</note> in which knowledge should abound, according to the prophecy of Daniel.

Secondly, this mode of philosophy is the most useful for the best purposes and serves best to support the main parts of natural religion—namely, the existence of God, of *genii* <note>original: "Genii"; spirits or guardian angels</note> or angels, and the immortality of the soul. For it is so absurd at first sight to think that a collection <note>original: "congeries"</note> or heap of particles or atoms should be capable of those most noble functions of imagination, memory, and understanding—or even of sense or personality. If it were not for this awkward idea that air, ether, and fire are continuous substances rather than a collection of particles, people would immediately be led to a necessary belief in spiritual substance properly so called. Then all the main articles of natural religion would be accepted easily <note>original: "go down glib and easie"</note>. But to deny that such liquid bodies consist of particles deprives us of some of the most significant help that philosophy offers against atheism and Epicureanism <note>original: "Epicurism"; the materialist belief that the world is made of atoms but lacks divine purpose or a soul</note>.

Thirdly, this mode of philosophy seems to be the most ancient (and "the oldest of everything is the truest" <note>original: "antiquissimum quodque verissimum"</note>). Indeed, it seems to have been the old <term>Moschical or Mosaical</term> <note>Many 17th-century scholars believed that atomism was originally taught by the biblical Moses, sometimes identified with a Phoenician philosopher named Moschus</note> philosophy, as may appear from what I have written in the *Appendix* to the *Defense* of my *Cabbala Philosophica*, Chapter 1, Section 8.

## SECTION XVIII.

Seventhly, you say, "Though I do not go to the extremes of <term>Louis le Grand</term> in his work *On Fire* <note>original: "Ludov. le Grand, *de Igne*"</note>, nor those of <term>Telesio</term> <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), an Italian philosopher who emphasized sensory observation.</note> or <term>Patrizi</term> <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), a Venetian philosopher and scientist.</note>, I wish that *Fire* were better studied." middle, and penetrating them both, that causes that marvelous phenomenon <note>original: "Phænomenon"</note>.

Furthermore, I would not only have such experiments as these considered, but I would have the very nature of *water* well examined <note>original: "sifted"</note> and studied. To anyone who possesses that impartial curiosity to study the nature of *water* as well as *fire*, I would recommend reading *Descartes’s Meteors* <note>original: "des Cartes’s Meteors", referring to René Descartes's 1637 work *Les Météores*</note>. In that work, he demonstrates with incomparable evidence that *water* consists of long, flexible particles. When these are joined together in a moderate, creeping motion side-by-side <note>original: "contiguously one by another"</note>, they create the phenomenon of *water*. However, when they are more swiftly agitated—as they are in an *aeolipile* <term>An early steam-powered device consisting of a hollow vessel with a nozzle; when water inside is heated, steam is forced out, often causing the device to spin.</term> <note>original: "Æolipyla"</note> set over a fire with some water in the bottom—these *aqueous* <note>water-based</note> particles are raised out of the water and set into a whirling motion. They strike against one another like people fighting with quarterstaffs <note>original: "Playing as it were at Quarter-Staff", a traditional English pole weapon</note> within the hollow part of the *aeolipile* that contains only air. As they compete for more space, they burst out of the opening <note>original: "Orifice"</note> of the *aeolipile* and create the phenomenon of a very noticeable, if not violent, wind.

Just as they are exhaled from the water in the *aeolipile* by the power of fire, so they are exhaled from the sea, rivers, and other moist places by the heat of the sun. Depending on certain degrees of motion or rest, and their distance from the Earth, they cause mists or clouds. When many of them cluster closely together in warm air, they cause raindrops; but in colder air, they form snow or hail. It is obvious to everyone that water is frozen into ice by intense cold. Ice is therefore a remarkably firm consistency of these same *aqueous* particles. While remaining *aqueous* particles, they can also take the form not only of clouds, snow, and rain, but also of blustering winds when that whirling motion is imparted to them.

These, I believe <note>original: "methinks"</note>, are sufficient indications that *water* is a substance <note>original: "Body"</note> consisting of oblong, flexible particles that can be separated by heat. Just as ice, though a solid body, is melted by heat into the fluid we call *water*, so too can the parts of this *water* be so loosened <note>original: "relaxated"</note> that they are thinned into vapors <note>original: "rarified into Vapours"</note>. Those vapors can then be so agitated that they take the form of wind. Among other things that align so well <note>original: "hit so handsomely"</note>, it is also observable that water is easily drawn out of a wet cloth when exposed to air or fire. In contrast, it is difficult to remove *oil* or grease in the same way. This suggests that water particles are long, smooth, and flexible, whereas those of *oil* are more branch-like <note>original: "ramose"</note> and become entangled with the cloth and with each other.

Anyone with any intuition or natural insight into <term>philosophy</term> cannot help but perceive the meaning of this: namely, that <term>water</term> must consist of such particles as <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), a French philosopher who proposed that matter was composed of particles of different shapes and sizes.</note> Descartes has described. It is not one uniform, continuous body; rather, although each long particle is strongly held together within itself, they are merely touching one another in <term>water</term>, though they are quite firmly joined in <term>ice</term>. But if they were uniformly continuous throughout <term>water</term>—that is, no more in one part than another—they might pass through the smallest pores and, like sunbeams (at least with some added force), strain themselves through glass. This plainly shows that <term>water</term> is not one uniformly continuous body, but consists of long particles, each being tough and flexible in itself, yet easily separable from one another. Since we find this so clearly discoverable in <term>water</term>, if we are not excessively shy or timid, how can we help but conclude that all other things, as well as <term>water</term>—especially if they can be made fluid—consist of some kind of particles or other? And this, I think, is the genuine result of our diligently studying the nature of <term>water</term>.

...if we may call it that, being so bright and splendid; a certain kind of particles loosened from the tallow or wax, which consists of them, are put into motion, just as they are in vapors. It is clear from this that *flame* is nothing more than these particles put into a specific kind of motion, different from that of *water*, and affecting or modifying the <term>medium</term> <note>the substance, such as air, through which a force or light is transmitted</note> in a different way. This creates the appearance to our eye that we call *flame*, which is actually just a more dense, bright vapor or <term>reek</term> <note>original: "Reek"; smoke, steam, or vapor</note>. In this way, the whole candle is gradually dissolved into particles. Nor is it the same individual flame at every moment, any more than the water running through a pipe is the same individual water until it has all run out.

So we see that studying *water* helps us better understand the nature of *fire*. It shows us that fire is nothing but a specific kind of motion and particles that modify our sight's <term>medium</term> so that the <term>phenomenon</term> <note>original: "Phænomenon"; an observable fact or event</note> we call *fire* or *flame* appears to us. *Flame* occurs when the <term>accended</term> <note>original: "accended"; set on fire or kindled</note> particles are <term>volatile</term> <note>evaporating rapidly; moving easily through the air</note>. However, it is called *fire* when the particles are more fixed, such as in the wick of a candle once the flame is gone, or in red-hot iron. In red-hot iron, the parts are not volatile at all (unlike wax, wood, and tallow), yet they vibrate sharply against the <term>medium</term> of our sight and cause the phenomenon of *fire*. I have studied the nature of fire with diligence and seriousness, and yet I confess I can make no more of it than this. But let us continue.

<header>The True Notion of a Spirit</header>

Anyone who knows that fire <note>original: *Ignis*</note> is a *substance* whose *form* <note>In traditional philosophy, "form" refers to the essential nature or organizing principle of a thing.</note> is the *active power of moving, lighting, and heating* <note>original: *Potentia activa movendi, illuminandi, calefaciendi*</note>—and understands that these effects, when received by dense, passive bodies, are merely their *accidents* <note>original: *accidents*; in this context, these are non-essential properties or secondary effects rather than the essence of the thing itself</note>—realizes that it is the *fiery substance* itself that is actively operating upon them. Anyone who conceives of *spirits* as nothing but *eminent fire* <note>original: *Ignis eminenter*; "eminent" here means a higher, more perfect, or refined version of the element</note>—that is, a purer *substance* than physical fire—understands them through their similarities to fire (which is the best way to conceive of them next to their essential nature). I believe such a person knows as much as I can grasp regarding the *substance* of created *spirits*.

Although you thought you were limited in space, I believe you have shown a very skillful ability to pack so much meaning into such a small compass. By this, I feel I am now able to understand your full meaning, which I suppose can be broken down into these following propositions:

First, that fire is a substance whose form is an active power of motion, light, and heat.

Secondly, that the motion, light, and heat that appear in dense, passive bodies are merely accidents of those bodies—such as those seen in a fire-stick, a candle, and the like.

Thirdly, that there is an active fiery substance operating upon the aforementioned dense, passive bodies, which is distinct from the bodies themselves.

Fourthly, that a spirit is to be understood simply as *eminent fire*.

Fifthly, that this *eminent fire* is a purer substance than ordinary fire.

Sixthly, that this purer substance, second only to its essential power, is best understood by the similarity it bears to the aforementioned fire.

Seventhly and lastly, that anyone who thinks of created spirits in this way knows as much of their substance as you can reach.
