### SECTION XXI.

*Certain questions regarding the previous propositions to discover what the Psychopyrist <note>A term coined by the author for someone who believes the soul is made of fire.</note> intends, and how much closer we are to the true knowledge of a spirit by his illustrations using fire.*

I shall now take the liberty to ask some questions regarding these propositions; such as whether in the first proposition, you mean that an "active power" is a power always putting itself into action, so that this fire is always moving, giving light, and providing heat. And is it these things not only *effectively* (producing the effect of fire) but <term>formally</term> <note>original: "formaliter"; meaning it possesses the actual essence or "form" of fire.</note>? Otherwise, why should it be called <term>fire</term> <note>original: "Ignis"</note>? 

That this question is to be answered in the affirmative seems clear from the second and third propositions, as they imply a *fiery* substance acting upon those substances or gross passive bodies that we call *fire*. Now, if this *fiery* substance is a real substance and not one of those <term>intermediate substances</term> <note>original: "Substantiæ Mediæ"; a philosophical concept of things that are neither fully material nor fully spiritual.</note>—following the philosophy of Judge Hale <note>Sir Matthew Hale (1609–1676), a prominent jurist and natural philosopher.</note>, which I have sufficiently refuted in my *Examination*—I ask here: what is this new *fiery* substance that has never been heard of before? Is it material or immaterial? 

If it is *immaterial*, it is not *fire*. If it is *material*, then there is no more reason to believe in a *material fire* distinct from the flame of a candle, a fire-brand, or red-hot iron, than there is to believe in a *material water* that is distinct from the water of a well, a river, or the sea. Rather, the matter of the water itself—that which we call "water"—is shaped into the phenomenon of water. In the same way, the matter of fire—even that which we call "fire"—is shaped into the phenomenon of fire without any other material *fiery* substance acting upon it. To an unbiased person, I think this will appear very clear and logical.

The next question concerns the fourth proposition: what is meant by <term>fire in an eminent sense</term> <note>original: "Ignis eminenter"; meaning something that possesses the qualities of fire in a higher, more perfect way.</note>? For if this is meant to reject the idea of a spirit being <term>fire in its essence</term> <note>original: "Ignis formaliter"</note> and suggests it is only *fire* in its effects, then God might be called <term>fire in an eminent sense</term>, just as He might be called all other things according to *Orphic* theology <note>Referring to the ancient Greek mystical teachings attributed to Orpheus, which often used pantheistic language.</note>. But the fifth and sixth propositions seem to favor the other meaning: that a spirit...

<header>The True Notion of a Spirit.</header>

A Spirit is <term>Formally Fire <note>original: *Formaliter Ignis*</note></term>, but only a more pure <term>Fire <note>original: *Ignis*</note></term>—that is, of a more thin or tenuous substance, as was observed above, than that very fiery substance mentioned in the Third Proposition. But I confess that to me, this is a fire without *light*; it does not enable me to conceive a bit better of the nature of a *Spirit* than if I were without this description.

For gross, visible fire is nothing but ignited <note>original: "accensed"</note> particles, or a certain type of particles put into a certain kind of motion. How does it appear that there is either any other fire besides this, or if there were, that it is anything other than more subtle particles moved in such a way? So, in all this fire and heat, we lack light to discover the real nature of a *Spirit*. 

Yet the sixth Proposition says that a *Spirit*, next to its formal power <note>original: "vertue"</note>, is best known by the similarity it bears with <term>Fire <note>original: *Ignis*</note></term> in the sense of the third Proposition. Thus, even if we knew that <term>Fire <note>original: *Ignis*</note></term>, it would only be a metaphorical illustration, which is not a good way to define the nature of things. As I suggested above, the nature of this <term>Fire <note>original: *Ignis*</note></term> can be nothing other than a more subtle consistency of particles, if it is anything at all. Therefore, it is very unsuitable <note>original: "inept"</note> to describe the nature of a *Spirit*, which is <term>a being that is one in itself and not through another <note>original: *Ens unum per se & non per aliud*</note></term>. All must grant this who admit there is any such thing as a *Spirit* properly so called. 

Therefore, I much doubt the truth of the last Proposition: that he who thus conceives of created *Spirits* knows as much of their substance as can be reached. For I believe you undervalue your own cognitive faculties in that assertion. I cannot help but believe we can pierce further than that, as I may perhaps <note>original: "haply"</note> show shortly; in the meantime, we pass to what follows.

*A transcription of a narrative, taken from the Natural History of Oxfordshire, concerning the strange events <note>original: "passages"</note> that happened at Woodstock in the year 1649, when the Commissioners for surveying the manor house, park, deer, woods, and other demesnes <term>demesnes: lands attached to a manor and retained for the owner's own use</term> belonging to that manor, sat and lodged there.*

**O**n October 13, 1646, the Commissioners and their servants, having arrived at the manor house, took up their lodging in the King’s own rooms: the Bedchamber and the Withdrawing Room. There, they stored the wood of that ancient standard <note>original: "standard," referring here to a large, standing tree of great age or size</note> in the High Park, known to all by the name of the *King’s Oak*. On the 14th and 15th, they had little disturbance; but on the 16th, something entered the bedchamber where two of the Commissioners and their servants slept. However, the next morning, finding the cords whole and a quarter of beef—which lay on the ground—untouched, they began to have other thoughts about what it was.

October 17. Something, to their thinking, removed all the wood of the "King's Oak" out of the dining room and into the presence chamber <note>The room where a monarch officially receives guests</note>, and hurled the chairs and stools up and down that room. From there, it came into the two chambers where the Commissioners and their servants lay and hoisted up the feet of their beds so much higher than the heads that they thought they would be turned over and over. It then let them fall down with such force that their bodies rebounded a good distance from the bed, and then it shook the bedstead so violently that they themselves confessed their bodies were sore from it.

October 18. Something came into the bedchamber and walked up and down, and bringing the warming pan <note>A long-handled metal pan filled with hot coals, used to warm bedding</note> out of the withdrawing room, made so much noise that they thought five bells could not have made more. October 20. This night, they also thought they heard whole armfuls of the wood of the King's Oak being thrown down in their chambers, but in the morning, they found that nothing had been moved.

Two specific knocks astonished all the neighboring residents, and it was thought they might have been heard from a great distance away. During these noises, which were heard in both rooms at the same time, both the Commissioners and servants were struck with such great horror that they cried out to one another for help. One of them, recovering from a strange state of distress <note>original: "Agony"</note> he had been in, snatched up a sword and nearly killed one of his colleagues who was coming out of bed in his nightshirt, having mistaken him for the spirit that was causing the mischief. 

However, they eventually all gathered together, yet the noise remained so loud and terrible, and shook the walls so much, that they thought the entire manor house would fall on their heads. When the presence departed, it took all the glass away with it.

November 1. They thought they heard something walking up and down the withdrawing room, which then made a noise in the dining room. The stones that had been left before and stored in the withdrawing room were all carried away this night, and a great deal of glass (unlike the previous glass) was thrown about again. 

November 2. Something came into the withdrawing room, treading, as they imagined, much like a bear. At first, it only walked for about fifteen minutes; eventually, it made a noise around the table and threw the warming pan <note>A long-handled metal container filled with hot coals, used to warm a bed.</note> so violently that it was completely ruined. It also threw glass and large stones at them again, along with horse bones, and all so violently that the bedstead and walls were dented <note>original: "bruised"</note> by them. This night they placed candles all around the rooms and built fires up to the mantelpieces <note>original: "Mantle-trees"; the wooden or stone beams across the top of a fireplace.</note> of the chimneys; but they were all put [out].

But before they could get out, a whole bowl's worth of stinking ditch-water poured down upon them. It was so green that it stained their shirts and sheets that color as well.

The same night, the windows were all broken by the throwing of stones, and there were most terrible noises in three different places at once, to the extraordinary wonder of all who lodged near them. Even the <term>coney-stealers: rabbit poachers</term> who were out that night were so frightened by the dismal thundering that, in their haste, they left their <term>ferrets: animals used to hunt rabbits</term> behind in the rabbit burrows beyond <note>Rosamonds-Well: A famous spring at Woodstock Palace, named after Rosamund Clifford, the mistress of King Henry II.</note>. Despite all this, one of them had the boldness to ask, "In the name of God, what is it? What does it want? And what have we done that we should be disturbed in this manner?" No answer was given, but the noise ceased for a while. 

At length it came again, and as they all said, it brought seven devils worse than itself. Thereupon, one of them lit a candle again and set it in the doorway between the two chambers. Another man, fixing his eyes on it, saw the likeness of a hoof strike the candle and candlestick into the middle of the bedchamber, and afterward make three scrapes on the <note>original: "snuff" — the charred part of a candle wick</note> to put it out. At this, the same person was bold enough to draw his sword, but he had scarcely gotten it out before another invisible hand grabbed hold of it too. The invisible hand struggled with him for it and, prevailing, struck him so violently with the <term>pummel: the rounded knob at the end of a sword's hilt</term> that he was stunned by the blow.

Then grievous noises began again, so much so that they called to one another, gathered together, and went into the <term>presence-chamber: the grand room where a high official or monarch receives guests</term>. There they said prayers and sang psalms, but despite all this, the thundering noise still continued in other rooms. After this, on November 3rd, they moved their lodgings to the rooms over the gate. The next day, being Sunday, they went to <note>Ewelin: Likely the village of Ewelme in Oxfordshire.</note>. The authors of these accounts did not know how they escaped [the disturbances] there; but returning on Monday, the Devil (for that was the name they gave their "Nightly Guest") did not leave them unvisited, nor on the Tuesday following, which was the last day they stayed.

# ADVERTISEMENT.

**T**HAT the matter of *fact* is true, we have all the *assurance* desirable from what the writer of the *Natural History of Oxfordshire* <note>The author refers to Robert Plot (1640–1696), who wrote *The Natural History of Oxfordshire* (1677).</note> declares before he comes to the narrative itself: namely, that he had several accounts put into his hands, and one of them was written by a learned and faithful *person* then living at the location. This was confirmed to him by several *eyewitnesses* of many of the details, and all of them were confirmed by one of the *Commissioners* themselves, who frankly confessed to him that he could not deny that what was written by the *person* mentioned above was all true. So, regarding the matter of *fact*, there can be no doubt. The historian only raises a doubt—which is very much in the fashion of this *age*—as to whether all these pranks might have been played by a conspiracy <note>original: "Combination," meaning a secret plot or collaboration between people.</note>. It being a sophisticated thing, and much in fashion, not to seem over-credulous that any such things are done by any demons or spirits. Yet the nature of some of these exploits mentioned here extorts a confession from him, even against his will, that they cannot be explained away as trickery <note>original: "Juggling," referring to sleight of hand or deceptive illusions.</note>.

Such things, says he, are:
(1st.) *The extraordinary noises beyond the power of man to make without such instruments as were not there.* 
(2.) *The tearing down and splitting of the bed-posts, and the putting out of so many candles and such great fires, nobody knows how.* 
(3.) *A visible shape seen of a horse’s hoof treading out a candle.* 
And (4.) *A tugging with one of them for his sword by an invisible hand,* by which I suppose is meant an imperceptible hand. For the hand must necessarily be invisible, the candle being put out at that time of the year; but it was such a hand that, even if the candle had been lit, could not have been seen. For although he felt that tugging for his sword in the dark, he could not feel or lay hold of the hand or arm, or any part of any tangible person who tugged with him. This may be said if this tugging for the sword was late in the night, around or past midnight; but if it was earlier in the night, the party might have seen the hand that tugged for the sword if it had not been a hand of its own nature invisible. For the moon was at least 7 or 8 days old, if I compute correctly using the second Ptolemaic Tables in Nicolaus Mulerius <note>original: "N. Mulerius," referring to the Dutch astronomer Nicolaus Mulerius (1564–1630) and his astronomical tables.</note>.

These indeed are the most significant arguments to prove that everything here was not trickery or conspiracy. And indeed, how could it be a conspiracy, when the story focuses on one *person* all along, call—

...calling it "the Thing" or "Something"? It seems that these events were all performed by a single person or power. Besides, regarding these experts in *mischief* <note>original: "Waggery"; refers to practical jokes or playful malice</note>, how could they train a dog to gnaw through bed-cords while refraining from eating beef when it lay so easily within reach on the floor? Furthermore, it would be a laborious <note>original: "operose"</note> task, and hardly worth the effort, for any single person to move all the wood of the *King’s Oak* from one room into another. It is even more unlikely that a person could make a noise as if they were doing it when they were not. The flinging of many wooden plates <term>trenchers</term> and stones near men—without hurting any of them—seems to me improbable to be within the skill of an ordinary man to perform. It is also difficult to explain the noise of whole armfuls of the *King’s Oak* being flung down by their bedsides on the floor of their chamber, when not a single stick was actually found to have been thrown there.

The whining and fearful yelp of the *dog* <note>original: "Bitch"</note> was also a strong sign of the approach, not of an ordinary man, but of some "evil thing," as the common people call it. What a skillful *prankster* <note>original: "Wag"</note> must he be who could so perfectly imitate the *gait* <note>original: "Gate"</note> of a *bear*, as if such a *beast* had entered the *room*? Or who could have such strength as to split the feet of a bedstead in two without using an *ax* or *saw*? 

Did these pranksters combine their efforts so that some set up ladders to climb to the top of the chimney to fling down bricks, while others played different tricks in the chamber? The entire structure of the story is such that it argues these things were not done by human conspiracy and mischief, but by the frolicsome activity of some spirits or *demons* <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>. 

In conclusion, how exceedingly improbable is it that the residents in the house, after being molested two or three times, would not secure their doors so firmly that no man could reach them? It is also unlikely that they were not well-armed enough that no single man would venture alone to play so many odd tricks and frolics to terrify and scare them. Such a person, even if he escaped being killed on the spot, might be apprehended and severely punished; the residents had power on their side, even if they did not have the legal right—whatever *Mr. Hobbes* <note>A reference to the philosopher Thomas Hobbes, whose materialist views often clashed with belief in spirits</note> may judge in such cases.

Therefore, it is manifest that these pranks were played by *demons*. That learned physician, *Dr. Willis* <note>Thomas Willis (1621–1675), a founding member of the Royal Society and a pioneer in anatomy</note>, readily acknowledged this to me many years ago. He affirmed that such things as are related here in the story are undoubtedly true, as I had the opportunity of conversing with him at *Lord Conway’s* estate at *Ragley* in *Warwickshire*.

## RELATION II.

*Another transcription from the previously mentioned history regarding a strange account concerning the family of a certain Captain Wood—formerly of Bampton, now of Brize Norton, and a captain in the recent wars for the King <note>original: "Late Wars for the King"; referring to the English Civil War (1642–1651), where he fought for the Royalist cause</note>. This account describes the strange knockings that were heard shortly before the deaths of family members.*

**T**HE first knocking that was heard (or at least noticed) occurred about a year after the Restoration of the King <note>The restoration of the monarchy under Charles II in 1660</note>. It happened in the afternoon, shortly before nightfall, as perceived by Mrs. Eleanor Wood, mother of Captain Basil Wood. She was the only one who heard it, as no one else was in or near the house at the time. She was very disturbed by it, thinking it foreshadowed some misfortune for her or her family. Within fourteen nights, she received news of the death of her son-in-law, Mr. George Smith, who had died in London.

About three years after that, three loud knocks were heard quite clearly by everyone then in the house: the aforementioned Mrs. Eleanor Wood, Mr. Basil Wood and his wife, Mrs. Hester, and some servants. These knocks were so remarkable that one of the maids came from the well, which was about twenty yards from the spot, to see what was the matter. Mrs. Eleanor Wood and another maid who was inside the house saw large pans of lard shake and wobble so much on a shelf in the milk-house <term>milk-house</term> <note>A cool room or dairy used for storing milk, cream, and fats like lard</note> that they were nearly knocked down. 

Upon hearing this violent knocking, Mr. Basil Wood and his wife—who were in the hall at the time—immediately went into the milk-house to find their mother. Finding her somewhat distressed and asking the reason, she replied that only God Almighty knew the cause; she could say nothing except that she heard the knocking. Because the sound occurred inside the house, Mr. Basil Wood concluded it must signify a death for someone in the family at home; he believed that a knocking upon the door signified a friend abroad. This proved to be true: three members of the family (matching the number of knocks) died within a little more than half a year. These included Mrs. Hester Wood, wife to Mr. Basil Wood, and a

**Th**ese prognostic <note>original: "prognostick"; signs that foretell or predict a future event</note> signs occurring before the death of certain men are things noted by *historians* and *philosophers*. These are sometimes made by the *apparition* of a deceased *person* of the same *family*, or by some other *specter*; sometimes they occur by an audible *voice* calling the person by name, which I have heard has happened to some *seamen* at *sea*. Sometimes they occur through *music*, as I heard credibly reported regarding an entire *family* that died one after another in a short time. Always, some time before any member of the *house* fell sick, *music* was heard coming from the *house*—though nothing was seen—playing continuously. Several people, out of curiosity, would follow it and observed it passing through the *field* until it reached a *wood*, and there they left it or lost track of it. This happened in *Suffolk* and was told as a certain truth to a friend of mine by *Mr. Samson*, who was recently a Fellow of *King's College* here in *Cambridge*. Sometimes the appearance of *lights* presages the death of family members, with the number of deaths corresponding to the number of *lights*. This happened only a few years ago to a *family* of high social standing <note>original: "great Quality"</note> in *Ireland*, where three *lights* danced upon a place they call *Fairy-Mount*. All his working instruments were being damaged—some of them broken, some of them cut—and yet he could not discover by what means this harm was done. New and extraordinary attacks began, involving the throwing of stones in through doors and windows, and down through the top of the chimney. This new and painful trouble forced Mr. Campbell to reveal to the parish minister and to some other neighbors and friends what he had, until then, endured in secret. 

Yet, despite this, his trouble increased. Not long after, he frequently found his warp and threads <note>Parts of a loom used for weaving cloth.</note> cut as if with a pair of scissors, and the reed <note>original: "Reed"; a comb-like tool used to separate and space warp threads on a loom.</note> broken. Not only this, but their apparel was cut in the same manner, even while they were wearing it—their coats, bonnets, hose <note>stockings</note>, and shoes—yet they could not determine how or by what means. It only pleased God to preserve their persons so that not the least harm was done to their bodies. However, during the night, they were deprived of the ability to sleep, as something would come and pull their bedclothes and linens off them, leaving their bodies naked.

Next, their chests and trunks were opened, and all the items inside were scattered here and there. Likewise, the parts of his working tools that had escaped destruction were carried away and hidden in holes and crevices of the house, where they could hardly be found again. Indeed, whatever piece of cloth or household item was in any part of the house, it was carried away and so cut and ruined that the master of the house <note>original: "Good-man", a term for a male head of a household.</note> was forced to move with all haste and speed. He transported the rest of his belongings to a neighbor’s house and was himself compelled to quit the practice of his trade <note>original: "Calling".</note>, which was his only means of supporting his family. 

Yet he resolved to remain in the house for a time. During this period, some local people who were not very wise advised him to send his children out of the family to various places to see which person the trouble followed most—assuring him that this trouble was not against the whole family, but against one specific person. He obeyed them too willingly. For the space of four or five days afterward, there were no remarkable attacks as there had been before.

The minister, hearing of this, showed him the evil of such a course of action and assured him that if he did not repent and call back his children, he could not expect his trouble to end in a proper way. When the children who were nearby were called home, no trouble followed until one of his sons, named Thomas, who was the farthest away, returned. The Devil answered and said, "That passage of Scripture is written in the 13th chapter of *Zechariah*: 'In that day, I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land.' But afterward it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.'"

The minister answered, "We are fortunate that our *blessed* Shepherd was struck, and by that, he has bruised your head. And although in the hour of his sufferings his disciples forsook him (*Matthew* 26), yet now, having ascended on high, he sits in glory and is *preserving*, gathering in, and turning his hand upon his little ones; and he will save his poor ones in this *family* from your malice."

The minister stepped back a little and stood upon the *floor*. The Devil said, "I did not know these Scriptures until my father taught them to me. I am an evil spirit, and *Satan* is my father, and I have come to torment this *house*." Presently, there appeared a naked *hand* and an *arm* from the elbow down, beating upon the *floor* until the *house* shook. The Devil also *uttered* a most fearful and loud cry, saying, "Come up, Father! Come up! I will send my father among you! See, there he is behind your backs!"

The minister said, "I saw indeed a *hand* and an *arm* when the stroke was given and heard."

The Devil said to him, "Did you see that? It was not my hand; it was my father’s. My hand is blacker in the *palm* <term>original: "Loof"; a Scots and Northern English word for the palm of the hand</term>. Would you see me? Put out the *candle* then, and I shall come into the *house* among you like *fireballs*."

After this, everyone went to prayer, during which time it did no harm, nor did it at any other time when God was worshiped. When prayer was ended, the Devil said, "( *Mister John* <term>original: "Mes John"; a common, often informal or slightly derogatory title for a Presbyterian minister</term> ), if the *goodman's son's prayers* at the *University of Glasgow* <note>original: "College of Glascow"</note> did not prevail more with God than yours, my..."

From April to July he had some respite and ease. In this painful and sad affliction, Mr. *Campbell* resolved to appeal to the Synod of Presbyters <note>A regional governing council of the Presbyterian Church</note> for advice and counsel on what to do. The meeting was scheduled to convene in October 1655 to decide whether or not they should abandon the house and the area. Among other intentions, they were to petition God on behalf of that poor, afflicted family. In *August*, he was completely free from disturbances. Around that time, the Devil began new assaults. # ADVERTISEMENT.

*This narrative I have transcribed almost word-for-word <note>original: "verbatim"</note> from the* Miscellaneous Observations *of Mr. George Sinclair <note>George Sinclair (died 1696) was a Scottish mathematician and philosopher who famously wrote about witchcraft and spirits.</note>, which are added to his* Treatise of Hydrostatics <note>original: "Hydrostaticks"; the study of fluids at rest.</note>. *Only the certainty of its truth and its usefulness for refuting <term>Sadduceism</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Sadduceism" referred to the denial of the existence of spirits or the resurrection of the dead, essentially meaning atheism or skepticism toward the supernatural.</note> could have tempted him to insert it, as it is an observation so different <note>original: "Heterogeneous"</note> from all the rest of his work.*

*Therefore, I thought it worthwhile to move it to a more appropriate place. Sinclair himself acknowledged it was a somewhat unsuitable piece for the structure <note>original: "Contexture"</note> of the rest of his book, but he included it only to convince the skeptical world of the existence of spirits. He believed this account more than probably proves their existence—that is to say, it demonstrates it, assuming it is true. The narrative itself seems to sufficiently confirm this truth, as the disturbances there were so long-lasting, so public, and so frequent. Furthermore, these things were written by Mr. Campbell’s own son, who knew the details exactly, and I have heard the truth...*

To be brief, I have more certainty about the truth of this story than I think appropriate to state publicly.

The most remarkable part of the whole narrative is the appearance of a naked arm from the elbow down, which appeared by itself without any other parts of a visible person—much like the shape of a horse's hoof in the first story, which appeared without any other parts of a horse. This reminds me of the apparition "Elkerken," mentioned by Wierus <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician and demonologist</note> in his book *On the Illusions of Demons* <note>original Latin: "De Praestigiis Daemonum"</note>. This spirit used to haunt the highway in a heathy area not far from Emmerich <note>original: "Embrica"</note>, in the Duchy of Cleves in lower Germany. Nothing was seen but a lone hand, which would beat travelers as they passed, pull them off their horses, and overturn carriages.

As for the cutting and snipping of objects, that is something that has happened frequently to those plagued by witchcraft. A respected and learned friend of mine told me of a notable example involving a man's daughter in North Cadbury, Somerset. For several months, whenever she put on clean linen or her best clothes, they would be snipped and slashed full of holes, as her father certainly reported to my friend. Besides the account of Gilbert Campbell, there is another recent example of this snipping from a story within the last three or four years concerning witchcraft practiced on the family of William Metcalf of Lessingham (Sections 12, 13, 18), which follows below.

### ACCOUNT IV.

A true account of how Alice, the daughter of William Medcalfe, a yeoman <term>a farmer who owned and worked his own land</term> in the parish of Leasingham <note>original: "Leffingham"</note> in Lincolnshire, was disturbed by an apparition, along with other acts of witchcraft practiced upon that family. This account was sent from Mr. William Wyche, who lives in the same parish, to Mr. J. Richardson, a Fellow of Emmanuel College in Cambridge.

<margin>1.</margin> In the year 1678, on the Sunday after Twelfth Day <note>January 6, the end of the Christmas season</note>, William Medcalfe and his wife went to church, leaving their only daughter, Alice, at home. While they were away, Alice heard a noise in the yard. Looking out of the window, she saw a man of medium height with light flaxen hair standing at the stable door. She called out the window and asked what he was doing there. He replied that he had come for a horse he had borrowed from her father. She answered him, saying she knew nothing about it and that he would get no horse until her father came home. He accepted this answer and left for the day.

<margin>2.</margin> The next day, while her father and mother were away at Sleaford Market, she saw him again at the stable door. She questioned him as before. He told her she "might go look" <note>likely a dismissive or rude remark similar to "find out for yourself"</note>. Then he asked her where the horses were. She answered him just as curtly, telling him he "might go look." At this, he began to soothe and flatter her, using many persuasive words as he walked toward the door, as if he intended to come inside. Noticing this, Alice hurried to bolt the door fast. He then threatened her—though she cannot recall exactly what his threats were—but someone knocked at the door on the other side of the house. Realizing it was a neighbor, she opened the door and told her neighbor everything that had happened. They both ran into the yard together to see if he was still there, but they could not find him, nor did they know which way he had gone.

<margin>3.</margin> After this, she was left in peace for some time, until about two weeks before Shrove Tuesday <note>original: "Shrove-tide"; the period preceding Lent</note>. At that time, a man named Follet, a cobbler who was suspected to be—

## S E C T. X.

### *An Appeal to the internal sense of the Mind, to see if she be not surrounded by a certain infinite Extension; together with a waking of the Nullibist out of his Dream, by the sound of Trumpeters surrounding him.*

**T**HE Reasons of the *Nullibists* <note>Nullibists: From the Latin *nullibi* (nowhere). Philosophers, often followers of Descartes, who believed that because the soul is a thinking thing and not a physical thing, it exists "nowhere" in space.</note> by which they endeavor to maintain their Opinion, are sufficiently weakened and overthrown. Nor do we need any more Arguments to establish the contrary *Doctrine*. I will only ask, in passing, that he who thinks his *Mind* is no *where*, would test his own faculty of *Thinking*; and when he has pulled himself away from all thought or sense of his *Body*, and fixed his *Mind* only on an Idea of an indefinite or infinite *Extension* <note>Extension: The quality of taking up space or having physical dimensions. In this period, philosophers debated whether only matter was "extended" or if spirits were too.</note>, and also perceives himself to be some *particular thinking Being*, let him try, I say, whether he can any way avoid it: he must at the same time perceive that he is *somewhere*, namely, *within this immense Extension*, and that he is surrounded by it on all sides. Truly, I must honestly confess, I cannot conceive of it otherwise; I cannot help but conceive an Idea of a certain *Extension, infinite and immoveable*, and of necessary and actual Existence. This I most clearly perceive was not drawn in by the outward senses, but is innate and essentially inherent in the Mind itself. Thus, it is the genuine *object* not of *Imagination*, but of the *Intellect*; and it is only perversely and without judgment decided by the *Nullibists*, or *Cartesians*, that whatever is extended is also <term>imaginable</term> <note>original Greek: φανταστὸν (*phantaston*), meaning something that can be pictured in the mind's eye or perceived by the senses.</note> or the *Object of Imagination*. Yet there is nothing imaginable, or an *Object* of Imagination, which is not *sensible* <note>Sensible: Able to be perceived by the physical senses (sight, touch, etc.).</note>: For all *Mental Images* are drawn from the *Senses*. But this infinite *Extension* has no more to do with things that are *sensible* and fall under *Imagination*, than that which is most *Incorporeal* <note>Incorporeal: Having no physical body or substance; purely spiritual.</note>. But of this perhaps it will be more appropriate to speak elsewhere.

## RELATION V. <note>Relation refers to a formal report or account of an event.</note>

### *A true and faithful narrative of the disturbance that occurred in the house of Sir William York, in the parish of Lessingham in Lincolnshire, sent by the same person <note>original: "the former hand"</note> to the same recipient.*

1. **IN** May 1679, while Sir *William York* was away from home, a great noise was made by the lifting of the latch on the outermost door. This continued with rapid movement and loud noise for two or three hours, until between ten and eleven o'clock at night. His wife <note>original: "His Lady"</note>, who was then at home with a few servants, feared they were thieves; consequently, they went to the door and spoke to them. Afterward, they blew <note>original: "winded"</note> a horn and alerted the townspeople. When the townspeople arrived, the noise stopped, and nothing more was heard of it until the following *May*.

2. Then, while Sir *William* was in *London*, the same noise occurred at the door as before for two or three nights in a row. At that point, they began to believe it was caused by some supernatural <note>original: "extraordinary"</note> means. This was heard by twenty different people then in the household, who, looking out of the windows above the door, heard the noise but saw nothing. About a month later, after Sir *William* had returned from *London*, he was in bed and his wife was getting ready to join him when he heard the same noise again. It lasted about seven or eight minutes <note>original: "half a quarter of an hour"</note> and then stopped, starting again several times that night. The same people were in the house and took great care to find the source. At the end of this knocking, there was a sound like a knee thrusting against the door, only more violent.

3. Around the middle of *July*, while Sir *William* and his wife were both away from home, the servants were staying up waiting for their return that night. They heard a noise in the hall, which was the next

# ADVERTISEMENT.

*This is a very true and reliable diary of the chief incidents during those disturbances made in Sir William York’s house, though it is a very brief one. This led me to ask Mr. Richardson to send certain questions regarding several passages, which were answered by a very sure and authentic source. By virtue of those answers, I shall be able to put a stop to all the <term>tergiversations</term> <note>evasions or shifting of arguments</note> of the skeptics and their <term>evasorious</term> <note>deceitful or intended to escape the truth</note> pretenses—as if these things might be explained away as a <term>waggish combination</term> <note>a mischievous prank or conspiracy</note>. As for example:*

*Section 1. I was assured (so that no one can claim that the party making that noise with the latch simply snuck away when the horn was blown before the townspeople could arrive) that the noise continued until the people of the town reached the gate. It was impossible for any person to have been within the yard without being discovered, because there is a wall about ten feet high around the yard, so there was no way to escape. Furthermore, it happened at that time of year when there is twilight nearly all night long, which is sufficient to see any person if there were anyone there to be seen; it is unlikely, if there had been a need, that some of the company would not have come with lanterns or other lights.*

*Section 2. Those persons who looked out of the window toward the place where the noise was made could not have failed to see if there were any man there to make that noise. It was done by moonlight (as was stated in the answer to my question on this passage), which was bright enough to reveal if any person had been there, and if so, who it was. Since this careful observation was repeated for several nights together and nothing was seen, it is manifest that the noise was made by some demon or spirit, and not by any human.*

*Section* 5. *Note* that it could not be determined whether the noise at the door of the room under the stairs was on the inside of the door or the outside, as was answered in one of my *Queries* <note>original: "Queries"; specific questions or points of inquiry sent to the witnesses.</note>. Therefore, *Sir William*, seeing no one on the outside who could cause that noise—which he would have easily seen by his candlelight if anyone had been there—went into the room to see if he could discover anyone inside. But finding no one, he locked the door; and yet the noise began again in the same room. Upon a second search, however, no one was found within. This noise, and the diligence of searching the same place several times in one night, performed by someone naturally skeptical of such extraordinary events and receiving full satisfaction from the results, should, I think, shake the most stubborn *Sadducee* <note>original: "Saducee"; a reference to the biblical sect that denied the existence of spirits, here meaning a person who refuses to believe in the supernatural.</note> and make him ashamed of his foolish *Incredulity* <note>disbelief</note>.

But now, regarding the fact that the knocking stopped whenever anyone came near a door where the knocking occurred: this was no obstacle to the certain *Experience* of what happened under the stairs. Because they could see plainly by candlelight—though from some distance—that there was no one on the outside of the door, and they found no one within the room or small space, which was locked. Despite the knocking ceasing, they could be sure that the knocking was not made by the hand of any mortal. Indeed, I will further add from certain *Information* that there was hardly anyone in the house who has not seen the door at the same time the noise was made while no one was near it. *Sir William* himself, in particular, has seen the door from the top of the stairs with a light in his hand several times while the noise was occurring; the sound sometimes continued until he came down several steps, and once until he was directly across from the door, within a yard of it or thereabouts, yet he saw no one. So certain an experiment is this of *Demoniacal operations* <note>original: "Demoniacal operations"; activities or manifestations attributed to demons or spirits.</note>.

*Section* 6. Bringing the whole *Family* into one room was very effective; for by doing so, it was plain that none of the *Family* played these tricks, nor made them worse by any playful imitation. It is unbelievable that any stranger would venture to do it, as I understand by the answer to my fifth *Query*. This assures me that on the first night, the house was searched everywhere, the doors were always locked, and *Sir William* was given the keys. What stranger, therefore, in his *right mind*, would venture upon such bizarre pranks—in which he gained so little for himself—when he was in such obvious danger of being caught in such a large *Family*?

### Sect. 9.
*The fact that the disturbances continued all night also argues that it was probably not a man. For who would exhaust himself a whole night merely to deceive <note>original: "amuse"</note> others for no reward? But that battering noise at the door demonstrates it was not the act of any mortal. And besides this noise, as Mr. Edward Brown the elder—who was there that very night—writes to Mr. Richardson: the iron latch of the great door of the room, which was just under the one in which he lay, seemed to him to move with such wonderful swiftness up and down, and with such very great noise, that he could not think any human skill or dexterity could achieve it. He also describes the battering noise he heard at that door. "There seemed," he says, "sometimes to be such extraordinary thumping and knocking against the said door with such a wonderfully loud noise, as if some had used an exceptionally large piece of timber with the greatest skill to give it the maximum advantage to force the door open or break it in pieces; and upon reflection <note>original: "in deliberate Thoughts"</note>, I could not conceive how the strongest doors or walls could stand before such force as was threatened by such a very great and loud noise." These two kinds of noises, he says, continued in his hearing until about daybreak, with frequent short intervals; and yet in the morning, both the iron latch and door were found unchanged, in the exact same state they were left when they went to bed. And very intelligent people in the family said that when they went to the door, or went out during the time of such disturbances, they could see nobody, nor perceive any motion in anything upon which the invisible agent seemed to be acting. This is the very same thing I heard from the aforementioned physician <note>original: "Doctor of Physic"</note> in his letter to me. Mr. Brown, in his conversation with Mr. Richardson in the country regarding this thumping noise at the door, told him he could compare it to nothing better, in terms of its force, than a Roman battering ram <note>original: "Roman Ram"</note> with which the Romans battered down walls. But it being experienced on all hands that the noise seemed to come from a force against the door that would, if it had been real, break the—*

Section 10. My seventh query was on this section, namely: whether when Sir William went into the great parlor with a candle in his hand to walk there, did the noise cease at his approach or before? Section 11. My eighth query belongs to this section and to part of the former, namely: whether when the drumming occurred, the candle was put out, and the chairs moved, were the outer doors of the house locked so that no one could escape? To which it is answered: They were locked, and Sir William kept the keys. This was indeed done every night, as was noted in the sixth section. Therefore, it is incredible that any man would venture to make such a thundering noise on the wainscot <note>wood-paneled</note> doors—imitating the various beats of drums—or perform any other detectable feats in such a large family where there were so many people to find and capture him, especially with the doors shut so that he could not escape. To this you may add that the dogs were never observed to bark at any of these disturbances, as most of the family affirm; all of them agree that the dogs never barked more than once (a detail also noted in the story of the *Devil of Mascon* <note>original: "Maschon"; refers to a famous 1653 account of a poltergeist in Burgundy, France</note>). Yet the noise was external, heard alike by the whole family and other watchers.

These were my main queries regarding this narrative, and I must admit that I am fully satisfied by the answers to them. Nor will I omit what goes beyond these queries. This applies to more details than I could propose by way of a query, which so far has only touched upon factual matters. And there were at least forty people who were eyewitnesses, or rather ear-witnesses—the disturbance being caused by noises, not apparitions properly so called—and most of the servants who were there at the time of the disturbances are still in Sir William’s household. So, if anyone has the curiosity to inquire about the truth of the matter, they may easily find full satisfaction in the parish of Lessingham.

My last query was whether anyone was suspected to be the cause of these disturbances, and upon what occasion. But the answer was prudent and Christian: that though someone might be suspected, since the proof was not complete, he was unwilling to lay so heavy a charge on anyone. It was also restricted by time; for unless it began at* eight, nine, *or* ten *o'clock, it did not come at all that* night, *and it usually stopped around* eleven *or* twelve—*with the exception of only that one* night *when Mr.* Brown *was there. Finally, when Sir* William *was in his greatest difficulties,* (Section 12), *and intended to have his* wife *and* children *join him in* London *and to place his* father *with Mr.* Brown *at* Horbling <note>original: "Horblin"</note> *to avoid further trouble, the disturbance ceased entirely. But Sir* William’s Christian faith *and* courage *in the midst of those disturbances, while they continued, was very eminent and conspicuous; and I know of no injury done to him or anyone else by my passing on the memory of these events to future* ages.

# RELATION 6.

*A story of the extraordinary condition of one Robert Churchman of Balsham, some six or seven miles from Cambridge, when he was enticed into Quakerism; how strangely he was possessed by a spirit that spoke within him and used his organs of speech in spite of him while he was in his fits. And how he was recovered from his error and restored to the Church by the devotions and diligence of Dr. J. Templar, who is still the Minister of that place, as it is set down in his letter to a friend, which is as follows.*

SIR,

**Y**our desire to be acquainted with some events concerning the *Quakers* in this town obliges me to give you the following account. At my first settlement here, I found them very busy in enticing my people to comply with their persuasions in religion. They attempted to accomplish this goal by distributing their papers among them. I kept a particular eye upon two of my parishioners, namely *Robert Churchman* and his wife. As they were persons of very good character and possessed a significant estate <note>original: "plentiful Estate"; meaning they were wealthy and influential in the local community.</note>, I feared that their departure from the Church might be a means to induce others to do the same. In the many conversations I had with him, Robert manifested a very strong inclination toward the principles of the *Quakers*. His wife was so far involved that the *Quakers* commonly reported that "a principle was wrought in her" <note>This phrase refers to the Quaker belief in the "Inner Light" or a divine seed taking root in a person's soul.</note>.

As I was one day in conference with the said *Robert Churchman*, I asked him that whenever any of their books came into his hands, he would do me the kindness of bringing them to me so that we might read them over together; I assured him that I was not unwilling to listen to whatever should appear reasonable. He performed what I requested not long after. When I had received the paper into my hand, before I began to read, I suggested to him that it would be convenient to send for the person who had been the cause of his <term>seduction</term> <note>original: "seduce-ment." In this context, it refers to being led away from the orthodox teachings of the Church of England.</note>, so that they might hear

When he had delivered his message, that which spoke within him charged him to denounce wrath against them. It declared that fire and brimstone would fall upon them, as it did upon *Sodom* and *Gomorrah* <note>Biblical cities destroyed by God as punishment for their wickedness.</note>, if they did not obey; and so he returned to his own house. There, upon the floor of a low room, he stood naked for about three or four hours. All that while he was acting in a very unusual manner; sometimes the *spirit* within forced him to sing, and sometimes to bark like a dog. When his brother and sister, who followed him, were very insistent that he resist it, the spirit commanded him to kill them, using these words: *“These my enemies, who would not that I...”*

At this, the *spirit* pronounced a curse against him, saying, "*Depart, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire,*" <note>Quoting Matthew 25:41.</note> and then left him with an intense heat throughout his body.

After this, he believed himself <note>original: "he was in his own apprehension"; meaning his own perception or understanding</note> to be in a very comfortable condition. While he was considering what had happened, a voice within him spoke to him, saying that the spirit which was previously upon him was a spirit of delusion, but now the true Spirit of God had entered him. It informed him that the doctrine of the Trinity was true, and that God had an <term>Elect People</term><note>In Reformed theology, the "Elect" are those chosen by God for salvation.</note>. It said that those whom the Father elected, the Son has redeemed; and those whom Christ redeems, the Holy Ghost sanctifies. The voice told him that the minister of the town would further instruct him about the truth of these things.

On Thursday morning around daybreak, it set him upon his knees while he was in bed and bid him farewell. The same day, it came upon him in the field as he was going to and coming from the market, and it pressed him to believe that he was being moved by the good spirit—which he still doubted. One night that week, among many arguments it used for that purpose, it told him that if he would not believe without a sign, he might have whatever sign he wished. Upon that, *Robert Churchman* requested that if it were a good spirit, a wire candlestick standing upon the cupboard might be turned into brass. The spirit said it would do so. Immediately, there was a very unpleasant <note>original: "unfavoury"</note> smell in the room, like that of a candlewick <note>original: "snuff"</note> just extinguished; however, nothing else was done toward fulfilling the promise.

On the following <term>Lord’s Day</term><note>Sunday</note>, while he was at church, the spirit came upon him. When the chapters were named, he turned to them in his Bible but was unable to read. When the psalm was sung, he could not pronounce a single syllable. On Monday morning, his speech was completely taken from him. When I came to him and asked him how he was, he moved his head toward me but was unable to speak. I waited an hour or two in the room, hoping that his speech might return to him so that I might gain some account of his condition. 

But finding no change, I asked those present to join with me in prayer. As we were praying, his body was thrown out of bed with much violence; then, with great vehemence, he called out to me to hold my tongue. When the prayer was finished, his tongue was bound as before, until at last he broke out into these words: "*Thine is the Kingdom, Thine is the Kingdom*," which I believe he repeated over a hundred times. Sometimes he was forced into extreme laughter, and sometimes into singing; his hands were usually employed in beating his chest. All of us who stood by could see unusual heavings in his body. My second *reason* for including it is because it is such a notable *example* of the danger people put *themselves* in when they leave the true *Church* of *Christ*. <note>The author defines the "true Church" as the Reformed/Protestant tradition which he believes aligns with the Bible.</note> This Church possesses the seal and testimony of Christ and is, in the main, aligned with his Word—just as the Universal Church was before the Apostasy, and as the Reformed Churches are since the "rising of the witnesses." <note>A reference to Revelation 11, often interpreted by theologians of this period as the Protestant Reformation.</note> They put themselves in danger when they follow the seductions of any private *spirit*, especially those like the *Quakers* were at first. And my third and last *reason* is *because* this *story*, along with others concerning *Toldervey*, *Gilpin*, *James Naylor*, and the like, <note>These were individuals associated with early Quakerism who were often cited by critics as examples of religious delusion or blasphemy; Naylor famously re-enacted Christ's entry into Jerusalem.</note> will better justify that satirical *passage* in *Joseph Glanvil’s* letter to me. However, a more tolerable assessment can be made of them now (though some shameful marks of Familism still cling to them—and indeed, all the ugly traits that remain in them are of that sort, even if they do not realize it). I shall remark on this in my *advertisement* <note>original: "Advertisement" (here meaning a formal notice or commentary)</note> regarding that *letter*, which follows.

## REVEREND and LEARNED

# Dr. HENRY MORE, D.D.

---

### SECTION I.

*His Answer to certain Questions and Queries regarding the disturbances made by the Drummer of Tedworth.*

Honored Sir,

**T**he scrupulous care you take in examining the story of the disturbance at *Tedworth* <note>Tedworth (now Tidworth) was the site of a famous 1661 poltergeist case involving the Mompesson family and a vagrant drummer.</note> is no more than what is expected of a philosopher and one who is unwilling to be deceived. Without such a cautious and detailed inquiry, you could not answer the murmurs and petty evasions of willful unbelievers. Those objections you gathered at *Cambridge* have the misfortune of being proven wrong in almost every circumstance, and they are unlikely to be believed except by those at a great distance. Some of them I could have answered from my own knowledge; and concerning the rest, I made a strict inquiry of *Mr. Mompesson* himself and others when I was last in those parts. Based upon reliable information, I give you this account:

To the first point (1) which says, *“The house is rented, and this is a scheme to lower the value of it.”* I answer from his own mouth: the house is his own, and so the foundation of this excuse <note>original: "shift"</note> is overturned. The second point, from those who say, *“It is a trick to get money from those who come to see the wonder,”* <note>original: "prodigy"</note> has

# Reflections on

There is as little truth, but much more malice, in the first inventors of these rumors than in the previous group. For this gentleman, being a man of property, I am confident scorns such a base and lowly tactic; he is so far from making any profit from this situation that it has caused significant harm to his finances and affairs. And those strangers who came to see the phenomenon <note>original: "Prodigy," meaning an extraordinary or supernatural event</note> usually leave nothing behind them except thanks for the hospitality they received. 

It is true, (3.) as others say, *that the house is paneled on the outside—or at least a large part of it.* But there are no cellars, as the objection adds, except only under the parlor, and the disturbance was mostly in other rooms. And whereas (4.) it is objected *that a knight who offered to go down into the cellar was not permitted*, I am told in response that the gentleman might have gone down had he pleased; indeed, his servant did go down and made a careful search, but could find nothing that might be a cause of the noise. The servant affirmed the noise was above him and did not come from the cellar. 

And to disprove what other objectors say—namely, (5.) *that there was no drumming in the middle of any room, but only a striking on the floorboards as if with a hammer in a corner of the outside of the house*—I say, to nullify this pretense, Mr. Mompesson and others assured me that the noise was often in the middle of the room and often overhead. He says that there is scarcely a man or child in the village who has not heard it and can witness to it. And after the first month, it was almost always inside the house. Thus, Sir, to the objections of others which you have gathered, and to your own queries, I provide this response:

Where you inquire (1.) *what part of the children’s bed did the demon <note>original: "Dæmon," referring here to the unseen spirit or poltergeist</note> beat, and what noise did it make?* It is answered that it beat against the head and posts of the bed. When hands were laid on each side of them, the posts would shake as if they would fall to pieces, but nothing else could be perceived or felt. The noise was like that of striking with a hammer. 

And then, (2.) *to the question of whether the drummer's drum was ever looked at while it beat, or if it was only in the dark:* I am assured that it was seen while the noise was made upon it, by the light of both fire and candle. 

(3.) To the query, *what were the boards that moved, by what light was their motion seen, and by whom?* Mr. Mompesson answers: they were seen moving forward and backward in the light of clear day, before the sun had set, and by a whole house full of people. 

And whereas (4.) you ask, *in what clarity of light were the chairs seen walking about, and by what witnesses?* It is answered that they were seen to do so by candlelight and by several people.

Regarding what I witnessed myself, I add these details to satisfy your questions <note>original: "Queries"</note>: The children were in bed when the scratching and panting occurred, but I am certain they did not contribute to those noises. I saw their hands above the blankets <note>original: "Cloaths"</note> during the scraping and searched the area where the noise originated. To this I might add that they were small, harmless, and modest girls who could not have been suspected of such bold trickery <note>original: "juggle"</note>, even if it had been possible for them to perform it. As for the panting, I am certain there was no dog in the bed; I felt the bed with my hand in all parts, especially in the spot where the motion began. We also searched under the bed, but no dog or any other creature could be found there. As I mentioned, the floor shook noticeably from the panting, even though it was as strong and solid a floor as is usually seen. However, the children did not seem very concerned, as they were used to those and even louder <note>original: "ruder"</note> noises, and there were others in the room to reassure them.

## SECTION II.

### *The affected habit of mockery <note>original: "drollery"</note> as a cause for the disbelief in witchcraft, apparitions, and spirits. Also, how shallow-minded such mockers are regarding matters that require deeper insight <note>original: "searching Wit"</note> and solid judgment.*

**T**HUS, sir, I have briefly answered the objections of others and your own questions. Because I am inclined to say a little more, I will consider—something you know as well as anyone alive—the reasons why people are so prone to find fault with these kinds of accounts, preferring to believe almost anything rather than the truth of such a narrative. The main reasons, I believe, are an affected habit of mockery and scoffing, and a far worse cause: atheism.

Regarding the first reason, the subject of *witches* and *apparitions* provides a frequent and convenient opportunity for mockery. Furthermore, the deception of frauds <note>original: "Impostures"</note>, the delusions <note>original: "Conceits"</note> of depression <note>original: "Melancholy"</note>, the gullibility of the uneducated <note>original: "Ignorance"</note>, and the pranks of mischievous people <note>original: "Waggery"</note>,

# Reflections on

the more solemn vanities of superstition and the tales of old women: these are excellent topics for a playful and unrestrained imagination <note>original: "frolic and wanton fancy"</note>. And the desire the humorist <term>humorist: in this context, someone driven by whims or a mocking disposition rather than reason</term> has to be someone important, and to have a reputation above those of common understanding, will be sure to activate his scoffing vein. In the exercise of this, if he has punned <note>original: "quibbled"</note> luckily and made people laugh, he is encouraged to take every such opportunity to prove himself a wit and to show he has a clever way of playing the fool. And when he has played around for a while and playfully toyed in his affected amusements, his *reason* becomes an obedient servant to his *imagination* <note>original: "fancy"</note>. He makes himself believe (by those arguments that at first were intended only to make him laugh), and in the end concludes in earnest, that there is neither *witch* nor *apparition*—and it is well if he stops there.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now these, Sir, are the "wits" (if we are to believe them), and their admirers take every jest for an argument, and a loud laugh at an idle tale of a *devil* or a *witch* for a demonstration of the *non-existence* of such beings. And thus this disposition spreads, and *Sadduceeism* <term>Sadduceeism: a denial of the resurrection, the existence of spirits, or the supernatural, named after the ancient Jewish sect of Sadducees</term> becomes the fashion. Nor is this all; but by the same method, everything that is sacred or serious has been exposed, and both *government* and *religion* have been made the objects of idle and fantastic buffoonery.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And must we call this *wit*? Sir, I confess there are few things that provoke me more to indignation than to hear that name, which deserves to signify something better, to be so harmfully applied. Certainly *wit* is not an odd *metaphor*, or a lucky *simile*, a *wild stretch* <note>original: "wild fetch"</note>, or an unexpected *inference*, a mimicking *action*, or a clever *knack* for telling a tale; rather, it is a faculty to dive into the depth of things, to find out their causes and relations, agreements <note>original: "consonancies"</note> and disagreements, and to make fit, useful, and unobvious applications of their respective relations and dependencies. For these great and noble exercises of the mind, the *droll* <term>droll: a buffoon or jester who mocks serious subjects</term> is the most unfit and incompetent person in the world; and those who on this account assume the prerogative of being the only wits are, of all men, the most incapable of being so. For that trivial and petty <note>original: "peddling"</note> way of *imagination* and *humor* to which they are addicted weakens <note>original: "emasculates"</note> their minds and makes them superficial, flashy, and fantastical by employing them on trivialities <note>original: "effeminacies"</note> and little apish fooleries. And by these darling entertainments of a too fondly indulged *imagination*, the mind is made incapable of serious and deep reflections, which provide it the noblest and most valuable improvements. So that I have observed that the mocking humorists are, for the most part, remarkably defective in close reasoning <term>ratiocinations: the process of logical reasoning</term>, and the worst in the

### Drollery and Atheism.

World by inference. This is no wonder, since imagination <note>original: "Fancy"</note> is a wandering and inconsistent faculty; when it is not under the guidance of a strict judgment, it is not able to keep itself to a steady and resolved attention, much less to make coherent chains of logical reasoning. So it is nearly impossible for such "wits" as these to achieve anything more than a habit of scoffing at what they do not understand. They are under an almost invincible temptation to do so with everything that is too great for their comprehension. For the mood that drives them is proud and arrogant; it does not want anything to be valued that it is incapable of understanding. Therefore, it belittles all nobler and more honorable matters—which it has great reason to despair of ever achieving—and endeavors by ridiculous and insolent scorn to lift itself above them.

And yet this supposed wit, which raises them to such high standing in their own conceit, is but an immature and boyish mood. These exercises of imagination are merely the first attempts of youthful creativity, which more mature minds outgrow. For you know, Sir, our senses are the first powers we exercise and indulge in our earliest years. From them, our imaginations gradually grow, and their actions and gratifications are the pleasures and entertainments of youth. This is easy to observe in the small outbursts, puns, and tricks of imagination with which the younger students in the universities are so much delighted and carried away. 

But when age and experience ripen the judgment (which is the faculty of slowest growth), we then slight this playfulness and toying of our imaginations, and apply ourselves to pursuits that are more manly and important. When the judgment has come to its full exercise and peak, and has overcome and silenced the trivialities and prejudices of imagination, we are then, and not until then, grown into manhood. Those who never arrive at this stability, but spend their lives fooling with their imaginations, are still children, though they have gray hairs; they are still boys, though they are past their great <term>Climacterical</term> <note>The "Grand Climacteric" was historically considered a critical turning point in life, specifically the age of 63.</note>.

I confess, Sir, I am not so cynical and harsh that I would deny even the most refined geniuses their relaxations and pleasant intervals. Even the wise *Socrates* himself sometimes rode a boy's hobby-horse. Imagination may be permitted its playfulness and harmless jokes, so long as they are governed by the rules of virtue and prudent judgment. No doubt God himself allows all our powers and faculties their innocent gratifications. Indeed, I acknowledge a delightful charm in the results of a managed and wise imagination, while it is employed

...in exposing **Vice** and conceited **Follies** to deserved **Scorn** and **Laughter**.

But when **Imagination** is rampant, loose, and ungoverned—when it knows no bounds and observes no sense of decorum, but shoots at random and insolently attacks all things that are majestic and venerable—its outbursts are then vicious and detestable excesses. Those who have this disposition are merely a sort of sneering buffoon—that is, a better kind of ape in the judgment of the wise, though they consider themselves "wits."

### SECT. III.

*His just reprimand of the <term>quibbling debauchees</term> <note>original: "quibling Debauches"; refers to individuals who use clever but trivial wordplay to justify or distract from their immoral behavior</note> for their lack of reverence toward government and religion. And what an abhorrence and antipathy they have against all noble theories of philosophy, which are above the level of their weak intellectual abilities.*

**B**UT, Sir, I suggested a greater charge against these <term>quibbling debauchees</term>, namely: that they are the enemies of government and religion. I shall prove it with this addition: that they are also enemies of all the better types of knowledge.

<margin>*</margin> Regarding government, you know, Sir, that its influence depends upon the reverence its rulers receive from the people. Since they are only men, there will inevitably be mistakes in public affairs and the management of the state. If all the mistakes and faults of the supreme ministers of rule are tattled about and exaggerated among the common crowd, the government will thereby be exposed to the scorn of the masses and lose a great part of its power along with its reverence. In this regard, the state suffers infinitely from the mocking <term>Phantasticks</term> <note>original: "Phantasticks"; people governed by erratic or delusional imagination rather than reason</note>, who blow on the sores until they have infected them with their malicious and poisonous breath. They shoot libels at the government until they have made deep wounds in its reputation and reverence, and they turn every tongue into a weapon of war against it. In this way, these *Chams* <note>original: "Chams"; a reference to the biblical figure Ham (sometimes spelled Cham), the son of Noah, who was cursed for showing disrespect by looking upon his father's nakedness (Genesis 9:22). The author uses this to describe those who shame their leaders.</note> discover their father's nakedness and rejoice to publish the shame of those whose failures and infirmities should be concealed out of loyalty, prudence, and regard for public peace.

# Drollery and Atheism

Nor, (2.) is religion any more indebted to them. For a mind that tends to drift aimlessly among the whims <note>original: "levities of Fancy"</note> of imagination will find itself very poorly suited for the serious and solemn practices of piety. This lack of interest will grow into a deep aversion, which will surely prompt the joker <note>original: "Humouriſt," here meaning someone governed by fickle moods or a desire to be funny</note> to take every opportunity to mock it. Consequently, he soon jests at the Scriptures, makes a mockery of sin, plays with the idea of eternal flames, and scoffs at those who fear them. It is as if the sacred Oracles <note>The Bible</note> were nothing but a collection of pointless tales, and sin were merely a name invented by imagination and empty fears. He acts as if hell were but a painted fire, and the religious were merely a group of timid fools who are afraid of imaginary monsters <term>original: "Buggs"; refers to bugbears, hobgoblins, or terrifying imaginary creatures</term> and the imagery of dreams. 

Even if these are not yet the real articles of their creed, their extravagant whims and base desires are likely, in a short time, to incline these impure spirits to make them so. This sort of "wits" are either atheists, or—if they are not—they are just as great examples of folly. For it is a monstrous thing to believe in a God who made, sees, and will judge them, and yet to scoff at 그 tremendous Majesty before whom their fellow "wits" in the underworld <note>original: "Brother Wits below"; likely referring to fallen angels or the damned</note> tremble. It is madness to think the Scriptures are the inspirations of the God of Heaven, the laws for souls, and the primary instruments of eternal happiness, and yet to make light of them <note>original: "to Droll upon them"</note> and jest with the records of eternity. To believe in endless torments and everlasting joys in the state immediately following our short and uncertain lives, and yet to joke about the wrath of God and make light of eternal terrors—to talk trivializingly of heavenly joys <note>original: "beatifical Enjoyments"</note> and to treat Heaven as flippantly as they do an imaginary *Elysium* <note>The paradise of Greek mythology</note>—these, I say, are follies. These are degrees of impudence beyond all exaggeration or possibility of expression. If sad experience did not show them to be real, one would scarcely believe such prodigious monsters existed in nature. And to these things I add:

(3.) These idle jokers <note>original: "Drolliſts"</note> have an utter antipathy toward all the nobler and more generous kinds of knowledge. I have already said enough to prove that they are perfectly unsuited for philosophy and all deep research. I add this observation to confirm it: among the numerous youths I have seen educated in great schools and in the universities, I have noted that those who were most remarkable for playfulness <note>original: "Waggiſhneſs"</note> and jesting seldom reached any great maturity or capacity for matters of consequence and weight. Indeed, a frolicsome imagination and a solid judgment require temperaments of the brain that are very different; they seldom meet in high degrees except in a very few extraordinary individuals.

### Reflections on

Tempers. But generally, I believe the *mocker* <note>original: "Droll"; a person who uses cynical humor or satire to trivialize serious subjects</note> is very unfit for matters of sublimity and substance. Therefore, as I mentioned, he endeavors through his insults and mockery to make them appear as much below his serious notice as they are indeed above his reach. In this design, he has many great advantages for his abuses. For the intellectual arrogance of debaters who make a loud claim to knowledge, the vanity of the extreme sort of *chemists* <note>original: "Chymists"; likely referring here to alchemists or those making grand, unsubstantiated claims about matter</note>, the foolish boasts of some bold pretenders to *philosophy* <note>original: "Philosophy"; in this context, it refers to natural philosophy or what we now call science</note> and experimental research, the strangeness of things that more serious researchers declare to be possible but have not yet achieved, and the humble and seemingly trivial nature of many subjects the experimenter is often obliged to deal with—all these provide plausible arguments for *mocking* harangues. These advantages are taken to make the most useful theories and efforts appear ridiculous and vain.

And to encourage the *fanciful person* <note>original: "Phantastick"</note> in his rude attitude of injustice and abuse, there is a certain *envy* in mankind against those who attempt anything extraordinary. This makes people willing to embrace and applaud anything that exposes what they themselves cannot do or understand. Because of this poor character in the general public—and even among some who claim to be knowledgeable—this kind of *wit* becomes the most destructive enemy to *knowledge* and its improvement, especially to *scientific wisdom* <note>original: "Philosophick Wisdom"</note>. For *philosophy* can shame and invalidate all the reasons that can be urged against it, but jests and loud laughter cannot be disproved. Yet, these are more effective at degrading a subject in the eyes of certain types of people than the most powerful demonstrations. The tragedy of it is that these *quibblers* and *buffoons*, who have some small scraps of learning matched with a great deal of confidence, commonly have the luck to be celebrated among the common people as men of great talent and knowledge; that public opinion then gives credibility to their insults and abuses.

But, *Sir*, I see that my zeal against those *peddlers* of *wit* has led me to trouble you. I therefore make a sudden return to my other mentioned reason for people’s disbelief in the existence of *witches* and *ghosts* <note>original: "Apparitions"</note>, which is:
