## S E C T. IV.

*Atheism, another cause of disbelief in apparitions and spirits. With an account of his discourse with a professed atheist, and a brief look at one special cause of the increase of atheism: namely, the placing of religion in opinions.*

<margin>(11.)</margin>
**A**THEISM—the folly of which accursed madness you, Sir, have so fully revealed to the world in your incomparable works, and so thoroughly understand the mysteries of that black conspiracy against Heaven—it would be foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> for me to think I could suggest any notion on the subject that you could not already teach. But Sir, I have an account about this matter to share with you, which I believe you will be interested to hear. I shall share it once I have noted that there is a *hidden atheism* at the root of the *Sadducean* <note>original: "Saducean Principle"; referring to the Sadducees, a sect described in the New Testament as denying the existence of spirits and the resurrection of the dead.</note> principle. For too many people deny the existence of witches simply because they believe there are no spirits; and they are so persuaded because they recognize no being in the world except matter and the results of physical motion, and consequently can acknowledge nothing of a God.

It has indeed been a question whether it is possible for such a monster as a *speculative atheist* <note>One who arrives at atheism through philosophical reasoning rather than just immoral living.</note> to exist in nature, and I could wish it were still a matter of doubt. But alas! Our age and experience have ended that dispute. We do not need to search the dark and barbarous corners of *America*, nor seek the monster among the wild men of the desert; we have found him in times of enlightenment, in a witty and civilized region, and in an age of the greatest knowledge and improvement. He does not skulk among the thickest woods, nor seek out caverns for concealment, but braves the sun and appears in the clearest day. And the fool is not as modest as he was in the days of the Royal Prophet <note>original: "Royal Prophet"; referring to King David, author of the Psalms, specifically Psalm 14:1: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God."</note>, to say only in his heart, *There is no God*. We know a bolder sort of infidel, and I can say, Sir, from personal experience, that there are those who deny the existence of a Deity. I met with one such man some years ago in *London*, who confidently and without hesitation denied that there was any such Being, and challenged me to prove it. I wondered at the boldness, as well as the impiety of his statement; and because I had great compassion for someone in such a deplorable state, I resolved not to

# Reflections on

...provoke him with anger, harsh words, or condemning judgments, but calmly and without showing emotion, I discussed the matter with him. I granted him everything I safely or reasonably could, and everything that might help my plan to convince him, before we began our close debate. I did this so he might be less biased against the words of someone he could see was not narrow-minded, and so that I wouldn't face the disadvantage of having to attack principles that seem plausible because of the famous names or reasoning of eminent philosophers—especially those principles not strictly necessary to defend the argument I had undertaken.

\* Such principles included the *Platonic Anima Mundi* <note>original: "Anima Mundi"; Latin for "Soul of the World," a concept where the universe itself possesses a soul</note> and the eternity and immensity of the world. Sir, although I would not affirm these, I chose not to deny them at that time. Instead, I quietly accepted them as hypotheses <note>propositions or starting points for an argument</note>, being willing to let him keep these beliefs in order to succeed in convincing him and correcting his main and deadly conclusion. By making these concessions, I gained the advantages I expected. Through this, he was deprived of all the plausible arguments I noticed he usually used to support those doctrines. I saw that when he was pressured with the necessity of a "First Cause" of all things, his refuge was that old *Epicurean* <note>referring to the philosophy of Epicurus, who proposed that the universe is made of eternal atoms and void</note> idea of eternal, infinite matter. 

When his careless opponents would try to disprove this by attempting to demonstrate that the world had a beginning and is finite, they gave him the opportunity for a believable defense and distracted him from the main thesis <note>the central argument being debated</note>. That main point could be proven even if the immensity and eternity of the universe were granted; yet, by arguing over the world's age, they let him escape from an assertion that is most impious and absurd to move to another which is reasonably logical and attractive. The final result would be that since the debater could not prove the world was not infinite and eternal, he could not prove that God exists. By following that procedure, the arguer fails at a proposition that is the most demonstrable in nature, falling instead into another that cannot be resolved without assuming the very thing in question.

But besides this tactic, which my concession made useless: when my atheist opponent was challenged by the order, harmony, design, and wisdom visible in all creatures, he would retreat to his *Anima Mundi*. When the other opponents he had dealt with would try to overthrow that idea, they took on a task much harder to prove than the main conclusion itself.

I say therefore, Sir, I allowed him to assume these principles, and then proved that even if the world were immense and...

However, I asked him whether he considered it to be a substance that was *intelligent*, or one devoid of *reason* and perception. When he seemed to incline toward the latter, I showed him that such a principle—one that had no sense or knowledge—offered no more help to his cause than if he had remained stuck in the *hypothesis* of mere *matter* and motion. But when he finally allowed his "great Soul" to be an *intellectual being* (as he eventually did), and admitted that it was *immense* and *eternal* (as he was forced to do by his assertion that this Soul was diffused through the whole mass of his *infinite* and *eternal matter*), I showed him that, in effect, he had been brought by his own principles to the acknowledgment of a God, even though he gave Him another name.

Thus, Sir, I pursued my *infidel* into all his hiding places and retreats. I drove him from one assertion to another (even its contradictory) and then back again to his original thesis. I continued this until, at length, he began to be ashamed of his evasiveness <note>original: "shuffling"</note> and confessed that I had said more to him than he had ever heard before, and mentioned some things that he would consider. He requested that I give him the substance of my discourse in writing, which I prepared for him; I shall perhaps, before long, give an account of these and other related matters to the *public*.

After the heat of the engagement was over, I was interested to learn by what means he had fallen into such desperate *infidelity*. I understood from him *that he had run through the several stages of modern sects, not stopping until he reached that pit <note>original: "sink"</note> of folly and madness, Quakerism, and from there took a step into atheism—which is no great leap, for extremes eventually meet and become the same.* Certainly, for anyone who places their *religion* in *opinions*, and judges it to lie in one form of belief today and another tomorrow—when he comes to consider the vast variety of *sects*, the confidence each has in its own *reasoning*, the pretences of all to *scripture, reasoning*, and *antiquity*, the antipathy they have for one another, and the doubtfulness (if not falsehood) of things that each of them holds sacred and certain—I say, he that takes *religion* to be an adherence to *sects* and opinions, based on the...

Section 2. *And must we call this wit, sir, etc.* Certainly not *wisdom*, nor *wit* in the true sense and meaning of the word—which signifies a sound and capable faculty of the *mind*, whether natural or improved, to distinguish and judge things. But the *wit* that is so called nowadays is more like the *paralytic* <note>original: "Paralytick"; here used to mean uncontrolled or jerky movements</note> motions or *bizarre* dances of that faculty, rather than its genuine operations. It is the demoting of that faculty to lesser tasks, though God gave it to us for better purposes. As *J.G.* <note>Joseph Glanvill, the original author of the work.</note> phrases it, they turn into *jesters* <note>original: "Drolls"</note> and *fiddlers* for the *atheist*, just to make his "Worship" merry. This is a very lowly employment for such a noble being as the *rational soul* of *man*.

Section 3. *For government you know, sir, etc.* What the writer of this letter says in this section is worth the most serious consideration of all men who are not as loyal to the *government* as they ought to be. Its authority is certainly most sacred, and their rule—if it is at all tolerable—is exceedingly commendable. Those in high places face such strong temptations from the flattery and deception of cunning *sycophants* <note>original: "Parasites"</note> and the forceful pressure of events that attack them daily. ### Sect. 4.
*Such were the Platonic* Anima Mundi <note>original: *Anima Mundi*; translated as "World Soul," a concept where the universe itself has a soul</note>, *the eternity and immensity of the world, which, Sir, though I should not assert it, yet I would not at that time deny, etc.* This passage is written with caution and discretion, in that he professes these concessions were only <term>ad hominem</term> <note>original: *ad hominem*; an argument based on the opponent's own premises rather than absolute truth</note>. They were used so well that he caught his adversary in his own net. The opponent was forced by the strength of the argument to acknowledge that the *phenomena* <note>original: *Phænomena*; observable events or things in the natural world</note> of the world must come from an intelligent principle. However, to avoid the profession of a Deity, the opponent attributed this to his "World Soul." By granting—because of the eternity and immensity of matter—that this "Soul" was immense and eternal as well as intelligent, he was forced to acknowledge a Deity in a significant way, whether he wanted to or not. It is better to go this far than to be a downright, foolish **atheist**. But I must confess, I do not consider anyone an orthodox **deist** <note>In this context, a "deist" refers to a believer in a creator God, though the term later took on the meaning of believing in a God who does not intervene in the world.</note> who does not believe that **matter** was created by God, as well as arranged by His wisdom into such phenomena as appear in the world.

Besides, he might have puzzled and defeated the **atheist** by demonstrating that the world (being an orderly continuation of things in successive motion and duration) could not have existed <term>ab æterno</term> <note>original: *ab æterno*; from eternity, or without a beginning</note>. First, because it is plain and undeniable that in a sequence of time, every moment that is past was once present. Therefore, since they all must occur one after another, all of them—or at least all but one—were once in the future. This plainly proves the world could not have existed from eternity. Again, this is most certainly true: even if you suppose the world has existed from eternity, yet according to the order of nature and time, there was **life** before there was any **death**, and a **state of perfection** for spirits before any **fall**. He might here, therefore, ask the atheist how long it was before any...

-> # Drollery and Atheism <-

...death existed, or the decline of any order of beings into a worse state. Was there an infinity of time before that? And thirdly and lastly: if there has been an eternal and infinite succession of time until now, how is it that we find ourselves existing? 

For if, starting from our current time "B" and looking backward, the sequence of time is infinite, it is likewise infinite *ab aeterno* <note>original: "ab æterno"; Latin: "from eternity"</note>, or from a hypothetical point "A" to our present "B." And just as one can never travel backward from "B" to reach "A" because the distance is infinite, so too—the sequence from "A" to "B" being equally infinite—it could never have become our turn to exist. Nothing but a stable duration without sequence <note>original: "unsuccessive duration"</note> can be infinite, as it contains nothing past and nothing to come. From this eternal *nunc stans* <note>original: "NUNC STANS"; Latin: "standing now," a philosophical concept of eternity as a single, unchanging moment</note>—where there is nothing yet to happen and which cannot be divided into a sequence (and therefore nothing can be argued from it by pretending it *is* a sequence)—successive duration begins. It is equally impossible for this successive duration to be eternal or infinite.

Indeed, if infinity were not a sequence but existed all at once like infinite space, I grant that we might exist at a specific point within it. This might look like a boundary where, for example, an "Eastern Infinity" bordered us. From that boundary, you might imagine an infinite line extending eastward, such that neither we nor any other moving thing could ever reach its end, because it is infinite. 

And it is just as certain that no moving object, starting its journey from the far end of that "Eastern Infinity," could ever reach us or the point where we are. The distance traveling forward from that infinity is just as infinite as the distance traveling back toward it from us; there is the same distance, as *Aristotle* mentions somewhere, *from Thebes to Athens as from Athens to Thebes*. 

This further illustrates the impossibility of our current existence if the world's sequence of time had existed from eternity. Since the distance from point A to point B is as infinite as from B to A, it is manifest that our turn to exist would never have arrived, as an infinite distance from A could never be crossed. 

I only need to touch upon this point—the impossibility of successive time being eternal or infinite—here, as I have handled it fully in my *Enchiridion Metaphysicum* <note>Latin: "Manual of Metaphysics," a major work by Henry More published in 1671</note> and cleared it of all objections and evasions. See Chapter 10 and the *Scholia* <note>Explanatory comments or annotations</note> on it. There, you may also see how little reason there is to believe the matter of the world is infinite. It is part of the *essential sanctity* and unique *transcendency* <note>original: "Transcendency"; the state of being beyond the range of normal physical experience</note> of God’s exalted nature that He alone is eternal in duration and immense in *amplitude* <note>original: "Amplitude"; greatness of extent or reach</note>.

# Reflections on

Allowing God to be a mere *Anima Mundi* <note>Latin: "Soul of the World."</note>, though it served J. G.'s purpose in that argument, is also greatly against the *Essential Sanctity* of the *Divine Majesty*. It is infinitely below God's excellence to grow, as it were, into one *Suppositum* <note>original: "Suppositum"; a philosophical term for a distinct individual person or substance.</note> with the visible world. This error might have been a primary foundation or support for much of the idolatry of the ancient pagans. There is no *Anima Mundi* except for that which is purely a created being, and that is the *Spirit of Nature*. This spirit is so far from being a God that it scarcely has any consciousness, possessing only an *Omniform Plastic power* <note>A Neoplatonic term for a formative force that gives shape to matter without conscious thought.</note>, or *Vital Laws* for organizing the *matter* of the *world*, which are fundamentally imparted to it from the *Wisdom* of God. To call this an *Anima Mundi* may make good enough sense. 

However, the Platonic <term>Divine Soul</term> <note>original Greek: Θεία ψυχή (Theia Psyche)</note>, or *Anima Divina*, which corresponds to the Holy Spirit in our Christian Trinity, is the third *Hypostasis* <note>original: "Hypostases"; the distinct persons or essences of the Godhead.</note> of the pure Deity in both systems. It is of an eternal, necessary, and immutable essence and existence; therefore, it is in no way a created thing, but purely Divine, and existed before the world ever was or could be.

Now that the *world* exists, there is no need for any *Hypostatical Union* <note>A theological term for a personal, fundamental union (like that of the two natures of Christ), here applied to God and the physical world.</note> between it and the Platonic *Divine Soul* for God to be aware of what happens here, or to govern the matter of the world. The latter is done by the *Spirit of Nature*, and the former requires no such union, since we ourselves have the perception of things that are not part of our own *Suppositum* <note>that is, we can perceive objects without those objects being part of our physical "self."</note>. Just as we see things reflected from a mirror without our eye having any hypostatic union with it, so are all the *energies* of this exterior creation reflected into the perception of the Deity, without any such degrading union of the Godhead with it. This is expressed in *Psychozoia* <note>Henry More's 1642 philosophical poem, "The Life of the Soul."</note>, Canto 1, Stanza 50:

> In this clear, shining mirror, the Soul sees
> All that falls under sense, whatever is done
> Upon the earth, the deserts, shaken trees,
> The mournful winds, the solitary haunt <note>original: "wonne"; a dwelling or place where one stays.</note>
> Of dreaded beasts, the Libyan lions' moan,
> When their hot entrails scorch with hunger keen,
> And they to God for meat do deeply groan;
> He hears their cry, he sees them while remaining unseen,
> His eyes encompass all that in the wide world has been.

# Reflections on

God has a perception of all the active forces of creation while they are *in the process of becoming* <note>original: *in fieri*</note>, and he sees that they are now *becoming* when they were not before. This exists alongside his *Intellectual comprehension*, which is *simultaneously from eternity to eternity*. In an infinite *Life* such as God is, there can be no *distraction*, as his *attention* <note>original: *animadversion*; here meaning the mind's ability to perceive or notice things</note> is necessarily infinite. If we do not grant him this outward-facing perception, we cannot be assured that he knows when we pray to him. This, I think, would be a foul defect and a great discouragement to our devotion. However, the other opinion does not only encourage *Devotion*, but naturally inspires a proper awe and reverence toward him in our *prayers* <note>original: *Addresses*</note>.

I know there are some overly abstract thinkers <note>original: "dry Contemplators"</note> who would prefer God to have no new perceptions *as things arise* <note>original: *pro re nata*</note>, lest he might seem *physically alterable or changeable*. But these are the very *useless trifles* <note>original: *Cobwebs* and *Quisquiliæ* (Latin for dross or waste)</note> of the Scholastic philosophers. They thinned and stretched every *attribute* of God to such infinite excess as they could, forgetting the one necessary measure of all his attributes: *that they should be applied to him only so far as they imply perfection. This is a point worth our most serious consideration.* 

Certainly, it would be an imperfection in God if he did not know *that past things are past, that present things are present, and that future things are yet to come. He could not know them to be past when they were yet to come or present, nor could he know they are present when they are still to come or already past, or that they are yet to come when they are already present.* Therefore, you must either assume God is ignorant of things here below, or accept that his outward perceptions change as the landscape of things changes *externally* <note>original: *ad extra*</note>. Otherwise, his perceptions will prove false, which is intolerable to admit in either philosophy or theology. I have strayed further than I intended, but I hope it is not a useless digression. For nothing can move a man more to do all things with *faithfulness and proper behavior* <note>original: *Decorum*</note>, both in private and before others, than to remember that the *all-present God* is truly a *hearer* of his *words* and a *seer* of his *actions*.

The writer mentions that he had run through the several stages of modern religious sects, not stopping until he reached that "sink of folly and madness," *Quakerism*, and from there took a step into *Atheism*, etc. This is a remarkable passage of his letter and worth our consideration. I must confess that his expression here regarding the condition of *Quakerism* is very sharp and mocking <note>original: Satyrical</note>—to call it that *sink of madness and folly*. I believe he said this with an eye toward their first appearance, which was very strange and wild <note>original: *uncouth and frantick*</note>, and not at all like the appearance of the Apostles of *Jesus Christ*, but rather like *people possessed by demons* <note>original: *Demoniacks*</note>. # Drollery and Atheism

I have written enough about it in my *Mystery of Godliness*, book 4, chapter 6, and book 10, chapter 13. And the previous story of the man at *Balsham* who was enticed into *Quakerism* <note>original: "inveigled in Quakerism"</note> is of the same kind. But to deal impartially regarding them, if we judge them by *Robert Barclay's Apology*—which represents them as they were when he wrote it, which was not more than <note>original: "passing"</note> five or six years ago—they have changed very much for the better since they first began. I have made a most just and impartial assessment of them and their way in my *Scholia* <term>scholarly notes or commentaries</term> on my *Divine Dialogues*, Dialogue 5, Section 15. Anyone who is curious may examine this in the second volume <note>original: "Tome"</note> of my *Philosophical Volume* <note>original: "Volumen Philosophicum"</note>. 

But that *Apology* by Robert Barclay was written many years after this letter from *Joseph Glanvil* to myself, which better excuses Glanvil for the severity of that passage. I have noted how natural and easy a step it is from *Enthusiasm* <term>in this era, "enthusiasm" referred to a belief in direct, private divine inspiration, often viewed with suspicion by established churches</term> into *Atheism* in my book *Enthusiasm Conquered* <note>original: "Enthusiasmus Triumphatus"</note>.

But the examples of the man at *Balsham* and this *atheist* with whom *Joseph Glanvil* <note>original: "J. G."</note> conversed are striking instances of how dangerous it is to forsake the communion of the *Truly Catholic Church*—one that is purged from the gross dregs of *Antichristian superstition and idolatry*. To forsake the sentiments of the ancient Apostolic Church to follow any *private spirit* <note>an individual's personal interpretation or subjective inner feeling over established church doctrine</note> is such a piece of folly and giddiness that its extravagance is beyond words. The danger is so obvious that anyone who is not very blind and stupid must see it at first sight. The Reformed Churches, freed from the filth of the predicted Great Apostasy, represent this ancient church, and the *Church of England* does so in a special way.

Not everyone is born to be a *philosopher* or a *theologian*, or has the faculty to decide controversies by the sharp edge of their own wit and reason. Therefore, it is both a duty and a matter of safety to adhere to the consensus of the Catholic <term>universal</term> Church as it existed before the Great Apostasy—specifically, the church as it was for about four hundred years after *Christ*. Within that timeframe, the *divinity of Christ* and the *Trinity* <note>original: "Triunity"</note> *of the Godhead* were professed as public articles of the Church, and the distinction between *bishops* and *presbyters* <term>priests or elders</term> was recognized. 

From this, it is demonstrable how innocent the latter is and how *orthodox* the former. For if the articles of the *divinity of Christ* and the *Trinity of the Godhead* were false, they would also have been idolatrous. If that were the case, the Great Apostasy would have begun much earlier than it is predicted to begin in that wonderful book of prophecies, the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. Nor would the late Reformation be the *Rising of the Witnesses* (though it certainly is, and I have undeniably demonstrated it in the second part of my *Appendix* to my *Exposition of Daniel's Visions*). For they would have been strange witnesses indeed if they were to still profess the *divinity*...

Regarding the witches, he <note>Referring to the Devil</note> had drawn some hundreds of children to him and made them subject to his power. It was reported how he had been seen traveling in a visible form through the country and appeared daily to the people; how he had targeted the poorer classes by presenting them with meat and drink, and in this way allured them to himself, along with other circumstances to be mentioned later. The inhabitants of the village added, with very great lamentations, that although their children had told everything and they themselves had sought God very earnestly through prayer, the children were still carried away by him. Therefore, they begged the Lords Commissioners to root out this hellish group so that they might regain their former rest and quiet; they noted that the children who used to be carried away in the district of *Elfdale* <note>modern Älvdalen</note> had remained undisturbed ever since some witches had been burned there.

That day, which was the 13th of *August*, was the final Day of Humiliation <note>original: Humiliation-day; a day set aside for public fasting and collective repentance to seek God's mercy during a crisis</note> instituted by the authorities for the removal of this judgment. The Commissioners went to church, where a considerable assembly of both young and old appeared. Most of the children could read and sing psalms, as could the women, though they did not do so with any great zeal or fervor. Two sermons were preached that day, in which the miserable condition of those people who allowed themselves to be deluded by the Devil was explained; these sermons concluded at last with very fervent prayer.

After public worship was over, all the people of the town—nearly three thousand of them—were called together to the parson’s house. Once silence was commanded, the King’s Commission <note>the official document authorizing the investigators to act on behalf of the monarch</note> was read publicly in the hearing of everyone. They were charged under severe penalties to conceal nothing of what they knew and to say nothing but the truth—especially those who were guilty—so that the children might be delivered from the clutches of the Devil. They all promised obedience; the guilty did so insincerely, but the innocent wept and cried bitterly.

On the 14th of *August*, the Commissioners met again to consult on how they might withstand this dangerous tide. After long deliberation, and following an order from His Majesty, they resolved to execute those against whom the facts of the crime could be proven. Upon examination, no fewer than seventy <note>original: Threescore and ten</note> people were discovered in the aforementioned village. Twenty-three of them, freely confessing their crimes, were condemned to die. Of the rest, one claimed she was pregnant and the others denied the charges and pleaded not guilty; these were sent to *Faluna* <note>modern Falun</note>, where most of them were later executed.

Fifteen children, who also confessed to being involved in this witchcraft <note>original: "Witchery"</note>, died like the others. Thirty-six of them, between nine and sixteen years of age, who were considered less guilty, were forced to run the gauntlet <term>run the gauntlet: a military-style punishment where a person runs between two rows of people who strike them with sticks or rods</term>. The previously mentioned thirty-six children were also sentenced to be lashed in this manner once a week for an entire year. The total number of seduced children was about three hundred.

On August 25th, the execution of the notoriously guilty was carried out. The day was bright and glorious with the sun shining, and several thousand people were present to witness the spectacle. The order and method used during the examination were as follows:

First, the commissioners and the neighboring justices prayed together. After this, the witches were brought before them. Most of these witches had children with them, ranging from four to sixteen years old, whom they had either seduced or attempted to seduce into witchcraft. Some of the children complained piteously <note>original: "lamentably"</note> of the misery and harm they were occasionally forced to suffer because of the witches.

When the children were asked if they were certain that the Devil had carried them away at any time, they all declared that they were. They begged the commissioners to be freed from that intolerable slavery.

Then the witches themselves were asked if the children’s confessions were true. They were urged to confess the truth so that they might turn away from the Devil and toward the living God. At first, most of them stubbornly <note>original: "stifly"</note> denied it without shedding a single tear, though this was very much against their will and natural inclination.

Afterward, the children were examined individually to see if their confessions matched. The commissioners found that all of them—except for some very young children who could not recount all the circumstances—agreed exactly on the specific details of their confessions.

Meanwhile, the commissioners who were members of the clergy examined the witches but could not get them to confess. All of them remained steadfast in their denials until, at last, some of them burst into tears. Their confessions then matched what the children had said. These individuals expressed their abhorrence <note>original: "abhorrency"</note> of the crime and begged for pardon, adding that the Devil, whom they

### 1: *Of their Journey to Blockula. The Contents of their Confession.*

We of the province <note>original: Provence</note> of *Elfdale* confess that we used to go to a gravel pit which lay near a crossroads, and there we put a vest over our heads and danced in a circle. After this, we ran to the crossroads and called the Devil three times: first with a quiet voice, the second time somewhat louder, and the third time very loud, with these words: "*Antecessor* <note>Latin: "one who goes before" or "leader"</note>, come and carry us to Blockula." Whereupon he usually appeared immediately, but in different outfits <note>original: Habits</note>. For the most part, we saw him in a gray coat and red and blue stockings; he had a red beard, a high-crowned hat with linen of various colors wrapped around it, and long garters on his stockings.

Then he asked us whether we would serve him with soul and body. If we were content to do so, he set us on a beast which he had ready there and carried us over churches and high walls; and finally, we came to a green meadow where *Blockula* lies. We must obtain some scrapings from altars and filings from church clocks; then he gives us a horn with an ointment <note>original: Salve</note> in it, with which we anoint ourselves, and a saddle with a hammer and a wooden nail to fix the saddle. Whereupon we call upon the Devil, and away we go.

Those who were from the town of *Mohra* made essentially the same declaration. Being asked whether they were sure of a real, physical transportation <note>original: personal Transportation</note>, and whether they were awake when it was done, they all answered in the affirmative. They added that the Devil sometimes laid something down in their place that was very like them. However, one of them confessed that he only took away her strength while her body lay still upon the ground; yet sometimes he took even her body with him.

When asked how they could pass with their bodies through chimneys and broken panes of glass, they said that the Devil first removed everything that might hinder them in their flight, so they had enough room to pass.

Others were asked how they were able to carry so many children with them. They answered that when the children were asleep, they came into the bedroom and laid hold of them. The children immediately awoke and were asked if they would go to a feast with them. Though some answered "yes" and others "no," they were all forced to go. The witches gave the children only a shirt, a coat, and a doublet <note>original: "Doublet"; a man's short, close-fitting padded jacket worn from the 14th to the 17th century.</note> that was either red or blue. Then they set them upon a beast provided by the Devil and rode away.

The children confessed to the same thing, and some added that they were very willing to go because they had such fine clothes put upon them.

Some of the children concealed this from their parents, but others revealed it to them immediately.

The witches declared, moreover, that until recently they never had the power to carry away children, except for this year and the last, and that the Devil forced them to do it at this time. Previously, it was sufficient to carry only one of their own children or a stranger's child with them, which happened seldom. But now, he plagued and whipped them if they did not procure children for him, so much so that they had no peace or quiet because of him. And whereas formerly one journey a week from their own town to the aforementioned place would suffice, now they were forced to run to other towns and places for children, bringing fifteen or sixteen children with them every night.

Regarding their journey, they said they made use of all sorts of instruments: beasts, men, spits <note>original: "Spits"; long, thin metal rods used for roasting meat over a fire.</note>, and posts, according to whatever opportunity they had. If they rode upon goats and had many children with them, they would stick a spit into the backside of the goat so that everyone would have room, and then they were anointed with the aforementioned ointment. What the true nature of their journey is, God alone knows. This much was established: if the children at any time named the names of those who had carried them away, they were again carried by force either to <term>Blockula</term> <note>A legendary meadow where Swedish witches were said to gather with the Devil; the name is often associated with the Blåkulla of Swedish folklore.</note> or to a crossroads and there miserably beaten, to such an extent that some of them died from it. Some of the witches confessed to this and added that they were now exceedingly troubled and tortured in their minds because of it.

The children treated this way looked very pale, sickly, and beaten. The judges could not see the marks of whip lashes on them, except for one boy who had several wounds and holes in his back that had been inflicted with thorns; however, the witches claimed these marks would quickly disappear.

After this ordeal, the children are extremely weak. If any are carried away during the night, they cannot recover their strength the next day. They often fall into fits <note>original: "fits"; in this context, these describe seizure-like episodes or sudden physical collapses</note>, the onset of which they recognize by an extreme paleness that overcomes the children. If a fit begins, the children lean against their mothers’ arms (who sometimes sit up with them all night). When the mothers notice the paleness appearing, they shake the children, but it does no good.

They further observe that the children’s chests grow cold at such times. Sometimes they take a burning candle and stick it in the child's hair, yet the hair is not burned by it. The children faint during this paleness, and this fainting spell lasts sometimes half an hour, sometimes an hour, or even two hours. When the children regain consciousness, they mourn, lament, and groan miserably, begging desperately for relief. Two old men declared this under oath before the judges and called all the inhabitants of the town to witness it, as most of them had experience with these strange symptoms in their own children.

A little girl from *Elfdale* <note>original: "Elfdale"; refers to Älvdalen, a parish in Dalarna, Sweden</note> confessed that when she spoke the name of ***JESUS*** while being carried away, she suddenly fell to the ground and got a large wound in her side. The Devil immediately healed it, and then he carried her away again. To this day, the girl confessed she still feels intense pain in her side.

Another boy also confessed that one day he was carried away by his mistress <note>original: "Mistress"; here meaning a female witch who controlled him</note>. To make the journey, he took his own father’s horse out of the meadow where it was grazing; upon his return, the woman left the horse in her own field.

The next morning, the boy’s father searched for his horse, and when he could not find it, he gave it up for lost. But the boy told him the whole story, and so his father went and brought the horse back; one of the witches also confessed to this event.

The place or house where they met had a gate painted with various colors. Through this gate, they entered a small meadow, separate from the other meadow where the beasts they rode upon were kept. The men who assisted them on their journey stayed in the house by the gate in a slumbering posture, sleeping against the wall.

In a very large room of this house, they said, there stood a long table at which the witches sat down. Just beside this room was another chamber containing very lovely and delicate beds.

The first thing they were required to do at <term>Blockula</term> <note>original: "Blockula"; refers to Blåkulla, or "Blue Hill," a legendary island in Swedish folklore where witches were said to hold their Sabbath with the Devil.</note> was to deny everything and devote themselves body and soul to the Devil, promising to serve him faithfully and confirming this with an oath. Upon this, they cut their fingers and wrote their names in his book with their own blood. They added that he caused them to be baptized as well, by such priests as he had there, and made them confirm their baptism with dreadful oaths and curses.

Following this, the Devil gave them a purse containing filings from clocks with a stone tied to it, which they threw into the water while being forced to speak these words:

> *As these filings of the clock never return to the clock from which they are taken, so may my soul never return to Heaven.*

To this, they added blasphemy and other oaths and curses.

The mark of their cut fingers is not found on all of them. However, one girl who had a scar on her finger declared that because she would not willingly stretch out her finger, the Devil had cruelly wounded it in his anger.

After this, they sat down at the table. Those whom the Devil esteemed most were placed nearest to him, but the children had to stand at the door, where he himself gave them food and drink.

The diet they usually had there, they said, was broth with <term>coleworts</term> <note>original: "Colworts"; a type of cabbage or leafy green vegetable.</note> and bacon in it, oatmeal, bread spread with butter, milk, and cheese. They added that sometimes the food tasted very good, and sometimes very poor. After meals, they went to dancing, during which they swore and cursed most dreadfully, and afterward, they began fighting with one another.

Those from <term>Elfdale</term> <note>original: "Elfdale"; refers to Älvdalen, a locality in Sweden that was a primary site of the 1668–1676 witch trials.</note> confessed that the Devil used to play a harp before them and would afterward go with those he liked best into a chamber, where he committed <term>sexual acts</term> <note>original: "Venerous Acts"; derived from 'Venus,' this is an archaic term for sexual intercourse.</note> with them; and indeed, they all confessed that—

He had sexual relations with them <note>original: "carnal knowledge"</note>, and the Devil had sons and daughters by them. He married these children to each other, and they coupled together and gave birth to toads and serpents.

One day the Devil appeared to be dead, leading to great mourning <note>original: "lamentations"</note> at *Blockula* <note>Blåkulla: a legendary meadow where witches were said to gather in Swedish folklore</note>; however, he soon woke up again. If he wants to be entertained by them, he makes them all ride on roasting spits in front of him. Afterward, he takes the spits and beats the witches black and blue, and then laughs at them. He tells them to believe that the Day of Judgment is coming soon. Therefore, he sets them to work building a great stone house, promising that he will protect them from God’s anger there and provide them with the greatest delights and pleasures. But while they are working extremely hard on it, a large section of the wall falls down again. Some of the witches are usually hurt by this, which makes him laugh, though he immediately cures them afterward.

They said they had sometimes seen a massive devil resembling a dragon, surrounded by fire and bound with an iron chain. The Devil who speaks with them tells them that if they confess anything, he will release that great dragon upon them, putting all of *Sweden* <note>original: "Swedeland"</note> in great danger.

They added that the Devil had a church there, just like the one in the town of *Mora*. When the royal commissioners <note>government officials sent to investigate the witchcraft claims</note> were arriving, he told the witches they should not fear them, for he would certainly kill them all. They confessed that some of them had attempted to murder the commissioners but had been unable to succeed.

Some of the children spoke often of a white angel who used to forbid them from doing what the Devil commanded. This angel told them that these events would not last long. He said that what had happened was permitted because of the people's wickedness, but the kidnapping of the children would soon be revealed <note>original: "made manifest"</note>. They added that this white angel would sometimes stand at the door between the witches and the children; when they arrived at *Blockula*, he pulled the children back, while the witches went inside.

### 3. Concerning the Harm or Evil that the Witches Promised to Inflict on People and Animals.

They confessed that they were required to promise the Devil they would do everything that is evil. They also claimed the Devil taught them how to "milk" <note>This refers to a folk magic belief where a witch could magically steal milk from a neighbor's cow from a distance.</note> in the following way: they would stick a knife into a wall and hang a kind of "label" <note>original: "Label"; likely a strip of cloth or leather used as a ritual object.</note> on it, which they would pull and stroke. As long as they did this, the people they had power over were miserably tormented, and the cattle were milked in this magical way until they sometimes died from it.

One woman confessed that the Devil gave her a wooden knife. She claimed that by carrying it into houses, she had the power to kill anything she touched with it; yet, there were very few who would actually admit to having harmed any man or woman.

When asked whether they had murdered any children, they confessed that they had indeed tormented many, but they did not know if any of them had died from those "plagues" <note>original: "Plagues"; here meaning afflictions or supernatural torments.</note>. They added that the Devil had shown them several places where he had the power to do mischief.

The Minister of *Elfdale* <note>modern: Älvdalen, a town in Dalarna, Sweden.</note> declared that one night, he felt as if these witches were upon the crown of his head, and from that moment on, he suffered from a long-lasting headache.

One of the witches also confessed that the Devil had sent her to torment that minister. She said she was ordered to use a nail and strike it into his head, but it would not go very deep; she claimed this was the cause of his headache.

The same minister also said that one night he felt a pain as if he were being torn with a flax-comb <note>original: "an Instrument that they cleanse Flax with"; a tool with long metal teeth used to separate flax fibers.</note>. When he woke up, he heard someone scratching and scraping at the window but could see no one. One of the witches later confessed that she was the person who did it, having been sent by the Devil.

The Minister of *Mohra* <note>modern: Mora, the central location of these famous 17th-century trials.</note> also declared that one night, one of these witches came into his house and grabbed him so violently by the throat that he thought he would be choked. Upon waking, he saw the person who did it but could not recognize her. For several weeks afterward, he was unable to speak or perform Divine Service <note>original: "Divine Service"; church rituals or leading a congregation in worship.</note>.

An old woman of *Elfdale* confessed that the Devil had helped her make a nail, which she struck into a boy's knee; because of this strike, the boy remained lame for a long time. She added that the boy would recover only after she was burned or executed by the hand of justice.

They also confessed that the Devil gives them a beast about the size and shape of a young cat, which they call a *Carrier*; and that he gives them a bird too, as big as a raven, but white. These two creatures they can send anywhere, and wherever they go, they take away all sorts of food <note>original: victuals</note> they can find—butter, cheese, milk, bacon, and all sorts of seeds—and carry it to the witch. What the bird brings they may keep for themselves, but what the *Carrier* brings, they must reserve for the Devil. This is brought to *Blockula* <note>Blockula (or Blåkulla) is the legendary meadow in Swedish folklore where witches were said to meet the Devil.</note>, where he gives them as much of it as he thinks fit.

They added likewise that these *Carriers* sometimes fill themselves so full that they are forced to vomit <note>original: spue</note> on the way. This vomit <note>original: spueing</note> is found in several gardens where cabbages <note>original: colworts</note> grow, not far from the houses of those witches. It is of a yellow color like gold and is called *Butter of Witches* <note>This likely refers to *Nostoc commune* or *Fuligo septica* (slime mold), which often appears suddenly in nature and was historically associated with witchcraft.</note>.

The Lords Commissioners were indeed very earnest and took great pains to persuade them to show some of their tricks, but to no purpose. For they all unanimously confessed that since they had confessed everything, they found that all their witchcraft was gone, and that the Devil now appeared to them in a very terrible form, with claws on his hands and feet, horns on his head, and a long tail behind. He showed them a burning pit with a hand reaching out, but the Devil thrust the person down again with an iron fork; he suggested to the witches that if they continued in their confession, he would deal with them in the same manner.

The above-mentioned account is taken from the public register, where all this is related with more detail. And at this time, through all the country, there are weekly prayers in all churches to the end that Almighty God would pull down the Devil’s power and deliver these poor creatures who have hitherto groaned under it.

### *An Account of what happened to a Boy at* Malmö <note>original: Malmoe</note> *in* Scania <note>original: Schonen</note>, *in the Year 1678, supposed to be caused by Witchcraft, and attested by the ablest and most judicious Men of that Town.*

**H**aving in the preface of the preceding narrative mentioned the Swedish Envoy Extraordinary, it may be appropriate to the subject of these papers to give the world an account of a very strange event <note>original: passage</note> which the said Envoy took great pains to investigate for himself. He possesses the public testimony regarding this event from the town where it occurred as recently as the year 1678. In Malmö, Scania—a city belonging to the King of Sweden—there was a boy about thirteen years of age named Abraham Mechelburg, the son of an alderman or senator <note>In this context, a "senator" refers to a member of the city council</note>. One morning around 6:00 a.m., as is the custom in that place, he went to school. He stayed there until 8:00 a.m. and then went home for his breakfast. After he had eaten and was returning to school, he found a little bundle of linen rags lying right before the door, close to the bottom step. Out of curiosity, the lad picked it up and opened it, but found nothing inside except for some pins—some crooked, some laid across each other, and some without points—as well as broken horse-nails, nails without heads, horsehair, and similar trash. When it did not meet his expectations, he tore it apart and threw it away.

A few days later, the boy fell ill and remained so for some time; no physician was able to guess what ailed him. At last, he began to pass <note>original: void</note> small stones from the opening of his penis. Gradually, these stones became larger and larger. Some were perfect pebbles of all sorts of colors, and in time, there came forth great, uneven stones like pieces of rock, appearing as if they had been broken off from a larger stone. The Envoy has two of these with him: one given to him by the boy's father, and the other by the King’s surgeon <note>original: chyrurgeon</note>. I have thought it proper to provide the reader with the dimensions of both.

Before the stones were passed, there was a strange movement in his belly, as if something were alive in it. The stones seemed to crack within him, and a sound was heard as if a large stone were being violently broken; it was at these times that he felt the greatest pain. When the stones were ready to come out, the penis

The penis was drawn in so deep that the bystanders could not see any part of it. When the stones came forth, the boy felt no pain. The pain was greatest when the stones within seemed to crack, and shortly before they were passed. The fit was then so violent that four or five men were forced to hold him down. In the meantime, the boy slept well at night and ate and drank as heartily as ever. He was never discomposed except when the fit of passing these stones was coming upon him. 

This lasted for two years. The parents had the boy prayed for at church and constantly besought God at home—whenever any of those fits came upon him—to "turn the stream" and stop the devil’s power. The boy is now as healthy as ever; he rides his horse out and does all things as he used to do before this accident befell him. 

The Envoy <note>A diplomatic representative or messenger</note> spoke with both the father and the boy. He tells me they are not poor people but are well-to-do <note>original: "well to pass"</note> and are persons of very good reputation in the town of Malmö <note>original: "Malmoe"</note>. 

While this misfortune lasted, the King of Sweden, being then only a short distance away, sent some of his surgeons <note>original: "Chyrurgeons"</note> to the place to discover the truth of the matter. They were present when the lad passed very strange stones from the orifice of the penis and gave the King an account of it. One of them, to be thoroughly satisfied, held his hand under the penis after it had retracted, and a very odd stone—broad and angular—dropped into his hand.

**B**E it known that during the years 1678 and 1679, a very wonderful thing happened in this city of *Malmö* to one of the town’s aldermen named *John Mechelburg* and his wife, *Abla Kruthmeyer*. God having blessed them with three sons, one of them named *Abraham*—a boy about sixteen years old at the time—has been strangely afflicted with an unnatural passing of stones. Over the course of those two years, he passed several hundred stones, both large and small, through his penis <note>original: "Virga of the Penis"</note>. When weighed together, these stones totaled no less than twenty-one pounds, avoirdupois <note>original: "Aver-du-poise"; a system of weights based on a pound of 16 ounces</note>. Some weighed 6, 7, 8, or even 9 ounces; they were full of sharp angles and looked much like pieces of rock broken by force or by tools made for that purpose. 

These broken stones sometimes came out of the boy’s mouth, and sometimes he passed them by <term>stool</term> <note>original: "siege"; an archaic term for a bowel movement</note>. The child's parents have assured us with confidence that before this misfortune, the boy had been sick for several weeks and was bedridden. During this illness, something was seen moving in his body as if it were a living thing. After this sickness, the aforementioned stones appeared. The first to come out was no larger than half a pea, but a short time later, they increased to a greater size. When they were ready to be passed, the boy complained significantly of the spine of his back where, as he said, he felt incredible pain. 

While this lasted, he neither urinated nor had a bowel movement—sometimes for two months and sometimes not for a quarter of a year. Sometimes the stones, after they had passed through the penis, appeared bloody, and on one of them, there appeared a kind of *talc* <note>original: "Talch"</note>. Despite all this misery, the boy continued to eat his food <note>original: "Meat"; in this period, the word often referred to food or solid nourishment in general</note> very heartily, nor was he troubled by this pain at all during the night, but slept quietly as he usually did. Toward the end of this unprecedented suffering <note>original: "Passion"</note> and misery, about 64 stones—mostly small—came out very quickly, one after another. Since September 20, 1679, this misfortune has totally left him, and he is as well as ever. After all those torments, there is no defect to be found or perceived in either his body or the boy’s aforementioned member, but he continues safe and sound to this day.

Since many people will likely mock these accounts as being fictional because they were not eyewitnesses, we whose names are written below—at the request and desire of Lord *John Leyonberg*, Envoy Extraordinary of *Sweden*—have once more spoken and conferred with the boy's parents. The difference between editions 3 and 4 is unimportant. In front of the title of the Second Part in the 4th edition is a plate <note>An engraved illustration</note> containing six small pictures, which I think is listed in the Price's Library Catalogue. At the end of the First Part is a four-page list of contents for the First Part—this is included in the 4th but not in the 3rd edition. Near the end of both (in the 4th and 3rd editions) is a ten-page further introduction to the Swedish case <note>Refers to the 1669 witch trials in Mora, Sweden</note> by Anthony Horneck, Doctor of Divinity.

The Tedworth case <note>original: "Tedworth case"; refers to the "Drummer of Tedworth," a celebrated haunting case from 1661 investigated by Glanvill</note> (located about the middle of the book) looks the same in both editions. ### THE

### TO THE
# READER.

Reader,

**Y**ou cannot justly blame either the author or myself that you have not enjoyed this long-expected edition sooner. Not myself, for I could not publish the book before I had it; nor the author, because many unexpected circumstances drew his mind to other matters and interrupted him in his current project—so much so that he was snatched away by death before he had quite finished it. 

But although the learned world may very well lament the loss of such an able and ingenious writer, regarding this specific point—if it may mitigate your sorrow—in all likelihood, this book would not have seen the light of day so soon if he had lived. So many emerging occasions gave him new interruptions and offered him new temptations to delay further. Indeed, it would have been desirable for it to have had the polishing of his final revisions <note>original: "last Hand"</note>, as the reviewer <note>original: "Peruser"</note> of his papers indicates in his last*

advertisement; but to compensate for this loss, the aforementioned examiner—a friend to both the author's goals and his person—has organized the materials he left behind into a clear and distinct order. He has connected the various parts and supplied additional information in his notes <note>original: "Advertisements"</note> so that a discerning reader will find nothing missing that is necessary for the goals of this intended treatise. This is not even to mention the significant additions that are included here, which likely would not have been present had the author finished the work himself. Besides the notes from the diligent examiner of his papers and that notable recent story of the **Swedish Witches** (translated from **German** into the **English** tongue), there is also added a short treatise on the true and genuine notion of a spirit. This was taken from **Dr. Henry More’s** *Manual of Metaphysics* <note>original: *Enchiridion Metaphysicum*</note> to entertain those who are more inquisitive seekers into the nature of these things. 

The number of stories has also been greatly increased beyond what was originally designed by **Mr. Glanvill**, though none were admitted except those that seemed very well-attested and highly credible to his aforementioned friend. These stories, when rightly understood, contain nothing but what is consistent with right reason and sound philosophy—as I have heard the editor earnestly declare—though it would have been too tedious to have explained them all. It may be more pleasing to the reader to be left to exercise his own intelligence and ingenuity <note>original: "Wit and Ingeny"</note> upon the rest. These are the advantages this edition of **Mr. Glanvill’s** *Drummer of Tedworth* <note>original: "Demon of Tedworth"</note> and his *Considerations about Witchcraft* have over any previous edition. Indeed, the last edition was so quickly sold out <note>original: "bought up"</note> that there was not a copy to be found in all of **London** or **Cambridge**; the examiner of his papers was even forced to take apart his own copy to provide the text for the printing press. # To the Reader.

*...invite you to the reading of so pleasant and useful a treatise; yet I can add one thing more regarding the story of the* **Demon of Tedworth** <note>original: Damon of Tedworth; this refers to the "Drummer of Tedworth," a famous 17th-century haunting involving rhythmic pounding sounds at the home of John Mompesson</note> *which is very significant. Indeed, it is not for me to comment on that pettiness of spirit* <note>original: meanness of Spirit</note> *found in those who dismiss stories of apparitions and witches—a spirit which strangely revealed itself in their rejection of that well-attested narrative concerning the disturbances* <note>original: stirs</note> *in* **Mr. Mompesson’s** *house.*

*In that house, although those who came to be spectators of the marvelous things done by invisible agents were given all the liberty imaginable—even to the ripping open of the bolsters* <note>long, thick pillows or cushions</note> *to search and see if they could discover any natural cause or clever trick by which such strange feats were performed—and although many who had free access day after day were fully satisfied of the reality of the matter (that the house was haunted and disturbed by demons or spirits), yet a few years after the disturbances had ceased, the truth of this story sat so uncomfortably in the minds of those who detest such things that they started a rumor. Even though none of them—not even the most diligent and inquisitive—could detect any trick or fraud themselves, they claimed that both* **Mr. Glanvil** <note>Joseph Glanvill (1636–1680), a philosopher and clergyman who defended the scientific study of the supernatural</note> *himself, who published the narrative, and* **Mr. Mompesson**, *in whose house these wonderful things happened, had confessed the whole matter to be a cheat and a hoax. They were so diligent in spreading this gross untruth that it became common belief in all three kingdoms of* **England, Scotland**, *and* **Ireland**. *This is a shocking revelation of the character of such men. As I said, although it is not my place to dwell on this, I will not hesitate to point it out, as it serves both my own interest and the interest of truth: those reports raised concerning* **Mr. Glan-**

<summary>The author defends the authenticity of the "Demon of Tedworth" haunting, arguing that skeptics spread false rumors of a confession by Joseph Glanvill and Mr. Mompesson to discredit the well-attested supernatural events.</summary>

<meta>This page appears to be the conclusion of a preface or "To the Reader" section, likely written by Dr. Henry More (Dr. H. M.) for Joseph Glanvill’s work on witchcraft and apparitions, such as *Saducismus Triumphatus*.</meta>

# To the Reader.

...Glanvill <note>original: "vil", likely the end of the name Joseph Glanvill (1636–1680), a philosopher and apologist for the existence of the supernatural</note>, through his preface to the second part of the book; that regarding Mr. Mompesson <note>original: "Mr. Mompesson", John Mompesson, whose home was the site of the famous "Drummer of Tedworth" haunting in 1662</note>, through two letters of his own—one to Mr. Glanvill, the other to myself—which are added to the end of that preface. This fact alone may justly be considered to add great weight to the value of both that story and this current edition. 

However, I will not, under the pretense of exciting your interest, keep you from satisfying it with an overly long preface. Yet, if this preface seems lacking in any way, the Doctor’s letter (where among other things you will find that famous and well-attested story of the **Apparition of Anne Walker’s Ghost to the Miller** <note>A famous 1631 murder case from County Durham where a ghost allegedly appeared to a miller to identify her killers</note>) will, I hope, provide a full supplement. I shall add nothing more myself, other than that I am

->Your humble servant, etc.<-

# Dr. Henry More’s <note>original: "Dr. H. M."</note> Letter with the *Postscript* to *Mr. Joseph Glanvill* <note>original: "Mr. J. G."</note>, reminding him of the great *expedience* and *usefulness* of his newly intended edition of the *Demon of Tedworth*, and briefly representing to him the *marvellous weakness* and *deception* <note>original: "gullerie"</note> of *Mr. Webster’s* display of *Witchcraft*.

---

-> SIR, <-

**W**hen I was in London, I called on your bookseller to learn the progress of this newly intended printing of the story of the *Demon of Tedworth*. This edition will correct the public's perception regarding that rumor spread abroad—the claim that Mr. Mompesson and you yourself had admitted the matter was merely a trick or imposture. 

However, because the story, along with your clever considerations <note>original: "ingenious Considerations"</note> regarding witchcraft, has been printed so often already, the bookseller said he needed to be careful about venturing on a new printing unless he had some new material of that kind to add which might make this new edition more certainly marketable <note>original: "sailable"</note>. Therefore, he was waiting for the outcome of that rumored story of the spectre at Exeter, which has been seen so often to reveal a murder committed some thirty years ago. 

But as the outcome of this business, in terms of legal proceedings <note>original: "juridical process"</note>, did not answer expectations, he was discouraged from making use of it, as many things were reported to him from there in favor of the party most concerned. 

Nevertheless, I told him a story of a certain Mrs. Britton appearing to her maid after her death. This account is very well-attested, though not of such a tragic kind as that of Exeter, and he thought it noteworthy. But regarding the discovery of murders, I never met with any story more plain and unexceptionable than the one in *Mr. John Webster’s* <note>Webster was a critic of the witch trials, though he still believed in some supernatural phenomena.</note> *Display of Supposed Witchcraft*. I confess the book itself is but a weak and irrelevant piece; yet that story is weighty and convincing—one that Webster himself (though otherwise a pretentious critic <note>original: "affected Caviller"</note> against almost all stories of witchcraft and apparitions) is forced to agree with, as you shall see from his own confession. For your convenience, or because you perhaps may not have the book, I shall transcribe it...

...from the writer himself, though it was some time ago, around the year of our Lord 1632 (as near as I can remember, having lost my notes and the copy of the letters to *Serjeant Hutton* <note>Sir Richard Hutton (1561–1639), a respected judge of the Common Pleas.</note>, but I am sure that I perfectly remember the substance of the story). Near *Chester-le-Street* <note>A town in County Durham; "Chester in the Street" was a common older name.</note>, there lived one *Walker*, a yeoman <term>A farmer who owned and cultivated his own land, occupying a social class below the gentry.</term> of good estate and a widower. Sharp was a collier <term>A coal miner.</term>, or one who dug coals underground, and was born in *Blackburn* Hundred in *Lancashire*. After this, she was not heard from for a long time, and little or no noise was made about it.

In the winter time following, one *James Graham* (or *Grime*, for that is what they call them in that part of the country) was a miller living about two miles from the place where *Walker* lived. One night, very late, he was alone in the mill grinding corn. Around twelve or one o’clock at night, he came down the stairs after putting corn in the hopper. Although the mill doors were shut, there stood a woman in the middle of the floor with her hair hanging down about her head; she was all bloody, with five large wounds on her head.

Being greatly frightened and amazed, he began to bless himself <note>A traditional defensive gesture or prayer, such as making the sign of the cross, to ward off evil spirits.</note> and at last asked her who she was and what she wanted. To this she said, "I am the spirit of the woman who lived with *Walker*. Having been made pregnant by him, he promised to send me to a private place where I would be well looked after until I had given birth <note>original: "brought in Bed"</note> and recovered, and then I was to return and keep his house. And accordingly," said the apparition, "I was sent away late one night with one *Mark Sharp* who, upon a moor"—naming a place the miller knew—"killed me with a pick, such as men dig coals with, and gave me these five wounds. He then threw my body into a coal pit nearby and hid the pick under a bank. Since his shoes and stockings were bloody, he endeavored to wash them, but seeing the blood would not come out <note>original: "forth"</note>, he hid them there."

The apparition further told the miller that he must be the man to reveal this, or else she would continue to appear and haunt him. The miller returned home very sad and heavy-hearted, but spoke not one word of what he had seen. Instead, he avoided <note>original: "eschewed"</note> as much as he could staying in the mill at night without company, thinking he might thereby escape seeing that frightful apparition again. Nevertheless, one night when it began to grow dark, the apparition met him again. She seemed very fierce and cruel, and threatened him that if he did not reveal the murder, she would continually pursue and haunt him. Yet despite all this, he still concealed...

[He] concealed it until St. Thomas’s Eve <note>December 20, the night before the feast of St. Thomas</note> before Christmas, when, soon after sunset while walking in his garden, she appeared again. There were some who reported that the ghost appeared to the judge, or the foreman of the jury, who was alive in Chester-le-Street <note>original: "Chester in the Street"</note> about ten years ago, as I have been credibly informed; however, of that I have no certainty. There are many people still alive who can remember this strange murder and the discovery of it; for it was, and sometimes still is, as much discussed in the North Country as almost anything that has ever been heard of, and the account was printed, though it is now impossible to obtain. I relate this with the greater confidence (though I may fail in some of the specific details) because I saw and read the letter that was sent to Serjeant Hutton, who then lived at Goldsborough in Yorkshire, from the judge before whom Walker and Mark Sharp were tried and by whom they were condemned. I had a copy of it until about the year 1658, when I had it and many other books and papers taken from me. I confess this to be one of the most convincing stories, being of undisputed truth <note>original: "verity"</note>, that I ever read, heard, or knew of; it carries with it the most evident force to satisfy even the most skeptical spirit that there truly are, at times, such things as apparitions.

While Mr. *Webster* mentions that some reported the apparition appeared to the judge or the foreman of the jury, he admits he had no certainty of this. This confession of his shows he would not write anything in this story of which he was not certain regarding the main facts. Here, Mr. *Smart* provides a very timely addition: he affirms that he heard a Mr. *Fairhair* give evidence under oath that he saw the likeness of a child standing upon *Walker*’s shoulders during the trial. It is likely that this Mr. *Fairhair* was the foreman of the jury. Because the judge was so visibly troubled, it is possible that he also saw the same apparition, as the rumors suggested to *Webster*. The only mistake in Mr. *Webster*’s account is his claim that it was the apparition of a woman; however, the appearance of this child was very appropriate and well-placed...

## Dr. H. More's Letter.

...on his shoulders as one who was justly loaded or charged with the crime of getting his kinswoman pregnant, as well as of plotting with *Sharp* to murder her.

The letter he mentions, written by the judge who heard the trial to Sergeant *Hutton*, is clearly from Judge *Davenport* according to Mr. *Smart's* testimony. In all likelihood, this was a very full and precise <note>original: "punctual"</note> account of the entire matter. This enabled Mr. *Webster* to be more specific about some significant details than Mr. *Lumley*. However, the accounts agree so exactly on the main points that there is no doubt regarding the truth of the apparition. As for the claim that this was not the soul of *Anne Walker* but her "astral spirit"—this is merely a fanciful <note>original: "fantastick"</note> notion of *Webster* and his *Paracelsians* <note>Followers of Paracelsus, a Swiss physician and alchemist who proposed that humans possessed an "astral body" intermediate between the soul and the physical body.</note>. I have sufficiently shown the folly of this idea in the *Scholia* <note>original: Latin for explanatory notes</note> of my book *The Immortality of the Soul* (*Philosophical Volumes, Vol. 2, Page 384*).

I think you would do well to include this story of *Anne Walker* among your additions in the new edition <note>original: "impression"</note> of your *Demon of Tedworth*. It is excellently documented and entirely beyond reproach in every respect. You should hasten that edition as fast as you can to enlighten the "half-witted" world. These people exult and triumph in extinguishing the belief in that story, as if discrediting the truth of the *Demon of Tedworth* were the same as actually slaying the Devil. They think they can now sing that mad, drunken song <note>original: "catch"</note> with more gaiety and security than ever:

->Heigh-ho! The Devil is dead, etc.<-

Although mentioning this wild song may seem like a piece of lightheartedness <note>original: "levity"</note>, believe me, its application carries a serious and weighty meaning. Specifically, these sorts of people are deathly afraid that spirits might exist, because that would imply there is a Devil and an accounting for one's life after death. Therefore, they are intolerant of anything that suggests such a thing, so that they may indulge their own lusts and whims in this life with full abandon and total security from any future reckoning. I know from long experience that nothing rouses them out of that dull lethargy of *atheism* and *Sadducism* <note>Sadducism refers to the denial of the existence of spirits or the afterlife, named after the ancient Sadducees.</note> as much as stories of this kind. Because they are "thick and gross" spirits themselves, the most subtle and solid logical arguments have little effect on them. However, these kinds of sensory experiences <note>original: "sensible experiments"</note> sting them deeply and startle them. Even a story far less significant than that of the *Drummer of Tedworth* or *Anne Walker* once caused a doctor of medicine...

cried out immediately, "*If this be true, I have been in the wrong box all this time, and must begin my calculations anew.*" <note>original: "wrong Box"; an idiom meaning to be mistaken or in an embarrassing situation.</note>

And I remember an old gentleman in the country of my acquaintance—an excellent Justice of the Peace and something of a mathematician—but you may understand what kind of a philosopher he was from a rhyme of his own making. He commended this rhyme to me as I was mounting my horse in his yard, which rhyme is this:

->*Ens* <note>original: Latin for "Being" or "Existence."</note> is nothing until Sense finds it out:<-
->Sense ends in nothing, and so nothingness goes around.<-

This rhyme of his gave him such a sense of rapture that, upon reciting the second verse, the old man spun himself around on his toe as nimbly as one might observe a dry leaf whisked around in the corner of an orchard path by some little whirlwind. I have had many discussions with this "philosopher" concerning the immortality of the soul and its distinct nature. When I had completely defeated him with reason, he would only laugh at me and say, "This is logic, Henry," calling me by my first name. To this I replied, "This is reason, Father L." (for that is what I and some others used to call him), "but it seems you prefer the 'New Lights' and immediate inspiration." <note>The "New Lights" were radical religious groups who claimed direct divine revelation rather than using reason or tradition.</note> I confess he cared as little for those as he did for logic; I only said it to tease him back then. 

The truth is, nothing but physical experience would move him. Being a bold man who feared nothing, he told me he had performed every magical ceremony of conjuration he could to summon the Devil or a spirit, having a most earnest desire to meet one, but he could never succeed. However, he told me that once, when he wasn't even thinking about it—while his servant was pulling off his boots in the hall—some invisible hand gave him such a slap upon the back that it made his whole body ring. "Now," he thought, "I am invited to converse with my spirit." Therefore, as soon as his boots were off and his shoes were on, out he went into the yard and the neighboring field to find the spirit that had given him this friendly <note>original: "Familiar"; here meaning intimate, but also playing on the term "familiar spirit."</note> slap on the back, but he found no one in either the yard or the field.

But although he eventually thought this event was a mere delusion (finding that nothing came of it), yet shortly before his death it had more force with him than all the philosophical arguments I could use. Even though I could out-maneuver <note>original: "wind him"</note> and baffle <note>original: "non-plus him"</note> him as I pleased, all my arguments, however solid they were, made no impression upon him; where-
