Therefore, after several arguments of this nature by which I tried to prove to him the soul’s distinction from the body and its immortality, I found that none of these subtle considerations had any more effect on his mind than lightning is said to have when it melts a sword while leaving the fuzzy <note>original: "fuzzy"; referring to the soft or fibrous texture of a leather scabbard.</note> scabbard intact. 

"Well," I said, "Father L, though none of these things move you, I still have something else—something you yourself have acknowledged to me to be true—that may do the job. Do you remember the slap on your back when your servant was pulling off your boots in the hall? Assure yourself," I said, "Father L, that the goblin <note>In this context, "goblin" refers to a ghost or supernatural spirit that the man had previously encountered.</note> will be the first to welcome you into the other world." 

Upon that, his facial expression changed visibly, and he was more unsettled by this rattling of his memory than by all the rational or philosophical arguments that I could produce.

Indeed, if any modesty remained in mankind, the histories of the Bible would be enough to assure people of the existence of angels and spirits. But these "wits," as they are called, are so suspicious and "wise" that they suspect everything offered to them as established religion to be a piece of political trickery. This is just as silly and childish as the whim of a friend of yours when he was a schoolboy in the lowest grade of a country grammar school. He could scarcely believe that men like Cato, Aesop, Ovid, Virgil, and Tully <note>original: "Tully"; the Roman orator and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> ever existed, much less that they wrote such books. Instead, he thought it was a trick played by our parents to keep us inside for so many hours of the day and stop us from enjoying our innocent games in the open air—the pleasure of planting little flower gardens, or hunting butterflies and bumblebees.

Furthermore, although something that is once true never becomes false—so that it can never be said that it wasn't once true—these "shrewd wits" suspect the truth of things simply because of their antiquity. For that very reason, they think them less credible. This is as "wise" as the story of the old woman who was at church the week before Easter. Hearing the tragic description of all the details of our Savior's crucifixion, she was in great sorrow. She was so troubled by the matter that she came to the priest after the service with tears in her eyes, dropped a curtsy, and asked him how long ago this sad accident happened. When he answered, "About fifteen or sixteen <note>The text says "fifteen or sixteen Years ago," but in most versions of this common anecdote, the priest says "sixteen hundred years," leading the woman to hope the story is no longer relevant or true.</note> years ago," she immediately began to feel comforted and said, "Then, by the grace of God, it may be true." At this level of wit, found in children and old wives, is the reasoning of our professed <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<header>Dr. H. More's Letter.</header>

...but "Wit-would-be's" <note>original: "Wit-would-be's"; a term for pretenders to intellect or wisdom.</note> of this present age, who will catch at any slight occasion or pretense for disbelieving those things that they cannot endure to be true.

And forasmuch as such coarse-grained philosophers as those *Hobbians* <note>Followers of Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), whose materialist philosophy was often accused of leading to atheism.</note> and *Spinozians* <note>Followers of Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose rationalist views on God and nature were highly controversial.</note>, and the rest of the rabble, slight religion and the Scriptures because there is such express mention of spirits and angels in them—things that their dull souls are so inclined to conceive to be impossible—I look upon it as a special piece of Providence that there are every now and then such fresh examples of apparitions and witchcraft. These may stir up and awaken their benumbed and lethargic minds into a suspicion at least, if not an assurance, that there are other intelligent beings besides those that are clad in heavy earth or clay <note>That is, human bodies.</note>. 

In this, I say, it seems to me that divine Providence plainly outwits the powers of the dark kingdom by permitting wicked men and women, and vagrant spirits of that kingdom, to make leagues or covenants with one another. The confession of witches against their own lives is such palpable evidence—alongside the miraculous feats they perform—that there are bad spirits. This will necessarily open a door to the belief that there are good ones, and lastly, that there is a God.

Wherefore, let the small, philosophic "Sir-Foplings" <note>original: "Sir-Foplings"; a derogatory term for foolish men who affect sophistication or learning.</note> of this present age deride them as much as they will. Those who spend their efforts in committing to writing certain well-attested stories of witches and apparitions do real service to true religion and sound philosophy. This is the most effectual and suitable way to confound infidelity and atheism, even in the judgment of the atheists themselves. They are as much afraid of the truth of these stories as an ape is of a whip, and therefore they force themselves with all their might to disbelieve them because of the dreadful consequences these truths would have for them. 

"The wicked fear where no fear is, but God is in the generation of the righteous" <note>A reference to Psalm 14:5.</note>; and he who fears God and has his faith in Jesus Christ need not fear how many devils there are, nor be afraid for himself or his own immortality. Therefore, it is nothing but a foul, dark conscience within, or a very gross and dull constitution of blood <note>In early modern medicine, the quality of one's blood was thought to influence their temperament and spiritual receptivity.</note>, that makes men so averse to these truths.

But however, be they as averse as they will, since this is the most suitable medicine for this disease, the diligence and care for mankind shown by those who make it their business to apply it is much to be commended. They are resolved to continue, even though the peevishness and perverseness of the patients makes them pull off their plaster <note>original: "Plaiſter"; a medical dressing or remedy.</note>, as they have done with this excellent one of the story of the

## THE
# Postscript.

---

**T**his letter sat with me for some time before I thought it appropriate to send it. In the meantime, I met more than once with people who seemed to hold a high opinion of Mr. Webster's criticisms and interpretations of Scripture. They spoke as if he had handled himself so well that no proof of the existence of a <term>witch</term> can ever be expected from the Bible again—which is the very goal he earnestly pursues. Reflecting on the passage in my letter that does not hesitate to condemn Webster's entire book as a weak and irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent" – in this context, meaning "not to the point" or "irrelevant" rather than "rude"</note> work, I decided (so you would not think my judgment was too hasty or unfair) to write a brief postscript. Since showing every weakness and irrelevance in his discourse would be an endless task, I will instead point out the flaws in the section considered his masterpiece. This will show you that my judgment of the whole work was not rash.

To do this, we must first notice the true aim of his book. If you read it, you will certainly find it to be this: that the people usually considered <term>witches</term> and <term>wizards</term> are only "knaves and queens" <note>original: "queans" – a term for a disreputable woman or a harlot</note> (to use his phrase), absolute cheats, or suffering from deep <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "melancholists" – people believed to suffer from a mental illness caused by an imbalance of "black bile," often used by skeptics to explain away supernatural visions</note>. He argues they have no more to do with any evil spirit or the Devil—nor the Devil with them—than he does with any other sinners or wicked men. Secondly, we must impartially define the true concept of a <term>witch</term> or <term>wizard</term>, which is necessary to expose Webster’s irrelevant arguments.

Regarding the words "witch" and "wizard," based on their <term>etymology</term> <note>original: "notation"</note>, they signify nothing more than a "wise man" or a "wise woman." This is obvious at first glance in the word "wizard." And I believe the simplest and least laborious <note>original: "operose"</note> derivation of the name <term>witch</term> is from "wit." Its derived adjective might have been "wittigh" or "wittich," which was later contracted to "witch," just as the noun "wit" comes from the verb "to weet" <note>original: "to weet" – an archaic verb meaning "to know"</note>, which

<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<summary>The author begins a postscript to his letter, intending to debunk John Webster's skeptical views on witchcraft by critiquing Webster's scriptural interpretations and providing a proper definition of a witch.</summary>

# The Postscript.

...which is, to know. So that a <term>Witch</term>, thus far, is no more than a knowing woman; which answers exactly to the Latin word *Saga*, according to that of *Festus*: *Sagæ dictæ anus quæ multa sciunt* <note>original: "Saga is the name given to old women who know many things." Sextus Pompeius Festus was a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note>. This is the general meaning. But usage, without question, had appropriated the word to a specific kind of skill and knowledge that was out of the common road, or extraordinary. Nor did this peculiarity imply anything unlawful in itself. 

However, there was later a further restriction—the most proper of all, and the only way in which the words <term>Witch</term> and <term>Wizard</term> are used nowadays. And that is for one who has the knowledge or skill of doing or telling things in an extraordinary way, and that by virtue of either an express or implicit association or confederacy with some evil spirit. This is a true and adequate definition of a <term>Witch</term> or <term>Wizard</term>; whoever fits this description is one, and vice versa. 

But to prove or defend the idea that there neither are, nor ever were any such people, is, as I said, the main goal of <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a critic of the witch hunts who argued in *The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft* (1677) that many phenomena attributed to magic were actually natural or fraudulent.</note> Webster’s book. To achieve this, he endeavors in his sixth and eighth chapters to nullify all the testimonies of Scripture. I shall now show, with all possible brevity and clarity, how weakly and irrelevantly he has done this.

The words that he comments upon are *Deuteronomy 18:10–11*:

> *There shall not be found among you any one that uses divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a <term>necromancer</term> <note>original: "Necromancer" — one who communicates with the dead to predict the future.</note>.*

The first word or name in the Hebrew is קוסם קסמים (*Kosem Kesamim*), a <term>Diviner</term>. Here, because *Kasam* (divine) sometimes has a neutral sense—meaning to divine by natural knowledge or human prudence and sagacity—Webster argues that nothing concerning the kind of <term>Witch</term> who is imagined to make a visible league with the Devil can be deduced from this word. He mocks the idea of a witch having her body sucked by him <note>A reference to the "witch's mark" or "teat," where an animal familiar or the Devil was believed to feed.</note>, having sexual intercourse with him, or being transformed into a cat, hare, wolf, or dog. 

This is a fine inference indeed, and greatly to the purpose, as is apparent from the previous definition! But even though that specific imagery cannot be deduced, this <term>Divination</term> is plainly declared abominable and cursed in verse 12. It is manifest that the type of <term>Divination</term> understood here is one that truly is abominable; this cannot well be conceived unless it implies either an express or implicit entanglement with some evil invisible powers who assist with any of those types of <term>divinations</term> included under this general term. So, this is plainly one name for <term>witchcraft</term> according to its genuine definition. Furthermore, the very words of King Saul to the Witch of Endor are קסומי נא לי באוב—that is to say, "Divine for me, I pray you, by the spirit."

By your familiar spirit. This is more than natural knowledge or human wisdom.

The next word is *Megnonen* [מעונן]. Although our English translation—deriving it from *Gnon* [ענן], meaning "time"—renders it as "an observer of times" (which should rather mean someone who declares whether a time is favorable or unfavorable for success, something often asked of witches), the common meaning given by scholars of the language is *Praestigiator* <note>Latin: an impostor or one who uses illusions</note>, one who deceives the sight. "The ancient sages," says Buxtorf <note>original: *Sapientes prisci*. Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a celebrated Hebraist and scholar.</note>, "derived it from *Gnajin* [עין, 'eye'] and said that *Megnonen* [מעונן] refers to 'one who holds and restricts the eyes so that they see falsehood as truth'" <note>original: *Sapientes prisci... a עין [Gnajin, Oculus] deduxerunt & מעונן [Megnonen] esse eum dixerunt, qui tenet & praestringit oculos, ut falsum pro vero videant.*</note>. Look! Here is another word that signifies a witch or a wizard, which is named specifically for its power to deceive the sight and make bystanders believe they see shapes or transformations of things that are not there. For instance, when *Anne Bodenham* <note>Anne Bodenham was executed for witchcraft in Salisbury in 1653; her case was famous for its reports of demonic transformations.</note> transformed herself into the shape of a large cat before *Anne Styles*, Styles's sight was so deceived that the transformation seemed real to her, though her eyes were merely deluded. 

Certainly, such a delusion cannot be achieved without an alliance with evil spirits. To believe the word signifies *Praestigiator* in the sense we use for an English "juggler" or a "hocus-pocus" performer is such a foolish idea that no man of any deep intelligence could tolerate it. As if a cheerful juggler performing sleight-of-hand <term>legerdemain: skillful use of one's hands when performing conjuring tricks</term> at a fair or market were such an abomination to the God of *Israel* or his lawgiver *Moses*! Or as if a mere "hocus-pocus" performer were important enough to be consulted as an oracle! For verse 14 says, "*For the nations which you shall possess, they consulted* Megnonenim" [מעוננים]. What? Do they consult jugglers and street performers? No, they certainly consult witches, wizards, and diviners, just as *Anne Styles* consulted *Anne Bodenham*. Therefore, this is clearly a second name for a witch.

The third word in the text is *Menachesh* [מנחש], which our English translation renders as "an enchanter." And with the permission of Mr. *Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a critic of witch-hunts who argued many cases of "magic" were actually fraud or natural phenomena.</note>—who mocks their supposed ignorance—I believe they have translated it very learnedly and wisely. Since charming and enchanting are the same thing—as *Webster* himself admits and the words suggest—the word *Menachesh* [מנחש] here may very well signify enchanters or charmers. However, it specifically refers to those who kill serpents through their charming, derived from *Nachash* [נחש], which means "a serpent," from which comes *Nichesh* [נחש], meaning to kill or remove serpents. For a verb in the *Pihel* form <term>Pihel: a Hebrew verb structure often used to indicate an intensive action or, occasionally, the removal of something related to the root noun.</term> (especially when formed from a noun) sometimes has an opposite 
->signification.<-

...fication. Thus from the root <term>Sheresh</term> <note>Hebrew: שרש, meaning "root"</note> comes the verb <term>Sheresh</term>, meaning "he uprooted roots" <note>original Latin: *radices evulsit*</note>. From the word for "ashes," <term>Deshen</term> <note>Hebrew: דשן</note>, comes the verb <term>Deshen</term>, "he removed ashes" <note>original Latin: *removit Cineres*</note>. From the word for "sinned," <term>Chata</term> <note>Hebrew: חטא</note>, comes the verb <term>Chata</term>, "he purified from sin" <note>original Latin: *expiavit à peccato*</note>. Finally, from the word for "serpent," <term>Nachash</term> <note>Hebrew: נחש</note>, is derived <term>Menachesh</term> <note>Hebrew: מנחש</note>, which means "he freed from serpents," specifically by killing them or driving them away through incantations.

Therefore, there seems to have been a great deal of skill and depth of judgment in our **English** translators who rendered *Menachesh* as an "Enchanter." This is especially true when compared to terms like "Augur" or "Soothsayer"—which the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> calls *Oionizomenon* <note>Greek: Ὀιωνιζόμενον, meaning one who predicts the future by observing the flight of birds</note>. Because there are many harmless types of augury, that term might seem less appropriate for this "black list" of abominations. For instance, there is no great sin in venturing to predict that harsh weather is approaching when one sees wild geese flying high in large groups and cackling loudly. However, to rid a place of serpents by using a charm is above the power of nature. Therefore, it indicates a person who has the assistance of some invisible spirit to help him in this exploit, as happens in several other cases. Consequently, this is another name for one who is truly a witch.

The fourth word is <term>Mecasseph</term> <note>Hebrew: מכשף</note>, which our **English** translators render as a **Witch**. I have no quarrel with this translation, unless people understand it in a way that excludes others from being witches in the sense I have defined—which is impossible. This is simply another term for the same thing: a witch in general. Here, the word refers specifically to the "prestigious" <note>In this context, "prestigious" refers to *prestigium*, or the act of creating illusions and delusions</note> imposing on the sight of onlookers.

**Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a celebrated Hebraist</note> tells us that the scholar **Aben Ezra** defines the *Mecassephim* as "those who change and transform natural things in the appearance of the eye" <note>original Latin: *qui mutant & transformant res naturales ad aspectum oculi*</note>. These are not merely jugglers and "Hocus-Pocus" performers, as the author **Webster** <note>John Webster (1610–1682), a skeptic who argued that many biblical "witches" were actually just clever stage magicians</note> would ridiculously suggest. Rather, it refers to what I described regarding the second name: these are various titles for a witch, who may have more properties than a single name suggests.

It is no wonder, then, that translators do not always render these terms the same way. So many names are listed here in this section of the **Law of Moses** so that, much like in our own Common Law, the "fence" may be more secure, leaving no room for evasion. It is clear that this name does not refer to the simple tricks of sleight of hand <note>original: "tricks of Legerdemain"</note> used by common jugglers who delude the sight of people at a market or fair. Instead, it is the name for those who raise magical specters to deceive human sight, and who are therefore most certainly witches. This is plain from **Exodus 22:18**: *“Thou shalt not suffer a* <term>Mecassephah</term> <note>Hebrew: מכשפה, the feminine form of Witch</note> *to live.”* Such a law would be extremely severe, or rather cruel, if it were directed at a poor "Hocus-Pocus" for his simple stage tricks.

# The Postscript.

The fifth name is חֹובֵר חֶבֶר <note>original: *Chobher Chebher*</note>, which our English translators render as "Charmer," which is the same as "Enchanter." John Webster's commentary on this name is very tedious and dull; he uses many words with very little substance in them. I shall explain the meaning briefly as follows: This *Chobher Chebher*—that is to say, <note>original: *Socians Societatem*, meaning "one who joins in a society or partnership"</note>—is another name for a witch. It is specifically called this either because of the charming together of serpents (which has led men to usually translate it as "Charmer" or "Enchanter," following the example of the Septuagint's <note>original: ἐπάδων ἐπαοιδῷ (epādōn epaoidō), "one who chants charms over charms"</note>), or else from the society or compact of the witch with certain evil spirits. Webster acknowledges that this was the opinion of two very learned men, Martin Luther and William Perkins; and I will add a third, Abraham ibn Ezra (as Martinius has noted), who gives this reason for the word *Chobher* meaning an enchanter, which signifies "one who joins" or "associates": <note>original: *Quòd malignos Spiritus sibi associat*, meaning "Because he associates evil spirits with himself."</note> 

And certainly, one may charm for a long time—even until his heart aches—before he makes a single serpent assemble near him, unless he is helped by this confederacy of spirits that drive them to the charmer. Webster makes a fuss <note>original: "pudder"</note> over the sixth verse of the fifty-eighth Psalm to no purpose. Whereas from the Hebrew, if you repeat the phrase "to the voice" <note>original: *apo koinou* (ἀπὸ κοינוῦ), a grammatical term meaning a phrase is shared between two clauses</note> before the word for "charmer," you may easily and exactly translate it like this: *That does not hear the voice of muttering charmers, nor even the voice of a confederate wizard or charmer who is skillful.* 

But seeing as charms can have no such effects by themselves—except in the minds of those who are very shallow and foolishly gullible—there is every reason in the world (as the very word implies, and as Ibn Ezra has declared) to attribute the effect to the assistance, alliance, and cooperation of evil spirits. Thus, *Chobher Chabharim* or *Chobher Chebher* will plainly signify a witch or wizard according to their true definition. However, as for J. Webster's rendering of this verse on page 119 as: <note>original: *Quæ non audiet vocem mussitantium incantationes docti Incantantis*, meaning "Which will not hear the voice of those muttering incantations of a learned enchanter"</note> (which he says is undoubtedly the most genuine translation of the passage), let any skillful man apply it to the Hebrew text, and he will immediately find it to be grammatical nonsense. If that had been the sense, the Hebrew word order would have been different.

The sixth term is שואל אוב <note>original: *Shoel Obh*</note>, which our English translation renders as "a consulter with familiar spirits"; but the Septuagint uses the term <note>original: *Engastrimythos* (Ἐγγαστρίμυθος), literally "belly-speaker" or "ventriloquist," referring to those through whom a spirit was thought to speak</note>. This, therefore, must necessarily signify the person who has this familiar spirit. Therefore, I believe *Shoel Obh* (considering the other words are understood this way) should be understood as referring to the witch or wizard.

->The wizard himself who asks counsel of his familiar spirit, and does by virtue of him give answers to others.<-

The reason for the name *Obh* <note>original: אוב (*Obh*); a Hebrew word often translated as "medium" or "spirit of a dead person."</note> was likely first taken from that spirit that was in the body of the person, and swelled it to a bulge <note>original: "protuberancy"</note> like the side of a bottle. But afterward, without any relation to that circumstance, *OBH* signifies as much as *Pytho* <note>original: *Pytho*; referring to the Pythian spirit of Apollo, used here to mean a divining spirit</note>; as *Pytho* also—though at first it took its name from the *Pythian Prophets* <note>original: *Pythii Vates*</note>—signifies nothing more than a *spirit of divination* <note>original: *Spiritum Divinationis*</note> in general: a spirit that tells hidden things or things to come.

And *OBH* and *Pytho* also agree in this: they both signify either the divining spirit itself or the person who has that spirit. But here in *Shoel Obh* <note>original: שואל אוב (*Shoel Obh*); literally "one who consults a spirit"</note>, it being rendered by the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as *Engastrimythos* <note>original: *Ἐγγασρίμυθος*; literally "belly-speaker" or ventriloquist</note>, *OBH* is necessarily understood as the spirit itself, just as *Pytho* is in Acts 16:16. This is especially true if you read it as *a spirit of Python* <note>original: *pneuma pythona* (πνεῦμα πύθωνα)</note>, as Isaac Casaubon <note>A renowned classical scholar (1559–1614) who studied the New Testament</note> does; but if read as *of Python* <note>original: *pythonos* (πύθωνος)</note>, it may be understood either way.

Of this "spirit of Python," it is recorded in that passage, *That Paul, being grieved, turned and said to that spirit: I command you, in the name of Jesus Christ, to come out of her. And he came out at that very hour.* This signifies as plainly as anything can be signified that this *Pytho*, or spirit of divination—this *OBH*—was inside her. For nothing can come out of the sack that was not in the sack, as the Spanish proverb says; nor could this *Pytho* come out of her unless it was a spirit distinct from her.

Therefore, I am amazed at the profane impudence of John Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a famous critic of the witch trials who argued that many "supernatural" phenomena were actually natural diseases or fraud</note>, who makes this *Pytho* in the maid mentioned there nothing but a wicked habit <note>original: "humour"</note> of cheating and deceptive <note>original: "couzening"</note> divination. And he adds that this spirit was no more cast out of that maid than the seven devils were out of Mary Magdalen—which he would have us understand only as her various vices. This foolish "Familistical" <note>Referring to the Family of Love, a radical religious group often accused of interpreting the Bible allegorically to deny the existence of literal spirits or devils</note> whim <note>original: "conceit"</note> he attributes to Theodore Beza <note>A major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin</note> as well as Thomas Ady <note>An English physician and author of "A Candle in the Dark," which was skeptical of witchcraft</note>. 

In this, as he is most unjust to Beza, he is also most grossly impious and blasphemous against the Spirit of Christ in St. Paul and St. Luke. He makes them both look like such fools as to believe there was a spirit or divining devil in the maid, when according to him there is no such thing. Can anything be more frantic or ridiculous than this passage of St. Paul if there was no spirit or devil in the young woman? But what will this profane trickster <note>original: "shuffler"</note> hesitate to do out of his deep devotion to his beloved hags? He is their sworn advocate and determined patron, right or wrong.

But to proceed: it is manifest from Leviticus 20:27 that *OBH* signifies the divining spirit itself, not only the person who has it: "A man or woman when there shall be [a spirit/Obh] in them" <note>original Latin: *Vir autem sive mulier cùm fuerit [בהם אוב] in eis*</note>...

# The Postscript

*Pytho* <note>original: A spirit of divination</note>. And 1 Samuel 28:8: "I pray you, divine for me [by a familiar spirit]" <note>original Hebrew: *be-obh*</note>. In the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> it is *en tō engastrimythō* <note>meaning "in the belly-speaker" or ventriloquist</note>, that is, by that spirit that sometimes enters into the body of the person and gives answers from within; but here it only signifies a **familiar spirit** <term>a supernatural entity believed to assist a medium or witch</term>.

And lastly, **בעלת אוב** [*Bagnalath Obh*] in 1 Samuel 28:7: "She who has a spirit" <note>original Latin: *Quæ habit Pythonem*</note>; there *OBH* must certainly signify the spirit itself, of which the woman of Endor was the owner or possessor; that is to say, it was her familiar spirit. But see what brazen and stupid impudence will do here: *Bagnalath Obh*, according to **Webster** <note>John Webster, author of *The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft* (1677), who argued against the reality of spirits</note>, must not signify someone who has a familiar spirit, but the "Mistress of the Bottle." Who but a "Master of the Bottle"—or rather, someone of whom the bottle had become master, and whose wits had become excessively muddy and frothy by guzzling—could ever stumble upon such a foolish interpretation? 

But because *OBH* in one place in the Scripture signifies a bottle <note>Job 32:19</note>, Webster insists it must signify so here. He claims it must be the instrument, forsooth, out of which this cheating woman of Endor whispers, peeps, or chirps like a chicken coming out of its shell (pp. 129, 165). And does she not, I ask you, also put her beak into it sometimes, as if into a reed—as is said of that bird—and cry like a *butterbump* <note>a bittern, a bird known for its booming call</note>? Certainly, he might as well have interpreted *Bagnalath Obh* as the great **Tun of Heidelberg** <note>a massive wine vat famous in the 17th century</note>, which **Tom Coryate** <note>Thomas Coryate (c. 1577–1617), a famous English traveler and writer</note> takes such special notice of, as to call it a "bottle."

And truly, as far as I can see, it would have to be some such huge vat in the end, rather than a bottle—that is, such a spacious tub as he, in his inventive imagination, fancies **Manasseh** to have built. He calls it a *manteion* <note>original Greek: *μαντεῖον*, an oracular shrine</note>, or an oracular building for cheating rogues and women to play their deceiving tricks in, based on that passage in 2 Chronicles 33:6: "And he made a spirit" <note>original Latin: *Et fecit Pythonem*</note>. Now, says Webster, how could Manasseh *make* a familiar spirit? Or *make* someone who had a familiar spirit? Therefore, he argues, he must have made a "bottle," a "vat," or a large "tub"—an oracular building for cheating rogues or women to play their deceiving tricks in. 

This is very wisely argued, and comes out of the very depth of his ignorance of the Hebrew language. If he had looked into **Buxtorf's** dictionary <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a celebrated Hebrew scholar</note>, he might have understood that *asah* signifies not only "he made" <note>original Latin: *fecit*</note>, but also "he prepared," "he acquired," "he procured," or "he supported" <note>original Latin: *paravit, comparavit, acquisivit, magni fecit*</note>. None of these words imply the physical manufacturing of an *OBH* in Webster's sense, but rather the appointing of them to be gathered and giving them official support. For in Webster's sense, Manasseh did not "make" **ידעני** [*Idegmoni*] either—that is, **wizards**—and yet Manasseh is said to have "made" them both alike: "And he made a spirit and wizards" <note>original Latin: *Et fecit Pythonem & Magos*</note>. 

It is so plain, then, that *OBH* signifies a "spirit of divination" <note>original: *Pytho*</note>, and that it matches the same sense that *Pytho* does: either a familiar spirit, or the person...

But rest assured, if you read his book carefully, you will plainly see that his main goal—as I noted above—is to prove there is no such thing as a witch who has anything more to do with the Devil than any other sinner has. However, despite the conclusion he stated just before this, he falls infinitely short of proving it. Therefore, this sixth chapter (which is about thirty folio pages long) is a complete piece of irrelevance <note>original: "impertinency"</note>. Witches will continue to exist despite all this, whether or not these specific details are observed in them. For it was enough for Moses to name those sinister terms in general, which describe a witch according to the general definition I provided above. If having anything to do with evil spirits is prohibited, then being suckled by them or having lustful or sexual <note>original: "venous," likely a misspelling of "venereous," meaning sexual</note> dealings with them is even more strictly forbidden.

But some of these specific details also seem to be hinted at in some of the words, especially as they are sometimes translated by skilled interpreters. For example, *Mecasseph* <term>Hebrew: מכשף, a term for a sorcerer or magician</term> is translated by Vatablus and the Latin Vulgate as *Maleficus* <note>Latin: an evildoer or sorcerer</note>, and by the Septuagint <note>the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> as *pharmakos* <note>Greek: φαρμακός, a word meaning "poisoner" or "sorcerer"</note>, which signifies *Veneficus* <note>Latin: a poisoner or practitioner of dark magic</note>. This word suggests doing enough mischief to both humans and animals. 

Furthermore, the word *Mecasseph* also carries the meaning of transformation. Perhaps this is the difference between *Mecasseph* and *Megnonen* <term>Hebrew: מעונן, often translated as a "soothsayer" or "observer of clouds"</term>: the former uses magical transformations to cause great harm. For instance, Olaus Magnus <note>a 16th-century Swedish historian and clergyman</note> tells of those who—in people's minds—transformed themselves into wolves and immediately began attacking sheep. Others, transformed in their "astral spirit" into various shapes, enter houses and harm men and children, as I recall Remigius <note>Nicolas Rémy, a French judge known for his involvement in witch trials and his book 'Daemonolatreiae'</note> reports. Therefore, it is no wonder that the strict Law of Moses is directed against the *Mecassephah* <note>the feminine form of *Mecasseph*</note>, such a witch as this:

> *You shall not permit a witch to live*;

This may be a more specific meaning of that word. As for making a pact with the Devil, how naturally does the name *Chobber Chebber* <term>Hebrew: חובר חבר, literally "one who binds with charms" or "weaver of spells"</term> signify that act as well? But as for suckling and sexual intercourse, though it may be true when properly explained, I admit there is no hint of it here—as it was not necessary for the other points to be mentioned either. These behaviors are the very dregs—the *faex magorum et sagarum* <note>Latin: "the dregs of magicians and hags"</note>—who wallow in those abominations. As I move on to the eighth chapter, I will briefly note the shameless impudence of J. Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a prominent skeptic who argued in *The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft* (1677) that "witches" were merely frauds or suffered from mental illness.</note>, who, in favor of his beloved hags—so that they might never be thought to do anything with the Devil's assistance—claims the victory of Moses (with whom God's mighty hand was) or of Christ (who was the Angel that first appeared to Moses in the Burning Bush and led the children of Israel out of Egypt to the Promised Land) was merely a victory over a few "hocus-pocus" performers. He treats them like mere jugglers who were apparently skilled in sleight of hand <term>legerdemain</term>. This is the lowest insult to the glory of that victory and a vile reproach against the God of Israel and the person of Moses that either the malicious wit of a devil could invent or the dullness of a fallen soul could stumble upon. 

Certainly, there was a real conflict here between the Kingdom of Light and the Kingdom of Darkness and its evil spirits, who assisted the *Hartummim* <note>Hebrew: הרטמים, usually translated as "magicians" or "scribes" in the context of the Egyptian court.</note>, the magicians of Egypt. Before that name is even used, to ensure no one is mistaken, they are called *Mekhashephim* <note>Hebrew: מכשפים, a term for sorcerers or those who practice "black magic."</note>. These are the kind of magicians who can display various deceptive transformations through diabolical help. Good interpreters translate this as *maleficia* <note>Latin: "evil-doing" or "sorcery."</note>, as I noted above; that is, they were wizards or "he-witches." The very same word is used in that severe Law of Moses: "You shall not allow a witch to live" <note>Exodus 22:18.</note>. Are these magicians not clear enough examples that witches exist? That is to say, such wretched people <term>wights</term> who perform strange, miraculous things through the assistance or companionship of evil spirits?

"Oh no," says Mr. Webster, "these are only *Chachamim*" <note>Hebrew: חכמים, meaning "wise men."</note>—wise men and great naturalists—and everything they did, they did *be-lahateihem* <note>Hebrew: בלהטיהם, translated in the King James Version as "with their enchantments."</note>, by their "bright glittering plates" <term>laminae</term>, for that is supposedly what *lahat* must mean. 

But why must *lahat* mean "plate"? There is only the excuse of that one passage in Genesis 3:24, *lahat ha-cherev* <note>Hebrew: להט החרב, "the flaming sword" guarding Eden.</note>, where it is actually *ha-cherev* (the sword) alone that signifies the blade <note>original: "lamina"</note>, and that is a long form, hardly common for those small magical plates with celestial signs on them that J. Webster is suggesting. Rather, *lahat* simply means "flame" <note>original: "flamma"</note>. Therefore, by this logic, *be-lahateihem* must mean "by their flames," if it comes from the root *lahat*, meaning "to burn" or "to flame" <note>original: "ardere, flammare"</note>.

For this reason, Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a famous Hebrew scholar whose dictionaries were standard reference works in the 17th century.</note> judiciously places the word under the root *lut*, meaning "to hide" or "to wrap" <note>original: "abscondit, obvolvit"</note>. He reads it not as *be-lahateihem* but as *be-lateihem*, which is as much as to say "by their secret magical methods" <note>original: "occultis suis rationibus Magicis"</note>, which is...

This agrees marvelously well with the Hebrew *Mecassephim* <note>original: *Mecaſſephim* (מכשפים)</note>, which means "magical conjurers" <note>original Latin: *Praeſtigiatores Magici*</note>, or those who perform strange, wondrous things in a hidden way by the help of evil spirits. But the idea that the *Egyptian magicians* performed the acts recorded in *Exodus* by virtue of any <term>Lamels</term><note>Small metal plates or amulets (lamellae) inscribed with astrological symbols used in ritual magic.</note> or plates of metal with certain sculptures or figures created under a specific constellation is so "sottish" <note>foolish or drunkenly stupid</note> and foolish that no man—unless he is himself bewitched by some old hag or hobgoblin—could ever use it as a sanctuary to save himself or his "old dames" from being classified as witches based on the history in *Exodus*. For if there can be he-witches—that is, *magicians* like those of *Egypt*—I leave *John Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), author of "The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft," who argued that witchcraft was largely a result of fraud or natural causes.</note> to scratch his head to find any reason why there may not be she-witches as well.

And indeed, the account of the *Witch of Endor*—to move finally to the eighth chapter—is as plain a proof of this as could be desired by any man whose mind is not blinded by prejudice. But here *John Webster* (not irrelevantly, I confess, in general terms—though I discount the many tedious and irrelevant details with which he has cluttered his discourse) relies on two methods to show there was nothing of a witch in that entire narration. First, he pretends that the whole transaction on the *Woman of Endor’s* part was nothing but collusion and a cheat, claiming that *Saul* was not in the same room with her, or at least saw nothing if he was. Secondly, he argues that the *Samuel* who is said to appear could neither be *Samuel* appearing in his body out of the grave, nor in his soul; nor was it a devil that appeared. Therefore, Webster concludes, it must have been some colluding rogue hired by the witch. To discover the weakness of his first allegation, we need only appeal to the text itself, which is *1 Samuel 28:8*:

### The Postscript.

...take a <term>dram</term> <note>original: "Dram"; a small drink of liquor</note> of the bottle to make her wits quicker and more <term>divinatory</term> <note>capable of foretelling the future</note>. Who but someone who had taken too many drinks from the bottle could ever fall into such a foolish whim? Therefore, *Obh* <note>Hebrew: אוב; often translated as "familiar spirit," though sometimes literally meaning "skin bottle"</note> in this passage does not—as it doesn't anywhere else—signify an oracular bottle or a <term>prophetic vessel</term> <note>original Greek: μάντιον</note> into which Saul might have desired the woman of Endor to retreat while he waited for answers in the next room. Instead, it signifies that <term>familiar spirit</term> <note>a demonic spirit believed to assist a witch</note> through whose help she was believed to perform all those wondrous duties of a <term>wise woman</term> <note>a common term for a female healer or sorceress</note>. But we proceed to Verse 11.

*Then said the woman, Whom shall I bring up unto thee? And he said, Bring me up Samuel.* Surely Saul and the woman are still in the same room, since the woman asked, "*Whom shall I bring up to you?*" and he answered, "*Bring up Samuel to me.*" This implies that Samuel was brought up in a way that Saul could see him, and not just the witch alone. But we go on to Verse 12.

*And when the woman saw Samuel, she cried with a loud voice; and the woman spoke to Saul, saying, Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul.* Though the woman might have had some suspicions before that it was Saul, once she saw Samuel appear—and in a different manner and appearance than her usual spirits, as is likely for such a holy soul—she immediately cried out with a loud voice. She did not mutter, chirp, or "peep" like a chicken coming out of its shell <note>The author is mocking the idea that the "spirit" was just the woman performing ventriloquism</note>. She was now certain it was Saul; she was not so foolish as to think her own magic could call up the real Samuel, but rather that the presence of Saul was the cause of it. 

And *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian</note> writes explicitly: <note>original Greek: Ὅτι θεασάμενον τὸ γύναιον ἄνδρα σεμνὸν καὶ θεοπρεπῆ ταράττεται, καὶ πρὸς τὴν ὄψιν ἐκπλαγέν, ὃ σὺ, φησὶν, ὁ Βασιλεὺς Σάουλ;</note> "*The woman, seeing a grave, god-like man, was startled; and, astonished at the vision, she turned to the king and said, 'Are you not King Saul?'*" 

Verse 13.
*And the king said unto her, Be not afraid; for what did you see? And the woman said unto Saul, I saw gods ascending out of the earth.* The King here assures the woman that although he was Saul, no harm would come to her, and so he tells her not to be afraid. But since she turned her face toward Saul as she spoke to him, and he toward her, her sight was taken off the object. Saul then asked her, "*What did you see?*" and she answered, "*I saw gods,*" etc. For "gods," I suppose any free translator in Greek, Latin, or English would say <term>spirits</term> <note>original Greek: δαίμονας</note>, <term>genies</term> <note>original Latin: Genios</note>, or spirits. And *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: אלהים</note> signifies...

# The Postscript.

Angels as well as gods; and it is likely these wise-women <note>original: "Wife-women," likely a typographical error for "wise-women," a common term for folk healers or witches</note> take the spirits they converse with to be good angels. This is similar to what Anne Bodenham the witch told a worthy and learned friend of mine: that these spirits, such as she possessed, were good spirits and would do a man all helpful services all the days of his life. It is likely this Woman of Endor held the same opinion of her spirits, and therefore we need not wonder that she calls them *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים (gods or divine beings)</note>, especially with Samuel appearing among them, to say nothing of the presence of Saul. As for the fact that more than one spirit appears at a time, there are repeated examples in Anne Bodenham's magical evocations of them, whose history, I must confess, I take to be very true.

The case stands therefore thus: the woman and Saul being in the same room, she turns her face away from Saul and mutters to herself some magical formula for the evocation of spirits. Whereupon, as they begin to appear and rise up, seemingly out of the earth, she sees Samuel's face and cries out to Saul. Turning her face toward him, she speaks to him. Now, the fact that Saul had seen nothing until this point, though in the same room, might be either because the body of the woman was positioned between his eyes and the spirits, or because the "vehicles" <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "vehicle" was the semi-material body that a spirit used to manifest in the physical world</note> of those spirits were not yet refined to that <term>conspissation</term> <term>conspissation: the thickening or condensation of a fluid or spiritual substance into a visible form</term> that would strike the eyes of Saul, even though they were visible to the witch. There is an instance of some seeing an object while others do not in the story of the child upon Walker's shoulders, who appeared to Mr. Fairhair and perhaps to the judge, but was invisible to the rest of the court; there are many such examples. But I proceed to Verse 14.

> And he said unto her, "What does he look like?" And she said, "An old man is coming up, and he is covered with a mantle <note>cloak</note>."

He asks here in the singular form because his mind was only fixed on Samuel. And the woman's answer is exactly according to how the spirit appeared to her when her eye was upon it—namely, *ish zakan oleh* <note>original Hebrew: איש זקן עלה</note>, "an old man coming up." For he was only just ascending when she looked upon him, and she describes him accordingly. For the word *oleh* there is a present tense participle, and the woman describes Samuel by his age, clothing, and the motion he was in while her eye was upon him. So the true and grammatical meaning of this answer to "What does he look like?" is this: "An old man is coming up, and the same is covered with a mantle"; this is the form and condition in which I saw him. ...changing their postures or positions, or **Samuel** by this time having sufficiently thickened <note>original: "conspissated"</note> his spiritual form <note>original: "Vehicle"; in Neoplatonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle or airy body that allows a spirit to become visible</note> and adjusted it for **Saul’s** sight as well, the text continues: *And Saul perceived it was Samuel, and he stooped with his face to the ground and bowed himself.*

Oh, the impudent profanity and foolishness <note>original: "Sottishness"</note> of these perverse tricksters and deceivers <note>original: "Shufflers and Whifflers"</note>! Upon hearing this passage, they have the nerve to deny that **Saul** saw anything at all, merely because the word "*perceived*" is used instead of "*saw*." Yet the word "*perceived*" clearly implies that he saw **Samuel** and something more: specifically, that through his previous familiarity with him, he was certain it was he. **Samuel** appeared so perfectly and convincingly to **Saul's** senses that he could not help but acknowledge (which is what the Hebrew word *yada* <term>ידע</term> signifies) that it was indeed him. Otherwise, why would he bow his face to the very ground to honor him?

No, no, says **J. Webster** <note>John Webster (1610–1682), author of *The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft* (1677), a skeptical work that argued against the reality of the apparition at Endor</note>, **Saul** saw nothing himself, but stood waiting like a "drowned puppet" in another room to hear what would happen. (Notice what a base and rude spirit this "defender of witches" <note>original: "Squire of Hags"</note> has, using such language about a prince in his time of distress!) Webster claims that everything **Saul** understood came from the woman's cunning and lying accounts. That this champion of witches should dare to abuse a prince in this way—portraying him as much more foolish in his intellect as he was taller in height than the rest of the people (standing head and shoulders above them)—merely to protect "old wives" from even the possibility of being suspected of witchcraft, is something extremely crude and intolerably vile. 

Indeed, considering that **Saul** is said to have bowed to **Samuel** (which clearly implies there was a **Samuel** present who was the object of his sight and reverence), Webster’s confidence fails him in this wild argument. He then shifts to the idea that it was a co-conspirator—a rogue that the **Woman of Endor** sent into the room where **Saul** was to play the part of **Samuel**, having first dressed him in her own short cloak, which she used along with her wicker basket <term>Maund</term> under her arm when riding to fairs or markets. According to Webster, King **Saul**—bowing with his face to the very ground—must have made his profound gesture of respect to this clumsy provincial fellow <term>County-slouch</term> dressed in a woman’s cloak. Were a market-woman's cloak and **Samuel's** mantle—which the historian **Josephus** calls a *diploïda hieratikēn* <note>original: διπλοΐδα ἱερατικὴν</note>, a priestly robe <term>Sacerdotal Habit</term>—really so similar? And if not, how did this woman, being caught so suddenly by surprise, manage to provide herself with such a priestly garment?

Could she find clothing to disguise her partner-in-crime <note>original: "confederate Knave"</note> in? Besides, scoundrels do not usually say what is true, but what is pleasing. And moreover, this Woman of *Endor*, though a medium <note>original: "Pythoness"</note>, was of a very good and kind nature, which the historian *Josephus* takes notice of and praises her greatly for. Therefore, she could take no delight in laying a further burden on the oppressed spirit of the distressed King *Saul*. This is another sign that this scene was acted in good faith <note>original: "bonâ fide"</note>, and that there was no cheating in it. Another sign is that she spoke so magnificently of what appeared to her, saying that she "saw gods ascending." Could she then possibly venture to present a clumsy countryman wearing a beggar-woman’s cloak <note>original: "Maund-womans Cloak"</note> to act the part of so god-like and divine a personage as *Samuel*? *Samuel* was "like some great god" <note>original: "$\Theta\epsilon\tilde{\varphi}$ $\tau\iota\nu\grave{\iota}$ $\mu\epsilon\gamma\alpha\lambda\tilde{\varphi}$ $\hat{o}\mu\omicron\iota\omicron\varsigma$"</note>, as the woman describes him in *Josephus's Antiquities of the Jews, Book 7, Chapter 15*. And the Son of Sirach <note>referring to the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the Apocrypha</note>, in Chapter 46, says that *Samuel* himself prophesied after his death, referring to this story of the Woman of *Endor*. 

But as for our "newly inspired" seers or "saints"—*Saint Scot*, *Saint Adie*, and if you wish, *Saint Webster*, the sworn advocate of witches—who so madly and boldly argue against all sense and reason, against all antiquity, all interpreters, and against the inspired Scripture itself, they insist there was no *Samuel* in this scene, only a cunning accomplice. Whether the inspired Scripture, or these conceited buffoons <note>original: "inblown Buffoons"</note>—puffed up with nothing but ignorance, vanity, and dull lack of faith—are to be believed, let anyone judge.

## The Postscript.

Ten arguments are given to disprove this assertion, and all are little to the purpose—so little, indeed, that I think it is unnecessary to answer them individually. Instead, I shall mention only a few truths that will defeat the entire group of them.

Therefore, I say that departed souls, like other spirits, possess a "self-governing power" <note>original Greek: *αὐτεξούσιον* (autexousion), meaning free will or the power of self-determination</note> within them, just as souls do in this life. They have both the ability and the right to move of their own accord, provided there is no specific law against the particular purpose toward which they are moving.

Furthermore, they have the power to appear in their own personal forms to those who have a need—just as **Anne Walker's** soul did to the **Miller**. Since this is a capability of theirs, whether natural or acquired, doing so is not a miracle.

Thirdly, it was the intense, piercing desire and the deep distress and agony of mind in **Saul**, in his troubled circumstances, combined with the great compassion and goodness of spirit in the holy soul of **Samuel**, that acted as the effective "magic." This drew Samuel down to condescend to converse with **Saul** in the **woman's** house at **Endor**—just as a sharp sense of justice and revenge caused **Anne Walker’s** soul to appear to the **Miller** with five **wounds** in her head.

Regarding the rigid and harsh severity that **Webster** <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a skeptical author who argued that "apparitions" were often delusions or natural phenomena rather than the actual spirits of the dead</note> imagines **Samuel’s** ghost would have used against the **woman**, or the sharp reproofs he would have given to **Saul**: as for the latter, it is somewhat described in the biblical text. **Saul** had his excuse ready, and the good soul of **Samuel** was sensible of his troubled condition. As for the former, since the soul of **Samuel** might indeed have terrified the poor **woman**—unhinging her so much that she would be fit for nothing afterward, without actually converting her—it is no wonder he ignored her. Goodness and forbearance are more befitting a holy, angelic soul than the bluster and fury imagined by that "rude goblin" who drives the body and pen of **Webster**.

As for the idea that departed souls never care for or regard any of their fellow souls here on Earth, this is expressly contradicted by the known example of that Great Soul and universal Pastor of all good souls <note>A reference to Jesus Christ</note>, who appeared to **Stephen** at his stoning and to **St. Paul** before his conversion. Though he appeared in his glorified body, this was an even greater condescension than that of the soul of **Samuel**, which appeared to a prince upon whose shoulders lay the great affairs of the people of **Israel**. I will also mention that other notable example of the angel called **Raphael**—so named because of his office at that time, or because of the angelic order he was adopted into after his death—who was indeed the soul

For when he says, *I am Raphael, one of the seven holy Angels who present the prayers of the Saints, and who go in and out before the glory of the Holy One*, in the <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>original: "Cabbalistick"; referring to mystical or symbolic interpretations of scripture.</note> sense it signifies no more than this: that he was one of the universal society of the holy angels (and a *Raphael* within the "Order of Raphaels") who serve the saints. But certainly, *Saul* was a brave prince and commander, as *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> justly describes him. He was a "reprobate" only in a <term>symbolic sense</term> <note>original: "Type"; in theology, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows or symbolizes something else.</note>, as were *Ishmael* and *Esau*—which is a mystery, it seems, that *J. Samuel appeared to settle Saul's mind by telling him plainly the <term>final outcome</term> <note>original: "upshot"</note> of the whole matter: that he would lose the battle, and he and his sons would be killed. This allowed Saul to show the greatest bravery ever achieved by any commander; he would not allow his country to be over-run by the enemy without resistance while he was still alive. As for the other opinion, which the majority of Protestant theologians hold—that it was the Devil who appeared in **Samuel’s** form—even **Grotius** seems inclined toward it. He cites a passage from **Porphyry’s** *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, where he describes one kind of spirit as: <term>γένος ἀπατηλῆς φύσεως, παντομορϕόν τε καὶ πολύτροπον, ὑποκρινόμενον καὶ θεוὺς καὶ δαίמוνας καὶ ψυχὰς τεθνηקότων</term> <gloss>a race of a deceptive nature, taking all forms and many turns, pretending to be gods, demons, and the souls of the dead</gloss>.

I admit this is very relevant to this story, and I do not doubt that in many of these necromantic <note>original: "Necromantick" – relating to communication with the dead</note> apparitions, they are playful or deceptive spirits rather than the souls of the deceased that appear. Nevertheless, I am certain that it was the soul of **Samuel** who appeared in this story, for the reasons argued above. I am equally certain that in other instances of necromancy, it may be the Devil or the kind of spirits Porphyry describes, *who transform themselves into all sorts of forms and shapes, acting at one time as demons, another time as angels or gods, and another time as the souls of the dead*. I confess that such a spirit could have impersonated **Samuel** here, despite anything **Webster** <note>John Webster, author of "The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft" (1677), who argued against the reality of many supernatural phenomena</note> has argued to the contrary; for his arguments are indeed wonderfully weak and poorly constructed, as can be understood from what has been said.

I have alluded to the previous opinion, but I cannot provide further details now.

I have unknowingly made my *Postscript* much longer than my letter. However, I do not need to elaborate for you, as you are already so well-versed in these matters and can, by your quick wit, judge the whole from a small part <note>original: "collect the whole measures of *Hercules* by his Foot"</note>. By now, you surely understand that it was no rash judgment on my part to say that *Webster’s* <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was the author of *The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft* (1677), a skeptical work that argued many witchcraft accusations were the result of mental illness or fraud.</note> book is a weak and irrelevant piece of work. Even its most important parts are so feeble and off-target that they fail to achieve his goal. His real aim was to prove that there is no such thing as a witch or wizard—at least, that there is no mention of them in Scripture as someone who had more to do with the Devil than any other wicked person. He denies that anyone, through a covenant <note>A formal agreement or contract with the Devil, either implied or stated outright.</note> (either implicit or explicit), performs strange feats with the help of evil spirits. Instead, he claims in his very title page that these are merely various types of deceivers and impostors, or people suffering from the passive delusions of melancholy <term>a state of depression or "black bile" believed at the time to cause hallucinations</term> and imagination.

In this way, he plainly suggests that the entire business of witches' feats is nothing but fraud <note>original: "Couzenage"</note> or mental illness. To soften or hide the crudeness of this false assertion, he adds that there is no physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> league between the Devil and the witch, and that the Devil does not suck the witch's body, nor has sexual intercourse with her, nor do witches turn into dogs or cats, and so on. As you can see in his book, he interprets all these things in the most literal way imaginable—as if the "imps" of witches had physical mouths to suck them, or bodies of flesh to lie with them. By this logic, he might as well claim a physical league does not exist unless a lawyer drew up the document and wrote it formally on vellum <term>high-quality parchment made from animal skin</term>, with witnesses and the hand and seal of the party involved! 

He also denies transformations into dogs or cats unless they are physical and literal. Yet none of the "witch-mongers"—as he rudely and disrespectfully calls learned and serious men like *Dr. Casaubon* <note>Meric Casaubon (1599–1671), a scholar who defended the reality of spirits and supernatural phenomena.</note> and others—actually believe that. The question of their physical transformation is a debated case between *Bodin* <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and influential writer on demonology.</note> and *Remigius* <note>Nicolaus Remigius (c. 1554–1612), a French magistrate and author of *Daemonolatreiae libri tres*.</note>, which I discuss further in my *Scholia* <term>explanatory notes or commentary on a text</term>. But the idea that a woman cannot be considered a witch without this literal, physical transformation is such a foolish assumption that *Webster* himself should certainly be ashamed of it.

Therefore, if his *Book* was written only to prove that there is no such thing as a *Witch* who makes a contract on parchment with the *Devil* by the advice of a *Lawyer*, and is physically <note>original: "Really and Carnally"</note> turned into a *Dog*, *Cat*, or *Hare*, etc., and is sucked by the *Devil* with physical lips, or is one with whom the *Devil* has sexual relations; then the purpose of his work is clearly irrelevant, since neither *Dr. Casaubon* <note>Meric Casaubon (1599–1671) was a scholar who argued that denying the existence of spirits led to atheism.</note> nor anyone else believes in such things. 

But as for the true and accurate concept of a *Witch* or *Wizard*, such as I described at the beginning, all of his arguments are far too weak and irrelevant to disprove the existence of such a person. This true *Witch*—positioned between his "deceivers," "impostors," and "melancholies" <note>At the time, "melancholy" (depression or mental illness) was often used by skeptics to explain away supposed supernatural visions.</note> on one hand, and those absurd, exaggerated *Witches* he describes on the other—escapes like a *Hare* in a green <term>balk</term> <note>A "balk" is a strip of unplowed land acting as a boundary between two plowed fields.</note> between two fields of *Corn*. None of his arguments reach her or even catch sight of her. Meanwhile, he himself stands on the side of the *Deceivers* and *Impostors*; his *Book*, regarding the main *Design* he pursues, is a mere *Cheat* and *Impostor*.

->**C. C. C.** <note>Likely referring to Corpus Christi College.</note> May 25.<-

<note>original: "ADVERTISEMENT." In this context, it refers to an introductory note or public announcement by the editor.</note>

**Th**is letter from Dr. Henry More <note>original: "Dr. Moor"</note> was found among other papers belonging to this new intended edition by Mr. Joseph Glanvill <note>original: "Mr. Glanvil"</note>. Because I perceived in a letter from Mr. Glanvill to the Doctor that he intended for this letter to be published along with his book, it has been included and placed at the beginning, as a natural method requires. The *Letter* is encouraging <note>original: "Hortatory"</note>, meant to urge Mr. Glanvill to quickly finish his intended new edition to correct the world's misunderstandings. The *Postscript* also contains many points that have a general influence on the entire book. 

However, to ensure that the Doctor's reputation does not suffer from the publication of his *Letter* and *Postscript*—due to their occasional sharp and satirical tone—I will explain his reasons for using that style of writing. I shall transcribe a passage from a letter he wrote to his friend Mr. Glanvill regarding this matter: 

*I pray you, send me word whether that Postscript will counter all the evasive arguments <note>original: "elusory Cavils"</note> of that irreverent fool <note>original: "profane Buffoon"</note> regarding those passages of Holy Scripture. His unworthy usage of Holy Writ, and his mocking <note>original: "derisorious"</note> interpretations of it on behalf of his beloved hags <note>Referring to the subjects of witchcraft trials</note>, provoked my indignation. It led me to use such methods of mocking and exposing him, which I otherwise would never have stooped to.* 

This is sufficient evidence of the Doctor's natural dislike for such a manner of writing. But as theologians tell us that anger and punishment are God’s *strange work* <note>original: ***Opus alienum***</note>—meaning they are contrary to His nature, yet He occasionally performs them for the good of the universe—so I think it is not unbecoming for good men to sometimes stoop (as the Doctor calls it) to disciplining irreverent jesters <note>original: "drolls"</note> and those who abuse holy things. They may use a deserved mockery and satirical rebuke for such erratic and impious arrogance <note>original: "freakish and impious Sauciness"</note>, provided it is done sincerely and for the public good.

# The Epistle Dedicatory.

...for the justification of the belief in <term>Witches</term> <note>original: "Witches"; in this period, the existence of witches was seen as proof of a spiritual world, countering "atheistic" materialism</note>, as it suggests clear and current evidence of our immortality, which I am exceedingly anxious to have proven true.

For truly, my Lord, if we make our calculations like rational men and do not allow ourselves to be deceived by the flatteries of the senses and the deceitful pleasures that steal us away from God and from ourselves, there is nothing that can make the thoughts of this strange life tolerable except for the expectation of another. And wise men have said that they would not live a single moment if they thought they were not to live again. 

This perhaps some may take to be the discontented paradox of a melancholy, troubled person of low social standing <note>original: "mean Condition"</note>, who is pinched by financial hardship <note>original: "straitness of Fortune"</note> and envies the heights of others' happiness and grandeur. But by the time those who judge this way have spent the passions of their frolicsome youth and have passed through the several stages of vanity—when they sit down to make sober reflections upon their pleasures and pursuits and sum up the account of all they have and all that lies before them—I do not doubt that their thoughtful considerations will reach Solomon’s conclusion <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Ecclesiastes, often attributed to King Solomon, which famously concludes that earthly pursuits are "vanity of vanities."</note> and find that it is nothing but a misery to live, if we were to live for nothing else. 

So that if the contentment of the present life were all I had in exchange for the hope of immortality, I would be very unwilling to believe that I was mortal for that reason alone. For certainly, the pleasures that result from thoughts of another world—in those who not only see it painted in their imaginations but feel its beginning in their souls—are as far beyond all the tickling pleasures of the senses as a real, lasting happiness...

<meta>This page transitions from the introductory dedication to the main body of the work, specifically engaging in a theological and linguistic debate about the nature of demonic possession as described in the Bible.</meta>

<header>Proof of Apparitions, etc.</header>

Again, this writer alleges that "to have a devil" and "to be mad" seem to be synonyms in Scripture (p. 35). I answer: possession caused a certain *mania* <note>original: μανία (Greek)</note>, *fury* <note>original: furor (Latin)</note>, and madness. Therefore, when anyone acted extravagantly, the Jews said in common speech that they "had a devil," just as we say, "The Devil is in you"—meaning, "You are acting unreasonably and madly." But just as we do not mean to exclude the belief in a *real* possession by using this metaphor, neither did they. Indeed, the very phrase "has a devil" or "the devil is in him"—when applied to those who act furiously and recklessly—implies that there is such a *real thing* as diabolical possession, which madness and extreme folly resemble.

Observe, then, how the defenders <note>original: "Patrons"; here referring to those who argued against the reality of witchcraft</note> of witches argue: "The Jews sometimes used the phrase 'having a devil' metaphorically; therefore, no other kinds of possession exist, or therefore all those passages of Scripture in which they are described literally and plainly mean nothing else." Indeed, if we only argued from the mere words and expressions of "having devils" and "casting out devils," there would be a bit more plausibility <note>original: "colour"</note> to our adversaries' reasoning. But since we draw our conclusions chiefly from the clear circumstances of history and fact, their argument has no force at all.

## SECTION X.

### The ignorance of the author of *The Grand Apostasy* in his interpretation of the word *daimonion*. <note>original: Δαιμόνιον (Greek)</note>

But what does this writer mean when he tells us *daimonion* <note>original: Δαιμόνιον (Greek)</note> can hardly signify anything else properly but an unusual affliction from God, such as madness? Everyone—even schoolboys—knows that as a noun <note>original: "Substantively"</note>, it is the same as *daemon* <note>original: Δαίμων (Greek)</note>, or "demon," which is already used in Scripture in a negative sense to mean an impure spirit. As an adjective, it sometimes signifies "something divine" <note>original: "Divinum quid" (Latin)</note>, but that is not how it is understood in the passages we are debating. For example, in Luke 4:35: "When the devil had thrown the possessed man down in the midst of them, he came out of him"; here, the word used is *to daimonion* <note>original: τὸ Δαιμόνιον (Greek)</note>. The same being in verse 33 is called a "spirit of an unclean demon" <note>original: "πνεῦμα δαιμονίου ἀκαθάρτου" (Greek)</note>. 

From this, and the subsequent details of the story, it clearly appears that *to daimonion* <note>original: τὸ δαιμόνιον (Greek)</note> is to be understood as a noun referring to a *person*—namely, an evil spirit. The same is true in the story of the devils entering the herd of pigs,

# P R E F A C E.

...the right way if he attempts anything that is really excellent; instead, he must study *small ways to please* <note>original: "little plausibilities"</note> and adapt to the mood of the MANY, who are the *active distributors of fame*. As for these people, it is one of my chief concerns to make myself as unconcerned by their criticisms <note>original: "Censures"</note> as I am by the cackling of a flock of geese, or by the sharp displeasure of those little snarling *animals* <note>Likely referring to small dogs.</note> that are angry when I walk along the streets. Nor can any man be either wise or happy until he has arrived at that greatness of *mind* where he considers the *gossip* of the *masses* no more than the whistling of the *wind*. 

This is not because I think the *common people* should be despised <note>original: "contemned"</note> for the weakness of their *understanding*; it is an arrogant pettiness of spirit that does that. But when conceited ignorance sits in the *judgment seat* and gives final *verdicts* upon things beyond its *reach* <note>original: "Line"</note>, the wise man smiles and passes by. For such people (if this may serve to keep them from troubling themselves with the following C O N S I D E R A T I O N S), I want them to take notice from me that I did not write these things for people like them. They would do well to give up the book upon reading this *notice* <note>original: "Advertisment"</note>, unless they are willing to hear this: that although *philosophical discourses* intended to justify the common belief about *witches* mean nothing at all to them or those of their caliber, they are nonetheless very timely and necessary for our age, in which *atheism* begins with *Sadducism* <note>original: "Sadducism"; a term used in the 17th century to describe the denial of the existence of spirits or the supernatural, referencing the ancient Jewish sect of Sadducees who denied the resurrection.</note>.

### P R E F A C E.

And those who do not dare to say bluntly, "*There is NO GOD*," satisfy themselves (as an easy first step and *Introduction*) by denying that there are *SPIRITS* or *WITCHES*. This type of *Infidel* <note>original: "Infidels"; here referring to those who lack faith in the spiritual world</note>, though not common among the ordinary <term>vulgar</term> <note>original: "meer vulgar"; referring to the common people or the uneducated</note>, is quite numerous among those with a slightly higher level of education. Anyone with knowledge of the world knows that most of the more dissolute *Gentry*, and those who superficially pretend to *Philosophy* and *Wit*, generally mock the belief in *Witches* and *Apparitions*.

If this were only a minor and purely theoretical mistake, I would not bother myself or them about it. But I fear this error has a *core* that is worse than *Heresy*. Therefore, regardless of how little I care about what people believe or teach regarding matters of personal *opinion*, I believe I have reason to be concerned about a matter that so closely affects the greatest *Interests* of religion. 

Indeed, I am sometimes astonished to consider the kind of age we live in, where some of the greatest *Impieties* <note>Acts of disrespect toward God or sacred things</note> are considered nothing more than *bugs* <note>original: "Bugs"; here meaning "bugbears" or imaginary scares used to frighten children</note>, scary *names*, invisible *trifles* <note>original: "Tittles"; very small particles or unimportant points</note>, *peccadillos* <note>minor sins</note>, or *fantasies* <note>original: "Chimera’s"; mythical creatures used to mean figments of the imagination</note>. 

The most tragic and significant examples are *SACRILEGE*, *REBELLION*, and *WITCHCRAFT*. Regarding the first two, there is a certain type of person (who is far from being a self-proclaimed enemy of religion) of whom I am unsure whether they even acknowledge such vices exist. We find no mention of them in their most detailed *Confessions*, nor have I noticed them in those sermons that contain the longest *catalogues* of the sins of our age and nation. ### PREFACE.

...who should be found guilty. But my business at present is not with these people, but with the other subject, *WITCHCRAFT*, which I am certain was a sin in earlier times. How does it happen that our *age*, which so greatly surpasses former times in all other kinds of wickedness, should be entirely innocent in this one? I believe I have demonstrated in the following *CONSIDERATION* that there *MAY* be *WITCHES* and *apparitions* in our day, despite the objections of the modern <term>Sadducee</term> <note>original: "Sadduce". Historically, the Sadducees were a Jewish sect that denied the resurrection and the existence of spirits; here, Glanvill uses the term for contemporary skeptics who deny the supernatural.</note>. In that section, I did not primarily intend to provide direct proof, but rather a *DEFENSE*, as stated in the title of the first edition, which has been restored in these later mentioned versions.

And if it should be objected that I have mostly used suppositions and conjectures to vindicate common belief, and that I do not speak with absolute, point-blank certainty in my specific answers as I do in my general conclusion, I need only say this: the proposition I defend is a *matter of fact*, which disbelievers attack by alleging that it *cannot be* or is *not likely*. In response, if I show how those things *may* exist—and probably do, despite their allegations—it is enough for the purpose of a *defense*, even if I do not provide a definitive *proof*. I do not claim to know the exact way these things occur, but when someone says a thing cannot be, and I show how it possibly may be, I defeat their objection. This makes way for the evidence of the thing <term>de facto</term> <note>Latin: "in fact" or "in reality".</note>, which I have now added from the <term>divine Oracles</term> <note>original: "divine Oracles"; a reference to the Holy Scriptures or the Bible.</note> and two modern accounts that are clear and beyond reproach.
