# PREFACE

I have no inclination or delight in telling stories, and I do not publish these for the gratification of those who do. Instead, I record them as *arguments* for the *confirmation* of a truth which has indeed been attested to by a multitude of similar evidence in all places and times. However, things that are *remote* or *long past* are either not believed or are forgotten; whereas these accounts—being *recent* and *near*, and accompanied by all the circumstances of credibility—it may be expected that they should have more success against the obstinacy of unbelievers.

But after all this, I must confess there is *one argument* against me that cannot be dealt with: namely, a *mighty confidence* grounded upon *nothing*, which boasts, blusters, and swears there are no **Witches**. As for such *philosophers* as these, let them enjoy the *opinion* of their own superlative *judgments*, and let them rank me among the greatest *fools* for trusting my *senses*—and those of the entire *world*—over their *sworn dictates*. If they choose to believe in *Scot* <note>original: "Scott"; referring to Reginald Scot (c. 1538–1599), whose book *The Discoverie of Witchcraft* argued that belief in witchcraft was irrational and unbiblical.</note>, *Hobbes* <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the materialist philosopher whose work was often seen as denying the existence of incorporeal spirits.</note>, and *Osborne* <note>Francis Osborne (1593–1659), a popular author known for his skeptical and secular "Advice to a Son."</note>, and think them more *infallible* than the *Holy Scriptures* <note>original: "sacred Oracles"</note>, the *history* of all *ages*, and the full experience of our *own*, who can help it? They must not be *contradicted*, and they are resolved not to be *persuaded*. Regarding this sort of men, I never attempt to convince them of anything. If I can avoid it, I throw nothing before them, *lest they should turn again and tear me to pieces* <note>original: "rend me"; a reference to the biblical warning in Matthew 7:6 regarding "throwing pearls before swine."</note>. Their *opinions* entered their heads by chance, at a time when their limited *reasoning* <note>original: "little Reasons"</note> took no notice of their entry; they must be left alone to leave the same way they entered. # PREFACE.

To make much noise to disturb these infallible *Huffers* <note>original: "Huffers"; a 17th-century term for blustering, arrogant critics or braggarts.</note>—and they cannot hear a little for their *own noise*—I softly step by them, leaving only this whisper behind me: That although their *worshipful ignorance* and *fottishness* <note>original: "fottishness"; meaning foolishness, stupidity, or mental dullness.</note> can relish nothing of a discourse that does not minister to sensuality and unbelief, yet my **CONSIDERATIONS** have had the good fortune of a better reception from braver and more generous spirits than my fondest hopes could have expected. 

Persons whose good thoughts I have reason to value have assured me that their kindness toward my book has improved upon second and more careful perusals. I mention this for a specific purpose: that those who need my remarks, but cannot "feel" or understand them in a *running* <note>original: "running reading"; meaning a quick, superficial, or hasty reading.</note> reading, may please to turn their eyes back and deliberately think over what I have offered. From such a course, I dare promise them more *satisfaction* than they will find from their *haste*.

*Bath, June*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*8. 1668.*

As for skepticism <note>original: "Infidelity"</note>, we should be grateful to such people if they believe in either angels or spirits, the resurrection of the body, or the immortality of souls. These concepts are linked together in a chain of connection—at least in the theories <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note> of these men—and it is only by a lucky chance if a person who has lost one link in the chain still holds onto another. Since the vital core of religion is so deeply connected to this subject, it will be a useful task to discuss it in detail.

To prove that there have been and are illegal alliances <note>original: "Confederacies"</note> with evil spirits—through which these hellish accomplices perform acts beyond their natural abilities—I must first state that this is a matter of fact. As such, it can only be proven by the evidence of history <note>original: "Authority"</note> and the senses; and by both of these, the existence of witches and diabolical contracts is most fully confirmed. All *histories* are filled with the deeds of these instruments of darkness. The testimony of every age—not only from the uneducated and primitive <note>original: "rude and barbarous"</note> but also from the most civilized and refined parts of the world—brings news of their strange performances. We have the testimony of thousands of eyewitnesses and ear-witnesses. These are not just easily deceived commoners <note>original: "Vulgar"</note>, but wise and serious observers; and this evidence comes from times when they had no reason to conspire in a shared lie. 

I say we have the light of all these circumstances to confirm our belief in things done by people of pathetic <note>original: "despicable"</note> power and knowledge—acts that are beyond the reach of human skill <note>original: "Art"</note> or ordinary nature. Permanent public records have been kept of these well-documented accounts, and major eras <note>original: "Epochas"</note> have been defined by those unusual events. Laws in many nations have been enacted against these vile practices; the laws among the *Jews* and our own are well known. Such cases have often been decided in our own regions by wise and respected judges based on clear and convincing evidence, and thousands in our own nation have been executed for their evil agreements <note>original: "Compacts"</note> with fallen spirits <note>original: "Apostate-Spirits"</note>. 

I could prove all of these with many specific examples, but it is not necessary. Those who deny the existence of witches do not do so out of ignorance of these arguments—which they have probably heard a thousand times—but from a belief that such a conviction is absurd and the events impossible. Based on these assumptions, they despise all proof of this nature and are hardened against being convinced. ## S E C T I O N II.

Objection 1. *The concept of a spirit is impossible and contradictory; consequently, so is the concept of witches, since the belief in them is based on that doctrine.*

**T**o this objection, I answer: First, if the concept of a <term>spirit</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "spirit" was an incorporeal substance, as opposed to physical "matter."</note> is absurd, as is claimed, then the concept of a God and a <term>soul</term> <note>The non-physical, immortal essence of a human being.</note>—distinct from <term>matter</term> and immortal—are also absurdities. If that were true, it would mean that the world was jumbled into this elegant and orderly structure by chance, and that our souls are only parts of matter that came together from some unknown place in an unknown way, and shall soon be dissolved again into those loose <term>atoms</term> <note>The author is likely critiquing "atomism" or "corpuscularianism," which some feared led to atheism by explaining the world through physical particles alone.</note> that make them up. It would mean that all our thoughts are nothing but the pushing of one part of matter against another, and the ideas in our minds are merely blind and accidental motions. These, and a thousand more of the most glaring impossibilities and absurdities (the consequences of the proposition *that the concept of a spirit is absurd*), would become sad certainties and proven facts. I would stop debating with anyone who asserts such things.

And yet, secondly, even if it were granted to them that an immaterial substance <note>A substance that is not made of physical matter; a spirit.</note> is as much of a contradiction as they imagine, why should they still not believe that the air and all the regions above us might have their own invisible, intellectual agents of nature? These would be like our souls—whatever those may be—and some of them at least as corrupt as the most vile and mischievous of men. This *hypothesis* <note>original: "Hypothesis"; a proposed explanation or theory.</note> would be sufficient to establish the possibility of *witches* and *apparitions*. And that all the upper levels of the universe are occupied by inhabitants is an infinitely reasonable conclusion to draw from the analogy of *nature*. For we see there is nothing so lowly or insignificant in the world we live in that does not have living creatures dwelling upon it: the earth, the water, the lower atmosphere, the bodies of animals, the flesh, the skin, the internal organs, the leaves, the roots, and the stalks of plants—even all kinds of minerals in the regions underground.

I say, all of these have their own proper inhabitants; indeed, I suspect this rule may hold true for every distinct kind of physical body in the world: *that they all have their own specific animals.* The certainty of this will, I believe, be revealed by improvements in *microscopical* <note>original: "Microscopical"; relating to observations made with a microscope. In the 17th century, the recent invention of the microscope revealed a "new world" of tiny organisms, which the author uses here to argue for the existence of other invisible beings.</note> observations. From this I infer that since this little speck of a world is so densely populated in every *atom* <note>original: "Atome"; the smallest possible unit of matter.</note> of it, it is a sign of weakness to think that all the vast spaces above us and the hollows underground are deserted and uninhabited. And if both the higher and lower regions of the universe also have their inhabitants, it is—arguing from the same analogy—exceedingly improbable that they are all purely physical beings. Rather, it is likely that at least some belong to the *rational and intellectual* orders. Once this is assumed, there is a good foundation for the belief in *witches* and *apparitions*, even if the concept of a spirit should prove to be as absurd and unphilosophical as I consider the denial of it to be. ## S E C T. III.

**Objection II.** **T**HERE are actions in most of those accounts ascribed to witches which are ridiculous and impossible in the nature of things. Such are: (1) their flying out of windows to remote places after they have anointed themselves; (2) their transformation into cats, hares, and other creatures; (3) their feeling all the injuries in their own bodies which they received while in those animal forms; (4) their raising tempests by muttering some nonsensical words or performing ceremonies that are as irrelevant as they are ridiculous; and (5) their being sucked in a certain private place on their bodies by a familiar <note>original: "Familiar"; a demonic spirit or supernatural entity believed to serve and assist a witch</note>. These are presumed to be actions inconsistent with the nature of spirits and beyond the power of those poor and miserable agents. Therefore, the objection supposes them to be performed only by the fancy, and that the whole mystery of witchcraft is but an illusion of a disordered <note>original: "crasie"</note> imagination.

**T**O this multi-part objection I reply: (1) In general, the more absurd and unaccountable these actions seem, the greater confirmations they are to me of the truth of those accounts and the reality of what the objectors seek to destroy. Because these circumstances are exceedingly unlikely when judged by the standards of common belief, there is a greater probability that they are not fictitious. For the creators of fictions usually form them as closely as they can to the most believable realities, endeavoring to make them look as much like truth as possible in their main assumptions, even if they make the specific circumstances strange. 

None but a fool or a madman would relate, with the intention of being believed, that he saw in Ireland men with hoofs on their heads and eyes in their breasts. Or, if anyone should be so ridiculously vain as to be serious in such an incredible romance <note>original: "Romance"; here meaning a fictional tale or tall story</note>, it cannot be supposed that all travelers who visit those parts after him should tell the same story. 

There is a large field for invention in fiction; and if all those accounts were arbitrary compositions, the first storytellers would undoubtedly have framed them to be more agreeable to the common doctrine of spirits. At the least, after these supposed absurdities had been laughed at a thousand times, people by this time would have learned to correct those offensive extravagances; and though they may have no more truthfulness <note>original: "veracity"</note> than the...

And if they are *fancies*, it is somewhat strange that *imagination*, which is the most varied thing in all the world, should endlessly repeat the same *concept* <note>original: "conceit"</note> in all times and places.

But again, (2) the strange *actions* related to *witches*, and presumed impossible, are not attributed to their own powers, but to the agency of those wicked *confederates* they employ. To affirm that those evil *spirits* cannot do what we imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> to be impossible is to boldly limit <note>original: "stint"</note> the powers of creatures whose natures and faculties we do not know; it is to measure the world of *spirits* by the narrow rules of our own powerless *beings*. We see among ourselves that the achievements of some exceed the understanding <note>original: "conceits"</note> and perceived possibilities of others. We know many things may be done through *mathematics* and *mechanical skill* <note>original: "mechanic artifice"</note> that ordinary people <note>original: "common heads"</note> think impossible to be achieved through the honest methods of *art* <note>In this context, "art" refers to human technology or craftsmanship.</note> and *nature*.

And doubtless, the subtleties and powers of those *mischievous fiends* are as far beyond the reach and activities of the most knowledgeable *experts* <note>original: "agents"</note> among us as those experts' abilities are beyond the wit and ability of the most rustic and illiterate person. So the most that any man’s reason in the world can amount to in this particular case is only this: that he cannot conceive how such things can be performed. This only proves the weakness and imperfection of our *knowledge* and *understanding* <note>original: "apprehensions"</note>, not the impossibility of those performances. We can no more form an argument against them from this than we can against the most ordinary effects in *nature*. 

We cannot conceive how the *fetus* is formed in the *womb*, nor even how a plant springs from the earth we tread on. We do not know how our souls move our bodies, nor how these distant and extreme natures are united—as I have abundantly shown in my *Scepsis Scientifica* <note>Joseph Glanvill’s 1665 book, which argued for a skeptical approach to science and philosophy, suggesting that human reason is too limited to understand the deep mysteries of the world.</note>. And if we are ignorant of the most obvious things around us, and the most significant things within ourselves, then it is no wonder that we do not know the constitution and powers of the creatures to whom we are such strangers. Briefly, then, matters of *fact* that are well-proven ought not to be denied simply because we cannot conceive how they can be performed. Nor is it a reasonable method of reasoning <note>original: "inference"</note> to first presume a thing is impossible and then conclude from that assumption that the fact cannot be proved. (3) I think there is nothing in the *instances* mentioned, but what may as well be accounted for by the *rules of reason* and *philosophy*, as the ordinary affairs of *nature*. For in resolving *natural phenomena*, we can only assign the probable *causes*, showing how things *may be*, not presuming how they *are*. And in the particulars under our *examination* <note>original: "Examen"</note>, we may give an account how it is *possible*, and not unlikely, that such things (though somewhat varying from the common road of *nature*) may be acted. And if our narrow and contracted *minds* can furnish us with understandings of the way and manner of such performances—though perhaps not the true ones—it is an argument that such things may be effected by *creatures* whose powers and knowledge so vastly exceed ours. I shall endeavor therefore briefly to suggest some things that may render the *possibility* of these performances conceivable, in order to the removal of this *objection*: that they are *contradictions* and *impossible*.

For the FIRST then, that the *confederate spirit* <note>original: "confederate Spirit"; a spirit or demon acting in league with a witch</note> should transport the *witch* through the *air* to the place of general *rendezvous*, there is no difficulty in conceiving it; and if that be true which great *philosophers affirm* concerning the real *separability* of the *soul* from the *body* without *death*, there is yet less difficulty. For then it is easy to apprehend that the *soul*, having left its gross and sluggish body behind it and being clothed only with its *immediate vehicle of air*, or more *subtle matter*, may be quickly conducted to any place it would be at by those *helpful spirits* <term>officious spirits: in the 17th century, "officious" meant dutiful or eager to serve, rather than meddlesome</term> that attend it. And though I venture to affirm nothing concerning the truth and certainty of this *supposition*, yet I must say it does not seem to me unreasonable. Our experience of *apoplexy*, *epilepsy*, *ecstasies*, and the strange things *men* report to have seen during those *fainting fits* <term>deliquiums: a period of fainting, swooning, or loss of consciousness</term>, look favorably upon this *conjecture*. This seems to me to contradict no principle of *reason* or *philosophy*, since *death* consists not so much in the *actual separation of soul and body*, as in the *unsuitability* and *unfitness of the body* for vital union, as an excellent *philosopher* has made good. On which *hypothesis*, the *witch's* anointing herself before she takes her flight may perhaps serve to keep the *body* habitable <note>original: "tenantable"</note> and in fit *disposition* to receive the *spirit* at its return. of his predictions; for if he had foretold the King's good success and victory, the woman and he, the confederate <note>original: "Confederate"; meaning an accomplice or secret partner in a deception</note>, would consequently have been sure of reputation, favor, and further rewards if it happened so. But no evil could have befallen them from the contrary success: for if Saul was killed, the falsehood of the prediction would be buried with him (for we do not read that the two servants were present at this communication, which in all likelihood was private) and no other evil was likely to ensue.

So that if it were a confederate knave, as the witch-advocates <note>The author's term for skeptics like Reginald Scot and John Webster who argued against the reality of witchcraft and spirits</note> have contrived, who gave the answers, he was not as cunning as Mr. Scot, Mr. Webster, and the rest pretend, but indeed a very silly juggler <note>original: "Juggler"; here meaning a common street magician or fraud</note>. He speaks very severe and disobliging things, and such as were not likely to result in his advantage; and indeed, they were the kind of things that do not at all look as if they proceeded from a confederate cozener <note>original: "Couzener"; a swindler or cheat</note>. They have that gravity, majesty, religion, and virtue in them that became the true Samuel, and are very unlike the words of a vicious, cheating knave.

To which may be added, that this woman, though otherwise an ill one, seems to have been of a kind and benign nature, by the courteous entertainment she gave the afflicted Prince; and Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Jewish historian</note> extols her much for her good nature. So it is very improbable that she would, by herself or her confederate, lay such a heavy load of trouble and desperation upon the King, who was in such distress before. I think all these things put together are abundantly sufficient to disprove and shame the ungrounded fancy of the witch-advocates—that all was done by a confederate. And consequently, it was a real apparition that Saul saw and to which he did civil obeisance <note>original: "Obeyſance"; a gesture of respect, such as bowing</note>.

->*That it was Samuel himself who appeared, not the*<-

BUT the "witch-advocates" <note>the author's term for skeptics who argued that witchcraft was either a delusion or a fraud</note> have another argument to prove an imposture in this business. For, they say, the person pronouncing the fate of Saul could not be the true Samuel, nor the Devil in his likeness; therefore it must be either the woman or some cheating accomplice. This conclusion does not follow, for it is possible it might be a good spirit impersonating Samuel. The Scripture assures us that these are often employed in errands and ministries here below, and on those occasions, they clothe themselves in human shape and appearance. So it is not absurd to think it might be thus here; but I do not affirm this. Who it actually was has been a great matter of debate among interpreters, and considerable authors have been on either side. My cause does not require that I should positively determine who the appearing person was; it might be one of them, though I cannot tell which.

I confess it seems to me most probable that it was the true Samuel, for the Scripture calls the apparition so five times—that is, as often as he is mentioned. And "when the woman saw Samuel" (v. 12); and "Saul perceived that it was Samuel" (v. 14); and "Samuel said to Saul" (v. 15); then "said Samuel to Saul" (v. 16); then "Saul was sorely afraid because of the words of Samuel" (v. 20). These expressions are from neither Saul nor the woman, but from that Spirit that inspired the Holy Scriptures. And if after all this, Samuel was a scoundrel, or the witch, or the Devil, what assurance can we have in interpreting the Scripture? I know that...

## SECTION IV.

<margin>Objection III.</margin> **BUT** (III) I come to another prejudice against the existence of *witches*, which is: that it is very improbable that the *Devil*, who is a wise and mighty *spirit*, should be at the beck and call of a poor *hag*, and have so little to do that he would attend to the *errands* and weak lusts of a foolish *old woman*.

**T**O which I might answer: (1) That it is much more improbable that the whole *world* should be deceived in matters of *fact* and circumstances of the clearest evidence and conviction, than that the *Devil*, who is wicked, should also be *unwise*. He who persuades all his *subjects* and *accomplices* out of their wits might very well act in accordance with his own *temptations* and *persuasions*. In brief, there is nothing more strange in this *objection* than the fact that wickedness is inherently base and servile; the *Devil* has the leisure to serve those he has the leisure to tempt and is industrious to ruin. 

And again: (2) I see no necessity to believe that the *Devil* is always the *witch's confederate*. Instead, it may be worth considering whether the *familiar* <note>A supernatural spirit or demon believed to serve a witch, often taking the shape of an animal.</note> might be some departed *human spirit*—one forsaken by *God* and goodness, and swallowed up by an insatiable desire for mischief and revenge, which it perhaps cannot execute directly because of the *laws* and limitations of its current state. 

I know no reason why we should assume that the *Devil* should have the liberty of wandering up and down the *earth* and *air* (when he is said to be held in "chains of darkness"), and yet believe that the departed *souls* of the wicked—of whom no such thing is affirmed in any *sacred record*—should be thought so imprisoned that they cannot possibly move from the place of their *confinement*. I am confident this misconception has prejudiced many against the belief in *witches* and *apparitions*. They are unable to conceive that the *Devil* would be as ridiculous as appearing *spirits* are sometimes reported to be in their "frolics," and they assume that *souls* who have departed never revisit the free and open *regions* of the living. I know of nothing to justify such confidence. For since good *men* in their state of separation are said to be *equal to angels* <note>original: ἰσάγγελοι (isangeloi). See Luke 20:36.</note>, I see no reason why the wicked may not be supposed to be *equal to demons* <note>original: ἰσοδαίμονες (isodaimones).</note> in the worst sense of the word. And if it is supposed that the *imps* of *witches* are sometimes wicked *spirits* of our own kind and nature...

**T**O this seemingly persuasive objection, I have these things to answer: (1) *Providence* is an unfathomable depth. This way of acting by subtle and invisible instruments is ordinary and familiar in all natural operations <note>original: "Efficiencies"</note>. ## SECTION VI.

**Objection V.** It might then be argued that if wicked spirits can hurt us at the direction and desire of a witch, one would think they should have the same power to injure us without any prompting or *compact* <note>original: "compact"; a formal agreement or contract with the Devil</note>. If this were true, it is a wonder that we are not constantly harassed and infected by them.

**To** which I reply: (1) The laws, liberties, and restraints of the inhabitants of the other *world* are utterly unknown to us. By debating this, we can only end up confessing our own ignorance—which every person must acknowledge, unless they are as arrogant as they are ignorant. It must be granted by all who acknowledge the existence, power, and malice of evil spirits, that the security we enjoy is wonderful, whether they act through *witches* or not. To speak as philosophers, we cannot say by what laws they are kept from preying upon us. Indeed, why they should be permitted to tempt and ruin our souls, yet be restrained from touching or hurting our bodies, is a mystery that is not easily explained. 

(2) However, even though we acknowledge their power to vex and torment our bodies as well, a reason can still be given as to why <meta>catchword: they</meta>

They are less frequent in this kind of mischief for this reason: <note>original: "viz." (namely)</note> because their main designs are leveled against the interest and happiness of our souls. They can best promote these designs when their actions are most *sly* and *secret*. On the other hand, if they usually persecuted men's bodies, their agency and wicked influence would be discovered and create a great stir in the world. As a result, people would be awakened to a suitable and vigorous opposition by using methods that would engage Providence <note>God's divine intervention or protective care</note> to rescue them from the spirits' rage and cruelties, ultimately defeating them in their great purpose of *undoing us eternally*.

Thus, we can understand that the security we enjoy is entirely consistent with the power and malice of those evil spirits. For this reason, we may suppose that they have their own laws prohibiting unlicensed injuries—not because there is any goodness in their nature, but to carry out the projects of the *dark kingdom* more successfully. This is similar to how generals forbid plundering, not out of love for their enemies, but to ensure their own success. 

And therefore (3), we may suppose that a law allowing them to hurt us at the request of a sorceress fits well with the *policy* of *hell*. By gratifying the wicked person, the spirits encourage her in malice and revenge. This promotes the main goals of their *black confederacy*, which are to spread wickedness and ruin our *eternal interests*. 

And yet (4), it is clear to those who believe the *history* of the *Gospel* that wicked spirits have tormented the bodies of men without any *instigation* <note>prompting or urging</note> that we read of. Even today, it is very likely that many of the strange *accidents* and *diseases* that befall us may be *inflicted* by evil spirits, who are prompted to hurt us simply by the delight they take in *mischief*. So, we cannot argue that it is improbable for them to hurt *children* and others through *witches* based on our own sense of security and freedom from their malice—which we perhaps feel in more ways than we realize.

## SECTION VII.

Objection VI. **B**UT (VI) *another prejudice against the belief in witches is a presumption of the enormous force of melancholy <note>original: "Melancholy"; in this period, it referred to a clinical state of mental imbalance or depression believed to cause hallucinations</note> and imagination, which undoubtedly can do wonderful things and produce strange beliefs. To these causes, some people attribute the presumed effects of sorcery and witchcraft.*

To which I reply briefly, and yet I hope sufficiently:

(1) **T**O resolve all the clear *circumstances of fact*—which we find in well-attested and confirmed *accounts* <note>original: "Relations"</note> of this kind—into the power of *deceptive imagination* is to make *fancy* the greater *miracle* <note>original: "Prodigie"</note>. It is to suppose that imagination can perform stranger *feats* than are believed of any other kind of *bewitchment* <note>original: "Fascination"</note>. To think that *pins* and *nails*, for instance, can by the power of *imagination* be moved inside the *skin*; or that *imagination* should deceive so many who have been *witnesses* to *physical objects* <note>original: "Objects of Sense"</note> in all the *circumstances* of their *discovery*; this, I say, is to be infinitely more gullible <note>original: "credulous"</note> than those who support the existence of *sorcery* and *demonic contracts*. 

By the same reasoning, it may be believed that all the *battles* and *strange events* of the *world* which we have not seen ourselves are but *dreams* and foolish *imaginations*. It would be like saying those battles fought in the *clouds* <note>A common historical report of atmospheric phenomena interpreted as celestial armies</note> occur only when the *brains* of the deluded *spectators* are the only *theater* for those imagined *events*. 

And (2) to deny *evidence* of an *act* simply because the *narrators'* imaginations *might* deceive them—when we have no reason to think so other than a bare presumption that there is no such thing as what is related—is to completely destroy the credit of all *human testimony*. It would make *all men liars* in a larger sense than the *Prophet* <note>A reference to Psalm 116:11, "I said in my haste, All men are liars."</note> concluded in his haste. For not only the *melancholic* and the *fanciful*, but the *serious* and the *sober*—whose *judgments* we have no reason to suspect are tainted by their *imaginations*—have made reports of this *nature* based on their own *knowledge* and *experience*.

## S E C T. VIII.

Objection VII. **T**hat it is a *suspicious circumstance*, suggesting that *witchcraft* is but a *product of the imagination* <note>original: "Fancy"</note>, since the *persons who are accused* are commonly *poor and miserable old women*. These women are *consumed by discontent and melancholy* <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was thought to be a physical imbalance of "black bile" that caused depression and hallucinations.</note>, which makes them very *prone to delusions*. Furthermore, the *persons said to be bewitched* are for the most part *children* or *people who are very weak*, who are easily *deceived* <note>original: "imposed upon"</note> and are apt to receive *strong impressions from nothing*. Whereas, if there were any such thing *really*, it is unlikely that more cunning and subtle *desperados*—who could more successfully carry out the mischievous designs of the dark kingdom—should not be more often engaged in those black *conspiracies* <note>original: "Confederacies"</note>. One would also expect the effects of this hellish combination to fall upon *others* besides the innocent and ignorant.

Mankind is no more acquainted with the *reasons* and *methods of action* in the other world than poor *laborers* <note>original: "Cottagers"</note> and *tradespeople* <note>original: "Mechanicks"</note> are with the *intrigues of government* and *reasons of state*. 

Indeed, perhaps (2) it is one of the great designs, as it is certainly the *interest*, of those wicked agents and *plotters* <note>original: "Machinators"</note> to industriously hide their *influences* and *ways of acting* from us, and to work as much as possible *incognito* <note>original: "incognito" - in disguise or unseen</note>. Based on this supposition, it is easy to conceive a reason why they most commonly work by, and upon, the *weak* and the *ignorant*, who can make no clever *observations* or tell credible *stories* to detect their *trickery* <note>original: "Artifice"</note>. 

Besides, (3) it is likely that a strong *imagination*, which cannot be weakened or disturbed by busy and subtle *logical reasoning* <note>original: "ratiocination"</note>, is a necessary requirement for those wicked performances. I am very inclined to believe that there are as real *communications* and *interactions* between our *spirits* as there are between material *agents*. ## Section 9.

Objection 8. **T**he frequent *impostures* <note>original: "impostures" — frauds or deceptions</note> that are encountered in this field lead some to *believe* that all such *accounts* are *forgeries and fables*. If we provide the *evidence* of a *story* to support the *belief* in *witches* or *apparitions*, they will produce two others that seem just as strong and plausible, which ultimately turn out to be *mistakes* or *intentional deceptions*. From this, they infer that all other accounts are of the same *quality* and *credibility*.

->But such *arguers* should please consider:<-

(1) **T**hat a single *account* <note>original: "relation" — a report or narrative of an event</note> supporting an *affirmative* case, if sufficiently confirmed and attested, is worth a thousand *tales* of *forgery* and *imposture*. One cannot conclude a *universal negative* <note>A logical term meaning a claim that "nothing of this sort exists." The author argues you can't prove witches don't exist just because some reports are fake.</note> from such examples. So, even if all of the *objector's stories* were *true*, and there were a hundred times as many more such *deceptions*, yet one *account* in which no *fallacy* or *fraud* could be suspected to support our *affirmative* position would ruin any *conclusion* they tried to build upon them.

And (2), it seems to me a belief that is quite bold and unstable to assume that *all* these *reports* of *forgery* and *mistake* are certain, while not a single one among all those which attest to the *affirmative reality*—with circumstances as good as could be expected or wished—should be *true*; but rather, that all are *mythical* and *empty*. Those who can swallow such a large claim have no reason to accuse the *assertors* of *sorcery* and *witchcraft* of *credulity* <note>original: "credulity" — a tendency to be too ready to believe that something is real or true</note>. I desire such *objectors* to consider:

(3) Whether it is fair to infer that because there are some *cheats* and *impostors*, there are therefore no *realities*. Indeed, the frequency of *deceit* and *fallacy* warrants greater care and caution in examining evidence. It justifies *scrupulosity* <note>original: "scrupulosity" — extreme care or hesitation</note> and a *hesitancy* to *assent* to things where *fraud* has been practiced or may be in the least degree suspected. But to conclude that because an old *woman’s imagination* deceived her, or some *knavish* fellows played *tricks* upon the *ignorant* and *fearful*, that therefore entire *Assizes* <note>original: "Assizes" — periodic courts held in English counties for civil and criminal trials</note> have been deceived a thousand times in *judgments* upon matters of *fact*, and numbers of sober *people* have committed *perjury* in matters where *perjury* could not benefit them—I say, such *inferences* are as lacking in *reason* as they are in *charity* and *good manners*.

This account, I think, is not unreasonable, and it will fully answer the objection. For even if the matter is not exactly as I have conjectured, it still suggests how it *might* be understood; this voids the claim that the goal of witchcraft is inconceivable.

Thus was *Jerusalem* forewarned before its sacking by *Antiochus* by those *airy horsemen* who were seen throughout the city for almost 40 days together (2 Maccabees 5:2–3), as well as the other miraculous portents that preceded its destruction by *Titus*—which I mention because they are famous examples. And though, for my own part, I despise the common tales of prodigies that arise from superstitious fears and an ignorance of nature—and which have been used for bad purposes by the *zealous* and the *ignorant*—I still think the arguments brought by a recent, very clever author to dismiss all such warnings and predictions entirely are flawed and illogical, built upon too narrow a *hypothesis*. 

For if it is supposed that there is a class of spirits over us and around us who can make a probable guess at significant future events, I do not see why it may not be conjectured that the kindness they have for us, and their natural desire to foretell strange things and keep the world in expectation (which we find is very pleasing to our own natures), might incline them to give us some general notice of those uncommon events they foresee. I see no reason to imagine that everything of this kind must necessarily come either directly from heaven or from angels by extraordinary commission and appointment. 

Instead, it seems reasonable to me to believe that those helpful spirits <note>original: "officious spirits"; in this period, "officious" meant performing a duty or being helpful rather than meddlesome</note> who oversee our affairs, perceiving some mighty and sad changes at hand in which their charges are much concerned, cannot help—because of their *affection* for us—but give us some timely hints of those approaching calamities; their natural desire to predict strange future events may also play a part. By this *hypothesis*, the most likely probabilities and strongest logical arguments <note>original: "ratiocinations"</note> against prodigies may be rendered useless. But this is only an observation in passing.

# SECTION XIII.

I desire it may be considered further:

(3) That God himself grants his intimacy and conversation to *better souls* who are prepared for it; this is a *privilege* infinitely beyond *angelic correspondence*.

I confess that the proud and fantastical <term>fanciful or imaginary</term> claims to *divine communion* made by many of the conceited *melancholies* <note>original: "Melancholists"; in this period, "melancholy" often referred to people believed to be suffering from religious delusions or overactive imaginations.</note> in this age have prejudiced many intelligent people against believing in such a happy *granting of favor*. Consequently, they conclude that the *doctrine of immediate communion* with the *Deity* in this life is nothing more than a *high-flown notion of a heated imagination and overly sweet self-flattery*. I acknowledge that I myself have had thoughts of this nature, supposing *communion with God* to be nothing more than the exercise of virtue and the *peace* and *comforts* that naturally result from it.

But I have since considered that God’s more direct and *immediate* imparting of himself to the soul—prepared for that happiness by *divine love, humility*, and *resignation*—through a *vital touch and feeling*, is possible in itself and will be a large part of our heaven. *Glory* begins in *grace*, and God is pleased to give some excellent souls a *happy foretaste* <note>original: "Antepast"; literally an appetizer or preliminary meal, here meaning a taste of heavenly joy while still on earth.</note>. Holy men in ancient times *sought* and gloried in this *enjoyment*, and never complained so *bitterly* as when it was *withheld and interrupted*. The *expressions of Scripture* lean heavily in this direction, and the *best of modern* good men attest to it from their own experience. 

This *spiritualizes religion* and makes its enjoyments more *comfortable and delightful*. It keeps the soul under a *vivid awareness* of God and is a *great safeguard against temptation*. It holds the soul steady amid the *flatteries* of a *prosperous state* and gives it the *most solid anchorage and support* amid the *waves* of an *unfortunate condition*. It is the noblest encouragement to *virtue* and the greatest assurance of a *happy immortality*. 

I say, I considered these *weighty matters* and wondered at the carelessness and prejudice of the thoughts that caused me to suspect the reality of such a glorious privilege. I saw how little reason there is in denying matters of *internal feeling* just because we ourselves do not feel them or cannot form a concept of them in our minds. It is the worst way to defend a good cause or to disprove a bad one. 

I have therefore consistently presented the most persuasive points I could think of on behalf of the objectors, because I did not want to deceive my reader or myself. The stronger I make their premises, the more I will weaken their conclusion if I successfully answer them. Whether I have succeeded or not, I leave to the judgment of thoughtful and fair-minded <note>original: "ingenious and considerate"</note> people. As for the supposed inadequacy of my response, I suggest that if the character of the people involved, their goals, and the outcomes are the best ways to distinguish <note>original: "best Notes of Distinction"</note> between true miracles and forgeries—or between divine and diabolical ones—then I have said enough to protect the miracles of our Savior and the *holy Men* of ancient times.

They show that even if *apparitions*, *witchcraft*, and *diabolical wonders* are admitted, none of these can cast a slur or create a dangerous doubt regarding the miraculous works of *JESUS* and his Apostles. ## SECT. XV.

**T**HE *sin against the Holy Ghost* is said to be *unpardonable*. By this sad attribute, and the discourse of our *Savior in Matthew 12:22–33*, we may understand its nature. In order to do so, we consider that since the mercies of God and the merits of His Son are infinite, nothing can make a sin *unpardonable* except what makes it incurable; and there is no sin but what is curable by a strong faith and vigorous endeavor: *For all things are possible to him who believes.* So, that which makes a sin incurable must be something that makes faith impossible and obstructs all means of conviction. 

To find this, we must consider the ways and methods *Divine Goodness* has taken to create faith and cure *infidelity* <note>original: "Infidelity"; here meaning a lack of religious belief or skepticism</note>. This was attempted first by the *prophets* and holy men of ancient times, who—by the excellence of their *doctrine*, the greatness of their *miracles*, and the holiness of their lives—endeavored to convince and reform a stubborn and unbelieving world. But though few believed their *report*, and men would not be persuaded by what they did or what they said, their *infidelity* was not yet incurable. Further means were provided in the ministry of *John the Baptist*, whose life was more severe <note>original: "severe"; meaning strictly disciplined or ascetic</note>, whose doctrines were more plain, pressing, and particular; and therefore it was possible that he might have succeeded. For *miracles* are *God's seal* and the great and final *evidence* of the *truth* of any *doctrine*. And though, while these are only disbelieved as to the *fact*, there remains a possibility of persuasion; yet when the *fact* shall be acknowledged but the *power blasphemed*, and the *effects* of the adorable *Spirit* maliciously imputed to the *devils*, such a *blasphemy* and such an *unbelief* is incurable and, consequently, *unpardonable*. I say, in some, the *sin* against the *Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> seems to be a malicious *imputation* of the *miracles* wrought by the *Spirit* of *God* in our *Savior* to *satanic conspiracy* <note>original: "Satanical Confederacy"</note> and the *power* of *fallen* <note>original: "Apostate"</note> *spirits*. Nothing is more *blasphemous* than this, and nothing is more likely to provoke the *Holy Spirit*—which is so abused—to an *eternal abandonment* <note>original: "Dereliction"</note> of so vile and so incurable an *unbeliever*.

This account, as it is clear and reasonable in itself, so it is plainly found in the mentioned *discourse* of our *Savior*. And most of those who say other things about it seem to me to talk at random and perfectly without *scriptural authority* <note>original: "without Book"</note>. But to leave them to the fondness of their own *notions* <note>original: "Conceits"</note>, I think it now time to draw to a *conclusion* of the whole.

## S E C T. XVI.

**T**HEREFORE, briefly, Sir, I have endeavored in these papers—which my respect and your interest in the subject have made yours—to remove the main prejudices I could think of against the existence of *witches* and *apparitions*. And I am sure I have suggested much more against what I defend than I have ever heard or seen from any who opposed it; whose discourses, for the most part, have seemed to me inspired by a lofty scorn of *common belief* and some trivial notions of *commonplace philosophy* <note>original: "vulgar Philosophy," referring to the unrefined or standard scholastic ideas of the time</note>. In despising the common *faith* regarding matters of *fact*, and foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note> adhering to it in matters of *speculation*, they make a very gross and absurd mistake. For in matters of *fact*, the *people* are as much to be believed as the most subtle philosophers and speculators, since here, *sense* is the judge; but in matters of *notions* and *theory*, they are not at all to be heeded, because *reason* is to be the judge of these, and they do not know how to use it. 

And yet, so it is with those "wise" philosophers who will deny the plain *evidence* of the *senses* of mankind because they cannot reconcile *appearances* with the foolish whims <note>original: "fond Crochets"</note> of a *philosophy* which they happened upon by chance in the *highway* and will stick to at any risk. So, I profess for my own part, I never yet heard any of the confident declaimers against *witchcraft* and *apparitions* say anything that might move a mind that is in any degree instructed in the noble <note>original: "generous"</note> kinds of *philosophy* and the *nature* of things. As for the *objections* I have recited, most of them are such as arose out of my own thoughts, as I felt obliged to consider what was possible to be said on this occasion.

For though I have examined *Scot’s Discovery* <note>Reginald Scot’s *The Discoverie of Witchcraft* (1584), the most famous skeptical work of the era</note>, fancying that there I should find the *strong reasons* for men's disbelief in this matter, I profess I did not meet with the least suggestion in all that *jumble* <note>original: "Farrago"</note> but what would have been ridiculous for me to have tried to *answer*. For the author does little but tell *odd tales* and *silly legends*, which he refutes and laughs at, and pretends this to be a *refutation* of the existence of *witches* and *apparitions*. In all of this, his *reasonings* are trifling and childish; and when he ventures into *philosophy*, he is little better than absurd; so that it will be a...

It is a wonder to me if anyone but boys and buffoons develop any prejudices against a belief so thoroughly confirmed, based on the loose and weak suggestions of such a poor reasoner. 

However, observing two things in that *Discourse* that would pretend to be more than ordinary *Reasons*, I shall have the courtesy to examine them. *It is said then:*

(1) *That the Gospel is silent as to the existence of* WITCHES; *and it is not likely, if there were such, that our Saviour or his Apostles would not have given hints of their existence.*
->The other is,<-
(2) *Miracles have ceased, and therefore the supernatural things ascribed to Witchcraft are assumed to be dreams and frauds.*

In answer to the first in order, I consider (1) that though the *History* of the *New Testament* were granted to be silent in the business of <term>Witches</term> and <term>Compacts</term> <note>original: "Compacts" refers to formal contracts or agreements made between a human and a spirit or the Devil.</note>, yet the *Records* of the *Old Testament* mention them frequently. The *Law* in *Exodus* 22:18 against permitting them to live (which I mentioned in the beginning) is famous. And we have another remarkable *Prohibition* of them in *Deuteronomy* 18:10, 11: *There shall not be found among you any one who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, or who uses divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer.* 

Now this accumulation of names (some of which have the same sense and meaning) is a plain indication that the *Hebrew Witch* was one who practiced by compact with evil spirits. And many of the same expressions are put together in the charge against *Manasseh* in 2 *Chronicles* 33, namely: That he caused *his children to pass through the fire, observed times, used enchantments and witchcraft, and dealt with familiar spirits and with wizards.* 

So, even if the original word which we translate as *Witch* and <term>Witchcraft</term> should—as our <term>Sadducees</term> <note>original: "Sadducees" refers to contemporary skeptics who, like the ancient Jewish sect, denied the existence of spirits or the resurrection.</note> urge—signify only a *cheat* and a *poisoner*, yet those other terms mentioned speak clearly enough of the thing itself. I have given an account in the former *Considerations* of how a *Witch* in the common notion is a *poisoner*. But I believe the denier of *Witches* will find it hard to explain why mere *poisoning* should have a distinct law against it and not be included under the general law against *murder*; or why mere <term>leger-de-main</term> <note>original: "Leger-de-main" refers to sleight of hand or deceptive trickery.</note> and *cheating* should be so severely criticized as to be ranked with *enchantments, converse with devils,* and *idolatrous practices.*

They saw that strange things were done and events predicted by such rituals and such words. They could not tell how it worked, nor is it likely they inquired; they satisfied themselves with the general explanation that it was by the power of their "arts," and were not concerned with any other reason. This, I say, was probably the case for most of those predictors, though it may be that others among them advanced further into the more desperate parts of the mystery. I have now finished with **SCOT** <note>Reginald Scot (c. 1538–1599), author of "The Discoverie of Witchcraft," who argued against the existence of witches.</note> and his *presumptions*; and I am inclined to imagine that there is nothing more needed to be said to "discover the discoverer." # A further Defense of the...

## SECTION XXII.

### Of the Greek Fathers dividing Fire into Intellective, Sensitive, and Vegetative, and in what sense they are to be understood, and how the mode of the ancient Philosophy was Enigmatic and Hebraic.

**A**ND the Greek Fathers, you say, who called *spirits fire* and distinguished *fire according to its forms* <note>original: "Ignem per Formas"</note> into *intellective, sensitive, and vegetative* <note>In the philosophy of the time, "intellective" relates to reason, "sensitive" to the senses/feelings, and "vegetative" to basic biological growth and survival.</note> or visible fire (as it is in *ignited air* <note>original: "Aere Ignito"</note>), allowing for an incomprehensible purity of *substance* in the higher levels above the lower (just as, in *passive* elements, air is purer than water), I think spoke reasonably and as informatively as the *notions of penetrability* <term>Penetrability: The philosophical idea that a spirit can occupy the same physical space as matter.</term> and *indivisibility* <term>Indivisibility: The idea that a soul or spirit cannot be broken into parts like physical matter.</term>, though perhaps these may also be useful. If the words and passages of these Fathers had been cited, I would have given a more distinct and particular answer to them; but as it stands, my answer must be more indeterminate and general.

And first, I say, though great respect should be given to the Fathers in things that were within their expertise, it is apparent that some of them were not the best philosophers, as seen from their belief that the Earth was flat rather than spherical, and their denial of the *Antipodes* <note>Antipodes: People living on the opposite side of the Earth. Some early church fathers thought this was impossible or heretical.</note>. But then, in the second place, even supposing some of them did philosophize in the manner described above—dividing fire into intellective, sensitive, and vegetative—I would ask in what sense they spoke. 

Were they not speaking of the immediate instrument of operation in intellective, sensitive, and vegetative creatures? I can easily agree that this instrument is, at least for the most part, igneous <note>igneous: fiery</note> or ethereal, since the *vehicles of angels* <note>The "Vehicle" of an angel was thought to be a subtle, celestial body made of light or fire that allowed a spirit to interact with the world.</note> are acknowledged to be such. Or, were they speaking symbolically *by design* <note>original: "ex Destinato"</note>? Or perhaps they were using the symbolic expressions of the ancient philosophers out of ignorance, taking them for literal truths—for those ancients symbolically called a spirit "fire," and even referred to God himself (who is the most pure spirit conceivable) as fire. Perhaps it was from that source that these Fathers incautiously divided fire as if it were a real spirit into intellective, sensitive, etc. For *Clement of Alexandria* <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note> expressly takes notice that the ancient philosophers spoke enigmatically: *that their method of philosophy among them was Hebraic and enigmatic* <note>original: "ὅτι ὁ τρόπος παρ' αὐτοῖς τῆς φιλοσοφίας Ἑβραϊκὸς ϗ Αἰνιγματώδης"</note>. In which say—

## SECTION XXIII.

### *That the symbolic or enigmatic mode of ancient philosophy caused marvelous, foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> mistakes in those who were unaware of it, such as Aristotle and others who took the husk <note>original: <term>Cortex</term></note> for the kernel.*

**A**ND ignorance of that style of the old philosophers has caused ridiculous opinions. For instance, because the ancient Mosaic Cabala <note>The author refers here to the "Kabbalah," specifically a Christianized or philosophical interpretation of Jewish mystical traditions attributed to Moses.</note> described the nature of things using numbers, those unskilled in the mystery later claimed that numbers were the actual constitutive principle of all things. 

And Aristotle made a similar mistake. Parmenides, speaking symbolically and in the manner of Moses, declared that fire and earth were the principles of all things. This was undoubtedly a reference to the beginning of Genesis, where "light and darkness" <note>original Hebrew: <term>אור וחשך</term> (or v'choshech)</note> are the two principles of things—namely, *spirit* and *matter*. I say, Aristotle is so foolish as to take Parmenides literally, even though Aristotle himself acknowledges that Parmenides ranked "earth" among "non-entities" <note>original Latin: <term>Non-entia</term>; things that do not truly exist</note>. It would have been impossible for Parmenides to do this unless he were speaking symbolically. 

These two elements, fire and earth, are the same as the Pythagoreans' "light and darkness" <note>original Greek: <term>φῶς καὶ σκότος</term> (phōs kai skotos)</note>, as they also shared in the Mosaic Cabala. See my *General Preface to the second volume of my Philosophical Writings*, Section 13, as well as the *Appendix to the Defense of my Philosophic Cabala*, Chapter 7, Section 5, and I hope you will acknowledge that I have reason on my side. Therefore, the fact that the Church Fathers—along with ancient philosophers—used the word "fire" <note>original Latin: <term>Ignis</term></note> for "spirit" <note>original Latin: <term>Spiritus</term></note> does not justify us in thinking that actual fire belongs to the very nature and essence of a spirit, since the term may have been used symbolically.

## S E C T. XXIV.

### *That the Chaldean and Magic Oracles call not only the Soul but God himself Fire; but that it is not to be understood literally, but symbolically—proved by the commentaries <note>original: "Glosses"</note> of Michael Psellus and Pletho.*

**T**HAT *Fire* <note>original: *Ignis*</note> is used to mean *Spirit* by the ancients is repeatedly clear from the *Magic* and *Chaldean* <note>The "Chaldean Oracles" were a collection of spiritual and philosophical texts from the 2nd century AD, highly regarded by Neoplatonists.</note> Oracles (to say nothing here of *Ezekiel’s* Vision, where God the Father is represented by *Fire*, a depiction which the *Cabbalists* <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note> also follow). These Oracles, I say, do not hesitate to call the highest Deity, from whom all things come, *Fire*. I believe it would be very crude and absurd to understand this in a literal sense regarding God. Therefore, both *Pletho* <note>George Gemistos Plethon (c. 1355–1452), a Byzantine philosopher who revived Neoplatonism.</note> and *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar who wrote commentaries on the Chaldean Oracles.</note>, commenting on that Oracle—"All things proceed out of one Fire" <note>original: Εἰσὶ πάντα πυρὸς ἑνὸς ἐκγεγαῶτα</note>—offer interpretations. The one says, "Out of one fire—that is, from one God" <note>original: ἐξ ἑνὸς πυρὸς ἥτις ἐξ ἑνὸς Θεοῦ</note>. The other says, "This is our doctrine and it is true: 'For all things received their existence from one God'" <note>original: Πάντα γὰρ τὰ ὄντα ἀπὸ μόνου Θεοῦ ὑπόστασιν ἔλαβον</note>. In these instances, they translate *fire* <note>original: πῦρ</note> as *God* <note>original: Θεὸς</note>. Unquestionably, they understood God in their proper philosophical sense as a pure, immaterial, and intellectual Being; otherwise, they would be making his nature inferior to that of a created spirit.

For when a created spirit is called fire in those Oracles—as the soul is explicitly termed "a shining fire" <note>original: πῦρ φαεινόν</note>—*Pletho* interprets the phrase, stripping it of its symbolic shell <note>original: cortex</note>, as "a certain divine and intellectual substance" <note>original: θεία τίς οὐσία καὶ νοερὰ</note>. It is called fire symbolically here, just as God himself is, to suggest its kinship with the Divinity itself. This is seen in the same Oracle, which in full is:

> "Because the soul, being a shining fire by the power of the Father,
> Remains immortal and is the mistress of life."
> <note>original: Ὅτι ψυχὴ πῦρ οὖσα φαεινὸν δυνάμει πατρὸς, Ἀθάνατός τε μένει καὶ ζωῆς δεσπότις ἐστίν.</note>

The meaning of this is, *that the soul, being a shining fire by the power of the Father, remains immortal and the mistress of life.*

—that is, an undisturbed possessor or proprietor of life in itself. This is the true notion of a spirit, and not of any fire, for all fire is composed of particles and is dissoluble. I might provide more examples, but the matter is so plain that it is unnecessary.

Therefore, it is manifest that even if the Greek Fathers <note>The early Christian theologians who wrote in Greek, such as Origen or Gregory of Nyssa.</note> should elaborate upon that symbolic term for a spirit—namely, *fire*—and categorize it into intellective, sensitive, and vegetative <note>These three terms represent the traditional hierarchy of the soul: "intellective" (human reason), "sensitive" (animal sensation), and "vegetative" (plant-like growth and reproduction).</note>, there is no proof from this that every created spirit is *fire* and not properly a *spirit*. That is, such a substance as is a being that is one in itself and not by virtue of another <note>original Latin: *Ens unum per se & non per aliud*</note>, and consequently indiscerpible.

### S E C T. XXVI.

*Whether the Greek Fathers spoke informatively in the above-mentioned division. That metaphors are to be excluded from definitions, and why. That wind <note>Latin: "Ventus"</note> and smoke <note>Latin: "Fumus"</note> might as well have been divided into intellective, sensitive, and vegetative categories as fire. And how utterly incapable fire is of the plastic power <note>the "plastic power" was thought to be the soul's ability to form and organize the physical body</note>, perhaps even less so than frost and cold.*

**A**ND now, since you say they speak so informatively by calling a spirit *fire*, what a weak and slender bit of information is this for satisfying our reason? Metaphors and figurative speech certainly fill the "sails" of our imaginative faculty the most; to compare God to a *consuming fire* and a glorious light may serve the well-intended goals of religion and strike greater terror, reverence, and devotion into the minds of the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note>. However, literal <note>original: "proper"</note> language is most appropriate for sound philosophy and strict reason. When we investigate the distinct nature of things, we must say goodbye to allusions and

Metaphors: To inquire into the proper nature of a thing is to search out its adequate definition. According to *Aristotle*, this must be done in the most certain and clear terms possible. Therefore, metaphors are excluded from serving in a definition because "everything stated metaphorically is obscure" <note>original Greek: πᾶν ἀσαφὲς τὸ κατὰ μεταφορὰν λεγόμενον (*pân asaphes to kata metaphoran legomenon*)</note>. As he noted in his *Topics*, whatever is spoken metaphorically is *obscure and uncertain*.

Therefore, I do not see how informatively the *Greek Fathers* <note>The early influential theologians of the Christian Church who wrote in Greek.</note> speak when they use the term *Fire* instead of more proper words to describe the true nature of a *Spirit*. I must honestly declare that they might as well have divided *Wind* <note>original Latin: *Ventus*</note>, *Smoke* <note>original Latin: *Fumus*</note>, or the *steam* <note>original: *Reek*</note> of a cauldron into Intellective, Sensitive, and Vegetative <note>These are the three levels of the "soul" in traditional philosophy: thought, sensation, and basic biological growth.</note> as they did *Fire* <note>original Latin: *Ignis*</note>; *Fire* has no advantage over them in describing the proper nature of a *Spirit*.

The main argument is that it appears as if there were a *self-motion* <note>original Greek: αὐτοκινησία (*autokinēsia*)</note> in *Fire*, since it is in perpetual motion. But this is a plain fallacy; the parts of a flame are not *self-moved*, but are moved by something else. For example, when you use a lighted candle to light another, the parts of the wick and the wax or tallow are put into motion by the moving particles of the lighted candle. Thus, all the particles of the candle are gradually put into motion by the particles of the existing flame, with the air also assisting—which nevertheless passes away like a river, as I noted above. 

But if you allege that *Fire* and *Flame* are fitly used to describe the *self-activity* of a *spirit* because they are always in motion, I would say that *smoke* and *steam* are also in motion as long as they exist. *Wind* especially is like a *spirit* in this regard, as it is so difficult to find out what gives it its motion that it looks more like a *self-moving* being. There is so little information gained in calling a *spirit* "fire" rather than "smoke," "steam," or "wind" that the *instruction* provided must be very thin and weak. 

Just as no one would say that *smoke*, *steam*, or *wind* is of three kinds—Intellective, Sensitive, and Vegetative—it would appear at first sight to be mere *misinformation*. Similarly, to say that *fire* is distinguished into these categories would look like the division of a "whole" into parts that do not actually match that "whole." This would be a foul *misinformation* indeed, and contrary to the known rules of logic. I may be so bold as to assert this because I have demonstrated throughout my writings the incapacity of *matter* to perform such functions as these.

Is *fire capable of intellect*? If so, then the *sun* would certainly be among the first to possess it, and some *materialists* would claim this is the case. However, I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated the madness and contradiction <note>original: "Repugnancy"</note> of that opinion in my preface to *The Immortality of the Soul*. 

Is *fire capable of sensation*? I have proved in that *treatise* that no matter whatsoever—whether fire, water, or air—is capable of receiving the kind of impressions from physical objects that we ourselves are conscious of experiencing. 

To claim that fire is *vegetative*—that is to say, *formative* <note>original: "Plastical"; referring to the power to give shape or organize growth</note>—is wonderfully contrary to its nature. Whatever nature is *formative*, it is the *entelechy* <note>original: ’Ενδελέχεια (Endelechia); a Greek philosophical term for the vital force or formal cause that realizes a thing's potential</note> of the body which it forms and organizes. Therefore, it must *pervade* as well as *contain* <note>original: Δίειν (diein) as well as συνέχειν (synechein); meaning to pass through and to hold together</note>; it must hold together and bind matter as well as move it. In contrast, the property of *fire* is only to disperse and consume, for it puts everything into a state of agitation and motion. That is all we can rationally imagine that *fire* can do, whereas *frost* and *cold* form beautiful patterns and elegant flourishes in snow and ice, and upon the windows and doors of cellars. 

Perhaps you will say that the *Greek Fathers* <note>The influential early Christian theologians of the Eastern Church</note> did not mean *fire* in the sense I am using, which leads to such absurdities. I would then like to know in what sense they understood *fire*. Would it not have been more informative if they had precisely defined what they meant by *fire* before they proceeded to divide it into intellectual, sensitive, and vegetative categories? If they say one thing while meaning another, they inevitably lead the reader into error and misinformation. If they meant *spirit*, they should have said *spirit*. And if they meant spirit in its proper sense, they should have declared its nature as an *immaterial substance*—or something to that effect—before they categorized it into its various types.

# SECTION 27.

### That the *Greek Fathers*, in dividing *Fire* instead of *Spirit* into *Intellectual*, *Sensitive*, and *Vegetative*, do not speak as informatively as those who use the notions of *Penetrability* and *Indivisibility*; and that a *Specific Difference* in a *Species* implies an opposite *Difference* in the opposing *Species*.

And thus I think I have clearly shown that the Fathers <note>original: "Fathers"; referring to the early Christian theologians known as the Greek Fathers</note>, in dividing *Fire* into *Intellectual*, *Sensitive*, and *Vegetative*, do not speak adequately or informingly. From this, it will be a very easy task to show that they do not speak as *informingly* as those who use the notions of *Penetrability* and *Indivisibility*. For certainly, unless the *Greek Fathers* thought all existing things were material—which is highly unlikely, as the *Greek philosophy* of *Pythagoras*, *Plato*, and *Aristotle* was available to instruct them better—they would have spoken more clearly and more informingly if they had used the word *Spirit* instead of *Fire* and indicated it to be an *Immaterial Substance*. This, I believe, is undeniably true.

And now I appeal to yourself: since *Divisibility* and *Impenetrability* are the known and universally acknowledged *Essential Properties* or *Characteristics* of *Matter* or *Body*, it follows naturally—or rather, necessarily—that the opposite species to *Body*, namely *Spirit*, is found to be *Indivisible* and *Penetrable*. 

Consider those two opposite species under the category of *Animal*: namely, *Homo* <note>Latin: Man or Human</note> and *Brutum* <note>Latin: Brute or Beast</note>. If it is once acknowledged that a *Brute* is an *Irrational Animal* <note>original: "Animal Irrationale"</note>, and that being *Irrational* is the *Specific Difference* <term>specific difference: the characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus</term>, then its opposite species, *Man*, must necessarily be a *Rational Animal* <note>original: "Animal Rationale"</note>. 

This is so plain and convincing that I cannot help but remind you here of how you have undervalued your own cognitive faculties. I previously predicted that I would discover you are able to understand more about the nature of a created *Spirit* than you claimed in the last of those seven propositions I derived from that paragraph. For you have gone this much further: you have recognized that *Penetrability* and *Indivisibility* belong essentially and inseparably to the nature of a *Spirit*.

# SECTION XXVIII.

## *That God can create an Indivisible Being, though of a large Metaphysical Amplitude, or else he were not God.*

Regarding the possibility of these proper and essential attributes of a *Spirit*, I believe I have proven them in my short *Discourse of the True Notion of a Spirit* against all supposed objections. The greatest difficulty concerning the *indiscerpibility* <note>original: "Indiscerpibility"—the quality of being impossible to tear or divide into parts.</note> of a *Spirit*—even one acknowledged to have *metaphysical amplitude* <note>size or extent that is not physical</note> or *extension*—should be no problem for anyone who considers two things. First, it is much easier to conceive of something that is inherently one by its own essence as being indivisible than it is to understand how something made of parts could hold together at all. Second, one must acknowledge the immense essence of God, which is absolutely indivisible and cannot be torn apart, as well as the omnipotence of that same God. Therefore, God can easily create *spirits* in his own image; though they have a finite size, they are indivisible. That is to say, he can create a being (which, because it is a being, necessarily implies it has some extent) which is <term>a being one in itself and not by another</term> <note>original: *Ens unum per se & non per aliud*</note>. Such a being has an extent that cannot be divided, not because it is too small to be any smaller, but because of the immediate union—or rather the *oneness*—of its essence, no matter how large you may imagine it to be.

Otherwise, God would only be able to create *metaphysical monads* <note>monads: simple, indivisible units of being</note>, or *spiritual points*, corresponding to the physical points or *monads* of matter. To a wise and philosophical mind that is thoroughly persuaded of the divine omnipotence, nothing could be more absurd or ridiculous than this. If you argue that if God were to create such a spirit with *metaphysical amplitude* which he himself could not divide or sever into parts, he would be limiting his own all-powerfulness, the same could be said of the *metaphysical monads*. At that rate, he would be permitted to create nothing—not even matter,

### SECTION 29.

*How naturally the previously mentioned division by the Greek Fathers of "Fire" into Intellective, Sensitive, and Vegetative categories actually belongs to Spirit, according to the definition in the preceding discourse on the True Notion of a Spirit. And how the effects of the types of Spirit included in that general definition account for all phenomena in the world.*

**Therefore**, since these things are so plain, I believe it will not be overly bold of me to hope that my definition of a Spirit—which is "an immaterial substance intrinsically endowed with life and the faculty of motion"—will prove itself more informative than defining a Spirit as "fire." My definition virtually contains within it the concepts of *penetrability* and *indiscerpibility* <note>original: "Indiscerpibility"; the quality of being impossible to divide or pull apart into separate pieces.</note> (for "immaterial" includes those two qualities, as you have seen). Defining Spirit as fire may heat the fancy and "fill the sails of imagination," as I said before, but it instructs us little or nothing about the true and proper notion of a Spirit.

Furthermore, because it is noted in that definition that life and motion originate from within this *immaterial* substance, the Spirit, you may see here how appropriately the Greek Fathers' division—which they applied to fire—actually fits the Spirit, and what easy and natural sense it makes. In this way, I prefer to philosophize without exaggeration, pomp, or metaphors. "Fire" is indeed more "phantasmatical" <note>original: "Phantasmatical"; relating to mental images, imagination, or sensory illusions rather than pure reason.</note> and is an object of the senses and the imagination, but "immaterial substance" is more rational and is the object of our intellectual faculties.

## SECTION XXXI.

### *The Necessary Usefulness of the Notion of the Penetrability of Spirits.*

**A**nd now, regarding the *penetrability* of spirits, it is also plainly not only useful but necessary that they penetrate matter. Otherwise, how could they be its *entelechies* <note>original Greek: 'Εντελέχειαι *Endelechiæ*. In Aristotelian philosophy, an entelechy is the vital principle that guides the development of an organism and gives it form.</note> and give it form and action? And if they could not penetrate their own parts, how could they be contracted so as to be the same size as the body of a small *fetus* in the womb? I have heard from some skillful midwives that these have sometimes been found as small as a bee, and yet already in human shape and form. Unless we wish to stitch together a soul from pieces to allow it to match the size of the body when it reaches a man’s stature, that very *soul*—with nothing added to it that was not already contracted into such a small space—later expands itself by degrees to the size of the grown body of a man. This, therefore, plainly implies the *penetrability of spirits*, as well as demonstrates its *usefulness*. But it is sufficient to touch only upon these things.

## S E C T. XXXII.

*That Logical* **Matter** *and* **Form** *are nothing but* **Undetermined Amplitude and Difference,** <note>original: "Indeterminata, Amplitudo, and Differentia"</note> *the two* **Simple Principles of Being as Being,** <note>original: "Ens quatenus Ens"</note> *and therefore imply no* **Physical Materiality.**

---

**W**e have now reached the conclusion of your letter, but I will include your short postscript before I consider that. You describe a spirit, you say, as *Being, and therefore one, true, etc.* <note>original: "Ens, ideoque unum, verum, &c."</note> And you say that "True" denotes how well the thing corresponds to its own proper idea, and implies a right *Matter* and *Form* duly joined together. Upon this you raise this question: *Do you not here make Spirits Material?* But no doubt, you say, whether they are called "material" or "substantial," the "form" is not something added onto it; rather, the form of a simple essence is merely an incomplete concept, <note>original: "inadequate Conceptus," meaning a partial way of thinking about a single, unified thing</note> which does not create a physical composition.

To this I answer: I do not make spirits "material" in any sense that lessens their nature or perfections. And when I speak of "right Matter and Form," if you had noticed that the *Matter* and *Form* you speak of are the kind that belong to *Being as Being*, you could not imagine that this would imply any physical materiality in spirits. This is because it is "matter" in its most general sense, separated from all particular kinds of being whatever; therefore, it belongs to beings that are truly immaterial just as much as those that are material.

It is only *Logical Matter and Form* <note>original: "Materia and Forma Logica"</note> that is meant there. The "Form" is not joined to the "Matter" in a physical sense, except in cases where the Form and Matter are really distinct substances, such as the soul of a man and his body. But they are also called "matter" and "form" even when they are only distinct in our minds within certain other beings; consequently, they can only be said to be "joined" to one another mentally, as if they had once been two things, when in reality they are only one. As you rightly say, the "form" of any simple essence is merely an incomplete concept of that essence and creates no physical mixture or composition. See my *Metaphysical Manual*, <note>original: "Enchiridion Metaphysicum"</note> Chapter 2, Sections 7 and 8, and you will understand what I mean by *Logical Matter and Form*. These are the simple principles of *Being as Being*, and are nothing else but *Undetermined Amplitude* <note>the "space" or potential of a thing's existence</note> and *Difference* <note>the specific quality that makes it what it is</note>. Thus, I no longer need to dwell on this matter here.

<summary>The author clarifies that using the terms "matter" and "form" in a logical or metaphysical sense does not imply that spirits are made of physical matter. He argues these are abstract categories used to define any type of existence, whether physical or incorporeal.</summary>
