**N**ow for the conclusion itself, in which you ask pardon for these brief expressions of thoughts which I requested regarding the description of a spirit. ## SECTION XXXIV.

### The Impediments to True Knowledge; and the full Agreement of the Author of the foregoing Discourse with the Learned <term>Psychopyrist</term> <note>original: Psychopyrist; literally "soul-firer," likely referring to a philosopher like Henry More who viewed the soul as a spiritual fire</note> in the last Clause of his Letter, namely: *If God makes us truly Holy, we shall quickly know more to our satisfaction.*

**B**UT I leave everyone to think as well as they can in philosophical speculations, being certain that everyone would arrive at the Truth if they could reach it. It is an imperfection and a flaw for a person to be found in error; though I doubt whether all men take the best path to attain the Truth, they would gladly have it if they could get it without cost. They will not part with their beloved laziness, nor with their preconceived opinions—for which they have an affection because they happened to embrace them so long ago, and therefore cannot bear the thought of a divorce from them. They will not part with their sensual pleasures or worldly-mindedness, nor with that flattering conceit or pleasant presumption that what they believe is more likely to be true than the opinion of any other man, even though they offer no clear demonstration for it.

To come to the very last clause in your letter, which is the best, and in which I most firmly and heartily agree with you: *If God makes us truly Holy, we shall quickly know more to our satisfaction.* I believe that the purification of the soul from all impurity of flesh and spirit is absolutely required for anyone who would successfully study philosophy, especially in <term>metaphysical</term> <note>the branch of philosophy dealing with the fundamental nature of reality and being</note> or <term>theological</term> speculations. I commend your judgment in saying, *“If God makes us truly Holy.”* By virtue of this true holiness, I suppose we shall be freed not only from the dullness of superstition and the bluster of <term>enthusiasm</term> <note>original: Enthusiasm; in this period, the term often referred to religious fanaticism or the mistaken belief that one is receiving direct, private revelations from God</note>, but also from the prejudices of both our education and our temperament. We shall be freed from the lack of restraint and the force of our own self-will and desires in things that do not look so commendable; and also from any vain desire for knowledge itself, which has such a fair and commendable appearance. We shall, I say, condemn ourselves for great folly and misconduct,

# A further Defence of the

especially in metaphysical, theological, and moral contemplations. If we find such a false appetite in ourselves for these things—where we would *know* merely to *know*, or (what is worse) to be *known* by others.

This is not a sound state of mind, nor does it suit a holy man. A holy man has no false appetite for knowledge, but only the kind of appetite a healthy and temperate man has for his food <note>original: "Meat"</note>: to eat what and as much as enables nature to correctly and steadily perform all the functions of a natural life. Similarly, any desire for knowledge in those contemplations I mentioned before that exceeds the proper goals of such knowledge is misguided. Those goals are to strengthen <note>original: "coroborate"</note> our faith in God and in his Son *Jesus Christ*, to confirm our belief in a glorious immortality after this life, and to promote true devotion, mortification <note>the spiritual practice of subduing one's desires or "killing" the sinful nature</note>, and regeneration—or the renewing <note>original: "Renovation"</note> of our fallen <note>original: "lapsed"</note> natures back into the lost image of God. Any desire for knowledge that does not tend toward this end is like a disease to a truly holy man; it tastes no better to him than feeding on chaff, feathers, or dry straw would taste to a natural man.

And we may be certain that the person whose appetite is sound and regular—who desires no knowledge except what is the real nourishment for his "New-Birth" <note>the process of spiritual rebirth or regeneration</note>—will not fail to receive all wholesome and useful knowledge from the fountain of all true wisdom: the "Father of Lights," from whom comes every good and perfect gift. Conversely, a false appetite for knowledge, which only feeds our pride, will expose us not only to accidental errors but also to the ridiculous deceptions of wandering <note>original: "vagrant"</note> spirits who amuse themselves with the empty curiosities of deluded humanity. 

Furthermore, such a person wastes precious time that would be much better spent examining the sincerity of our own hearts and in earnest prayers <note>original: "Breathings"</note> to God. We should pray that he would be pleased to free us from that "bondage of corruption" <note>a biblical phrase from Romans 8:21 referring to the state of sin and mortality</note> we find ourselves held in, and that he would perfect our spiritual rebirth and complete the image of his Son within us. This is better than wearing out <note>original: "teasing"</note> unnecessary ideas into useless, endless distinctions and complexities that contribute nothing to our great and everlasting concerns. 

I say I am perfectly of your mind in this: that he who is truly holy will soonest gain the knowledge he needs to his satisfaction. For he who feeds the young ravens that call upon him will never allow his own spiritual children to starve for lack of proper food for the soul. He who philosophizes in this way—seeking no knowledge out of curiosity, but only to feed and strengthen the divine life <note>original: "Divine Birth"</note> within him—

# The Preface

Apparitions are viewed as things that are *ridiculous, incredible, foolish <note>original: "foppish"</note>, and impossible*. Therefore, all *accounts* <note>original: "relations"</note> that *assert* their existence are dismissed as *lies, cheats, and delusions*. Those who give any *credit* to them are seen as credulous *fools* <note>original: "gulls"</note> and simple, easy *believers*.

If these things should turn out not to be so, it would spoil many a *jest*. Those who thought themselves great *wits* would have the discomfort of finding they are mistaken. They would have to fall back into common and ordinary *belief* and lose their claim to extraordinary *insight* <note>original: "sagacity"</note>, a quality on which they valued themselves so much. They would be forced to fear another *world* and be subjected to the common *terrors* which they previously despised as the *tricks* <note>original: "juggles"</note> and *schemes* of *priests* and *politicians*. Thus, they would find themselves under the necessity of altering their *lives* or being ruined. These are very hard and painful things to accept, and therefore the *stories* of *witches* and *apparitions* must be debunked <note>original: "exploded"</note> and ridiculed, or else all is lost for them.

This is the case with many arrogant, confident *men* in our *days*. To deal with this *subject* is to offend them greatly, to provoke their *rage* and *contempt*, and to stir up the *devil* of their *wit* and *buffoonery*. Considering all of this, it must be admitted that it is a very bold and adventurous thing to undertake the *task* <note>original: "province"</note> in which I have engaged. Besides the provocation which it must surely give to the *blusterers* <note>original: "huffers"</note> and *petty wits* <note>original: "witlings"</note>, there is another group, whose

<summary>The author argues that skeptical "wits" reject stories of witches and apparitions not because of evidence, but because accepting them would require a painful change in their own lifestyle and moral accountability. He acknowledges that writing on this subject will provoke mockery and anger from these arrogant critics.</summary>

<keywords>skepticism, apparitions, witches, atheism, sagacity, huffers, witlings, religious debate, 17th-century philosophy</keywords>

## To the Reader.

I greatly value the good opinion of others. However, some serious and ingenious people—who have their own reasons for doubting the existence of witches—may be inclined to judge me as gullible <note>original: "guilty of Credulity"</note> because of the effort I have put into this matter. This has also caused me some trouble and discouragement.

Overall, I am already certain that no possible evidence of the facts would be enough to remove the stubborn prejudices of various determined men. Therefore, I know I must endure their heavy criticism <note>original: "censures"</note>. I have considered the worst they might say, and I hope I am well-prepared to bear even the harshest of it. But no one would expose themselves to all this for no reason, and neither have I. There were specific reasons for this commitment, which are briefly as follows:

Because I was at Mr. Mompesson’s <note>Joseph Glanvill is referring to the famous "Drummer of Tedworth" case (1662), where John Mompesson's house was reportedly haunted by a drumming sound after he confiscated a drum from a vagrant.</note> house during the time of the disturbance—having seen and heard some things myself and received an account of the whole trouble from Mr. Mompesson and other credible people—I was persuaded to publish it. I did this, and both were published together through two or three editions without much further trouble for me. 

But recently, I have heard from all over—and am amazed by it—that this strongly documented account <note>original: "Relation"</note> is being dismissed in most places as a delusion and a fraud <note>original: "Imposture"</note>. # The Preface

I have received word from known friends and strangers from many parts of the Three Kingdoms <note>The kingdoms of England, Scotland, and Ireland.</note>, such that I have been haunted almost as much as Mr. Mompesson's house. Most of them declared that it was widely reported and believed in all their respective regions that the whole business was a fraud <note>original: "Cheat"</note>—that Mr. Mompesson had confessed as much, and that I had done the same. As a result, I was quite exhausted from denying these claims and answering letters about them. To free myself from this trouble, I finally resolved to reprint the story on its own, along with my refutation <note>original: "Confutation"</note> of the lies <note>original: "Invention"</note> concerning me, and a letter I received from Mr. Mompesson (*now printed in this book*) which cleared his name regarding the matter.

Accordingly, I placed this in my bookseller's hands some years ago to be printed. However, since it was not published, I was continually pestered <note>original: "importuned"</note> by new requests and questions. At length, Mr. Webster’s arrogant <note>original: "confident"</note> book was published, in which he says:

Having indicated that I was now inclined toward the plan, I received great encouragement from some of the greatest *minds* <note>original: Spirits</note> of our age and nation, who earnestly encouraged me. Once I had resolved to do it, I thought about making a small *collection* of the most credible and best-attested stories of this kind that were recent and modern to accompany the second one I had printed, and to confirm and prove the main subject.

The grand jury found the evidence sufficient to proceed <note>original: "found the Bill"</note>, but the trial jury <note>original: "Petty Jury"</note> acquitted him, though not without some difficulty.

The witnesses testifying under oath were myself, Mr. William Maton, and Mr. Walter Dowse—all still living and, I believe, of as good a reputation as anyone in this county—and Mr. John Cragg, who was then the local minister but has since died. We all testified to several things that we believed were impossible to be done by any natural means <note>original: "natural Agents"</note>, such as the movement of chairs, stools, and bed-staves <note>wooden sticks used to hold bedding in place or beat mattresses</note> when nobody was near them; the beating of drums in the air above the house on clear nights when nothing was visible; the shaking of the floor and the strongest parts of the house on still and calm nights; along with several other similar occurrences. Through other evidence, these events were linked to him.

# An Introduction to the Proof of the Existence of Apparitions, Spirits, and Witches.

---

## SECTION I.

### *The great usefulness and timeliness of the present* argument *concerning* witches *and* apparitions *in support of* religion.

**T**HE question of whether there are *witches* or not is not a matter of idle speculation or of minor importance, but an inquiry of very great and weighty significance. For on the resolution of it depends the authority and just execution of some of our *laws*; and what is more, the main doctrines of our *religion* are closely concerned. There is no one who is not a total stranger to the world who does not know how *atheism* and *skepticism* <note>original: "infidelity"</note> have advanced in our days, and how openly they now dare to show themselves in asserting and disputing their vile cause. In particular, the *separation of the soul* from the *body*, the existence of *spirits*, and a *future life* are assertions extremely despised and opposed by men of this sort; and if we lose those articles of faith, all religion comes to nothing. They are clearly and fully asserted in the *Holy Scriptures* <note>original: "Sacred Oracles"</note>, but those skeptics <note>original: "Wits"</note> have set aside these divine

<keywords>witchcraft, apparitions, atheism, immortality of the soul, afterlife, skepticism, religious doctrine, 17th-century philosophy</keywords>

# The Introduction.

<warning>Significant ink bleed-through from the reverse side of the leaf is visible throughout the text.</warning>

Divine Writings <note>referring to the Holy Scriptures</note>. They are proved by the best philosophy and highest reason; but many unbelievers are too shallow to be capable of understanding such proofs, and those who are more subtle are ready to use skepticism to explain away those foundations.

But there is one category of arguments that troubles them greatly, and that is the topic of *witches* and *apparitions* <note>original: "Apparitions"; referring to ghosts or spirits appearing to the living</note>. If such things exist, it provides tangible <note>original: "sensible"</note> proof of *spirits* and another *life* <note>an afterlife</note>. This is an argument of more direct force than any speculations or abstract reasonings, and it is the kind of argument that confronts all types of *infidels* <note>those who do not believe in religious teachings</note>. For this reason, they labor with all their might to persuade themselves and others that *witches* and *apparitions* are nothing but *melancholic dreams* <note>original: "Melancholick Dreams"; at the time, "melancholy" was often used to explain away supernatural experiences as delusions caused by a physical imbalance of "humors"</note> or *crafty impostures*. It is generally here that they begin their influence on young men, whose understanding they intend to corrupt <note>original: "Debauch"</note>.

They expose and ridicule all *accounts of spirits and witchcraft*, providing these young men with minor arguments—or rather, the mere appearance of arguments <note>original: "Colours"; meaning a deceptive or superficial justification</note>—against their existence. And the youth are very ready to entertain such opinions as will help them to imagine <note>original: "fansie"</note> they are wiser than the general public. Once they have swallowed this opinion and are certain there are no *witches* nor *apparitions*, they are prepared to deny the existence of *spirits*, a *life to come*, and all the other principles of *religion*. 

Therefore, I believe it will be a significant and very timely service to religion to fully debate and settle this matter. I shall attempt to do so in the following pages, and I hope to do it in a way that does not deceive myself or others with empty rhetoric <note>original: "Rhetorications"</note>, legendary stories, or fallacious <note>original: "Sophistical"</note> reasonings. Instead, I will treat the question with the freedom and plainness that suits someone who is neither foolish, overly imaginative, nor gullible.

## SECTION II.

### *The true stating of the question by defining what a witch and witchcraft is.*

I know that in most controversies, a great deal of effort is often wasted on matters irrelevant to the main issue. Because of these irrelevancies, the minds of both parties become so confused that they stray far from the actual point of disagreement and eventually lose sight of it entirely. This would quickly happen in the debate over witchcraft—and usually does—unless care is taken beforehand to avoid it. However, I will do my best to ensure my efforts on this subject are not misdirected but are closely focused on the objective. To do so, I will briefly define the terms of the question and then establish what I concede to my opponents and what I require from them. Once these preliminary points are settled, we shall proceed with greater clarity and always understand where we stand, knowing how far any claim or proof goes toward resolving the main issue in the debate.

The question is whether <term>witches</term> exist or not. Mr. Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was an English physician and author of "The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft" (1677), where he argued that "witchcraft" was natural or fraudulent rather than supernatural.</note> accuses the writers on this subject of being deficient because they do not provide a perfect description of a <term>witch</term> or <term>witchcraft</term>, or explain what they mean (page 20). I do not know what he considers a "perfect description," but I believe I have described a witch or witchcraft in my *Considerations* <note>"Some Philosophical Considerations touching the Being of Witches and Witchcraft" (1666), a work by Joseph Glanvill.</note> clearly enough to be understood. The concept that I—and, I think, most people—hold is that a *witch* is someone who can perform, or appears to perform, strange things beyond the known powers of art or nature, by virtue of a <term>confederacy</term> <note>original: "Confederacy"; a formal alliance or pact, in this case with the demonic.</note> with <term>evil spirits</term>. I mean "strange things," not miracles; miracles are the extraordinary effects of divine power, identified and distinguished by their circumstances, as I shall show in the proper place. These "strange things" are

<sig>Q</sig>
<meta>catchword: are</meta>

...are actually performed, and are not all *impostures* and *delusions*. The *witch* provides the occasion, but is not the *primary cause* <note>original: "Principal Efficient"; in early modern philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent that brings a thing into being.</note>. She seems to perform the act, but the *spirit* carries out the wonder—sometimes immediately, as in *transportations* and *possessions*; sometimes by applying other *natural causes*, as in *raising storms* and *inflicting diseases*; and sometimes using the *witch* as an *instrument*, conveying *harmful influences* either through the eyes or by touch. These things are done by virtue of a *covenant* or *compact* between the *witch* and an *evil spirit*. By a *spirit*, I mean an *intelligent creature* of the *invisible world*, whether one of the evil angels called *devils*, an *inferior demon* or *spirit*, or a *departed wicked soul*. This entity is one that is *able and ready* for mischief; whether it is altogether *incorporeal* <note>without a physical body</note> or not does not concern this question.

## SECTION III.

### *That neither the origin of the name (which has various meanings) nor the false additions made by others to the concept of a witch can in any way destabilize the author’s definition.*

**T**HIS I take to be a plain *description* of what we mean by a *witch* and *witchcraft*. What Mr. Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a prominent skeptical author who argued that "witchcraft" was often the result of natural causes or fraud rather than demonic pacts.</note> and other advocates for *witches* say concerning the words used to express these things—claiming they are improper and metaphorical, signifying this or signifying that—is altogether idle and irrelevant. The word *witch* originally signifies a *wise man*, or rather a *wise woman*. The same is true of *Saga* <note>original: "Saga" in Latin; a term for a female fortune-teller or wise woman, derived from the verb "sagire," meaning to perceive keenly.</note> in Latin; and plainly, *wizard* in *English* signifies a *wise man*. They are commonly called "cunning men" or "cunning women." They do possess an art, knowledge, and cunning that...

<lang>English</lang>

...that is extraordinary; but it is far from true wisdom, and the word has degenerated into a negative sense, just as *Magia* <note>original: "Magia"; Latin for magic, which the author implies once had a neutral or positive meaning but became associated with evil.</note> has.

So then they are named, and we need look no further; it is enough that by the *word*, we mean the *thing* and *person* I have described, which is the common meaning. Mr. *Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), author of "The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft" (1677), a skeptical work that argued many accusations of witchcraft were based on fraud or delusion.</note> and the others prevaricate <note>original: "prevaricate"; here meaning to speak or act in an evasive way to avoid the truth.</note> when they make it signify an ordinary *cheat*, a *swindler* <note>original: "couzener"</note>, a *poisoner*, *seducer*, and I know not what else. Words signify what they are used for, and in common use, *witch* and *witchcraft* do indeed imply these things, but they imply more: namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, deluding, cheating, and hurting by the power of an *evil spirit* in a *covenant* <note>A formal agreement or contract, specifically with the Devil.</note> with a wicked man or woman. This is our concept of a *witch*.

I know Mr. *Webster* will not accept this as a perfect description. He adds to the concept of the *witch* he opposes ideas like sexual intercourse <note>original: "carnal copulation"</note> with the *Devil*, and *real transformation* into a *hare, cat, dog,* or *wolf*; Mr. *Wagstaffe* <note>John Wagstaffe (1633–1677), author of "The Question of Witchcraft Debated" (1669), another prominent skeptic of the era.</note> does the same. This is as if a man should define an angel as a creature in the shape of a boy with wings, and then "prove" there is no such being. Of all men, I would not have Mr. *Webster* create my definitions for me; we ourselves should be allowed to state what it is that we affirm and defend. And I have described the *witch* and *witchcraft* that reasonable <note>original: "sober"</note> men believe and assert. So much, briefly, for the definition.

Indeed, it is considered a sign of wit to laugh at the belief in *witches* as if it were nothing but silly credulity. There are ten thousand silly, lying stories of *witchcraft* and *apparitions* among the common people. Many stories of *witchcraft* and *apparitions* have been nothing more than melancholy fancies.

Fifthly, I know and concede that there are many strange natural diseases that have odd symptoms and produce wonderful and astonishing effects beyond the usual course of nature, and that these are sometimes falsely attributed to *witchcraft*.

<meta>This page continues the author's list of foundational principles (postulates) for investigating the supernatural, establishing the criteria for evidence and the limits of human understanding regarding spirits.</meta>

<header>The Introduction.</header>

Secondly, that matters of **fact** can only be proven by direct **sensory perception**, or the **testimony** of others, whether **divine** or **human**. To endeavor to demonstrate **fact** by abstract reasoning and speculation is as if a man should try to prove that **Julius Caesar** founded the **Roman Empire** by using **algebra** or **metaphysics**. Therefore, what **Mr. Webster** <note>original: John Webster (1610–1682), an author who argued against the reality of witchcraft in his book "The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft" (1677).</note> says on page 43—that the true and proper mediums to prove the actions of **witches** are **Scripture** and sound **reason**, and not the "improper" way of **testimony** (which he uses in opposition to Scripture and sound reason)—is complete **nonsense**.

Thirdly, that the history found in the **Scriptures** is not entirely **allegory**, but generally has a plain, literal, and obvious meaning.

Fourthly, that some **human testimonies** are credible and certain; that is, they may be so supported by circumstances as to leave no reason for doubt. Our senses sometimes report the truth, and not all of mankind are liars, cheats, and knaves—at least, they are not all liars when they have no **interest** <note>original: "interest" here refers to personal gain or a selfish motive to deceive.</note> in being so.

Fifthly, that which is sufficiently and undeniably proven ought not to be denied just because we do not know *how* it can be—that is, because there are difficulties in conceiving of it. Otherwise, **sensory perception** and **knowledge** are lost, as well as **faith**. For the **modus** <note>original: Latin for "manner" or "way."</note> of most things is unknown, and even the most obvious things in nature have inextricable difficulties when we speculate about them, as I have shown in my book ***Scepsis Scientifica*** <note>original: Glanvill's own work, "Scepsis Scientifica: or, Confess't Ignorance, the Way to Science" (1665), which argued for a skeptical, scientific approach to knowledge.</note>.

Sixthly and lastly, we are very much in the dark regarding the **nature** and **kinds** of **spirits**, and the particular conditions of the other world. We know of **angels**, **devils**, and the **happiness** or **misery** of **souls**, but we understand very little about what specific kinds exist under these general categories, or what actions, circumstances, and ways of life exist within those states. These are my **postulata** <note>original: Latin for "postulates" or "assumptions."</note> or demands, which I assume will be thought reasonable and in need of no further proof.

**T**HERE are several evasions by which some people endeavor to escape these texts. First, there are the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect during the time of Jesus that denied the resurrection and the existence of spirits or angels.</note> of old and the Familists <note>The Family of Love, a 16th-century radical religious group often accused of interpreting the Bible through purely allegorical or mystical lenses.</note> of more recent days. The former held that the angels we read of were only *divine graces*; the latter held that they were *divine phantasms* <term>phantasms: temporary illusions or ghosts that have no permanent existence</term> created to serve a specific occasion, which ceased to be as soon as they disappeared. One would think that no one who had ever read the Scriptures would entertain such a conceit as this, which is so contrary to the account they provide everywhere regarding those celestial creatures. But there is nothing so absurd that some men will not embrace it to support their own opinions.

Let us consider for a moment how differently the Scripture describes them compared to this vain fancy. They are called *spirits*, an attribute given to God himself—the primary *subsistence* <term>subsistence: a self-existing being or reality</term>—who is by way of eminence called the *Father of Spirits*, not of *phantasms*. And *spirits* implies as much *substance* as *body*, though without a coarse physical bulk. We read of *elect angels* and the *angels that stand before the throne of God continually*, and that always behold the face of God. We read of the *fallen angels* who did not keep their first station but are held in the *chains of darkness*; and of *everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels* against the judgment of the Great Day. Both groups had their order of superiority and inferiority: *Michael and his angels*, and the *Dragon and his angels*. We are made a little lower than the angels. In heaven, we shall be like the angels of God. Of the Day of Judgment, no man knows—no, not even the *angels*. Let all the *angels* of God worship him.

These descriptions of the nature, order, condition, and attributes of angels—and an infinite number of others throughout the Scriptures—are not applicable to *phantasms*. Instead, they demonstratively prove that the *angels* whose appearances we hear of so frequently there were real, permanent *beings* <note>original: "Subsistencies"</note> and not mere *phantasms* and *shadows*.

## SECTION III.

*That the angels who are said to have appeared in Scripture were not human messengers, but inhabitants of the invisible world; and whether they ate and drank or not.*

**B**ut were those angels who appeared in that way not special prophets or divine messengers—who are sometimes admittedly called "angels" in Scripture? They ate and drank with *Abraham* and *Lot*, which would seem to suggest they were real *men*. But whoever examines the alleged instances of the appearance of angels and reads them within the full context of the text will clearly see that they could not have been *men*.

Such could not have been the *angel* who spoke to *Abraham* and *Hagar* from *heaven*, who conversed with *Jacob* in a *dream*, who appeared to *Moses* in the *burning bush*, who appeared to *Manoah* and ascended in the presence of him and his *wife* in the *flame* of the *sacrifice*, who went before the *camp* of *Israel*, who stood before *Balaam* in the way (unseen by him), who struck the army of the *Assyrians*, or who appeared to *Zechariah* in the *temple* and to the *Marys* at the *sepulcher* <note>tomb</note>. These must be a type of *beings* superior to mankind—*angels* in the proper sense—who are sometimes called *men* in Scripture because they appear in our likeness.

But whether these beings receive nourishment <note>original: "refection"</note> or sustenance in their own world and state, I will not debate. It is very likely, as has been the doctrine of both the Church Fathers and philosophers, that they are vitally united to *ethereal* and *heavenly* bodies. These bodies might possibly need replenishment in some such way, and so the phrase "*angels' food*" may be more than just a metaphor. But they certainly cannot eat in our manner, nor feed on our heavy diet, except in appearance only. They may make a show of doing so, as the angel Raphael told *Tobit* he did (*Tobit 12:19*: *All these days I appeared to you, but I neither ate nor drank; you only saw a vision*) but in reality, they do not. Therefore, when *Abraham’s* and *Lot’s* angels are said to eat and drink with them, the Scripture is speaking as it appeared to them. And so the *Jerusalem Targum* <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> reads: *And they seemed as if they ate and drank.* And we may suppose that men’s conceptions...

[No]tions of angels were not very refined in those days. This is noted as an excuse for the offer in verse 16: "For *Manoah did not know that he was an angel of the Lord*." This implies that the invitation would have been absurd had he known the truth.

I have said this to answer the objection, though it does not affect my main argument. These are more than enough to prove my point: that real angels—inhabitants of the invisible world—did sometimes physically appear.

# SECTION IV.

## *That Angels are still ministering spirits, just as they were in the past.*

**B**ut some will say that when they did appear, it was for divine missions, and God sent them to serve the purposes of His government and providence. I admit this, but God Almighty still has the same goals. He governs the world now, and His providence is as watchful as ever. Angels remain the chief ministers of that providence, acting as ministering spirits for our benefit. The Gospel was introduced through the *appearance of angels*, and they performed many tasks to help it progress. I see no reason why we should think they cannot be sent, or why they should not appear on occasion today. However, this is more than I need to say for now, as my first step is only to show that spirits have interacted <note>original: "transacted"</note> with humanity.

# S E C T. V.

## *Proof from the Apparitions of evil Spirits, recorded in Scripture.*

**T**hose I have mentioned until now have been good and benevolent spirits, but *evil spirits* have also appeared and tangibly interacted with mankind. My first instance of this is one of the first events that occurred in the world: the temptation of *Eve* by the *Devil* in the form of the *Serpent*. This is an argument that those who strictly follow the literal meaning of those first three chapters [of Genesis] cannot avoid. Evil angels were sent among the *Egyptians* (Psalm 78:49) and they passed through and struck the land; but the destroyers—namely, the evil angels—were not permitted to enter the *Israelites’* houses (Exodus 12:23). When God asked *Satan* where he came from (Job 1:7), he answered, "From going to and fro on the earth." By divine permission, he raised the great wind that blew down the house on *Job's* children (verse 19) and struck his body all over with boils (Job 2:7). He tempted our Savior in a physical, sensory way, carrying him from place to place and urging the Son of God to worship him (Matthew 4). But more evidence of this will appear by considering the second topic proposed: namely, the *possession by evil spirits*.

Such a "possession" was never heard of—a *beast* possessed by a *man*. But *Saint Luke* tells us that it was the *devils* who went out of the *men* and entered into the *swine (Luke 8:33)*. The men did not go out of themselves; therefore, if what went out was not the *disease*, it was really the *devil* or *unclean spirit*.

It is very easy to understand what damage this would do to the truth and credibility of the entire history.

## SECTION VII.

### *That the defenders of witches <note>original: "Witch-Advocates"</note> cannot evade the scriptural evidence of demonic possession by claiming it merely reflects the common opinions of the time.*

**I.** We know that the Scripture often speaks according to the common opinions of men, even when those opinions are technically errors. It is not necessarily concerned with correcting such mistakes when they do not affect *morality* or *religion*.

But first, the doctrine of *spirits* and *devils* was not the common opinion held by all the *Jews*. The *Sadducees* <note>a prominent Jewish sect during the time of Jesus that denied the existence of spirits and the resurrection</note>, a significant group, held a different view. Therefore, the accounts of casting out spirits would have made Jesus and the writers look like impostors to them. Furthermore, the Scriptures were not written only for the *Jews* of that specific time, but for all places and all ages. Most of these cultures do not use the term *devils* to mean *diseases*. Among such people, the biblical history would either promote a false opinion or lose its reputation for truth.

Secondly, while the Scripture does not always deviate from common figures of speech when they are based on harmless or minor mistakes, it is deeply concerned with reforming and correcting errors when they are significant, dangerous, and harmful to the glory of God and the interests of religion. According to the beliefs of the *defenders of witches*, the doctrine of *possessions* is exactly such a dangerous error. They claim it leads to the belief in *witchcraft*, which they describe as a dismal and tragic error, a blasphemy, and an abominably idolatrous—even atheistic—doctrine. They call it the "grand *apostasy*" <note>referring to a total abandonment of faith</note>, the greatest that ever was or can be, claiming it "decapitates" Christ, removes God’s status, renounces both Christ and God, and makes the Devil equal to them, etc.—as the *author* of *The Grand Apostasy* <note>likely John Wagstaffe, who published "The Question of Witchcraft Debated" in 1669</note> raves.

And Mr. *Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), a physician and author who argued against the reality of witchcraft in "The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft"</note> says much the same of this opinion in his preface: namely, that it tends to promote superstition and "Popery" <note>a derogatory term for Roman Catholicism</note>, and is derogatory to the wisdom, justice, and providence of the Almighty. He argues it tends to exaggerate the power of the kingdom of darkness and to question the truth of the principal articles of the Christian—

## SECTION VIII.

### *An Answer to an Objection: Why Christ Did Not Mention Casting Out Demons to John’s Disciples Among Other Miracles.*

**B**ut, says the author of *The Grand Apostasy* <note>Likely referring to Wagstaffe's work or a similar skeptical treatise of the period.</note> on page 34, our Savior himself, in his answer to the disciples of John the Baptist in Luke 7, does not claim to be casting out demons, but only to be curing diseases and raising the dead. To this I say:

First, we should not argue from a negative position in Scripture regarding such matters; certainly, we ought not to argue from silence in one place against plain affirmations in many others.

Second, our Savior answers in reference to the things he was doing at that very moment. When the disciples of John came to him, verse 21 says: *And in that same hour, he cured many of their infirmities and plagues.* It must be admitted that evil spirits are also mentioned there. It is likely that some of those diseases were caused by evil spirits, just as the blindness and muteness of the possessed person was in Matthew 12:22. Therefore, the casting out of the evil spirit is implied when the disease is said to be cured.

Third, the purpose of John’s disciples was to inquire whether he was the Messiah, and it was appropriate that our Savior, in his answer, should give such proofs of his identity as were plain and palpable. *Go your way,* he says, *and tell John what things you have seen and heard* (Luke 7:22). They had likely heard him preach the Gospel and had seen him cure diseases. These things were plain and perceptible, and could admit of no...

Again, it is alleged by this writer that to "have a *devil*" and to be "mad" seem to be *synonyms* in Scripture (page 35). I answer: *Possession* produced a certain *manic fury* <note>original: "mania furor"</note> and *madness*; therefore, when anyone acted extravagantly, the *Jews* said in common speech that they "had a *devil*." We do the same today when we say, "*The devil is in you*," meaning you are acting unreasonably and madly. But just as we do not mean for this metaphorical *possession* to exclude the belief in a real one, neither did they. Indeed, the very phrase *has a devil*, or *the devil is in him*, applied to those who act furiously and recklessly, implies that there is such a real thing as diabolical *possession*, which madness and extreme folly resemble.

See, then, how the patrons of witches <note>Those who defend the idea that witches do not exist, or who protect them from prosecution by denying the supernatural.</note> argue. They claim the *Jews* sometimes used the phrase "having a *devil*" *metaphorically*; therefore, they conclude there are no other types of *possession*, or that all those passages of Scripture in which possessions are literally and plainly related intend nothing more than a metaphor. Indeed, if we argued only from the mere words and expressions of "having devils" and "casting out devils," there would be some more color <note>original: "colour"; here meaning plausibility or weight of argument</note> to our adversaries' reasoning. But since we draw our conclusions chiefly from the plain circumstances of history and recorded facts, their argument has no force at all.

### SECTION X.
### The ignorance of the author of *The Grand Apostasy* in his interpreting the word *Daimonion*.

But what does this writer mean when he tells us *Daimonion* <note>original Greek: *Δαιμόνιον*</note> can scarcely signify anything else properly but an "unusual affliction from God," such as *madness*? All men and schoolboys know that when used as a *noun*, it is the same as *Demon* <note>original: *Δαίμων* (*Daimon*)</note>, which is already used in Scripture in a negative sense to mean an impure spirit. When used as an *adjective*, it sometimes signifies *something divine* <note>original Latin: *Divinum quid*</note>, but that is not how it is understood in the places we are debating. 

In *Luke* 4:35, it says: "When the devil had thrown him" (the possessed man) "in the midst, he came out of him." The word used there is *the demon* <note>original Greek: *το Δαιμόνιον* (*to Daimonion*)</note>. The same entity in verse 33 is called a *spirit of uncleanness* <note>original Greek: *πνεῦμα ἀκαθαρσίας* (*pneuma akatharsias*); a common biblical term for an evil or "unclean" spirit</note>. By this, and the later circumstances of the story, it plainly appears that *the demon* is to be understood *substantively* as a person—namely, an *evil spirit*. The same is true in the story of the *devils* entering into the herd of swine in *Luke* 8.

## SECT. XII.

*Further proof of the dealings of evil spirits with their followers, from the history of the magicians of Egypt; the excuses proposed by Mr. Wagstaffe, Mr. Webster, and the author of "The Doctrine of Devils" are answered.*

In general, they all say the same thing: namely, that the magicians were jugglers who, by their tricks and <term>legerdemain</term> <note>sleight of hand</note>, deceived Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Mr. Wagstaffe is modest enough not to describe the manner of the performance. But Mr. Webster says this: "The magicians, holding a rod in their hands and appearing to throw it down upon the ground, could easily throw down an artificial serpent in its place and immediately and unperceivably whisk away the rod" (p. 154). This is his trick; and for the changing of water into blood and the producing of frogs, he says they were so easy to do in the same manner that they do not need any particular explanation (p. 155). This is his main answer, after a great deal of irrelevance, and Mr. Webster thinks he has finished his work.

But the author of *The Doctrine of Devils* has devised a more specific way for this juggle. He says it is probable that these men, having the art or knack of making, engraving, or carving the pictures of men, beasts, serpents, reptiles, and so on, also had the skill of coloring, painting, and <term>fucussing</term> <note>original: "fucussing" — from "fucus," meaning to beautify, disguise, or color something to make it look like something else</note> them. Thus, they might easily—especially in the dark or by juggling feats, as the text suggests—make a rod look like a serpent, etc. (p. 114). But besides these dishonest painters, the man has found other jugglers to help with the deceit: subtle and political orators who, with deceptive arguments, cunning pretenses, and plausible rhetoric, could so disguise the truth and embellish dishonesty and falsehood that falsehood would seem like truth, and truth like falsehood (p. 115).

Whatever the magicians of Pharaoh were, anyone who considers these answers would take the creators of them for "colorers," "changers," and perverters of the face of things (as this author speaks). They are cunning orators, jugglers, <term>hocus-pocus</term>, and <term>hiccius-doccius</term> <note>nonsense words used by jugglers or magicians during a performance</note>—whip! The serpents, blood, and frogs are gone. But let us look a little closer at the matter, and at these "subtle" men.

The Scripture says, *Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a serpent (verse 10). And in verses 11 and 12: The magicians of Egypt also did the same with their enchantments. For every man cast down his rod and they became serpents, but Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods.* Now, say the defenders of witches <note>original: "Witch-Advocates"; those who argued that magic was merely trickery or natural phenomena rather than supernatural influence.</note>, the magicians were merely *jugglers*; they did not actually do the same thing. They did not really cast down their rods, but used trickery to swap them; they were not serpents but *pictures*. These claims are plain contradictions to the text—arbitrary inventions that have no basis in reality. If men may invent whatever they wish and apply whatever borrowed sense they please to plain accounts of facts, all history will be like a nose of wax <note>original: "Nose of Wax"; a common idiom of the period meaning something easily twisted or shaped to fit any interpretation.</note> and be easily shaped however the interpreter desires.

Secondly, if this were true and the serpents were only artificial pictures, it is strange that neither *Pharaoh* nor his servants should perceive the difference between carved and painted serpents and *real* ones—unless they also suppose that *Pharaoh* organized the business in a dark room on purpose, as the author of *The Doctrine of Devils* <note>A skeptical work published in 1676, often attributed to John Wagstaffe, which argued that belief in witchcraft was a delusion.</note> seems to suggest. And it is stranger yet that neither *Moses* nor *Aaron*, who were motivated to expose an imposture that was so gross and obvious, should not discern it; or if they did, it is just as strange that they should keep the jugglers' secret and say nothing about it.

Thirdly, *Aaron's* serpents are said to have swallowed up those of the magicians. What, did they swallow wires <note>original: "Wiars"</note> and pictures? It seems they were very skillfully made indeed, if the true serpents mistook them for real ones, just as the birds once did with the painted grapes <note>A reference to the ancient Greek story of the painter Zeuxis, whose painted grapes were so realistic that birds tried to eat them.</note>. But it would be more wonderful still if all of this was merely the "oratory" of the *magicians*; for then the serpents would be nothing but their *words* and *rhetoric*.

Fourthly, *Moses* and *Aaron* turned the *rivers into blood (verse 20), and the magicians of Egypt did so with their enchantments (verse 22). They caused frogs to come up and cover the land (Chapter 8, verse 6), and the magicians did the same, bringing up frogs onto the land of Egypt (verse 7).* Now, how did the jugglers do this? Was it with painting and disguising <term>original: "Fucussing"; the act of beautifying or disguising something to give it a false appearance.</term>? Or how, by legerdemain <note>Sleight of hand.</note> and trickery, were the waters made into blood and the frogs brought up out of the rivers onto the land? To turn a little water into the appearance of blood was not the same thing as what *Moses* and *Aaron* did; and to show two or three artificial frogs was not the same as "bringing up frogs on the land of *Egypt*," which implies multitudes that covered the ground. So that

<summary>The author argues that the miracles of Pharaoh’s magicians were genuine supernatural events rather than mere illusions or trickery, asserting that dismissing them as "juggling" contradicts the plain meaning of the biblical text.</summary>

The *Hocus-Pocus* tricks, *juggling* <note>original: "Juggling"; in this context, it refers to sleight of hand or stage magic rather than tossing objects</note>, and *deception* <note>original: "Painting"; meaning to color or disguise the truth</note> will not disguise this part of the story. I should wonder at Mr. *Webster*—if he did not already give me so many reasons to be surprised by him—when he passed over this so lightly. He said on page 15, "As for changing water into blood and the producing of frogs, they were so easy to do in the same manner—namely, by wires <note>original: "Wiars"</note> and juggling—that they do not need any particular explanation; for by this, the method of their performance may most easily be understood." How shall one deal with these men, and what will their confidence not affirm?

Fifthly, it is also very strange how those *jugglers* could have known what signs *Moses* and *Aaron* would show, so that they could furnish themselves with counterfeit serpents, blood, and frogs in advance. Did they always carry those in their pockets? If not, it was great luck for them that *Moses* and *Aaron* should show the very miracles first that they were prepared to imitate.

Sixthly and lastly: If the *magicians* did all this by tricks and juggling, should one not fear what opinion these men have of the same things done by *Moses* and *Aaron*? It is true that Moses and Aaron outdid the others in several following instances, but might these skeptics not say that it was because they had more cunning and dexterity in the art of *juggling*? If they or their followers have a mind to say this, they may do so by their own principles, which will serve them to evade the history in reference to *Moses* and *Aaron* just as well as it does in relation to the *magicians*. With just as much modesty, they might turn the entire account into allegory and metaphor.

I think by all this it appears that this excuse of the "Witch-Advocates" <note>Those who argue against the reality of witchcraft</note> is very vain, and that what the *magicians* did was not mere *juggling*, much less only political oratory and rhetoric. It is as if those *magicians* could use their eloquence to persuade *Pharaoh* and his servants against the evidence of their own senses—as these patrons of witches endeavor to do to us. They are the greatest "witches" in their own sense of the word that exist, and some of them are rumored <note>original: "belyed"; here meaning spoken of or accused</note> to be so in other senses as well.

## S E C T. XIII.

### *That what the Magicians of Egypt performed was at least by a secret alliance with Evil Spirits.*

**W**ELL! If there is any truth in this history, the magicians were not merely cheats <note>original: "Couzeners," meaning swindlers or tricksters</note> and "hocus-pocus" men; there was something done that was extraordinary, beyond human art and contrivance or the effects of ordinary nature. Therefore, it must have had either **God** or some **Spirit** or **Demon** (one or more) as its author. No one claims the former; the hand of God in this was only permissive. Therefore, it is plain the **magicians** did this by **spirits**, who are creatures of the **invisible world**. The text says they did it by their **enchantments**, or *per arcana* <note>original Latin: "by secret means"</note> as the Latin Vulgate reads. Because this is a general word, Mr. Wagstaff <note>John Wagstaffe (1633–1677) was a prominent skeptical author who argued that witchcraft and magic were merely the results of trickery or "legerdemain."</note> seizes upon it and defines it as a secret and sly trick—those of **sleight of hand** <note>original: "Legerdemain"</note> and **cheating**—whereas the word is just as applicable to any kind of secret (including the diabolical arts and alliance) as it is to his interpretation. And that it should be understood this way here is plain from the facts of the history. By those *arcana* (others read *incantationes* <note>incantations</note> or *veneficia* <note>sorceries</note>), they did those strange things; that is, by a secret alliance with spirits, they forced them to perform these wonders.

But what did the spirits actually do? Were the serpents, blood, and frogs **real** or **apparent** only? I am not required to say who holds which opinion on this; it does not matter. The reality of the performance is the easiest explanation and the most suitable to the sacred story. There is no difficulty in conceiving that spirits might suddenly carry serpents (which **Egypt** abounded with) into the place of the rods, which they might unperceivably snatch away after they were thrown down. This they could do, even though the magicians could not do it themselves. Furthermore, the spirits might be prepared for these performances by knowing the command God had given **Moses** and **Aaron** concerning the things He would have them do—which the magicians could not have known, except perhaps through the spirits.

And as for the blood and the frogs: by infusion, or a thousand ways that we cannot know, the spirits might make the water appear bloody to all sight, or perhaps really transform some (we...

To make the inference from these *magicians* to my point yet more plain and demonstrative, I shall further take notice that if we do not suppose a confederacy and formal compact between them and the spirits they act by, it must at least be granted that those *magicians* had a way to oblige them to act, either by *words* or *ceremonies*. Even this is sufficient for what I would infer.

He tells stories and cites scraps from this man and from that, all of which serve only for ostentation and the deception of the injudicious, but signify nothing for any purpose of reasoning.

### S E C T. XV.

## The Evasion of Mr. *Reginald Scot* regarding the *Witch's Private Room* <note>original: "Closet"</note> proposed and refuted.

**Mr.** *Reginald Scot*, the father of the modern skeptics who deny witchcraft <note>original: "Witch-Advocates"</note>, explains the matter this way. When *Saul*, he says, had told her that he wanted *Samuel* brought up to him, she left his presence and went into her private room <note>original: "Closet"</note>. There, she undoubtedly had her spiritual assistant <note>original: "Familiar"</note>—specifically, some wicked, crafty priest. She made *Saul* stand at the door like a fool (as if he had his finger stuck in a hole) to hear the deceptive <note>original: "couzening"</note> answers, but not to see the deceptive handling of the matter or the faking of the event. And so she goes to work, using common words of magic <note>original: "Conjuration"</note>, and so on. Likely <note>original: "belike"</note>, after many such words were spoken, she said to herself: "Look! Now the matter is finished; I see wonderful things." Because of this, *Saul* hearing these words longed to know everything and asked her what she saw. From this, you know that *Saul* saw nothing, but stood outside like a blockhead <note>original: "Mome"</note> while she played her part in her room, as is most clearly shown by the 21st verse of this chapter, where it says, *Then the woman came out to Saul, etc.* (*Scot*, p. 108).

Now, this is not interpreting a story, but making one up; for we read nothing of her private room, or her leaving *Saul* to go into it. We read nothing of the crafty priest she had there, or of *Saul's* standing at the door like a fool—or like a "drowned puppy," as Mr. *Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), another skeptic of witchcraft.</note> puts it (very respectful language for a prince in distress). There is nothing about words of magic, or of the woman's talk to herself; all of this is whimsy and fiction.

According to this way of interpreting, a person may make whatever they want of all the histories in the Bible—indeed, in the whole world. If one may supply and insert whatever they please, anything can be made into anything.

But Mr. *Scot* says it clearly appears that *Saul* saw nothing, but stayed outside like a blockhead <note>original: "Mome"</note> while she played her part in her room. He claims it is evident from the 21st verse of this chapter, where it is said, *Then the woman came out to Saul*. Is it not evident from this that she had a room? How else could she come out? But the trouble is, there is nothing about "coming out" in the original text or any version of it. Our translation—

is, *And the Woman came unto Saul.* The common Latin translation <note>original: *vulgar Latin*, referring to the Vulgate</note> says, *She entered* <note>original: *Ingressa est*</note>, which implies that she went out of the house, rather than into her private closet. The *Septuagint* <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> reads *the woman entered* <note>original: εἰσῆλθεν ἡ γυνή</note>, being the same sense as the common *Latin*. The *Chaldee* Paraphrase simply says *she came*, as do the *Syriac* and *Arabic* versions; but we find nothing of her coming out of any specific room anywhere except in the writings of the *Discoverer* <note>original: "the Discoverer" refers to Reginald Scot, author of *The Discoverie of Witchcraft* (1584), who argued that the woman was a fraud using ventriloquism and secret rooms.</note>. What does this have to do with a secret closet?

### Section XVI.

->Two of Mr. Webster’s Arguments for the Witch’s<-
->Closet proposed and answered.<-

**B**ut Mr. *Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), a critic of the belief in witchcraft who argued that such phenomena had natural explanations.</note> pursues this matter on behalf of the *Discoverer*. First, he asks: if they were in the same room and *Samuel* was a visible object, how does it happen that *Saul* did not see him? Mr. *Glanvill* <note>Joseph Glanvill (1636–1680), the author of this work and a defender of the reality of spirits.</note>, he says, *must struggle* <note>original: "must pump"; meaning to work hard or strain to find a reason</note> *to find an answer (page 169).* 

But does Mr. *Webster* not know that it is common in *apparitions*—and he admits that such things exist—for a spirit to appear to one person while remaining invisible to another, even though they are in the same room and both are capable of seeing? In the famous story of *Walker* and *Sharp* <note>A well-known 1631 murder case in Northern England where the ghost of Anne Walker reportedly appeared to a miller to identify her killers.</note>, recited by him on *pages 299 and 300* (which he confesses is undoubtedly true), he says it was reported that the *apparition* appeared in court to the Judge or the foreman of the jury (and I have very credible testimony from others that this was indeed the case), but the rest of the people saw nothing. Many other well-attested stories of this kind mention similar things, and there are innumerable stories of people who have "Second-sight," as they call it—that is, a faculty for seeing specters when others cannot discern them. There is nothing impossible or unlikely in this; why then should it require so much effort to answer this objection?

## RELATION XVI.

### *The appearing of the Ghost of* Mrs. Bretton, *for the* recovery of some lands into the hands of the poor, taken from them by some mistake in law or right, *as it is in a narrative sent to* Dr. Henry More, *from* Mr. Edward Fowler, Prebendary of Gloucester.

**Dr.** *Bretton*, late Rector of *Ludgate* and *Deptford*, lived formerly in *Herefordshire*, and married the daughter of Dr. S------. ## SECTION XVII.

### Other Arguments by Mr. Webster for a Separate Room from the One Saul Was In, Proposed and Answered.

**M**r. *Webster*’s third argument to prove there was a "closet" <note>original: "closet"; here meaning a small private room or partitioned space used for deception</note> is that it would have been inconsistent for *Saul* to have asked, "What did you see?" if they had been in the same room. But where is the inconsistency, or why is it a wonder, if a man in his desperate condition should speak inconsistently?

His fourth and fifth arguments aim to prove that *Saul* had seen nothing yet when he asked the woman, following her outcry, what she had seen. These arguments prove that she saw the *apparition* <note>original: "Apparition"</note> first, which is granted; however, her being in another room cannot be inferred from that fact, as I have shown—even though that is the point he must prove, or else his entire argument is irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note>.

The sixth argument is that, after all, *Samuel* was only just "coming up." The text says, "*An old man is coming up*," which proves nothing for Mr. *Webster*, but rather counts against him. At this point, *she shows him to* Saul; *she saw the very beginning of his appearing, which* Saul *did not. When he had risen higher out of the earth, she shows him to the King, who, it is said, perceived then that it was Samuel and bowed himself (verse 14)*. This is a very simple and logical <note>original: "congruous"</note> explanation when applied to their being in one and the same room. Why then does Mr. *Webster* mock <note>original: "insult"</note> me in the conclusion of this argument with these words: *Now let Mr.* Glanvill *consider and answer whether it is not only hinted at, but clearly stated in the text, that either they were in two rooms, or that nothing visible appeared before Saul (page 171).* I grant that he saw nothing at first, but there is no basis for the idea of two rooms, and he does not prove it. Whether or not he saw *Samuel* afterward, I shall not investigate now. So far, I am only concerned with the fanciful idea <note>original: "conceit"</note> of the "closet" or the separate room which Mr. *Scot* <note>Reginald Scot (c. 1538–1599), author of *The Discoverie of Witchcraft*, who argued that such spirits were merely stage magic or delusions.</note> invented for the woman, and which Mr. *Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), a skeptic who argued against the reality of witchcraft and sought naturalistic explanations for biblical wonders.</note> tries to support with much effort but little success.

# S E C T. XVIII.

## Convincing arguments brought to prove that Saul saw Samuel, which frustrates the fiction <note>original: "Figment"</note> of two rooms.

Ultimately, if he really saw the *apparition*, the fiction of the two rooms <note>A skeptical theory of the time suggesting the medium and Saul were in separate rooms, allowing her to trick him with voices or descriptions without him seeing anything.</note> is debunked, or at least signifies nothing to their purpose; the text indicates this plainly. She said, *“An old man is coming up, and he is covered with a mantle”*; and it follows, *“And Saul perceived that it was Samuel, and he stooped with his face to the ground, and bowed himself” (verse 14).*

He *perceived it was Samuel*. He perceived it, says Mr. Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682), an author who argued that many reported supernatural events were actually the result of fraud or natural causes.</note>, by the description of the woman. But she had only said, *“An old man is coming up, covered with a mantle.”* This is only a very general description—why must that necessarily signify *Samuel*? Could the Devil represent no other old man in a mantle, or could none of the dead appear in that way except *Samuel* alone? By these words alone, *Saul* could not certainly *perceive* that it was he; but he *perceived* it in such a way that he could not help but know and acknowledge it, as the *Hebrew* word seems to imply. I say this word [*perceived*] implies more than bare seeing. It is that and something else, namely, that he saw him so clearly as to be convinced that it was he indeed; judgment was added to the evidence of the senses. So Mr. Webster's objection—that the text does not say he [*saw*] it was Samuel—is of no weight; the word [*perceived*] implies that he saw it so as to be assured. If the woman's words had been the only evidence, there would have been no assurance at all, and *Saul* could not have perceived or understood any certainty of the matter from them.

Secondly, it appears even more clearly that his *perceiving* implied seeing; for *he stooped with his face to the ground, and bowed himself*. Now, to what did *Saul* show this respectful reverence if he saw nothing? Was it to a *Samuel* existing only in his imagination? Mr. Webster says, *“Surely in rational consequence it could be nothing else” (page 171)*. This is a rather unusual courtesy to show to mere ideas and imaginations. But Mr. Webster gives a reason: *“Since all that the woman had done and said were undeniable lies and cheats, this also, by right and reason, must be judged to be so as well.”* This is simply assuming the very point that needs to be proved.

## SECTION XIX.

### *That it was a real Apparition, not a conspiring Scoundrel, as Mr. Webster imagines, whom Saul saw and bowed down to.*

**B**UT did she not bring out her *conspiring scoundrel* <note>original: "confederate Knave"</note> to play the part of *Samuel*? And was it not to him that *Saul* bowed? This is what *Mr. Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682), an author who argued that many reported instances of witchcraft and spirits were actually natural phenomena or fraud</note> offers as part of his answer. The woman, in verse 14, describes *Samuel* in the form of an old man covered with a mantle <note>A loose, sleeveless cloak or cape</note>; the conspiring scoundrel would have had to be placed in such a disguise. Perhaps he was an old fellow, or she made him look old; but let that pass. But where did she get the mantle? According to *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>, it was a *priestly garment* <note>original: "Sacerdotal Habiliment"</note>. Did the woman have a wardrobe of all costumes for every occasion? Or was it some short cloak of her own that she threw over him? We will assume whichever option best serves *Mr. Webster’s* argument. But how did the man himself, or the old woman <note>original: "Quean," an archaic term for a disreputable woman</note> for him, change his face to look like *Samuel*, or alter his voice so as to make *Saul*—who knew *Samuel* well—believe it was actually him? These are difficult questions.

Even if we were to indulge *Mr. Scot* <note>Reginald Scot (c. 1538–1599), author of "The Discoverie of Witchcraft," which challenged the reality of magic</note>, *Mr. Webster*, and the rest by not pressing them with such troublesome questions, one cannot help but ask how the *conspiring scoundrel* managed to accurately predict such uncertain events as the *Israelites* being defeated by the *Philistines*, and *Saul* and his sons being killed the next day, as recorded in verse 19. How could the *fraud* <note>original: "Cheat"</note>, or the woman in another room, know this? "Why!" says *Mr. Wagstaffe* <note>John Wagstaffe (1633–1677), an English writer who argued against the existence of witchcraft</note>, "he spoke it as a gamble," and *Mr. Scot* says he or the witch made a "shrewd guess" about the outcome. But what basis was there for such a guess? Since there was none, the accomplice might just as easily have chosen to tell *Saul* that he and his sons would live and be victorious. If he were as clever a man as these skeptics claim he was, he would have done exactly that. After all, the witch’s business and his was to profit from their trade, and the more likely way to get a good reward would have been to prophesy favorable and pleasant things to the distressed king. If the prophet knew nothing of the event, he could have just as easily chosen the good side as the evil one. This would have served his own interests and would have better protected the reputation of...

## SECTION XX.

### *That it was not the witch herself who performed everything, as Scot and Webster would suppose for another excuse—imagining she put herself into a trance and deceived Saul through ventriloquism.*

**BUT** was it not the witch herself who performed everything? Mr. Scot <note>Reginald Scot (c. 1538–1599), author of *The Discoverie of Witchcraft*, a skeptical work that argued against the existence of witches.</note> says that if the explanation involving a <note>original: "Confederate"; here meaning a secret human accomplice working with the witch.</note> accomplice does not please us, he can easily adopt the opinion that this <term>Pythoness</term> <note>original: "Pythoneſs"; a woman believed to be possessed by a spirit or capable of prophecy, named after the Delphic Oracle.</note>—being a <term>ventriloquist</term>, speaking as it were from the depths of her stomach—cast herself into a trance. He suggests she thus deceived Saul by answering in Samuel’s name with a fake, hollow voice (p. 111). To the same purpose, Mr. Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682), another prominent skeptic who sought naturalistic explanations for supposedly supernatural events.</note> also supposes *that what she did, or pretended to do, was only by ventriloquism or by casting herself into a fake trance. He imagines she lay groveling on the ground with her face downward, and by changing her voice, she did mutter, murmur, peep, and chirp like a bird coming out of its shell. Or, he suggests she spoke through a pipe or into a bottle in some hollow cave or vault, and so <note>original: "amused"; in the 17th century, this meant to distract, bewilder, or mislead.</note> misled and deceived poor, fearful, and despairing Saul (p. 165, 166).*

What nonsense is this? How should one deal with such men who stretch their wits to the breaking point to invent excuses? They are ready to assert any absurdity to twist the meaning of a plain and simple history. I have already argued against the "dream of an accomplice" by pointing out Saul’s recognition that it was Samuel, his bowing down because of it, and his acceptance of the voice as the Prophet’s. Furthermore, the appropriateness and gravity of the words, the complexity of the prediction, and its eventual fulfillment are just as strong against this "whim" as they are against that other silly imagination. Indeed, in some details, these arguments have even more force, as will appear to anyone who considers the matter properly.

As for <term>ventriloquism</term>—speaking from the depths of the stomach—I think it is as strange and difficult to imagine as anything in witchcraft. I do not believe it can be performed with any clarity of spoken words without the help of the spirits that spoke out of <term>demoniacs</term> <note>original: "Dæmoniacks"; people believed to be possessed by demons or spirits.</note>. I would dearly like any of the "witch-advocates" <note>The author's derogatory term for skeptics who defended those accused of witchcraft by denying the reality of their powers.</note> to show how this is naturally possible. Therefore, the very thing they propose would actually imply the supernatural element they wish to avoid. It certainly cannot be thought, in any reason,

### SECTION XXI.

->*That it was Samuel himself who appeared, not the*<-

BUT the *witch-advocates* <note>original: "Witch-Advocates"; those who argued against the reality of witchcraft or sought to explain away supernatural events as natural phenomena or fraud</note> have another argument to prove an imposture in this *business*. For they say that the person announcing the fate of *Saul* could not be the true *Samuel*, nor the *Devil* in his likeness; therefore it must be either the *woman* or some cheating *confederate*. This conclusion does not follow, for it is possible it might be a good *spirit* personating *Samuel*. The *Scriptures* assure us that these are often employed in errands and ministries here below, and on those occasions they clothe themselves in human *shape* and appearance. So it is not absurd to think it might be thus here; but I do not affirm this. Who it actually was has been a great matter of debate among *interpreters*, and considerable *authors* have been on either side. My cause does not require that I should positively determine who the appearing *person* was; it might be one of them, though I cannot tell which.

I confess it seems most probable to me that it was the true *Samuel*, for the *Scriptures* call the *apparition* that five times—that is, as often as he is mentioned. And when the *woman* saw *Samuel* (v. 12); and *Saul* perceived that it was *Samuel* (v. 14); and *Samuel* said to *Saul* (v. 15); then said *Samuel* to *Saul* (v. 16); then *Saul* was greatly afraid because of the *words of Samuel* (v. 20). He proves the first point by these reasons: First, His body had lain too long in the grave, so that it must have been disfigured. Secondly, it must have stunk. Thirdly, there was no tailor in the grave to make him a mantle <note>original: "Mantle"; a cloak or spiritual garment.</note>. Fourthly, it must have required an omnipotent power to have done this. Fifthly, a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> is brought to prove this contrary to the Scripture, which says, *That those who die in the Lord rest from their labors.*

For it is nonsensical to think that the gross <note>original: "gross"; meaning the physical or material body.</note> body came out of the grave. Therefore, if there is any argument in this, it falls under the next inquiry.

The sixth argument is a question, namely: Who joined the soul and body again? Not the *witch* nor the *devil*. He claims the opinion is erroneous, impious, and blasphemous. As for me, let him call it what he pleases; his strength lies in harsh words, which here—like the stones sometimes thrown by witchcraft—land as softly as wool, and here they are also far from the mark.

#### Three Arguments of Mr. *Webster* against the appearing of the Soul of *Samuel* proposed and answered.

**Therefore**, as to his arguments: First, he could not, says he, come whether God would or not. Right! Secondly, he would not run on an errand without God's consent. No doubt. Because they were never employed in ministries here below, as they were never created for any such end or purpose (page 173). They were never employed in ministries here below! ...out their souls? <note>original: "out their Souls?" But he [Mr. Webster] will say these were sent on an extraordinary occasion. Even if that is true, they are still sometimes employed in such ways, and so Mr. Webster must eat his words. If blessed souls are, or have been, employed at any time, how can he be so certain that the real Samuel was not sent here?

Thus, I have briefly addressed his bold assertion. But he offers a reason: *They were never created for this purpose.* Even if that were true, what of it? The stars were never created to fight against Sisera <note>Judges 5:20 describes the "stars in their courses" fighting against the Canaanite general Sisera.</note>, nor against anyone else. Nor were the waters created to drown the world <note>A reference to the Great Flood in Genesis.</note>. Nor were the ravens created to feed prophets <note>1 Kings 17:4–6, where ravens brought food to the prophet Elijah.</note> or other men. May they not, therefore, be used for those services?

Furthermore, no sentient being was made primarily for another’s sake, but rather to enjoy its own existence and to partake of the goodness of its Creator. May it not, therefore, minister to others? And does not every creature do so? All things serve Him. 

Thirdly, he says that the angels are "ministering spirits" ordained for that purpose. Does he think they were created *only* for the purpose of serving us? 

Fourthly, rational human creatures exist for one another. *Non nobis solum, etc.* <note>original: "Non nobis solum, &c." From the Latin proverb *Non nobis solum nati sumus*: "We are not born for ourselves alone."</note> Souls are most suited to serve others, not only here in this life, but in the next world. They are *isangeloi* <note>original: "ἰσάγγελοι." Greek: "equal to angels" (see Luke 20:36).</note>, or like unto angels, and they are at least as suitable for the service of men as angels are. They share our nature and feelings. They feel our weaknesses and care for us more than abstract spirits do. This is the reason given why our Savior did not take on the nature of angels, but of men <note>A reference to Hebrews 2:16: "For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham."</note>. 

Fifthly, departed souls possess life, sense, and motion, as well as the capacity—and no doubt the inclination—to be employed. Where could they be more appropriately sent than to those of their own nature, whom they love, are related to, and have so recently left? 

Sixthly, the angels are not confined to their heavenly home but are often sent to this lower world, as Mr. Webster and the rest admit. Why then should we think that the souls of the righteous are so limited and restrained?

And lastly, it is supposed by both Jews and Christians that the soul of the Messiah appeared to the Patriarchs and was the "Angel of the Covenant." We also know He was pleased to appear to St. Stephen at his martyrdom, though He was then in glory. Regarding the various appearances of angels recorded in Scripture, we have reason to believe that some were actually human souls, called "angels" because of their office <note>The word "angel" (Greek: *angelos*) literally means "messenger" and can refer to a person's role or duty rather than their biological nature.</note>.

So, on the whole, we see we have no cause to rely on Mr. Webster’s certainty that Samuel’s soul did not come by a divine command.
