## SECTION XXV.

### *Other Arguments of Mr. Webster against the appearing of the Soul of Samuel, proposed and answered.*

**B**UT Mr. Webster goes on: Fourthly, he says, *Mr. Glanvill has only affirmed, not proved it.* This is not so; I allege the same reasons I have mentioned here in my *Philosophical Considerations about Witchcraft, Section 16*. The frequent affirmations of the Sacred Text <note>The Bible</note> were sufficient ground for the assertion, even though no other reasons were added to them.

He argues, Fifthly, that miracles are performed to confirm truth, but this would have confirmed Saul and the Witch in their wicked ways, *page 174.* I answer: miracles are not always performed to confirm truth, but sometimes to declare it. These sorts of events are often for that purpose. Such was this case: to pronounce the final sentence and doom on Saul regarding the concerns of this world. Additionally, the Prophet’s appearing so contrary to the woman's expectation, and before she had even performed her spells, struck her with dread and amazement; thus, she could draw no encouragement from it to support her trade of witchcraft.

Sixthly, he says it is not credible that Samuel would not have reproved the sorceress. But that was not his business. It is likely that she, being part of that vile and diabolical profession, was forsaken by God and good spirits and given up to those evil ones that were her agents and <term>familiars</term> <note>original: "Familiars"; supernatural entities or spirits believed to assist or serve a witch.</note>. We sometimes read of such <term>derelictions</term> <note>original: "derelictions"; the state of being abandoned or forsaken by God.</note>. Certainly, if any course of sinning causes and brings such a judgment (as some no doubt do), this practice of witchcraft and <term>confederacy</term> <note>original: "Confederacy"; a secret alliance or contract, in this case with the devil.</note> with evil spirits is one that most justly may.

These arguments can only reveal our ignorance of the reasons behind Divine counsels and actions. Yet it may be said that God had indeed withdrawn all comfortable and guiding communications from him, but this appearance was of another sort: a further instance of the Divine displeasure,

# S E C T. XXVI.

## *That the Soul of* Samuel *might come of its own accord, as well as be sent by* Divine Command; *either opinion is defensible.*

**I** have briefly listed and, I hope, cleared away Mr. *Webster’s* objections, which he stretches out into great length and numerous irrelevancies <note>original: "impertinencies"</note>. Indeed, his arguments are often such confident nonsense <note>original: "confident Nothings"</note> that it is really a shame to go about answering them. But I shall never pass by any of his stronger points.

But though I have defended the opinion that *Samuel’s* soul was sent on a divine errand to *Saul* against Mr. *Webster’s* contrary claims; there is another possibility which is just as probable: namely, that *Samuel* came without any direct command, simply being permitted to do so, and that the earnest and desperate desire of *Saul* to have some communication with him in his distress invited and inclined him to it. It might have been this way, and there is no reason to doubt that blessed souls are sometimes allowed such liberty. I shall not presume to determine which of these it was; both are defensible, and either is sufficient for my purpose.

## SECTION XXVII.

### *Several other Objections against the appearing of the Soul of Samuel answered.*

**B**UT there are other objections, besides Mr. *Webster's*, against the tenet <note>original: "Tenent," a principle or belief held to be true.</note> that it was the soul of *Samuel*; I shall not hide any one that has any weight in it.

First, it is argued that *witches* and *magicians* have no power over the spirits of the righteous, and therefore this <term>Pythoness</term> <note>A woman who acts as a medium or witch; the term refers to the priestess of Apollo at Delphi, known as the Pythia.</note> could not raise *Samuel*. We do not say she did. He appeared (as is probable from the *Scripture*) before she had performed her *conjurations* <note>Spells or rituals used to summon spirits.</note>. This might be one reason why she cried out. He came either sent by God, or of his own will. The *Devil* and the *witch* had nothing to do with it.

But secondly, would God send *Samuel* at such a time, when Saul was seeking answers through enchantment? And why not? He did the same when he appointed the Prophet to meet the messengers of *Ahaziah* when he sent to *Beelzebub* (2 *Kings* 1). That King sent to the Idol of *Ekron* to inquire about his fate, and God informed him of it through his Prophet *Elijah*. Similarly, when *Balak* had asked *Balaam* to curse the *Israelites*, God put a prophecy into his mouth and made him bless them (*Numbers* 22, etc.).

Thirdly, the woman said she saw "gods arising"—a group of evil spirits (as some interpret it)—and what was *Samuel* doing among them? But "I saw gods" is more probably translated by others as "*a god*," meaning a divine personage; the plural number is used for the singular to show honor. That it should be understood this way is shown clearly by the singular pronoun that follows: *What form is he of?* (verse 14). Or, if more were meant, why could they not be good <term>Genii</term> <note>Guardian spirits or supernatural beings.</note> that accompanied *Samuel*—a great and divine personage, who was no doubt as eminent in the next world as he was in this?

Fourthly, some argue from the question asked by the apparition in verse 15: *Why have you disquieted me?* *Samuel*, they say—whether sent by God or coming of his own accord—could not be "disquieted" by appearing. Nor was there any real disturbance in it, but the spirit of the Prophet speaks in our language. We are prone to imagine that the dead rest in their graves and are disturbed in their re-

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword is "pose," completing the word "repose."</meta>

Fifthly, but he says that Saul and his sons should be with him, namely in the *Chamber of the Righteous* <note>original: "Thalamo justorum"</note>, which some think is not unlikely, believing that Saul was a sinner only in a symbolic sense <note>original: "reprobate only in Type"</note>. But it is more probable that the meaning is that he would be in the state of the dead in the afterlife <note>original: "another World"</note>, just as the prophet was.

Sixthly and lastly, the ghost <note>original: "Spectre"</note> said that *tomorrow* he should be with him, which was not literally true, for several days passed before the battle. But the word *tomorrow* does not need to be taken strictly; it can be interpreted broadly to mean a short time. He was to die in or during the fight, and the enemies were now ready for it, so the event was to happen within a very little while. The prediction of this was a prophecy of a very uncertain event <note>original: "contingent"</note>, and shows that the speaker was the real *Samuel*.

### *An Answer to that Objection, That if it was Samuel's Soul that appeared, it proves nothing regarding Witchcraft.*

**B**ut if it were the real *Samuel*, they will say, this story then contributes nothing to the belief in witchcraft. For *Samuel* was not raised by enchantment, but came either of his own accord, or on a divine mission. To which objection, I say:

First, here is at least proof of an apparition of a man after death.

Secondly, *Saul's* going to this *medium* <note>original: "Pythoness," a term derived from the Delphic Oracle's "Pythia," used here to mean a woman with a familiar spirit</note> with such an inquiry, and her undertaking to bring up the person whom he should name (or at least the appearance of him) as indicated in verse 11, are good proof that this had been her practice—though at this time she was overruled—and that she acted by an evil spirit. For certainly when *Saul* entreats her to *divine to him by her familiar spirit*, he did not mean that she should deceive and delude him by a *hired accomplice* <note>original: "Confederate Knave"</note>. I have already sufficiently disproved the senselessness of that theory <note>original: "Figment"</note>. That the woman...

## SECTION XXIX.

->*Those who hold that it was an evil spirit that appeared to Saul may still be correct, despite everything Mr. Webster <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a critic of the belief in witchcraft who argued that many "supernatural" events had natural explanations.</note> argues against it.*<-

**A**s for the opinion of various theologians—that the Samuel who appeared was actually an evil spirit in his likeness—though I do not consider it as likely as the other view (that it was the real Samuel), the interpretation is neither absurd nor impossible. And because I do not definitively decide either way, I shall defend that view against Mr. Webster’s opposing arguments, which prove nothing whether the theory is true or not. He says:

This continued back and forth at least twenty times until Mr. *Mompesson* forbade his servant from such familiarities. This occurred during the daytime and was seen by a whole room full of people. That morning, it left a sulfurous smell behind, which was very offensive. At night, the minister, a Mr. *Cragg*, and several of the neighbors came to the house for a visit. Mr. *Mompesson*, seeing that the spirit so severely harassed the small children, sent them to stay at a neighbor’s house. He kept his eldest daughter, who was about ten years old, in his own bedroom, where the disturbance had not occurred for a month. As soon as she was in bed, the disturbance began there again, continuing for three weeks with drumming and other noises. It was noted that the drumming would exactly mimic any rhythm that was beaten or requested.

After this, when the house where the children were staying became full of guests, they were brought back home. Since no disturbances had occurred in the parlor, they were put to bed there. However, their persecutor <note>original: "Persecutor"; refers to the unseen entity or spirit</note> found them there as well, though it only pulled their hair and nightclothes without causing any other trouble.

It was noted that even when the noise was at its loudest and occurred with the most sudden and surprising violence, none of the dogs at the house would react. This was despite the knocking being so boisterous and loud that it was often heard from a great distance in the fields and woke up neighbors in the village, none of whom lived very near the house. The servants were sometimes lifted up along with their beds and then set gently back down without injury. At other times, it would feel like a heavy weight resting on their feet.

Toward the end of *December* 1661, the drumming became less frequent. They then began to hear a noise like the jingling of money. This was thought to be caused by something Mr. *Mompesson’s* mother had said the day before to a neighbor who spoke of *fairies* leaving money. She had said she would be pleased if the spirit left them some money to make up for the trouble it had caused. The night after she said this, there was a loud clinking of money throughout the house.

Following this, the spirit stopped the louder noises and occupied itself with silly, "apish" <note>original: "Apish"; meaning mimicking or foolish behavior, like an ape</note> and less troublesome tricks. On *Christmas Eve*, shortly before dawn, one of the young boys got out of bed and was struck on a sore spot on his heel by the door latch. The pin it was fastened with was so small that it was difficult to remove. The night after *Christmas Day*, it threw the old lady’s clothes around the room and hid her Bible in the fireplace ashes. It frequently performed such silly tricks.

Afterward, it became very troublesome to one of Mr. *Mompesson’s* servants, who was a strong man of serious character <note>original: "sober Conversation"; meaning reliable and grave behavior</note>.

On *Saturday* morning, January 10, an hour before dawn, a drum was heard beating on the outside of Mr. *Mompesson’s* chamber. From there, it moved to the other end of the house where some visiting gentlemen were staying, playing four or five different tunes at and outside their door, and then it faded away into the air.

The next night, a blacksmith from the village was sharing a bed with *John* the servant. They heard a noise in the room as if someone were shoeing a horse, and something came toward them that felt like a pair of pincers, snipping at the blacksmith's nose for most of the night.

One morning, as Mr. *Mompesson* got up early to go on a journey, he heard a great noise below where the children slept. Running down with a pistol in his hand, he heard a voice crying, "*A Witch, a Witch*," just as they had heard once before. Upon his entry, everything became quiet.

One night, after playing some small tricks at the foot of Mr. *Mompesson’s* bed, it moved into another bed where one of his daughters lay. It passed from side to side, lifting her up as it moved under her. At that time, three different kinds of noises came from the bed. They tried to stab at it with a sword, but it constantly shifted and carefully avoided the thrusts, always moving under the child when they aimed at it. The following night, it came panting like a dog out of breath. When more people came up, the room was suddenly filled with a thick, foul <note>original: "bloomy noisome"</note> smell and became very hot, even though there was no fire during a very sharp and severe winter. It continued panting and scratching in the bed for an hour and a half, then went into the next chamber where it knocked a little and seemed to rattle a chain. It continued this for two or three nights in a row.

After this, the lady's Bible was found in the fireplace ashes with the pages facing downward. Mr. *Mompesson* picked it up and noticed it was open to the third chapter of St. *Mark*, which mentions unclean spirits falling down before our Savior, His giving power to the twelve apostles to cast out demons, and the Scribes' claim that He cast them out through *Beelzebub* <note>A name derived from a Philistine god, used in the New Testament to refer to the prince of demons or the Devil.</note>.

The next night, they scattered ashes over the floor of the room to see what footprints it might leave. In the morning, they found the likeness of a large claw in one place, a smaller one in another, and some letters in a third spot that they could not understand, along with many circles and scratches in the ashes.

He later found out upon inquiry when he returned home that she really was there at that time. The gentleman himself affirmed this to me, and he is a very sober, intelligent, and credible person. Compton had no prior knowledge of him and was a complete stranger to his wife. 

We shall meet the same man again in the story of the witchcraft of *Elizabeth Style*, whom he identified as a witch by predicting her arrival at a house and her departure without speaking, as described in the third *Relation*. By all accounts, he was considered a very strange person.

<meta>This page continues the defense of Mr. Mompesson’s character and the credibility of the supernatural events reported at his house, likely referring to the famous "Drummer of Tedworth" case of the 1660s.</meta>

Mr. *Mompesson* is a gentleman whose truthfulness in this account I have no reason to doubt. He is neither conceited nor gullible, but a sensible, wise, and mature <note>original: "manly" — in this context, meaning dignified, courageous, or possessing the sound judgment expected of an adult male.</note> person. The credibility of factual matters depends heavily on the narrators; if they are neither easily deceived themselves nor suspected of having any motive to trick others, they ought to be believed. All human faith is grounded on such circumstances; indeed, a matter of fact cannot be proven in any other way except by the direct evidence of the senses. 

Now, this gentleman cannot be considered ignorant of whether what he relates is true or not, as the scene of everything was his own house. He was a witness not just to one or two incidents, but to a hundred; and not just once or twice, but over the course of several years, during which he was an involved and inquisitive *observer*. Therefore, it cannot reasonably be suggested that any of his servants deceived him, since over all that time he surely would have detected the trickery. And what motive could any of his family have had (even if it were possible to have managed it without discovery) to continue such a troublesome and harmful deception for so long? 

Nor is it any more probable that his own "melancholy" <note>original: "humour" — referring to the Four Humors theory of medicine. "Melancholy" was believed to cause depression or hallucinations.</note> deluded him. Besides the fact that he is not a foolish or overly imaginative person, that state of mind could not have been so long-lasting and persistent. Even if he were so affected, can we really think he influenced his entire family and the many neighbors and others who so often witnessed these events? Such suppositions are wild and unlikely to convince anyone except those whose biases dictate their logic. 

So, overall, the primary *narrator*, Mr. *Mompesson* himself, knew whether what he reported was true or not—whether the things that occurred in his house were staged *frauds* or extraordinary *realities*. And if he knew the truth, what interest could he possibly serve by carrying out or ignoring a deceptive scheme and *imposture*?

He suffered because of it in his reputation, his property, all his business affairs, and the general peace of his family. Those who did not believe in spirits and witches took him for a *fraud*. Many others judged the fact that such an extraordinary evil was permitted to happen to be God's judgment upon him for some well-known wickedness or lack of piety. Thus, his name was continually criticized, and his estate suffered due to the crowds of people flocking to his house from all over, the distraction it caused from his business, and the fear it instilled in his servants—because of which he could hardly find anyone willing to live with him. To which if I add the constant state of upheaval his family was in, the fr-

# Of Accounts

The frights, frustrations, and the tossing up and down of his children, along with the sleeplessness and disturbance of his entire household (in all of which he himself must have been the most affected)—I say, if these things are considered, there will be little reason to think he could have any interest in perpetrating a fraud <note>original: "cheat"</note> upon the world, an act which would have most injured and harmed himself. Or, if he had designed and managed such an incredible and unprofitable delusion <note>original: "Delusion" - a deception or false belief</note>, it is strange that he should have troubled himself for so long with such a business, only to deceive others and be talked about. 

It is even more strange that none of those many inquisitive people who came there specifically to criticize and examine the truth of these matters could discover any trickery <note>original: "Jugling" - sleight of hand or deceptive performance</note>, especially since many arrived prejudiced against the belief in such things in general, and others were already resolved against believing this specific case. Yet all were allowed the greatest freedom to search and inquire. After things were weighed and examined, some who were previously very skeptical went away fully convinced. To all this I add that:

There are several details in the story in which no abuse or deceit could have been practiced, such as the movement of boards and chairs on their own; the beating of a drum in the middle of a room and in the air when nothing was to be seen; the great heat in a chamber that had no fire during excessively cold weather; the scratching and panting; and the violent beating and shaking of the bedframes, for which there was no observable cause or occasion. In these and similar instances, it is impossible to imagine how tricks could have been played on so many suspicious and inquisitive people who witnessed them.

It is true that when the gentlemen sent by the King were there, the house was quiet and nothing was seen or heard that night. This was confidently and triumphantly used by many as a refutation <note>original: "confutation"</note> of the story. But it was bad logic to draw a conclusion in matters of *fact* from a single *negative* result—especially one weighed against numerous *affirmative* reports—and thus claim that a thing was never done just because it did not happen at that specific time, or that nobody ever saw what one particular man failed to see. 

By that same reasoning, I might infer that there were never any robberies committed on Salisbury Plain, Hounslow Heath <note>These locations were notorious for highwaymen and robberies in the 17th century.</note>, or other well-known places, simply because I have often traveled those roads and was never robbed. Likewise, the *Spaniard* made a poor inference when he said *there was no sun in England because he had been here for six weeks and never saw it.* This is the common argument of those who deny the existence of *apparitions* <note>original: "Apparitions" - ghosts or supernatural spirits</note>: they have traveled at all hours of the night and never saw anything worse than themselves (which...

<summary>The author argues that the disturbances were too physically exhausting and unprofitable to be a hoax, noting that even skeptics failed to find evidence of trickery. He dismisses the failed investigation by the King's messengers, arguing that a single quiet night does not disprove many previous eyewitness accounts.</summary>

(As may well be) and from this they conclude that all alleged *apparitions* are merely *fancies* or *impostures*. But why do such reasoners not also conclude that there was never a <term>pickpocket</term> <note>original: "cut-purse"</note> in *London* just because they lived there many years without ever being targeted by their schemes? Certainly, he who denies *apparitions* based on the confidence of this negative argument—against a vast heap of positive assurances—is as foolishly credulous as someone believing there was never a *highwayman* in the world because he himself was never robbed. If he is to be fair, the *Assize trials* <note>original: "Trials of Assizes"; periodic courts held in England and Wales</note> and *testimonies* of those who have been robbed ought to move his agreement no more in that case than in the case of *witches* and *apparitions*, which have the very same evidence.

But as to the quiet of *Mr. Mompesson's* house when the *courtiers* were there, it may be remembered and considered that the disturbance was not constant, but stopped sometimes for several days, and sometimes for weeks. So, the lack of activity at that time might have been accidental. Or perhaps the *demon* <note>original: "dæmon"</note> was not willing to give such a public testimony of those events, which might possibly convince those whom he would rather have continue in their disbelief of his existence. But however it was, this circumstance provides only a very slender argument against the credibility of the story, except among those who are willing to take anything as an argument against things which they have a personal interest in not acknowledging.

I have thus related the summary of the story and noted some circumstances that confirm the truth of it. I confess the passages recounted are not as dreadful, tragic, and amazing as some other stories of this kind; yet, they are no less probable or true for being less monstrous and astonishing. And they are strange enough to prove themselves the effects of some invisible, extraordinary agents, and so demonstrate that there are *spirits* who sometimes perceptibly interfere in our affairs. And I think they do it with clear evidence. For these things were not done long ago, or at a great distance, in an ignorant age, or among a barbaric people. They were not seen by only two or three <term>melancholic</term> <note>in this period, "melancholy" was thought to cause hallucinations</note> and superstitious people, nor reported by those who made them serve the advantage and interest of a political party. They were not the events of a single day or night, nor the vanishing glimpses of an *apparition*; but these occurrences were nearby and recent, public, frequent, and lasted for several years. They were witnessed by multitudes of competent and unbiased *witnesses* and took place in a searching, skeptical age—arguments enough, one would think, to convince any modest and capable mind.

## ACCOUNT II.

### *Which concerns witchcraft practiced by* Jane Brooks *upon* Richard Jones, *Son of* Henry Jones *of* Shepton Mallet.

**O**n Sunday, November 15, 1657, at about three o'clock in the afternoon, *Richard Jones*—then a lively youth about twelve years old and the son of *Henry Jones* of *Shepton Mallet* in the County of *Somerset*—was alone in his father's house. Perceiving someone looking in at the windows, he went to the door, where one *Jane Brooks* of the same town (though her name was then unknown to the boy) came to him. She asked him to give her a piece of <term>close bread</term> <note>likely referring to dense or unleavened bread</note> and gave him an apple. After this, she also stroked him down on his right side, shook him by the hand, and so bid him good night. The youth returned into the house, where he had been left in good health when his father and a man named *Gibson* went out. But at their return, which was within about an hour or thereabouts, they found him ill and complaining of his right side, in which the pain continued for most of that night. 

On the following *Monday* evening, the boy roasted the apple he had received from *Jane Brooks*, and having eaten about half of it, he became extremely ill and was sometimes speechless. Once recovered, he told his father that a woman of the town, on the *Sunday* before, had given him that apple and had stroked him on his side. He asked again why she sat with one hand over the other. She replied that she was <term>accustomed</term> <note>original: "wont"</note> to do so. He inquired if anything was wrong with her hand; her answer was that it was well enough. The Constable requested to see the hand that was underneath. When she was unwilling to show him, he pulled it out and found it bloody, just as the boy had described. When asked how it happened, she said it was scratched by a large pin.

# Of Relations

On the 8th of **December, 1657**, the Boy, **Jane Brooks**, and **Alice Coward** appeared at **Castle Cary** before the justices, **Mr. Hunt** and **Mr. Cary**. Just as the Boy began to give his testimony, upon the entry of the two women and their looking at him, he was instantly struck speechless. He remained so until the women were removed from the room; then, in a short time upon examination, he gave a full account of the mentioned particulars.

On the 11th of **January** following, the Boy was again examined by the same justices at **Shepton Mallet**. Upon the sight of **Jane Brooks**, he was again struck speechless, but this did not happen afterward when **Alice Coward** entered the room to see him.

At the next appearance at **Shepton**, which was on the 17th of **February**, many gentlemen, ministers, and others were present. The Boy fell into his fits upon the sight of **Jane Brooks** and lay in a man’s arms like a dead person. The woman was then asked to lay her hand on him, which she did; thereupon, he startled and jumped out in a very strange and unusual manner. One of the justices, to prevent all possibilities of <term>legerdemain</term> <note>original: "Legerdemain"; meaning sleight of hand or trickery</note>, ordered **Gibson** and the rest to stand back from the Boy, and then that justice held the Boy himself. While the youth was blindfolded, the justice called out as if **Brooks** were about to touch him, but signaled to others to do it instead. Two or three people did so in succession, but the Boy appeared unconcerned. The justice then called on the father to take him, but had privately requested one **Mr. Geoffrey Strode** to bring **Jane Brooks** to touch him at the exact moment he called for the father. This was done, and the Boy immediately jumped in a very odd and violent fashion. He was afterward touched by several other persons and did not move, but when **Jane Brooks** was again made to put her hand on him, he startled and jumped twice or thrice as before. He remained in his fit during all of this and for some time after; being then laid on a bed in the same room, the people present could not bend <note>original: "bow"</note> either of his arms or legs for a long time.

Between the mentioned 15th of **November** and the 11th of **January**, the two women appeared often to the Boy, their hands cold, their eyes staring, and their lips and cheeks looking pale. In this manner, on a **Thursday** about noon, while the Boy had just been laid in his bed, **Jane Brooks** and **Alice Coward** appeared to him. They told him that they could not complete what they had begun; however, if he would say no more about it, they would give him money—and so they put a twopence <note>original: "Two-pence"</note> into his pocket. After this, they took him out of his bed, laid him on the ground, and vanished; the Boy was found there by those who next entered the room.

He fell at last at the door of a man named *Jordan* in *Shepton*, where he was found appearing dead for a time. But when he came to himself, he told *Jordan* that *Jane Brooks* had picked him up by the arm out of *Isles’* garden and carried him through the air, as is described.

At several other times, the boy suddenly vanished, and upon searching for him, he was found in another room appearing dead, and sometimes strangely hanging above the ground. His hands were flat against a great beam at the top of the room, and his entire body was two or three feet from the ground. He hung there for fifteen minutes <note>original: "quarter of an Hour"</note> at a time, and after regaining consciousness, he told those who found him that *Jane Brooks* had carried him to that place and held him there. Nine people at once saw the boy hanging from the beam in this strange manner.

From November 15 to the following March 10, the boy’s body was much wasted and he was listless <note>original: "unspirited"</note> because of his fits. However, after that time—being the day the two women were sent to jail <note>original: "Goal"</note>—he had no more of those fits.

*Jane Brooks* was condemned and executed at the *Chard* Assizes <note>The Assizes were periodic courts held in England and Wales until 1971</note> on March 26, 1658.

I believe this is strong evidence for the existence of witches. If the Sadducee <note>In this context, a "Sadducee" refers to someone who denies the existence of spirits or the supernatural, named after the ancient Jewish sect that denied the resurrection</note> is not satisfied by this, I would very much like to know what kind of proof he would expect. Here we have the evidence of the senses, the oaths of several credible witnesses, the precise and careful scrutiny of perceptive and sensible examiners, and the judgment of a court session <term>Assize: a periodic court held in English counties for civil and criminal cases</term> upon the whole matter. The security of all our lives and fortunes currently depends on evidence no stronger than this. If such proof cannot be believed, then no fact can be proved, no wickedness can be punished, no right can be established, the law is at an end, and "blind Justice" would have no way to decide anything.

# RELATION III.

## Which contains the Witchcraft of Elizabeth Style of Bayford, Widow.

**T**HIS Elizabeth Style of *Stoke Trister*, in the County of *Somerset*, was accused by various persons of credit <note>people of good reputation</note> upon oath before Mr. *Hunt*. She also particularly and extensively confessed her guilt herself, which was confirmed by the jury at her trial at *Taunton*. However, she prevented her execution by dying in jail <note>original: "Goal"</note> a little before the expiration of the term her partner demon <note>original: "Confederate Dæmon"</note> had set for her enjoyment of diabolical pleasures in this life. I have shortened the examinations and organized them into the order I think best for making the matter clear and understandable.

1. Examination: *Richard Hill* of *Stoke Trister*, in the County of *Somerset*, Yeoman <note>a farmer who owned his own land</note>; being examined upon oath on January 23, 1664, before *Robert Hunt*, Esquire, one of his Majesty's Justices for that county, concerning the bewitching of his daughter by *Elizabeth Style*, declares: That his daughter, *Elizabeth Hill*, about thirteen years of age, has been for about the last two months taken with very strange fits, which have lasted two or three hours or more. In her fits, she also usually describes what clothes *Elizabeth Style* is wearing at that moment, which the informant and others have seen and found to be true.

2. Examination of **William Parsons**, Rector of **Stoke Trister**, in the County of **Somerset**. Now, before I proceed further with the story, I will note that there are three credible witnesses swearing to the same details: specifically, that the child *Elizabeth Hill* would sometimes fall into strange fits. Despite all this, some will claim it is merely "melancholy" <note>original: "Melancholy"; in this period, it referred to a physical and mental condition often used by skeptics to explain away supernatural sightings as hallucinations</note> and imagination, or sleight of hand <note>original: "Leger-de-main"</note>, or a natural illness <term>natural Distemper</term>—anything but witchcraft. Or they will deny the facts entirely and claim the three witnesses committed perjury. Such confidence against the oaths of sober men tends to overthrow all testimony and history, making all law useless. I will therefore proceed to further proof, which will abundantly strengthen this case: the confession of *Style* herself.

I left Mr. *Hunt* and the other two gentlemen at the Constable’s house, where *Style* was held for further examination. There, she expanded upon the confession she had previously begun and detailed the entire matter then, and on two other occasions afterward, in the particulars that follow.

5. Examination of *Elizabeth Styles* regarding her confessions of witchcraft, *January* 26 and 30, and *February* 7, 1664, before *Robert Hunt*, Esq; She then confessed that the Devil appeared to her about ten years ago in the shape of a handsome man, and afterward as a black dog. He promised her money and told her that she would live grandly and have the pleasures of the world for twelve years if she would sign his paper with her blood—which meant giving her soul to him—and if she would observe his laws and let him suck her blood. 

After four such requests, the witness promised to do so. Upon this, he pricked the fourth finger of her right hand, between the middle and upper joint (where the mark remained at the time of the examination). With a drop or two of her blood, she signed the paper with an [ o ]. Following this, the Devil gave her sixpence and vanished with the paper.

She confessed that since then, he has appeared to her in the shape of a man, as he did last Wednesday night, but more usually he appears in the likeness of a dog, a cat, or a fly like a miller <note>original: "Millar"; likely a large, pale moth</note>. In this last form, he usually sucks her poll <note>the back of the head</note> at about four o'clock in the morning, as he did on *January* 27; she noted that it is usually painful to be sucked in this way.

When she desires to do harm, she calls the spirit by the name of *Robin*. When he appears, she uses these words: *O Satan, give me my purpose!* She then tells him what she wants done. Her contract with him specified that he should appear to her in this way.

About a month ago, when he appeared, she asked him to torment one *Elizabeth Hill* and to thrust thorns into her flesh. He promised to do so, and the next time he appeared, he told her he had done it.

A little over a month ago, this witness, *Alice Duke*, *Ann Bishop*, and *Mary Penny* met around nine o'clock at night on the common near *Trister Gate*. There, they met a man in black clothes with a little band <note>a neck-collar worn by clergymen or professionals</note>, to whom they curtsied and showed due respect; the witness truly believes that this was the Devil. At that time, *Alice Duke* brought a wax image <note>original: "Picture in Wax"; a doll or poppet used for magic</note> meant to represent *Elizabeth Hill*. The man in black took it in his arms, anointed its forehead, and said, *I baptize you with this oil*, and used some other words. He acted as the godfather, and the witness and *Ann Bishop* acted as godmothers. They called the image *Elizabeth* or *Bess*. Then the man in black, this witness, *Ann Bishop*, and *Alice Duke* stuck thorns into several places of the neck, wrists, fingers, and other parts of the said image. After this, they had wine, cakes, and roast meat (all provided by the man in black), which

She says that before they are carried to their meetings, they anoint their foreheads and wrists with an oil that the spirit brings them (which smells raw). They are then transported in a very short time, saying these words as they travel: "*Thout, tout, a tout, tout, throughout and about.*" When they leave their meetings, they say, "*Rentum Tormentum*."

At their first meeting, the man in black welcomes them, and they all bow low <note>original: "make low obeysance"</note> to him. He hands out wax candles that look like little torches, which they return to him when they leave. When they anoint themselves, they recite a long ritual prayer <note>original: "form of words"</note>, and when they stick thorns into the image of anyone they wish to torment, they say, "A pox on you, I will spite you!"

At every meeting, before the spirit vanishes, he appoints the time and place for the next meeting; when he departs, there is a foul smell. At their meetings, they usually have wine or good beer, cakes, meat, or similar food. They truly eat and drink when they meet in their physical bodies; they also dance and have music. The man in black sits at the head of the table, and *Anne Bishop* usually sits next to him. He says some words before the meal <note>original: "before meat"</note>, but none after. His voice can be heard, but it is very low.

She says they are sometimes transported in their physical bodies and their clothes, and sometimes without them; the witness thinks that their bodies are sometimes left behind. Even when only their spirits are present, they still recognize one another.

# Concerning Narratives
## 6th Examination

When they intend to bewitch a man, woman, or child, they sometimes do it by using a **wax figure** <note>original: "Picture"; in this context, it refers to a wax effigy or doll used in sympathetic magic</note> which the Devil formally baptizes. Sometimes they receive an *apple*, *dish*, *spoon*, or another object from their evil spirit, which they give to the person they intend to harm. Once this is done, they have the power to hurt the person who eats or receives it. Sometimes they have the power to do mischief by a touch or a curse; through these methods, they can harm livestock. They can also cause harm by cursing without touching, but never without the Devil’s permission.

She testified that she has been at several general meetings at night at *High Common*, a common near *Motcombe*, a place near *Marnhull*, and at other locations. At these places, she met *John Combes*, *John Vining*, *Richard Dickes*, *Thomas Boſter* (or *Bolster*), *Thomas Dunning*, *James Bush* (a lame man), *Rachel King*, *Richard Lannen*, a woman called *Dunford*, *Alice Duke*, *Anne Bishop*, *Mary Penny*, and *Christopher Ellen*. All of these individuals performed acts of reverence <note>original: "obeisance"</note> to the "Man in Black," who was present at every one of their meetings. Usually, they have a *baptized wax figure* at these gatherings.

The Man in Black sometimes plays on a pipe or cittern <note>original: "Cittern"; a wire-stringed instrument similar to a guitar or mandolin</note>, and the company dances. At the end, the Devil vanishes, and everyone is carried back to their various homes in a short amount of time. Upon parting, they say, ["*A Boy! Merry meet, merry part.*"] <note>This phrase was a traditional ritual greeting and farewell recorded in several 17th-century Somerset witch trials.</note>

She stated that the reason she caused *Elizabeth Hill* to be tormented more severely was that Elizabeth's father had said she was a witch. She also claimed to have seen *Alice Duke’s* familiar <term>a supernatural spirit, often taking the shape of an animal, believed to serve a witch</term> suckle her in the shape of a cat, and *Anne Bishop’s* familiar suckle her in the shape of a rat.

She stated that she never heard the name of God or Jesus Christ mentioned at any of their meetings.

She testified that about five and a half years ago, *Anne Bishop* brought a *wax figure* to their meeting, which was baptized by the Man in Black and named *Peter*. This was intended to harm *Robert Newman’s* child at *Wincanton*.

She also stated that about two years ago, she gave two apples to *Agnes Vining*, the late wife of *Richard Vining*. She had received one of the apples from the Devil, who appeared to her and told her, "*That apple will settle the matter for Vining’s wife*" <note>original: "do Vining's Wives business"; a phrase meaning to cause her death or ruin</note>.

->Taken in the presence of several serious<-
->and orthodox clergymen before me,<-

->*Robert Hunt*<-

# The Collection

6. Examination. **William Parsons**, Rector of Stoke Trister, examined **February 7, 1664**, before **Robert Hunt, Esq.**; concerning **Elizabeth Style’s** confession, says: That he heard **Style** before the Justice of the Peace, at the time of her examination, confess—as she has also done to the witness several times since—that she was in a covenant with the Devil, that she had signed it with her blood, and that she had been with the Devil at several meetings in the night. He says that at one of those meetings, a <term>picture in blackish wax</term> <note>In this context, a "picture" refers to a wax image or "poppet" used in folk magic or witchcraft to represent and harm a specific person.</note> was brought, which the Devil, in the shape of a man in blackish clothes, baptized by the name of **Elizabeth Hill**. She confessed that she stuck a thorn into the wrists of the image, that **Alice Duke** stuck thorns into the same, and that **Anne Bishop** and **Mary Penny** were present at that meeting with the Devil.

->Taken upon oath before me,<-

->**Robert Hunt.**<-

Subscribed,

->**William Parsons**, Rector of Stoke Trister.<-

This confession by **Style** was free and unforced, without any torture or <term>watching</term> <note>A common interrogation method where a suspect was kept awake and forced to walk for days to break their will and induce a confession.</note>; it was drawn from her by a gentle examination, coinciding with the convictions of a guilty conscience. She confesses that she desired the Devil to torment **Elizabeth Hill** by thrusting thorns into her flesh, which he promised and later said he had done. She says that an image was baptized for the said **Elizabeth**, and that she, the <term>familiar</term> <note>A supernatural spirit, often in animal form, believed to serve and assist a witch.</note>, and **Alice Duke** stuck thorns into several places of the neck, wrists, fingers, and other parts of it. This exactly agrees with the strange effects reported regarding the torments the child suffered. She confesses she did this mischief because the child’s father said she was a witch. She also confessed she gave two apples to **Vining’s wife**, one of which she received from the Devil, who said it "would do the business"—which also matches the testimony of **Vining** concerning his wife.

She confesses further that the Devil used to suck her on the <term>poll</term> <note>The back of the head or nape of the neck.</note> about four o’clock in the morning, in the form of a fly like a <term>miller</term> <note>original: "Millar"; a name for a moth with white, dusty wings, resembling flour on a miller's clothes.</note>. Concerning this, let us hear the testimony (the other particulars of her confession we shall consider as the occasion arises).

## Concerning the Reports

7. **Examination:** Nicholas Lambert, examined again on *January 26, 1664*, before *Robert Hunt, Esq.*, concerning what happened after *Style’s* confession. He testifies that after *Elizabeth Style* had been examined before the Justice, made her confession, and was committed to the officer, the Justice required this witness, *William Thick*, and *William Read* of *Bayford* to watch her, which they did. As this informant was sitting near *Style* by the fire and reading in the *Practice of Piety* <note>original: *Practice of Piety*; a very popular 17th-century Puritan devotional book by Lewis Bayly</note>, at about three o'clock in the morning, there came from her head a glistening, bright fly, about an inch in length, which settled at first in the chimney and then vanished. 

In less than a quarter of an hour after, there appeared two more flies of a smaller size and another color, which seemed to strike at the witness's hand in which he held his book, but missed it—one going over and the other going under at the same time. Looking steadfastly then at *Style*, he perceived her countenance to change and to become very black and ghastly; the fire also at the same time changed its color. 

Whereupon the witness, *Thick*, and *Read*, conceiving that her <term>familiar</term> <note>A demonic spirit or "imp" believed to serve a witch, often taking the form of a small animal or insect.</note> was then about her, looked at her <term>poll</term> <note>The back of the head or the scalp.</note> and, seeing her hair shake very strangely, lifted it up. Then a fly like a large <term>miller</term> <note>A common name for a moth, particularly one that looks dusty or flour-covered.</note> flew out from that place, settled on the tabletop, and then vanished away. 

Upon this, the witness and the other two persons looked again at *Style’s* poll and found it very red and like raw beef. The witness asked her what it was that went out of her head; she said it was a butterfly and asked them why they had not caught it. *Lambert* said they could not. “I think so too,” she answered. A little while after, the informant and the others looked again at her head and found the place to have returned to its former color. The witness demanded again what the fly was; she confessed it was her *familiar*, and that she felt it tickle her poll, and that this was the usual time when her *familiar* came to her.

->Taken upon oath before me,<-

->*Robert Hunt*<-

*Which is the Examination and Confession of* Alice Duke, *otherwise known as* Manning (*another witch of Style's circle*) *of* Wincanton, *in the County of* Somerset, widow; *taken* Jan. 27 *and* Feb. 2, 7, 10, 21, in the year 1664, *before* Robert Hunt, Esq.

Present there were *Anne Bishop*, *Mary Penny* of *Wincanton*, *Elizabeth Style* of *Bayford*, and a man in black clothes with a little band <term>a formal neck collar worn by men in the 17th century</term>, whom she supposes was the Devil. 

At the meeting, there was a wax image <term>original: "Picture in Wax"; an effigy or "poppet" used for sympathetic magic</term> which the man in black took in his arms. After anointing its forehead with a little greenish oil and saying a few words, he baptized it with the name of *Elizabeth* or "*Bess Hill*," for the daughter of *Richard Hill*. Then the Devil, the accused, *Anne Bishop*, and *Elizabeth Style* stuck thorns into the neck, head, wrists, fingers, and other parts of the image, saying, "*A pox on you, I will spite you.*" When this was finished, they all sat down—a white cloth being spread on the ground—and drank wine and ate cakes and meat. After everything ended, the man in black vanished, leaving an ugly smell <note>Sulfur or brimstone was traditionally associated with the Devil's presence</note> upon his departure. The rest were suddenly transported back to their homes.

On the Monday night after *Christmas Day* last year, she met the same group again near the same place. Then *Ann Bishop* (who was there wearing a green apron, a *French waistcoat*, and a red petticoat) brought a picture made of blackish wax in her apron. The Devil baptized it as he had before, giving it the name *John Newman*, for the son of *Robert Newman* of *Wincanton*. Then first the Devil, followed by *Ann Bishop* and this witness <note>original: "Examinant"</note>, thrust thorns into the picture; *Ann Bishop* stuck two thorns into its arms. *Ann Bishop* carried the picture away with her. They were all present there in their clothes, and the Devil appeared in the shape of a man dressed in black.

About five and a half years ago, the same people were present at the baptizing of another image named *Peter Newman*, another son of *Robert Newman*. Both of these sons have since died. At that time, *Ann Bishop* asked the witness to join her in bewitching *Peter* and *John Newman*.

At another time, she was carried to a meeting at night in a green area near *Marnhull*, as she was then told. *Ann Bishop*, *Elizabeth Style*, *Mary Penny*, and some others unknown to her were present. There, a wax image was also baptized by the Devil in the previously mentioned manner, by the name of *Ann* or *Rachel Hatcher* of *Marnhull*, as she was then informed. After the ceremony ended, they had wine, cakes, etc.

She likewise confesses that she was at another such meeting where twelve people were present. Many of them were unknown to her, but she noticed one lame man with blackish hair among them, as well as the Devil, as before.

She says that after their meetings, they all make very low bows <note>original: "Obeysances"</note> to the Devil, who appears in black clothes and a small collar <note>original: "a little Band," a style of 17th-century neckwear</note>. He welcomes them when they arrive and brings wine or beer, cakes, meat, or similar food. He sits at the head of the table, and usually *Ann Bishop* sits next to him. They eat, drink, dance, and have music. At their parting, they usually say, "*Merry meet, merry part*." She also states that before they are carried to their meetings, their foreheads are anointed with a greenish oil that they receive from the spirit, which smells like raw meat. For the most part, they are carried through the air. As they pass, they say, "*Thout, tout a tout, tout, throughout and about*." Returning back, they say, "*Rentum Tormentum*," and another word which she does not remember.

She confesses that her <term>familiar</term> <note>A supernatural spirit or demon, often in animal form, believed to serve a witch.</note> commonly sucks her right breast around seven o’clock at night in the shape of a little cat of a dull brownish <note>original: "dunnish"</note> color, which is as smooth as a <term>want</term> <note>A regional English term for a mole.</note>. When she is being sucked, she is in a kind of trance.

## 1. Examination
**Thomas Conway** of **Wincanton** in the County of **Somerset**, examined February 12, 1664, before **Robert Hunt**, Esquire, concerning **Alice Duke**, informs the court:

That about twelve months ago, **Alice Duke** (also known as **Manning**) brought a little pewter dish to this witness and told him that it was a good <term>hansel</term> for his daughter. The witness asked Alice to carry it to her, as she was inside by the fire, but she forced the dish into his hand and went away. Shortly after, he became extremely ill in all his limbs; the physicians to whom he applied could give no explanation for this illness. When she left him, she was very angry and muttered a great deal because he would not sign a petition on her behalf. She has since confessed to him that she received the dish from the Devil and gave it to him specifically to hurt him. Since then, he has been in great torment and has been much weakened and wasted away in his body, which he attributes to the evil practices of **Alice Duke**.

->Taken upon oath, before me,<-
->**Robert Hunt**<-

2. The examination of Mary, the wife of Thomas Conway, examined March 6, 1664, before Robert Hunt, Esq., concerning *Alice Duke*. She says that her husband, Thomas Conway, about a year ago, gave her a small pewter dish, telling her he had received it from *Alice Duke* as a "hansel" <note>original: "Hansel"; a gift given to bring good luck, often to celebrate a new beginning or a birth</note> for his daughter, who had recently given birth <note>original: "lain in"</note>. In this dish she warmed a little deer fat <note>original: "Deer-suet"</note> and rose water, anointing her daughter's nipples with it, which caused her extreme pain. Because of this, suspecting the dish was harmful, she threw it into the fire, where it immediately vanished, and nothing of it could be found afterward. Later, when she anointed her daughter's nipples with the same deer fat and rose water warmed in a spoon, the daughter did not complain of any pain. She further says that after her husband received the dish from the hands of *Alice Duke*, he became ill in all his limbs and remained in a very strange condition for a long time.

->Robert Hunt.<-

## RELATION VI.

### Containing further testimonies of the villainous deeds of that rampant hag Margaret Agar, of Brewham in the County of Somerset.

<margin>1st Examination</margin> Elizabeth Talbot of Brewham, examined March 7, 1664, before Robert Hunt, Esq., says: That about three weeks before her father Joseph Talbot died, Margaret Agar fell out with him because he, being Overseer for the Poor <note>A parish official responsible for providing relief to the poor and finding work for their children</note>, required Agar’s daughter to go into domestic service. She said to him that he was proud of his property <note>original: "Living"</note>, but swore by the blood of the Lord that he should not enjoy it for long. Within three weeks of this, he was suddenly seized in his body as if he had been stabbed with daggers, and he continued in great pain for four or five days, and then died.

*Robert Hunt.*

<margin>2nd Examination</margin> Joseph Smith of Brewham, husbandman <note>A tenant farmer or smallholder</note>, examined March 15, 1664, before Robert Hunt, Esq., says: That a few days before Joseph Talbot died, he heard Margaret Agar rail very much against him because he had caused her daughter to go into domestic service. She said that he should not keep his property, but be carried out upon four men’s shoulders <note>Meaning he would be carried in a coffin to his grave</note>; that she should tread upon his jaws and see the grass grow over his head, which she swore by the blood of the Lord.

Taken upon oath before me,
*Robert Hunt.*

3. Examination - *Mary*, the wife of *William Smith* of *Brewham*, examined March 8, 1664, before *Robert Hunt*, Esquire. 4. Examination - *Catherine Green*, also known as *Cornish*, of *Brewham*, widow, examined May 16, 1665, before *Robert Hunt*, Esquire. She did so, and having arrived there, they saw a little man in black clothes with a small <term>band</term> <note>original: "band," a piece of neckwear or a collar common in the 17th century</note>. As soon as they came to him, *Margaret Agar* took out of her lap a small <term>picture</term> <note>original: "picture," referring here to a "poppet" or wax image used in folk magic to represent a person</note> made of blackish wax, which she delivered to the man in black. He stuck a thorn into the crown of the image and then delivered it back to *Agar*; upon which she stuck a thorn toward the heart of the image, cursing and saying, *"A plague on you."* She told the witness this was done to hurt *Elizabeth Cornish*, who (as she has been told) has been very ill ever since that time.

She also says that a little over a year ago, *Joseph Talbot*, late of *Brewham*, being the <term>Overseer for the Poor</term> <note>A local official responsible for managing welfare and placing poor children into apprenticeships or service</note>, forced two of *Agar’s* children to go into service <note>to work as domestic servants or laborers</note>. Because of this, she was very angry and said, in the witness's hearing a few days before he fell sick and died, that she had trodden upon the jaws of three of her enemies, and that she should shortly see *Talbot* rot and would tread on his jaws. And when this witness asked her not to hurt *Talbot*, she swore by the blood of the Lord that she would confound him if she could. The day before he died, she said to the witness, *"By God's wounds, I will go and see him, for I shall never see him more."* The next day, *Talbot* died.

She also heard *Margaret Agar* curse *Mary Smith* and say that she should live to see her and her cattle fall and rot before her face.

->Taken upon oath before me,<-
->*Robert Hunt*<-

5. **Examination.** Mary Green of Brewham, a single woman, examined June 3, 1665, before Robert Hunt, Esq., says: That about a month before Joseph Talbot, late of Brewham, died, Margaret Agar argued with him about her child being sent out to work as a servant <note>original: "putting out of her Child to Service"</note>. After that, she saw a clay or wax figure <note>original: "Picture" – a poppet or image used in sympathetic magic to harm a victim</note> in Agar's hands, which Agar said represented Talbot. She saw Agar deliver the figure at Redmore to the Fiend <note>original: "Fiend" – a demon or the Devil</note> in the shape of a man in black, about an hour after nightfall. He stuck a thorn in or near its heart; Agar stuck another in the breast; and Catherine Green, Alice Green, Mary Warberton, Henry Walter, and Christian Green, all of Brewham, were present then and there and all stuck thorns into the figure.

At 그 time, Catherine Green spoke to Agar, asking her not to hurt Talbot because she often received gifts from him <note>original: "received somewhat from him often times"</note>. But Agar replied, "By the Lord's blood, I will confound <note>original: "confound" – destroy or ruin</note> him," or words to that effect.

Shortly before Talbot fell sick, Agar, while in the house where the witness <note>original: "Examinant"</note> lived, swore that she would soon "tread upon his jaws" <note>A phrase meaning to see him dead and buried</note>. # ADVERTISEMENT.

**B**efore we move on to other accounts <note>original: "Relations"</note>, it will not be out of place to further remark upon these cases taken from the examinations of *Mr. Hunt*. From the poisoned apples that *Jane Brooks* gave to *Richard Jones*, and *Elizabeth Style* to *Agnes Vining*, and the poisoned pewter dish that *Alice Duke* gave to *Thomas Conway* (*which dish and apples they had received from the Devil*), we may observe in what a specific sense *witches* and *wizards* are called *pharmakoi* <note>original: φαρμακοὶ (Greek), meaning sorcerers or poisoners</note>, *venefici*, and *veneficae* <note>original: venefici/veneficae (Latin), meaning male and female poisoners</note>, **poisoners**. They do not harm people ordinarily by natural poisons, such as *arsenic* and the like, but rather by some hellish malice infused into things by the art and spite of the Devil, or by the vapors <note>original: "steams"</note> of their own bodies which the Devil sucks. For the hand of *Jane Brooks* stroking down *Richard Jones's* side inflicted a pain there.

We may also observe what an outstanding <note>original: eximious</note> example of *Moses's* *mekhashepha* <note>original: Mecassephah (Hebrew), the word used in Exodus 22:18, "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live"</note> *Margaret Agar* is, and how incorrectly some interpreters translate *mekhashephim* <note>original: Mecassephim (Hebrew plural for sorcerers)</note> as *malefici* <note>original: malefici (Latin), meaning "evildoers"</note>, because of the great

Mischief they do and delight in; and what a great credit this *Agar* <note>original: "Agar"; likely a reference to a specific accused person or spirit mentioned in the text's preceding accounts</note> is to *John Webster* <note>John Webster (1610–1682) was a prominent skeptic of witch-hunts who argued many cases were due to natural causes or fraud</note> and the rest of the *Hag-Advocates* <note>The author's derogatory term for skeptics who argued against the reality of witchcraft</note>, who would make them out to be mere cheating *scoundrels* <note>original: "Queans"; a term for disreputable women or harlots</note>, or melancholy *fools* <note>original: "Fops"</note> that had nothing to do with the Devil. It is as if the "Man in Black" with a little neck-band were nothing more than someone like *J. Webster*, or any other *Hag-Advocate* who, in a moment of mischief, played the part of the Devil at *Hussey’s-knap* <note>Likely a local place name; "knap" refers to the crest of a hill</note> or some similar spot in a forest. And so, after the act, quickly and suddenly retreating behind a bush and "letting fly" <note>The author is mocking the skeptics' view, suggesting they believe "demonic" smells of brimstone are actually just humans breaking wind or using gunpowder</note> into the wind, the deluded *hags* took it for the vanishing of the actual Fiend and his perfuming the air with the smell of *brimstone*. One who can explain away all the feats of the *Hartummim* <note>original: "Hartummim"; the magicians of ancient Egypt mentioned in the Book of Exodus</note> of *Egypt* as mere tricks of *sleight of hand* <note>original: "Leger-de-main"</note> cannot be easily fooled by a stunt like this—the old *wives* being hard of hearing and carrying their spectacles in their pockets rather than on their noses.

And lastly, from the *Devil’s* contracting with *witches* for their *souls*, it may be observed that the old *hags*—acting in good faith <note>original: "bonâ fide"</note> and believing they have *souls* that survive their *bodies*—are better *philosophers* than the arrogant wits of our age who deny the distinction between *soul* and *body*. But if they do not have souls (as these *arrogant men* would have it) and the *hags* think so themselves, it is a clever paradox that these old *fools* should be able to outwit the *Devil* himself. He would not, in bartering for their *bodies* and *souls*, buy a "pig in a poke" <note>An old idiom for buying something without inspecting it first</note> (as the proverb says), but rather a "poke without a pig" <note>Meaning the Devil would be receiving an empty bag if the soul did not exist</note>. 

But I believe instead that these arrogant wits, as high-and-mighty as they are, might learn one true point of philosophy from these *hags* and their *familiars* <note>Spirits or demons believed to serve a witch</note>. These evil spirits certainly make their bargains wisely enough by contracting for the *witch's* soul. If that clause were not expressed, the *soul* would be free from the *familiar’s* jurisdiction after *death*. Therefore, it is a significant argument—these evil spirits contracting for the *soul* of the *witch*—that they know the *soul* survives the *body*. Thus, they make their bargain certain so they can possess it as their *private property* <note>original: "Peculium"</note> after *death*. Otherwise, if the *soul* were mortal, they would tell the *witches* so, the more easily to rush them into all kinds of wickedness and make them more eager to enjoy this present *life* through the spirits' service. But this *doctrine* of mortality is inconsistent with the form of the Devil's *covenant*, by which the witches are assured to him after *death*.

# ACCOUNT 7.

## Concerning *Florence Newton*, an *Irish Witch* of *Youghal*, taken from her *trial* at the *Assizes* <note>original: "Assizes"; periodic courts held in English and Welsh counties for civil and criminal cases</note> held for the *County* of *Cork*, *September* 11, *in the year* 1661.

**T**HIS *Florence Newton* was committed to *Youghal Prison* by the *Mayor* of the town on *March* 24, 1661, for bewitching *Mary Longdon*, who gave evidence against her at the *Cork Assizes* as follows:

*Mary Longdon*, having been sworn and examined regarding what she could say against the said *Florence Newton* for any practice of witchcraft upon herself, was ordered to look at the prisoner. Her face turned pale, and she was very afraid to look toward her, but at last she did. Being asked whether she knew her, she said she did, and wished she never had. Being asked how long she had known her, she said for three or four years. She stated that last *Christmas*, the said *Florence* came to the deponent <note>original: "deponent"; the person giving a legal statement under oath</note> at the house of *John Pyne* in *Youghal*, where the deponent was a servant. Florence asked the deponent to give her a piece of beef out of the powdering tub <note>original: "powdering-tub"; a tub used for salting and preserving meat</note>. When the deponent answered that she could not give away her master's beef, Florence seemed very angry and said, "*You might as well have given it to me,*" and then went away grumbling.

About a week later, as the deponent was going to the water with a pail of laundry on her head, she met the said *Florence Newton*. Newton approached her directly, knocked the pail off her head, and violently kissed her, saying, "*Mary, I pray you, let us be friends; for I bear you no ill will, and I pray that you bear me none.*" The deponent then went home. Within a few days, she saw a woman with a veil over her face standing by her bedside, and someone standing next to her who looked like a little old man in silk clothes. This man, whom she took to be a spirit, drew the veil off the woman's face, and she then recognized her as *Goody Newton* <note>original: "Goody"; a shortened form of "Goodwife," a polite title for a woman of humble social standing</note>. The spirit spoke to the deponent and tried to make her promise to follow his advice, telling her she would have everything her heart desired. To this, she says she answered that she would have nothing to do with him, for her trust was in the Lord.

Within a month after the mentioned *Florence* had kissed her, this deponent <note>original: "deponent"; a person who gives evidence or testimony in court</note> fell very ill with fits or trances. These would strike her suddenly and with such violence that three or four men could not hold her down. During her fits, she would often suffer from vomiting and would bring up needles, pins, horse-nails, stub-nails <note>original: "stubbs"; short, thick nails</note>, wool, and straw; this happened very frequently. 

When asked if she realized at those times what she was vomiting, she said she did; she explained that at those moments, she was not as mentally distressed <note>original: "distraction"; a state of mental disturbance or delirium</note> as she was during other parts of her fits. She also stated that shortly before her fits first began, many small stones would fall on her as she moved about. They would follow her from place to place and from one room to another, hitting her on the head, shoulders, and arms before falling to the ground and vanishing. She and several others saw the stones fall both on her and on the ground, but they could never catch them, except for a few that she and her master caught in their hands. Following advice, she tied one stone that had a hole in it to her purse with a leather strap; however, it vanished immediately, even though the leather remained tied in a tight knot.

In her fits, she often saw *Florence Newton* and cried out against her for tormenting her. She claimed that Florence would several times stick pins into her arms—some so deeply that a man had to pull three or four times to remove them, as they were stuck between the skin and the flesh. 

Sometimes she was removed from her bed into another room, or carried to the top of the house and laid on a board between two <term>loft beams</term> <note>original: "Sollar-beams"; beams supporting an upper room or attic</note>. At other times, she was put into a chest, hidden under a bundle of wool, placed between two feather beds she used to lie on, or tucked between the bed and the mat in her master’s chamber during the day. 

When asked how she knew she was moved in this way, given that she was in a state of violent delirium during her fits, she answered that she never knew where she was until her family and neighbors found her and removed her from those places. When asked why she cried out so much against *Florence Newton* during her fits, she answered that it was because she saw her and felt her performing the torture.

[David Jones] was indicted at the **Cork Assizes** <note>A periodic court held in English and Irish counties for civil and criminal cases.</note>, and the evidence is as follows:

**Eleanor Jones**, widow <note>original: "relict"</note> of the said **David Jones**, being sworn and questioned in open court about what she knew concerning any practice of witchcraft by the said **Florence Newton** upon her husband **David**, gave this evidence: That in April last, her late husband **David**, having been out all night, came home early in the morning and said to her, "Where do you think I have been all night?" To which she answered that she did not know. Whereupon he replied, "I and **Frank Besely** have been standing sentinel <note>original: "Centinel," meaning a guard or lookout.</note> over the witch all night." To this, **Eleanor** said, "Why, what harm is there in that?" "Harm?" said he, "Indeed <note>original: "marry," an archaic oath derived from "by the Virgin Mary."</note>, I suspect it is not one bit the better for me; for she has kissed my hand, and I have had a great pain in that arm. I truly believe she has bewitched me, if ever she bewitched any man." To which she answered, "The Lord forbid." Throughout that night, and continually from that time on, he was restless and ill, complaining exceedingly of a great pain in his arm for seven days. At the end of those seven days, he complained that the pain had moved from his arm to his heart. He then remained in bed night and day, grievously afflicted and crying out against **Florence Newton**, and about fourteen days later, he died.

**Francis Besely**, being sworn and questioned, said that around the time mentioned above, he met with **David Jones** and discussed the various reports then circulating concerning **Florence Newton** (who was then in prison at **Youghal** for bewitching **Mary Longdon**). These reports claimed that she had several <term>familiars</term> <note>Supernatural entities or spirits, often taking the form of animals, believed to assist a witch.</note> visiting her in various shapes. **David Jones** told **Francis Besely** that he had a great desire to watch **Florence Newton** one night to see whether he could observe any cats or other creatures visiting her through the prison bars <note>original: "Grate"</note>, as was suspected. He asked **Francis** to go with him, which he did. When they arrived, **David Jones** went to **Florence** and told her he had heard she could <unclear>not</unclear> say the Lord's Prayer. Then **David Jones** began to teach her, but she could not, or would not, say it, though she was often <unclear>taught</unclear> it.

She told him she had a great mind to have kissed him, but since the grate hindered her, she desired that she might kiss his hand instead. Thereupon, he gave her his hand through the grate and she kissed it. Toward daybreak, they went away and parted, and soon after, the witness heard that David Jones was ill.

The witness then went to visit him and found him, about two or three days later, very ill with a pain in his arm. He complained of it excessively and told the witness that ever since he had parted from him, he had been seized by that pain. He said that the old hag had bewitched him when she kissed his hand, and that she now had him by the hand and was pulling off his arm. He said, "*Do you not see the old hag, how she pulls me? Well, I lay my death on her; she has bewitched me.*" Several times afterward, he would complain that she tormented him and had bewitched him, and that he blamed her for his approaching death. After languishing for fourteen days, David Jones died.

## RELATION VIII.

### The Narrative of Mr. Pool, a Servant and Officer in the Court to Judge Archer in his Circuit, concerning the Trial of Julian Cox for Witchcraft; who being himself then present, an Officer in the Court, noted as follows, namely:

**J**ulian Cox, aged about 70 years, was indicted at *Taunton* in *Somersetshire*, around the Summer Assizes of 1663, before Judge *Archer*, then Judge of Assize there, for witchcraft, which she practiced upon a young maid. By this, the maid's body languished and her health was impaired because of strange fits caused by the said witchcraft.

The evidence against her was divided into two branches: First, to prove her a witch in general; and second, to prove her guilty of the specific acts of witchcraft contained in the indictment.

To prove the first point: The first witness was a huntsman, who swore that he went out with a pack of hounds to hunt a hare, and not far from the house of *Julian Cox*...

While they were burning, *Julian Cox* came into the house, raging and scolding, saying that they had abused her without cause. Fourthly, another witness swore that she had seen *Julian Cox* fly into her own chamber window in her full human form, and that she knew her very well and was sure it was she.

Fifthly, another piece of evidence was the confession of *Julian Cox* herself, given during her examination before a Justice of the Peace, which was to this effect: that she had been often tempted by the Devil to be a witch but had never consented. She claimed that one evening she walked out about a mile from her own house, and there came riding toward her three persons upon three broomsticks <note>original: "Broom-staves"</note>, borne up about a yard and a half from the ground. Two of them she had formerly known—a witch and a wizard who had been hanged for witchcraft several years before. The third person she did not know; he appeared in the shape of a black man <note>In period witchcraft accounts, the "black man" was a conventional description of the Devil, usually referring to dark clothing or a shadowy, soot-colored appearance.</note> and tempted her to give him her soul, or words to that effect. He asked her to signify this by pricking her finger and signing her name in her blood as a token. He told her that she had a desire for revenge against several persons who had wronged her, but she could not achieve her purpose without his help; he promised that upon the aforementioned terms, he would assist her in being revenged against them. However, she said she did not consent to it. This was the summary of the general evidence to prove she was a witch.

But now, regarding the second point—to prove her guilty of the specific witchcraft against the maid for which she was indicted—this evidence was offered:

It was proved that *Julian Cox* came to the house where this maid was a servant to ask for alms <term>charity or donations</term>. The maid told her she should have none and gave her a sharp answer that displeased *Julian*. At this, *Julian* was angry and told the maid she would repent it before nightfall. And so she did; for before night, she was seized by a convulsive fit. After the fit left her, she saw *Julian Cox* following her and cried out to the people in the house to save her from *Julian*.

But no one saw *Julian* except the maid, and everyone attributed it to her imagination only. During the night, she cried out about *Julian Cox* and the black man, saying they came onto her bed and tempted her to drink something they offered her. But she cried out, defying the "Devil's potions" <note>original: "Devils Drenches"</note>. This also they attributed to her imagination, and they told her to be quiet because those in the same chamber with her did not see or hear anything; they thought it was only her own delusion <note>original: "Conceit"</note>.

-> # ADVERTISEMENT. <-

**T**HIS is a copy of a narrative sent by Mr. *Poole* on *October* 24, 1672, to Mr. *Archer* of *Emmanuel* College, nephew to the *Judge*, at the request of Dr. *Bright*. But I remember here at *Cambridge*, I heard the main passages of this narrative when they were first spread abroad after the *Assizes* <term>Assizes: periodic courts held around England and Wales for civil and criminal cases</term>, and particularly by *G. Rust*, later the Bishop of *Dromore* in *Ireland*. Nor do I doubt that it is a true account of what was attested before *Judge Archer* at the *Assizes*. For it is altogether incredible to me that someone who was an *officer* or *servant* of the *judge*, and present in the court at the *examination* and *trial*, and who took *notes* there, would write a narrative that would be so vulnerable to being proven wrong <note>original: "obnoxious to the disproof"</note> by the many other ear-witnesses who were present as well as himself. It may not be out of place here to transcribe what Dr. *M.* wrote to Mr. *G.* concerning this story in a letter dated *December* 26, 1678.

This narrative, he says, has the most authentic confirmation that human affairs are capable of: the evidence of the senses and the sacredness of an oath. But yet I confess, I heard that *Judge Archer* has been criticized by some for being too credulous <note>too ready to believe things without enough evidence</note> for sentencing *Julian Cox* to death based on those evidences. But to speak freely, I suspect those critics are people who, out of their ignorance, misinterpreted several passages in the evidence, or were of such a dull, stupid *Sadducean* <note>original: "Sadducean Temper"; a reference to the Sadducees, an ancient sect who denied the existence of spirits or the afterlife. In the 17th century, this was a common label for skeptics who did not believe in the supernatural.</note> temperament that they believe there are no *spirits* nor *witches*.
