"Such is the life of men," says Cicero <note>original: "Tully" — Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman</note>, "that no one attempts a crime without the hope of benefit or reward" <note>original: "Sic vita hominum est... ut ad maleficium nemo conetur sine spe atque emolumento accedere"</note>.

I suspect those foolish people thought he was lying because they imagined his story implied *Julian Cox* had actually turned into a hare. She had not, nor did his report imply any such real <term>metamorphosis</term> <note>a physical transformation from one form to another</note> of her body. Instead, these playful <term>demons</term> <note>original: "Dæmons" — spiritual beings, often considered malevolent or mischievous</note> presented the shape of a hare to the sight of this huntsman and his dogs. One of them transformed itself into such a form, while others hurried Julian's body along nearby at the same speed. They placed themselves between that hare-like phantom and her actual body, altering the air so that witnesses saw only empty air where she was, or a view of the ground where the hare passed. I have heard of some painters who have depicted the sky in a large landscape so realistically that birds flew against it, thinking it was open air, and fell down. If painters and jugglers, using tricks of <term>sleight of hand</term> <note>original: "Leger-de-main"</note>, can perform such strange feats to deceive the eyes, it is no wonder that these airy, invisible spirits far surpass them in such deceptive acts, just as the air surpasses the earth in its subtle nature.

Similar <term>deceptive illusions</term> <note>original: "Præstigiæ" — tricks or illusions</note> may occur with the toad mentioned in the testimony. It might have been a real toad (though controlled and guided by a demon) that was cut into pieces, or the one that was whipped and eventually snatched out of sight (as if it had vanished) by these <term>aerial illusions</term> <note>original: "Aerial Hocus-Pocus's"</note>. If some jugglers have tricks to put hot coals in their mouths without being hurt, it is certainly not strange that a small attempt was not enough to burn that toad. I heard a credible report some time ago from someone in the Isle of Ely about such a toad, sent by a witch, that crawled up the body of the master of the house as he sat by the fireside; he and his wife together overpowered it and burned it in the fire. I have heard other stories of these demonic vermin as well, such as a rat that followed a man for many miles, trudging through thick and thin alongside him. There is little difficulty, then, in believing the story of the toad.

By this power, they can so modify the air immediately next to the person they wish to conceal that it looks like the open sky, or whatever landscape they please. This is similar to when they show in a "shew-stone" <note>a crystal ball or mirror used for divination</note> or glass the very room in which the person is—the demon, by the power of his imagination, at least modifying his own "vehicle" <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "vehicle" was the subtle, airy body that a spirit inhabited to manifest in the physical world</note>. 

Some members of the "Atheistic Brotherhood" cannot honestly deny this power, assuming they admit demons exist at all, since they attribute an even greater power to the imagination of a human being—as if it were able to transform the air into real birds or mice, or similar creatures that are momentarily alive. But it seems some would believe anything rather than the existence of witches and demons.

It will not be amiss here to take notice of what an eminent example this Julian Cox is of the terms Moses used: *Megnonenah* or *Mecaffephah* <note>Hebrew terms from the Old Testament (e.g., Deuteronomy 18:10) referring to soothsayers or sorcerers</note> taken in the same sense. That is, she is a witch thought to use a <term>deceptive art</term> <note>original: πλεξωνια</note> or prestigiatory power (though it is the Devil who performs these feats, not she) to transform herself into strange shapes and use other similar deceptions of the light. 

This is also a notable instance of the "astral spirits" of witches: how strongly, though separated by distance, they are tied together in a fatal sympathy with their physical bodies. Julian’s body was wounded by a stab aimed at her astral spirit. I have seen the same thing happen with Jane Brooks and an old woman in Cambridgeshire. In the latter case, the woman's astral spirit entered a man’s house (as he was sitting alone by the fire) in the shape of a huge cat. It sat itself before the fire, not far from him; he struck at its back with a fire-fork <note>a tool for tending a fire</note> and seemed to break its back, but it scrambled away from him and vanished, he knew not how. However, that same reputed witch was found dead in her bed that very night with her back broken, as I heard credibly reported some years ago.

The "magical sympathy" in this story of Julian Cox is also marvelous—the fact that burning the ears of the beast she had bewitched would put her into such a rage and torment. This is like the heating of the tile red-hot in the story of Florence Newton and pouring some of the bewitched maid's water <note>urine</note> upon it. # RELATION III.

## *Which is an account of* Thomas Goddard *of* Marlborough, *in the County of* Wiltshire, *Weaver, given on November 23, 1674.*

**H**e says that on Monday the ninth of this month, as he was going to Ogbourne at a stile <term>a set of steps for scaling a fence or wall</term> on the highway near Mr. Goddard’s ground around nine in the morning, he met the apparition of his father-in-law, one Edward Avon of this town, a glover <term>a maker or seller of gloves</term>, who died last May. The ghost had on, to his appearance, the same clothes, hat, stockings, and shoes he usually wore when he was living, and was standing by and leaning over that stile. When he came near, the apparition spoke to him with an audible voice these words: *Are you afraid?* To which he answered, "I am thinking of one who is dead and buried, whom you are like." To which the apparition replied with the same voice, "I am he that you were thinking of; I am Edward Avon your father-in-law. Come near to me; I will do you no harm." To which Goddard answered, "I trust in Him who has bought my soul with His precious blood; you shall do me no harm."

Then the apparition said, *How do things stand at home?* Goddard asked what things? Then it asked him, *how are* William *and* Mary, meaning, as he understood, his son William Avon, a shoemaker here, and Mary his daughter, who was Goddard’s wife. Then it said, *What!* Taylor *is dead*, meaning, as he thought, one Taylor of London, who married his daughter Sarah; this Taylor died around Michaelmas <term>The feast of St. Michael, celebrated on September 29th</term> last. 

Then the apparition held out its hand, and in it, as Goddard perceived, were twenty or thirty shillings in silver; it then spoke with a loud voice: *Take this money and send it to* Sarah; *for I shut up my bowels of compassion <term>a biblical phrase meaning to withhold pity or generosity</term> toward her during my life, and now here is something for her.* And then it said, *Mary* (meaning Goddard’s wife, as he understood) *is troubled for me; but tell her God has shown mercy to me contrary to my deserts <note>original: "deserts"—what is deserved, usually in the context of earned punishment</note>.* 

But the said Goddard answered, "In the name of JESUS CHRIST, I refuse all such money." Then the apparition said, *I perceive you are afraid; I will meet you some other time.* And immediately it appeared to go up the lane. So he went over the same stile, but saw it no more that day.

# ADVERTISEMENT.

**T**hat Thomas Goddard saw this apparition seems to be a thing beyond doubt; but whether it was truly his father-in-law’s ghost is more questionable. The former point is confirmed by a source that is at least impartial, if not skeptical of the story. This person, in his letter to Mr. G—, writes briefly to this effect:

1. That he truly thinks that Thomas Goddard himself strongly believes the story.
2. That he cannot imagine what motive <note>original: "interest"</note> Goddard would have for inventing such a story, as he brings shame upon his wife’s father and obliges himself to pay a debt of 20 shillings <note>About £1 in 17th-century currency, a significant amount for a laborer.</note>, which his poverty makes him very ill-able to spare.
3. That his father-in-law, Edward Avon, was a determined and tough man in his youth and served for many years as a bailiff <note>A court official authorized to serve writs and make arrests.</note>.
4. That Thomas Goddard had the reputation of an honest man, was as knowledgeable about religion as most people of his social status and education, and was a regular attendee of the Church until about a year before this happened, when he left it entirely to join the Non-Conformists <note>Protestants who did not follow the established Church of England, often facing social and legal scrutiny.</note>.

Up to this point, everything except for that last detail tends to confirm the story. Therefore, that last detail shall be the first argument used against its credibility. 
2. It is further alleged that perhaps the purpose of the story was to make Goddard appear to be someone extraordinary among the Dissenting party. 
3. That he is sometimes

...times troubled with *epileptic fits*. 4. That the *Mayor* sent men the next morning to dig in the place where the *specter* said the *murdered man* was buried, but they found neither bones nor any difference in the soil from the surrounding earth.

But we answer briefly to the first point: although his turning to the *Non-conformists* <note>Protestants who did not follow the established Church of England</note> may suggest a vacillation <note>original: "vacillancy"</note> of his judgment, it does not imply any defect in his external senses. He was no less able to perceive what he saw or heard than he was before. To the second point: it is a complete contradiction to his strong belief in the truth of his own story, which plainly implies that he did not invent it just to make himself seem like an extraordinary "somebody." To the third point: an *epileptic person*, when not suffering from a fit, has external senses as true and complete as a drunken man has once his drunken fit is over, or a man who has woken up after a night of sleep and dreams. Thus, this argument has not the slightest force, unless you intend to dismiss the authority of everyone's senses because they occasionally lack full use of them—namely, during sleep, drunkenness, or similar states. 

But now lastly, regarding the fourth point, which is the most significant: it still only makes it questionable whether this *specter* was the ghost of his father or some mocking <term>original: "ludicrous"</term> goblin trying to play a trick on *Thomas Goddard* by impersonating his father-in-law and pointing to a fake grave to make him look ridiculous. For what *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote about demons.</note> has noted, I do not doubt is true: that *demons* sometimes impersonate the souls of the deceased. However, if an uncoffined body is laid in ground exposed to wet and dry conditions, the earth may, in thirty or forty years, consume even the bones and transform everything into the surrounding soil—especially since some types of earth can do this in less than a fifteenth or twentieth of that time. Or, perhaps the ghost of *Edward Avon* might have forgotten the exact location (it being an unpleasant memory) where he buried the murdered man, and only guessed the spot because the ground had sunk slightly, as if the earth had settled as the buried body decayed. The rest of the story still naturally suggests that it was the actual ghost of *Edward Avon*. Besides, he explicitly stated that although the body was buried there, by this time it had all turned to dust.

But whether it was a mocking *demon* or *Edward Avon’s* ghost does not affect our purpose. It is sufficient that this is a reliable instance of a real apparition. I thought it appropriate here, as in the previous story, to be so faithful as to conceal nothing that anyone might use to try to diminish its credibility. Stories of the appearing souls of the departed are not usually to the taste <note>original: "for the tooth of"</note> of the *Non-conformists*; if they generally believe this one, as it is said they do, it must be because of the undeniable

Z

## RELATION XII.

->The appearing of Mr. Watkinson’s Ghost to his Daughter<-
->Toppam, contained in a Letter from Mrs. Taylor<-
->of the Ford by St. Neots, to Dr. Ezekias Burton.<-

SIR,

My respects to you and your lady. Now, according to your desire, I shall write what my cousin told me. Her name was Mary Watkinson; her father lived in Smithfield, but she was married to Francis Toppam and lived in York with her husband. He was a bad husband <note>original: "an ill one"</note> who had stolen her away against her parents' consent, so that they could not endure him. However, she visited them often, and when she was with her father just before their final parting, she expressed her fear that she should never see him again. He answered her that if he should die, and if God ever permitted the dead to see the living, he would see her again. 

About half a year after he had been buried, on a night when she was in bed but could not sleep, she heard music, and the chamber grew lighter and lighter. Being wide awake, she saw her father standing at her bedside. He said, "Mall <note>original: "Mall"; a common diminutive or nickname for Mary.</note>, did I not tell you that I would see you once again?" 

She called him "Father" and they spoke of many things. He told her to be patient and dutiful to her mother. When she told him she had given birth to a child since he died, he said that the child would not trouble her long <note>This implies the child would soon die, a common theme in such "providential" ghost stories.</note>. He told her to say whatever she wished to him now, for he had to go, and she would never see him again until they met in the Kingdom of Heaven. Then the chamber grew darker and darker, and he vanished to the sound of music. She said she never dreamed of him, nor did she ever see any apparition of him afterward.

He was a very honest, godly man, as far as I can tell.

Note: *This story Dr. Rust, who later became the Bishop of Dromore, told me, I remember, with great assurance.*

## RELATION XIII.

*The appearance of the Ghost of Dr. Ferrar’s Daughter to him after her Death, according to a brief Narrative sent from the Reverend Mr. Edward Fowler to Dr. Henry More on May 11, 1678.*

**T**HIS week Mr. Pearson, who is a worthy and good minister of the city of London, told me that his wife’s grandfather—a man of great piety and physician to the current King <note>King Charles II</note>, named Dr. Ferrar <note>original: "Farrar"</note>—was a close relative (I believe the brother) of the famous Mr. Ferrar of Little Gidding <note>original: "Little-Giddon"; referring to the famous Anglican religious community founded by Nicholas Ferrar</note>. 

I say, this gentleman and his daughter (Mrs. Pearson’s mother, a very pious soul) made a pact <note>original: "compact"</note> at his request: that the first of them to die, if they were in a state of grace <note>original: "if happy"</note>, should appear to the survivor after death, if such a thing were possible. The daughter consented to this with some difficulty.

Some time later, the daughter, who lived at Gillingham Lodge (two miles from Salisbury), went into labor. By mistake, she was given a harmful medicine <note>original: "noxious potion"</note> instead of the one prepared for her, and she died suddenly.

Her father lived in London. That very night she died, she opened his bed curtains and looked upon him. He had previously heard nothing of her illness; however, because of this apparition, he confidently told his maid that his daughter was dead, and two days later he received the news. Her grandmother told Mrs. Pearson this, as did one of her uncles and the aforementioned maid. I know this Mrs. Pearson, and she is a very sensible and good woman.

### RELATION XIV.

*The appearance of the ghost of a Mr. Bower of Guildford to a highwayman in prison, as recorded in a letter from Dr. Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezekias"</note> Burton to Dr. Henry More.*

About ten years ago, a Mr. Bower, an elderly man living at Guildford in Surrey, was found on the highway not far from that place. He had been newly and very barbarously murdered, having one large cut across his throat and another down his chest. Two men were seized on suspicion and put into jail <note>original: "Goal"</note> at Guildford, sharing a cell with another man who had previously been committed for robbery, as I suppose. That night, this third man was awakened about one o'clock and greatly terrified by an old man who had a large gash across his throat, almost from ear to ear, and a wound down his chest. The old man entered stooping and holding his hand on his back. He appeared in this manner but said nothing. The thief called out to his two new companions; they grumbled at him but gave no answer.

In the morning, he retained such a vivid impression of what he had seen that he spoke to them again for the same purpose, but they told him it was nothing but his imagination. However, he was so fully persuaded of the reality of the apparition <term>apparition</term><note>A ghost or ghostlike image of a person.</note> that he told others about it. Eventually, word reached my friend Mr. Reading, a Justice of the Peace in Surrey and a cousin to the gentleman who was murdered.

He immediately sent for the prisoner and asked him first whether he was born or had lived near Guildford. To this, the prisoner answered no. Secondly, he inquired if he knew any of the inhabitants of that town or the neighborhood. He replied that he was a stranger to everyone in the area. Then the Justice inquired if he had ever heard of a Mr. Bower. He said no. After this, he examined him to find out why those two other men were imprisoned. To this, he answered that he did not know, but supposed it was for some robbery.

AFTER these preliminary questioning sessions, he asked him to tell him what he had seen in the night, which he immediately did, exactly according to the account he had heard, and which I gave before. Additionally, he described the old gentleman so well by his pointed beard <note>original: "picked Beard"</note>, and that his face was (as he called it) "rough on his cheeks," and that the hairs of his face were black and white. *Mr. Reading* says that he himself could not have given a more exact description of *Mr. Bower* than this was. He told the highwayman that he must give his oath (though that would signify little from such a rogue), to which the man readily consented, and took an oath before the Justice regarding all of this.

*Mr. READING* being a very discreet <note>original: "discrete"</note> man, concealed this story from the jury at the <term>Assizes</term> <note>Periodic courts held in English and Welsh counties for civil and criminal cases.</note>, as he knew that this would be no evidence according to our law. However, the friends of the murdered gentleman had been very inquisitive and discovered several suspicious circumstances; one of which was that those two men had washed their clothes and that some stains of blood remained. Another was that one of them had denied he ever heard that *Mr. Bower* was dead, whereas he had confessed it in another place two hours earlier. Upon these and similar evidences, those two were condemned and executed, but they denied it to the last. However, one of them said the other could clear him if he would, which the bystanders did not understand.

AFTER some time a tinker was hanged (where the gentleman has forgotten), who at his death said that the murder of *Mr. Bower* of *Guilford* was his greatest trouble, for he had a hand in it. He confessed he struck him a blow on the back, which knocked him from his horse, and when he was down, those other men who were arraigned and executed for it cut his throat and robbed <note>original: "rifled"</note> him. This is the first story, which I had from *Mr. Reading* himself, who is a very honest, prudent person, and not easily fooled <note>original: "credulous"</note>.

I know you desire to have the names of all the persons referred to in this account, and the exact time and place, but *Mr. Reading* cannot recollect them now, though he tells me he sent an exact and full narrative of all to one *Mr. Onslow*, a Justice of the Peace.

# RELATION XV.

### *Another appearance of the ghost of a man from Guildford for the recovery of a field for his child, which was being unjustly kept by his brother; from the aforementioned letter of Dr. Hezekiah <note>original: Ezekias</note> Burton to Dr. Henry More.*

**A**n inhabitant of the previously mentioned town of Guildford <note>original: Guilford</note> owned some copyhold land <term>land held by a tenant according to the custom of the manor, rather than by a deed</term>, which was to descend to his children, or, in the absence of such children, to his brother. He died without any child yet born. His wife did not believe she was pregnant, and when her husband's brother asked her immediately after the death, she told him she believed she was not. However, she later proved to be pregnant. When she realized this, she went, encouraged by her neighbors, to her brother-in-law and told him the situation. He scolded her, called her a whore, and told her she had found someone to get her pregnant because she knew that such a field must be inherited by her husband's descendants. He declared that her "whoring" would not cheat him out of that estate. The poor woman went home troubled, not only because her child would lose the land, but even worse, that she would be considered a whore. Nevertheless, she quieted herself and resolved to accept the loss.

A gentlewoman who could not be distinguished from her late mistress, neither in her person nor her clothing. Some years after I received the previous narrative (namely, near four years ago), I happened to meet <note>original: "light into the company of"</note> three serious persons of good social standing who all lived in the city of Hereford, and I traveled in a stagecoach for three days with them. To them, I happened to tell this story, but I said it had occurred at Deptford; I assumed it was so because I knew that Dr. Bretton lived there. As soon as I had finished, they told me that the story was very true in its main points, but that I was mistaken as to the place. For it was not Deptford, but—as I remember they told me—Pembridge near Hereford, where the Doctor was the minister before the Restoration <note>original: "Return of the King" (1660)</note>. They assured me, based on their own knowledge, that to that day the poor enjoyed that piece of ground. They added that Mrs. Bretton's father could never endure to hear anything mentioned of his daughter's appearance after her death, but would always reply in great anger that it was not his daughter, but the Devil. Thus, he acknowledged that something appeared in the likeness of his daughter.

## RELATION XVII.

### *Concerning a Dutchman who could see ghosts, and the ghost he saw in the town of Woodbridge in Suffolk.*

**M**r. Broom, the minister of Woodbridge in Suffolk, met a Dutch Lieutenant one day in a barber shop in that town. The Lieutenant had been on the ship that blew up with Opdam <note>original: "blown up with Opdam." This refers to Admiral Jacob van Wassenaer Obdam (1610–1665), whose flagship, the *Eendracht*, exploded during the Battle of Lowestoft.</note> and was taken alive out of the water and brought to that town, where he was a prisoner at large <term>a prisoner allowed limited freedom of movement within a specific town rather than being confined to a cell</term>. During their conversation, the Lieutenant told Mr. Broom that he could see ghosts and that he had seen many of them. When Mr. Broom rebuked him for talking so foolishly, he insisted upon it very firmly. Some days later, meeting him again, Mr. Broom asked him whether he had seen any ghosts since his arrival in that town. To which he replied, "No."

But not long after this, as they were walking together up the town, he said to Mr. Broom, "Look, yonder comes a ghost." Seeing nothing, Mr. Broom asked him where it was. The other said it was across from a certain house and that it was walking while looking upward toward one side, swinging one arm with a glove in its hand. He said, moreover, that when it came near them, they must move out of its way. He added that he always did so himself, and that some who had not done so had suffered for it. Shortly after, he said, "It is right upon us; let us get out of the way!" Mr. Broom, believing the whole thing to be a fiction, took hold of the Lieutenant’s arm as soon as he spoke those words and kept him in the path by force. But as he held him, such a force came against them that he was thrown into the middle of the street, and one of the palms of his hands and one knee were bruised and broken by the fall, which caused him excessive pain for a while.

But seeing the Lieutenant lying like a dead man, he got up as soon as he could and went to his relief. With the help of others, he got him into the next shop, where they poured strong-water <term>distilled spirits, such as brandy or gin</term> down his throat, though for some time they could discern no life in him. At length, between the spirits and much rubbing of his limbs <note>original: "well chafing him"</note>, he began to stir. When he had come to himself, his first words were, "I will show you no more ghosts." Then he asked for a pipe of tobacco, but Mr. Broom—

...dead and without feeling, so that she could not walk but crawled upon the ground or was carried in people's arms like a child. But now, through the power of Almighty God, she has walked again. This came to pass in the following manner, as I have recorded it from her own mouth.

In the year 1676, around the 13th or 14th of October, in the night between one and two o'clock, this Jesch Claes <note>A Dutch woman whose miraculous recovery was a famous "relation" or account of the supernatural in the late 17th century.</note> was in bed with her husband, who was a boatman. She was pulled three times by her arm, which woke her, and she cried out, "O Lord! What could this be?" At this, she heard an answer in plain words: "Do not be afraid; I come in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Your illness, which has been upon you for many years, shall cease, and it shall be granted to you by Almighty God to walk again. But keep this to yourself until a further answer." 

Upon hearing this, she cried aloud, "O Lord! I wish I had a light, so that I might know what this is." Then she received this answer: "There is no need for a light; the light shall be given to you by God." Then a light filled the entire room, and she saw a beautiful youth about ten years of age, with curly yellow hair, dressed in white down to his feet. He went from the head of the bed to the fireplace with a light, which vanished shortly after. Immediately, something shot or gushed from her hip and spread through her leg like water into her big toe, where she felt life returning. She felt it with her hand and cried out, "Lord, give me back my feeling now, which I have not had in so many years!" And she continued crying and praying to the Lord according to her modest ability.

Yet she continued that day, Wednesday, and the next day, Thursday, as before until six o'clock in the evening. At that time, she sat at the fire preparing food. Then a rushing noise came into both her ears, and a voice said to her, "Stand. Your ability to walk is given back to you." Then she, who had crawled for so many years, immediately stood up and went to the door. 

Her husband met her and, being exceedingly afraid, drew back. Meanwhile, she cried out, "My dear husband, I can walk again!" The man, thinking she was a spirit, drew back, saying, "You are not my wife." His wife took hold of him and said, "My dear husband, I am the same woman who has been married to you for thirty years. Almighty God has given me back my walking." But her husband, being amazed, retreated to the side of the room until at last she clasped her hands around his neck. Even then, he doubted and said to his daughter, "Is this your mother?" She answered, "Yes, Father, we can plainly see it is."

## RELATION XXI.

### *Mr. Jermin’s Story of a Haunted House, and the Disturbance he Witnessed during a Visit to his Sister-in-law.*

One Mr. Jermin, the Minister of Bignor <note>original: "Bigner"; a village in West Sussex</note> in Sussex, went to see his sister-in-law and found her very depressed <note>original: "Melancholy"</note>. When he asked her the reason, she replied, *“You shall know tomorrow morning.”* When he went to bed, two maids accompanied him in his chamber; the next day, he understood that they did not dare to go into any room in the house alone.

In the night, while he was in his bed, he heard the trampling of many feet upon the lead roof <note>original: "the Leads"</note> over his head, and after that the firing of a gun, which was followed by a great silence. Then they <note>the unseen entities</note> came swiftly downstairs into his chamber, where they began wrestling and tumbling each other down, and continued this for a long while. After they were quiet, they began whispering and made a great buzzing noise, of which he could understand nothing. Then someone called at the door and said, *“Day has broken, come away,”* upon which they ran upstairs as fast as they could go <note>original: "as fast as they could drive"</note>, and he heard no more of them.

In the morning, his brother-in-law and sister-in-law came in to see him, and she said, *“Now, brother, you know why I am so depressed.”* After she had asked him how he had slept, he answered, *“I never rested worse in all my life, having been disturbed a great part of the night with tumblings and noises.”* She complained that her husband forced her to live there, despite their being continually scared. To this the husband answered that their disturbers never did them any other mischief.

At dinner, they were joined by a physician who was an acquaintance. As Mr. Jermin discussed this disturbance, the physician also remarked that no harm was ever done, of which he gave this instance: while dining there one day, a man in mourning <note>clothing worn to signal grieving</note> arrived in the yard on horseback. A servant went to find out his business and found him sitting there very dejected, but he could not get any answer from him. The master of the house and the physician went to see who it was; upon this, the man spurred his horse and rode into the house, up the stairs, and into a long gallery, where

## RELATION XXII.

### *Contained in a letter from Mr. G. Clark to Mr. M. T. concerning a haunted house in Welton, near Daventry.*

SIR,

**I** am sending you here an account of a very memorable instance of <term>witchcraft</term> <note>In this period, "witchcraft" was a broad term often used to describe any inexplicable or demonic activity affecting a location or person.</note>, as I suppose, which would suit Mr. More <note>Likely Henry More (1614–1687), a philosopher and theologian who collected such stories to prove the existence of the soul and spirits.</note> perfectly. I first heard the story told to Sir Justinian Isham by a reverend minister from his own experience. Sir Justinian would have had me go to the place, which I could not do at that time. 

But a little while later, while going to visit a friend and not thinking of this, my friend told me the story. The place was near him, and the principal man concerned in the story was a relative of his and someone with whom I myself had some acquaintance. He had occasion to go to this man’s house for some land deeds, and I went with him to seek confirmation regarding this story. I received it to the full, and I could not help but accept it as true, though otherwise I am very cautious and skeptical enough to find it hard to believe accounts of this nature.

The story is this: at **Welton**, within a mile of **Daventry** in **Northamptonshire**, there live together Widow **Cawley** (the grandmother), Widow **Stiff** (the mother), and her two daughters. At the next house but one live another Widow **Cowley** (sister to the first Widow **Cowley**), her son **Moses Cowley** (an acquaintance of mine), and **Moses's** wife. I have sent you one, but it is not a quarter as large as some of the others were. It was one of the largest of those that were left and kept in a bag. This vomiting lasted about a fortnight and has plenty of good witnesses.

There were many other things which are too long and tedious to write; it would take up a great deal of time.

The following is the account <note>original: "Relation"</note> of *Joan Winsor* of Long *Burton*, regarding her three-night stay there, recorded on the third day of *July*, 1677.

She neither heard nor saw anything as long as the candle was burning, but as soon as it was extinguished, something seemed to fall down by the bedside. Soon after, it began to strike the head of the bed with a staff and struck *Joan Winsor* on the head. She reached out her hand and caught it, but she was not able to hold it fast. She got out of the bed to light a candle, and a large stone was thrown after her, but it missed her. When the candle was lit, they got up and went down to the fire. One of them went up to fetch the bedclothes to make a bed by the fire, and there lay a heap of stones on the bed where they had been lying just moments before. As soon as the bed was made and they lay down to take their rest, there was an extreme scratching sound on the form <term>form: a long bench without a back</term> that stood by them. Then the entity came and heaved up the bolster <note>a long, thick pillow extending across the width of the bed</note> where they laid their heads, and it endeavored to throw them out of bed. At last, it grabbed hold of one end of the pillow and set it quite upright on its end, and there it stood for a considerable time. When it finally fell back into its place, they fell fast asleep and continued so for the rest of the night.

The staff that was spoken of before belonged to *Joan Winsor*, and she says she had left it downstairs in the kitchen. She says that the presence which caused the trouble intended to kill the people, if it had the power to do so. She pressed them to know the reason why they were so troubled, and they said they knew nothing, unless it was about the business of *Old Warren*. She was there for three nights, and the trouble was much the same each night, with nothing else more remarkable.

This is the truth of what I heard them speak from their own mouths, and they will testify to it if called upon to do so.

...ly in *Somerset*. And there is more than one *Burton* there, and also several *Leighs*, but this *Burton* is located at a distance of a little more than a mile and a half from *Leigh*. So, the topographical account is sufficiently exact. Furthermore, the style of the narrative is so simple, plain, and rural that it prevents any suspicion of fraud or deception by the storyteller.

The moving of objects from one room into another, and the striking of blows by invisible agents, reminds me of *Mr. Lloyd's* story. This account appears in *Mr. Glanvill's* papers <note>original: "Mr. Glanvil's Papers"; referring to Joseph Glanvill, a writer known for documenting the supernatural</note>, where Lloyd writes in a letter that Glanvill may rely on it as truth, as it was sent by a person of quality and integrity from that region. It concerns a house haunted by one *Walter Meyrick* of the parish of *Bleddfa* <note>original: "Blethvaught"</note>, in the county of *Radnor*, about twenty-two years ago. 

In that house, besides strange kinds of musical whistlings in rooms where no one was seen whistling, heavy stones were thrown down from a loft. The doors were found bolted or barred against the residents from the inside when they returned from church, even though nobody was in the house. During prayers at home, when some of the women held each other's arms out of fear, some invisible power would pull their arms apart against their will. By such an invisible force, one person sitting at supper was struck flat to the ground. A <term>trencher</term> <note>original: "Trencher"; a wooden plate or platter used for serving food</note> was knocked out of the hand of the maid who was waiting on them, and another person received a sharp box on the ear, though no visible thing was near them to do it. 

A purse was lost containing two gold rings and six shillings and fourpence. When the owner complained about the loss, the purse dropped down from the ceiling of the room (which had no room above it), but it contained only fourpence. The fact that men were struck down with stones and yet suffered no great injury shows plainly that the stones were not thrown, but carried by the spirits. One man, however, was beaten black and blue with two staffs, though no one could be seen beating him, even though it happened during the day.

We will pass over the incident of the frying pan being beaten with a small piece of iron and tinkling over a man’s head in the night. We also note a man being struck down with a stick by day while he was tending a roasting goose; the invisible striker seemed to have a plot to steal it. Similarly, the spirit knocked a pickaxe against the lid of a chest <note>original: "Coffer"</note>, appearing to have designs on a bag of money. 

The narrative relates these and similar feats. *Mr. Lloyd* assures *Mr. Glanvill* that he may rely on the truth of it, as he obtained the account from a Justice of the Peace. The Justice had taken the testimonies of the parties who lived in the house or were present on those occasions as eyewitnesses to the strange pranks played in that place. Because there is such a <note>original: "Congeneracy"; a shared nature or similarity</note> similarity between *James Sherring’s* story and this one, they mutually support each other's credibility.

## RELATION XIV.

*Mr. Andrew Paschall, formerly a Fellow of Queens' College in Cambridge, his narrative of three nights of disturbance at his father's house in London in Soper Lane, in August 1661.*

**T**he first night's disturbance: In the family were my father and mother, my eldest brother, and one of my sisters with a young maiden gentlewoman, her roommate <note>original: "bedfellow"</note> (who seemed to be the person principally concerned), besides a maid who lay in the same chamber.

The aforementioned gentlewoman was in bed with my sister in a chamber adjacent to the one where my father and mother slept (the maid lying in another bed nearby). While she was lying awake, it seemed to her that someone was walking in the room, as suggested by a noise like a long gown or some trailing garment brushing and sweeping up and down the room.

Soon after, there was a noise of shoes clattering under the bed, along with a scratching and tugging of the mat under the bed as well. This continued for some time; my sister was awakened and heard it, as did the maid. After this, my mother was called out of the next chamber where she was awake (preparing a <term>chemical water</term> <note>A distilled medicinal or alchemical solution that required constant monitoring over a fire</note> which required her to be up all night). She came in, as they were in a great fright. My brother also went up, as he had not yet gone to bed but sat below. A candle was brought, and the noise ceased while they were in the chamber. Immediately after they had left and the light was removed, the chamber door (which is difficult to shut) flew closed with a great bang <note>original: "bounce"</note>, even though it had been wide open before. It shook the room where my mother was busy with the aforementioned preparation. After this, one of the shoes that was by the bedside was flung over the bed with a mighty force against a <term>press</term> <note>A large cupboard or wardrobe used for storing clothes or linens</note> that stood on the other side. This put them into such a fright again that the gentlewoman got up. My brother went into the room again and sat up with them all night.

I received this account from my brother, who came to bed with me (as I had gone to bed first in the family because of some illness) early the next morning. I was confirmed in the details afterward...

# ADVERTISEMENT.

*This narrative, though it was not among Mr. Glanvill’s* <note>original: "Mr. Glanvil’s" – Joseph Glanvill (1636–1680), a philosopher and clergyman famous for his studies of the supernatural.</note> *papers, was found by chance in my own study. Yet, because it was written by an eyewitness whom I knew to be a person of judgment and integrity, I thought it fit to insert here. I did so especially because of that passage where, when he placed his hand upon the shoulder of the gentlewoman where the ghost was, a cool blast or puff of air seemed to push or blow against his hand. This is similar to Mr. Glanvill’s experiment of pressing the linen bag in which some spirit was moving like a living animal. These are notable instances of their easy passage* <note>original: "percribration" – a term for filtering or passing through small holes like a sieve.</note> *through porous bodies. This troublesome spirit I suspect to have been the ghost of some deceased person who wanted to say something, but did not have the skill of speaking clearly enough to be understood. When they can speak intelligibly, it is usually in a hoarse and low voice, as is observable in many stories. This is particularly seen in a very recent story of the ghost of a deceased man that spoke to Jacob Brent about two years ago—an apprentice then to a Mr. Lawrence in the Little Minories* <note>A street and area in London near the Tower of London.</note>. *I think it fitting to give some brief account of this for the very same reasons that I have inserted this account from Mr. Paschal: namely, that it comes from an eyewitness and a discreet and well-disposed young man, as those who know him testify. I will set down no more, nor even as much as he himself declared or acknowledged, not only to Dr. Cudworth* <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a prominent English philosopher.</note>, *Mr. Fowler* <note>Edward Fowler (1632–1714), later the Bishop of Gloucester.</note>, *and Mr. Glanvill, but very lately to myself also, namely:*

The great iron chest by the window, at the foot of his bed, which had three locks on it (and contained all the deeds and legal documents <note>original: "Writings and Evidences"</note> of the aforementioned Mr. Mallet’s estate) began to open: first one lock, then another, then the third. Afterward, the lid of the iron chest lifted itself up and stood wide open. Then the patient, Mr. Bourne—who had not spoken in twenty-four hours—lifted himself up also and, looking at the chest, cried: *“You say true, you say true, you are in the right; I’ll be with you by and by.”* So the patient lay down and spoke no more. Then the chest fell shut again on its own and locked itself, one lock after another, just as the three locks had opened. They tried to force it open but could not, and Mr. Bourne died within an hour afterward.

I have also heard Dr. Raymond and Mr. Carlisle relate it often with amazement, both being trustworthy individuals <note>original: "Persons of Credit"</note>.”*

The curious reader may be inquisitive as to what the meaning of the opening of the chest might be, and of Mr. Bourne saying, *“You say true, etc. I’ll be with you by and by.”* As for the former, it is noted by Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and occultist known for his work on medicine and the supernatural.</note> especially, and by others, that signs are often given of the death <note>original: "Departure"</note> of sick men lying on their deathbeds. This opening and closing of the iron <term>coffer</term> <note>A strongbox or chest for holding valuables.</note> or chest is more than ordinarily significant, especially if we consider the similarity in sound and meaning between "coffer" and "coffin," and recall the words of Virgil:

## ACCOUNT XXVI.

### The *Apparition* of *James Haddock* to *Francis Taverner*, near *Drum-bridge* in *Ireland*, contained in a *Letter* from *Thomas Alcock* to *Dr. Henry More.*

At Michaelmas <note>a Christian festival celebrated on September 29th</note> in 1662, Francis Taverner—then about 25 years old and a strong, robust man—was a general servant (and later a porter) to Lord *Chichester*, the Earl of *Donegal*, at *Belfast* in the North of *Ireland*, County of *Antrim*, and Diocese of *Connor*. While riding late at night from *Hillsborough* toward home, near *Drum-bridge*, his horse (though it was of high spirit <note>original: "good Metal"</note>) suddenly came to a stop. Supposing the horse was suffering from the <term>staggers</term> <note>a physical condition in horses causing them to stumble or fall, often due to neurological issues</note>, he dismounted to bleed the horse in the mouth <note>a common, though now obsolete, veterinary practice of the time</note> and then immediately remounted. 

As he set forward, two horsemen seemed to pass him, though he could not hear the sound of their hoofbeats, which amazed him. Immediately, a third figure appeared in a white coat right at his elbow, in the likeness of *James Haddock*, formerly a resident of *Malone*, who had died nearly five years earlier. At this, *Taverner* asked him in the name of God who he was. He replied, *“I am James Haddock.”*

"Haddock, and you may remember me by this sign: that about five years ago, I and two other friends were at your father's house, and you, at your father's direction, brought us some nuts. Therefore, do not be afraid," says the apparition. Upon this, *Taverner*, remembering the circumstances, thought it might indeed be *Haddock*. He believed the two figures who had passed by him earlier were the two friends who had been with Haddock when he gave them the nuts. He courageously asked the spirit why he appeared to him rather than anyone else. The spirit answered that it was because he was a man of more courage <note>original: "resolution"</note> than others; and if he would ride along with him, he would inform him of a business he had to deliver to him. *Taverner* refused to do so and insisted on going his own way (for they were now at a <term>quadrival</term> <note>A crossroads where four roads meet.</note>) and so he rode on toward home. But immediately upon their parting, a great wind arose, and he heard very hideous screeches and noises, to his great amazement. However, riding forward as fast as he could, he finally heard the cocks crow, which brought him comfort. He got off his horse and, falling into prayer, asked for God's assistance, and so arrived safely home.

The next night, the likeness of *James Haddock* appeared to him again. He commanded him to go to *Elenor Welsh* (now the wife of *Davis*, living at *Malone*, but formerly the wife of the aforementioned *James Haddock*, by whom she had an only son. The said *James Haddock* had left this son a lease in his will, which he held from the Lord *Chichester*, but the son had been deprived of it by *Davis*, who had married the boy's mother). He was to ask her if her maiden name was *Elenor Welsh*; and if it were, to tell her that it was the will of her former husband, *James Haddock*, that their son should be treated justly <note>original: "righted"</note> regarding the lease. 

But *Taverner*—partly reluctant to gain the ill will of his neighbors, and partly thinking he would not be believed but rather looked upon as deluded—neglected to deliver the message for a long time. For about a month's time, he was haunted every night by this apparition in several forms, each night becoming more and more terrible. These visits were usually preceded by an unusual trembling over his whole body and a great change in his facial expression, which was obvious to his wife. Although the apparition was frequently in her presence, it was not visible to her. At length, he went to *Malone* to see *Davis's* wife and asked whether her maiden name was *Elenor Welsh*; if it was, he said he had something to tell her. She replied that there was another *Elenor Welsh* besides her. Because of this, *Taverner* returned without delivering his message. That same night, while he was fast asleep in his bed (whereas the previous apparitions had appeared while he sat by the fire with his wife), he felt something pressing upon him...

## ACCOUNT XXVII. <note>original: RELAT. XXVII.</note>

### The Story of David Hunter, Cowherd to the Bishop of Down and Connor, at Portmore in Ireland, 1663. From the same source.

**D**avid Hunter, a cowherd <term>original: Neat-herd; a person who looks after cattle</term> at the Bishop’s house at Portmore, was visited one night by an old woman who appeared as he was carrying a log of wood into the dairy. This astonished him, for he did not know her; his fright caused him to throw away his log and run into the house. The next night she appeared to him again, and he could not help but follow her all night—and he did so almost every night for nearly nine months. Whenever she appeared, he was compelled to go with her through the woods at a very fast pace; the poor fellow looked as if he were bewitched and was exhausted from so much walking. Even when he was in bed with his wife, if she appeared, he had to get up and go. Because his wife could not keep him in bed, she would go too, walking after him until daybreak, even though she saw nothing herself. However, his little dog was so familiar with the ghost that it would follow her just as well as its master did. If a tree stood in her path, he observed that she always walked right through it. During all this time, she did not speak.

But one day, as David was crossing a hedge onto the highway, she came right toward him, and he cried out, "Lord bless me, I wish I were dead; shall I never be delivered from this mise-" <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword suggests the word is "misery."</note>

story? At which she said, *“And the Lord bless me too! It was very fortunate you spoke first, for until then I had no power to speak, though I have followed you for so long.”* "My name," she said, "is Margaret. I lived here before the War <note>Original: "the War"; likely referring to the Irish Rebellion of 1641 or the subsequent Cromwellian conflicts.</note>, and had one son by my husband. When he died, I married a soldier, by whom I had several children, whom my first son supported; otherwise, we all would have starved. He lives beyond the Bann Water <note>The River Bann in Northern Ireland.</note>; please go to him and tell him to dig under a certain hearth, and there he shall find 28 shillings. David Hunter told her he never knew her. "No," she said, "I died seven years before you came into the country, but for all that, if you will deliver her message, I shall never hurt you." However, he delayed doing as the apparition commanded him, and she appeared the following night as he lay in bed and struck him very hard on the shoulder. At this he cried out and asked her if she had not promised she would not hurt him? She said that was only if he delivered her message; if not, she would kill him. He told her he could not go now because the waters were flooded <note>Original: "the Waters were out"; meaning the river had overflowed its banks.</note>. She said she was satisfied for him to stay until they had receded, but charged him afterward not to fail her. So he ran her errand, and afterward she appeared and gave him thanks. *"For now,"* she said, *"I shall be at rest; therefore, please lift me up from the ground, and I will trouble you no more."* So David Hunter lifted her up from the ground, and, as he said, she felt just like a bag of feathers in his arms. Then she vanished, and he heard most beautiful music as she went off over his head, and he was never troubled again.

This account the poor fellow gave us every day, just as the apparition spoke to him. Lady Conway <note>Anne Conway (1631–1679), a philosopher known for her interest in the supernatural and mystical.</note> came to Portmore, where she asked the fellow the same questions and many more. I know this to be true, having been all the while with my Lord of Down <note>Likely Jeremy Taylor, the Bishop of Down and Connor, a prominent theologian.</note>, and the fellow being but a poor cowherd <term>neat-herd</term> there.

->Thomas Alcock.<-

# NOTICE.
<note>original: "Advertisement." In this period, the word meant a formal notification or a preface to the reader.</note>

**IT** is no small confirmation to myself of the *truth* of these two most recent *stories*, in both of which *Lady Conway* is mentioned, that I received two letters from that incomparable lady out of *Ireland* concerning them both. The first is dated *Lisburn, March 3, 1662*, in which she writes the following: "I have spoken lately with two humble country people who have been much troubled by two different persons who died recently. The stories are too long to relate, but the circumstances are such that I do not know how to disbelieve them. These people cannot be suspected of having any ulterior motive, and they were completely unacquainted with the families of those who appeared to them. Furthermore, they were entirely ignorant of the matters they now relate. They have been charged to demand the correction of certain wrongdoings committed by some trusted persons—matters which, it is supposed, they could never have heard of by any other means. There are many other probabilities, but all are dismissed by several people here. *And to give you a taste of their fine excuses, I will transcribe a passage from the other letter of the said excellent lady, dated Lisburn, April 29, 1663, wherein she writes thus:* The account I sent you of two people in this country is certainly liable to as little objection (there was mention of the *Drummer of Tedworth* <note>A famous 1662 case of a poltergeist in Wiltshire, England, involving a spectral drummer.</note> before) as any one shall meet with. This is evident from the diligent search some have made for a flaw or objection against the witnesses, who, as all must eventually confess, clearly have no personal interest in the matter. It would have been impossible for them to have learned what they delivered from anyone involved. However, the skeptics believe that either drunkenness or desperate melancholy <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was considered a physical ailment caused by an imbalance of "black bile," often blamed for hallucinations or madness.</note> enabled them by chance to hit upon greater truths than they themselves realized." *So far writes that excellent person. And it was enough for this noble lady only to recite this explanation of the phenomenon as* melancholy *and* drunkenness; *it was so trifling and silly that it required no further refutation than merely repeating it.*

That drink may reveal the secrets of the person who is drunk, as the poet observes, is reasonable enough; but that a man, by being drunk, is better able to understand the secrets of another man or his family is such a wild paradox that no sober man can admit it. And what is melancholy but a natural drunkenness when it ferments? Moreover, since it is supposedly only by "chance" that melancholy or drunkenness enables them to discover such things, why

<sig>Cc</sig>
<meta>catchword: may</meta>

<summary>The author presents letters from Lady Conway of Lisburn, Ireland, verifying accounts of spirits appearing to common people to demand restitution for past wrongs. He mocks the skeptical view that these witnesses were merely drunk or suffering from melancholy, arguing such states could not grant knowledge of other people's secrets.</summary>
<keywords>Lady Conway, Lisburn, Ireland, Drummer of Tedworth, apparitions, skepticism, melancholy, drunkenness, supernatural testimony</keywords>

--- Page 492 ---
<meta>This page continues a philosophical argument regarding how certain mental or physical states (like melancholy or intoxication) affect the soul's ability to perceive truth, before transitioning into a new account of witchcraft trials in Scotland.</meta>

Might not a *cheerful* <note>original: "Sanguine"</note> temperament and *sobriety* happen to do the same just as well, or even better, if there is any "betterness" in things that happen by chance? But if there is any advantage in the agitation of *melancholy* or *strong drink*, it is only because the *soul* is more excited and made more ready to discover its own inner contents <term>furniture</term>—meaning innate knowledge or thoughts—just as *men* in *drink* reveal their own *secrets*. But the *soul* has no innate *ideas* of specific things; therefore, the greatest effervescence of *drink* or *melancholy* will not make her one bit better disposed to the *knowledge* of specifics, but will instead make her less fit to receive information from the outside. So blindly do these *superficial thinkers* <note>original: "witlings"</note> *philosophize* regarding things of this *nature*.

And yet I dare say, this was the very best of their *excuses* <note>original: "evasions"</note>. Since it is no better than that against these two *stories*—which were so sifted and examined by a *person* of such quick *wit*, impartial *judgment*, and *sagacity* as I know that excellent *Lady* to have been—I must confess that to me it is a *confirmation* as strong as I could desire for the main points of the *stories*. I retain some of these in my *memory*, having heard a more particular *account* of them from her *Ladyship* immediately <note>original: "presently"</note> upon her return from *Ireland* about 15 years ago. Nor is there any doubt that *Mr. Alcock* has proven himself a faithful *reporter* <note>original: "reciter"</note> of them in the main; nor could anyone rightly be deemed more fit and able, as he was present at the *examination* of *Taverner* and lived at *Portmore* with the *Bishop of Down*, whose *servant Hunter* was.

She declares that the effigies produced in court are the same effigies she saw being made. She declares that the black man's name is *Ejoal*. 

This declaration was delivered before *James Dunlop* of *Househill*, *William Gremlaye*, and others, on January 27, 1677.

# ADVERTISEMENT.

**T**hese confessions and testimonies are transcribed from the copy in the same Scottish dialect in which I found them. There are several words which I admit I do not understand—for example, those concerning the "black man's" <note>The "black man" was a common contemporary description of the Devil appearing in human form.</note> voice, described as being *hough* <term>harsh or hollow</term> and *goustie* <term>ghastly, eerie, or echoing</term>. But if the voice of this "black man" is like that of the one who appeared to the witches whom Mr. Hunt examined, these words may signify a *loud* and *deep* voice.

# The Collection

There is another *Scottish Trial* of Witches among *Mr. Glanvill’s* papers, which bears the same general signature as this one: *Robert Martin*, Clerk to the Justice Court. However, that record is of too old a date—being from the year 1590—to fit strictly with the title of our current stories. 

But since it is a true and authentic copy of a public record, even if it is not recent, it may perhaps be worthwhile to briefly name some of the effects, types, or circumstances of witchcraft mentioned there—especially those that have not appeared in the previous stories. One such example is the power of giving and taking away the potency of various men's sexual organs, for which *Jannet Clark* was accused.

What is notable in the case of *John Fian* <note>original: "Fiene." John Fian was a schoolmaster and a central figure in the North Berwick witch trials of 1590</note> is that the Devil appeared to him not in black, but in white clothing. Yet, he proposed a covenant just as hellish as those demons who appear in black. The record also describes Fian lying as if dead for two or three hours while his spirit was "taken" (as the phrase in the record puts it). According to his own depositions, he was carried or transported to many mountains and, as he thought, through the entire world. 

He also claimed to have heard the Devil preach from a pulpit in a church <note>original: "Kirk"</note> at night by candlelight, with the candle burning blue. He stated that in a conventicle <note>A secret or unlawful religious meeting</note> of witches (whose names are specified in the record), he and the rest kissed the Devil's buttocks <note>original: "Breech"</note> upon parting; the original record uses even coarser language. 

The record further details his activities, such as skimming across the sea in a boat with those of his gang, and his foretelling of a leak in the Queen's ship with the Devil's help. He and the others were accused of raising winds during the King’s <note>James VI of Scotland, later James I of England</note> voyage to *Denmark* by casting a cat into the sea, which the Devil had delivered to them, teaching them to cry "*Hola*" when they threw it in. 

He was also accused of raising a mist during the King's return from *Denmark* by getting Satan to cast an object like a football (though it appeared to *John* like a clump of straw) into the sea. This caused a vapor or smoke to arise, intended to cause His Majesty’s ship to be cast away upon the coast of *England*. 

Fian also claimed to hear the Devil preach again from a pulpit while dressed in black. Afterward, the Devil pointed them toward graves to open and dismember the corpses within; once finished, they were immediately transported away without a word. His other sorceries included opening locks, such as one he opened simply by blowing into a woman's hand while he sat by the fire. He was also said to have caused four candles to appear on the <term>luggs</term> <note>Scottish term for ears</note> of a horse and another on the tip of the rider's staff in the dark of night, making it as light as day. The rider was so terrified that he fell down dead upon entering his home. Finally, the record describes him embarking in a boat with other witches, sailing over the sea, entering a ship, and
